20987-story-of-the-war-in-south-africa-1:
Cape Horn and the Cape of Good Hope owed their fame to trade routes, this history notes. For centuries, only those wild capes linked Europe to Pacific and Indian shores. The Story of the War in South Africa opens with that wide, lone frame.

Alfred Thomas Story tells the Boer War of 1899-1900 as it unfolded. Sieges, commandos, and British columns clash across veld and town. The war shook the British Empire and taught it harsh new lessons. This early account, written close to the events, keeps the shock and scale of a war that proved far harder than London had dreamed.
22620-researches-on-cellulose-1895-1900:
Researches on Cellulose, 1895–1900 is a scientific review gathering five years of work on the chemistry of cellulose, the fiber that builds plant cell walls. The catalog record names no author. Paper, cotton, and wood industries all rested on this substance, and chemists raced to learn its true makeup.

The sample weighs a claim about silica in the plant skeleton. Does it play a special structural role beside the cellulosic parts? Or does it merely sit among the ash left after burning? Notes and references crowd the discussion, as the review tests rival findings against each other. The volume shows industrial chemistry in its careful, cumulative mode. Historians of materials science can watch a field sorting signal from noise.
22807-a-difficult-problem-1900:
A Difficult Problem is a mystery story dated 1900, in which a widow reads a name and wonders whether she is dreaming. The catalog record names no author. Its problem begins with paper: a slip, a letter, and a name that cannot be what it seems.

My husband, the narrator says, was James Forsythe De Witt Holmes. His last letter, lying beside the cushion at that very moment, came dated from the Colonnade. Was I dreaming, she asks? Or had some frightful hallucination made me misread the name on the slip before me? A dead husband's name, alive in the wrong place, sets the inquiry moving. The tale belongs to the turn-of-the-century school of lady detectives and drawing-room puzzles.
a-phrenological-chart-of-character-with-:
A Phrenological Chart of Character, issued in 1900 under the name of J G Spurzheim, presents the founder's system in chart form with supplementary tables. Johann Gaspar Spurzheim, who died in 1832, had carried phrenology from Vienna across Europe and America with Gall's doctrine in his hands. A chart of character in his name kept that system in circulation nearly seventy years after his death.

The fifty-six pages give the faculties in tabular form, so a reader can score a head organ by organ and read off the character. Such charts were the everyday stationery of the phrenological trade. This late edition shows how long Spurzheim's map of the mind outlived him, still being sold as a working tool in 1900.
abramelin-book-3-mathers-1900:
The Sacred Magic of Abramelin the Mage claims to record the system Abraham of Worms learned from an Egyptian mage. S. L. MacGregor Mathers translated the French manuscript, and his edition appeared in 1900. Book Three, given here, is the book of magic squares, and it completes the three-book Mathers Abramelin in the library.

After the long holy operation of the earlier books, the magician receives word squares for many purposes. Each square of letters serves a stated end, from finding treasure to raising storms. The squares are the working tools the whole rite exists to deliver. Mathers's Abramelin shaped modern ceremonial magic deeply. Book Three is its toolbox, page after page of lettered power.
abramelin-sacred-magic-book-3-mathers-19:
Abraham of Worms was a Jewish traveler of the late 1300s. He wrote down a system of ritual magic that he said he learned in Egypt from a mage named Abramelin. S. L. MacGregor Mathers turned the French manuscript into English, and his edition appeared in 1900. The third book holds the working tools of the system.

Inside are grids of letters called magic squares, each square tied to a spirit and a stated aim, from finding lost goods to raising storms. After months of prayer and strict living, the mage was to call on these spirits and direct them through the squares. Later occult groups treated these pages as the heart of the whole Abramelin operation.
alchemical-treatises-by-christophorus-pa:
Alchemical Treatises by Christophorus Parisiensis, a manuscript collection of about 1500, gathers the writings and correspondence of Christophorus of Paris. The volume of ninety-nine leaves, described from the Bibliotheca Osleriana, includes his letter named the Sumetta on the art of transmutation. It was sent to Andrea Ogniben of Venice. It is dated from Paris on the fourteenth of September, 1472.

Two alphabets for the Sumetta follow, dated the eighteenth of August, 1473, giving the letter's coded terms. A Testamento, or Violetta, also stands among the pieces, and letters by and to Christophorus complete the dossier. The manuscript preserves an adept's working papers: doctrine, cipher, and correspondence from the Paris alchemy of the fourteen seventies.
alphonsus-uniformity-gods-will-1900:
Uniformity with God's Will is a short devotional treatise by Alphonsus Liguori, given here in a 1900 English translation of his Italian work. Liguori, a leading Catholic moral teacher, argues that peace comes from conforming one's own will to God's will in all things. The book is practical rather than speculative, aimed at ordinary believers facing hardship.

Liguori teaches his readers to accept sickness, loss, and disappointment as coming from God's hand, and to answer them with trust rather than complaint. Short chapters press the same lesson from many angles, with examples meant for daily life. It became one of his most loved works, and this translation keeps its plain, direct counsel.
arxiv-2510-00100:
Leonardo Bonino and four colleagues published this 2025 paper in theoretical particle physics. It concerns smashing electrons into polarized protons and catching one outgoing particle. Such semi-inclusive scattering reveals how spin is shared inside the proton. The team computed the relevant physics to next-to-next-to-leading order, a level of precision not reached before for these charged and neutral current cases.

The work gives the first results of this kind in a scheme called the Larin scheme. The authors also fix how earlier papers assigned parts of the math to the wrong particle channels. Their study of cross sections and spin asymmetries shows large electroweak effects in the numbers. Those effects must be included whenever polarized scattering data are read at high precision. The paper is a tool-building step for future spin experiments at new colliders.
arxiv-2510-00300:
Serena Gomez Wannaz wrote this 2025 study on a side effect of in-context learning guides for language models. Such guides are example packs placed in the prompt to steer a model's behavior. They raise task scores, but their effect on wider reasoning was untested. Wannaz compared a baseline GPT-OSS model against five guided variants on 840 tests.

The tests spanned general knowledge questions, logic riddles, and a mathematical olympiad problem. Guided models scored between ninety-one and ninety-nine percent on general knowledge. On riddles, though, their accuracy fell well below the baseline model's mark. The olympiad problem showed no meaningful difference between any of the variants. Wannaz names the pattern optimized fragility: guides buy efficiency at the price of flexible reasoning. The findings carry a warning for anyone deploying guided models on open-ended work.
arxiv-2510-00400:
Jiyoung Choe and six colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper testing how well galaxy properties can be recovered from photos alone. Astronomers infer a distant galaxy's mass and star formation rate by fitting its spectral energy distribution. For the earliest galaxies seen by the James Webb Space Telescope, that fitting had never been stress-tested. The team fit mock photometry of simulated galaxies whose true values they knew.

Even in the cleanest case, with no dust or emission lines, fitted masses ran about sixty percent too high. Recent starbursts pushed some low-mass galaxies' errors to a factor of five. Star formation rates came out about twofold too low, thanks to blurred age and metal content. Adding dust and glowing gas widened the biases further. One emission-free band helped separate starlight from line glow and cut the mass error. The authors warn that high-redshift catalogs carry these systematic offsets.
arxiv-2510-00600:
Pietro Mazzaglia and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on robot models that think before acting, but only when thinking helps. Vision-language-action models plan better when they first generate chain-of-thought text. The catch is speed: long thoughts delay every physical action. Their Hybrid Training framework teaches models from thoughts while making the thoughts optional later.

During training, the model learns several output modes side by side. At run time it can act directly, think first, or follow an instruction to reason. That flexibility lets operators trade deliberation for speed task by task. Simulated benchmarks and real-world robot trials evaluated the approach. The authors report keeping the chain-of-thought performance gains while shedding its latency when desired. The work comes from Qualcomm AI Research, targeting practical deployment on real hardware.
arxiv-2510-01200:
Alfaro extends a trusted fix for the fake singularities that plague gauge theory calculations beyond its original home. Certain convenient gauges create spurious poles in loop integrals, and the Mandelstam-Leibbrandt prescription tames them on the light cone. Many modern models, though, need the same medicine away from that special setting.

The generalized version keeps the two virtues practitioners rely on, naive power counting and gauge invariance. Dimensional regularization then yields closed forms for the basic integrals, divergent and finite parts alike. Simpler formulas should speed calculations across gauge theories. Non-local models, long hampered by these integrals, gain a new avenue of attack. Scale symmetry plus regularity conditions pin the integrals down uniquely. Higher-order poles fall out by differentiating the basic case. String and Chern-Simons calculations lean on these gauges heavily. Closed forms end arguments about prescriptions for good.
arxiv-2510-01400:
Zhang and co-authors automate the construction of phase diagrams for materials with many ingredients, at supercomputer scale. Phase diagrams tell synthesizers which structures survive at each temperature and recipe. Reliable ones demand free energies across fine grids, an enormous sampling burden.

Their workflow, exaPD, samples many phases and compositions simultaneously under one global controller. Standard dynamics and Monte Carlo engines do the sampling, including neural-network potentials of near-quantum accuracy. The free energies feed an established thermodynamic modeling package to draw the diagram. Near-ideal parallel scaling keeps the whole campaign practical. Solid solutions and liquids both enter the free energy ledger. LAMMPS supplies the simulation engine under the workflow. Parsl orchestrates the job flood across computing resources. Temperature-composition meshes define the campaign's grid. User-friendliness matters because phase diagrams serve many specialties. Automation turns a heroic calculation into a routine.
arxiv-2510-01500:
Madahar redesigns tree search for language-model reasoning so that promising-looking dead ends stop eating the whole compute budget. Large test-time budgets expose two failures: extra samples at a node mostly duplicate each other, and early scores prune branches whose payoff arrives late. His controller splits candidates into narrow mainlines and wide laterals.

Laterals are logically consistent but initially low-scoring ideas that earn cheap probes. A racing procedure spreads tiny tests across many laterals and promotes any that clears the mainline bar. Mainlines stay narrow so spare compute funds breadth where breadth is cheap. Math, code, and puzzle tasks improved in success per unit compute. Consistency and utility are scored separately, the conceptual key. Promotion discipline survives the widening of the frontier. Success per compute is the metric the design optimizes. Error profiles clean up alongside raw success rates.
arxiv-2510-01600:
Lawton and co-authors compare ways to fine-tune the two models inside a retrieval-augmented question answerer. One model fetches relevant documents, and a second writes the answer from them. Teams can tune each model separately, tune them together, or tune in two phases.

Across four pipelines and two question sets, every strategy improved quality by about the same amount. Costs differed sharply, with independent tuning the cheapest by far. Joint approaches earn their keep when labeled context data is missing. The practical advice depends on what labels and compute a team actually has. HotPotQA and PopQA supplied the test questions for the comparison. Quality gains were measured with exact-match and overlap scores on generated answers. Learning-rate searches change the calculus, since joint tuning multiplies the combinations. Cheapest first is the sensible default until labels run out. Equal gains hide unequal bills.
arxiv-2510-02200:
Brei and six co-authors turn natural language questions into graph queries through an exploring agent in this 2025 paper. Knowledge graphs answer rich questions, but only through SPARQL, a language most users never learn. Single-shot translation by a language model often fails on real schemas. Their system, ARUQULA, generalizes an earlier agent called SPINACH.

Instead of guessing the whole query at once, the agent explores the graph step by step. It reasons, executes partial queries, inspects results, and revises its plan in a ReAct loop. Exploration utilities give it structured ways to probe classes, properties, and links. The authors document the architecture and the reasoning behind each design choice. They also analyze the agent's behavior in depth to find where it stumbles. That behavioral audit points to concrete improvements for the next iteration. The work grew out of the Text2SPARQL challenge series.
arxiv-2510-02300:
Wang and Du reframe image generation around a learned energy landscape. Their 2025 machine learning paper introduces Equilibrium Matching, called EqM. Diffusion and flow models move through timed, uneven steps. EqM drops the clock entirely. It learns the slope of one steady landscape instead. Sampling becomes a downhill walk on that landscape. Users can change step sizes and compute budgets at run time. Theory in the paper supports learning the true data shape this way.

On ImageNet at standard size, EqM reached a top generation score. Its FID of one point nine beat diffusion and flow rivals. The same landscape handled several extra jobs. It cleaned partly noised images without retraining. It also flagged odd inputs and composed new images from parts. One model doing many jobs is the attraction. EqM also ties flow models and energy models closer together.
arxiv-2510-02700:
Lekhak and co-authors release a drone hyperspectral dataset for finding buried explosives safely. Their 2025 remote sensing paper documents a new benchmark. Landmines and unexploded shells threaten civilians for decades. Detection research needs shared, realistic test data. A drone carried a hyperspectral camera over a seeded field. The field held one hundred forty three realistic surrogate targets. Some sat on the surface, others partly or fully buried. The sensor recorded two hundred seventy light bands per pixel. Flights cruised near twenty metres above the ground.

Calibration used reference panels and a ground spectrometer. Cross-checks on known objects scored very low error. Alignment quirks from GPS drift remain in the release. The raw flight lines and ground points ship with it. Researchers can refine the georeferencing themselves. Shared benchmarks make detection claims comparable. Humanitarian demining needs tools proven before deployment.
arxiv-2510-03200:
Collorone and co-authors build the first retrieval model that unites motion, scene, and text. A movement makes sense only if the setting allows it. Sitting needs a chair, yet no tool checked that coherence. Prior models paired modalities two at a time at best. MonSTeR embeds all three into one shared latent space. Higher-order relations, not just pairwise links, shape that space. Retrieval then works in any direction among the three.

Tests show the unified model beats trimodal rivals. A user study checked the scores against human judgment. Retrieval rankings matched what people found coherent. The latent space also transfers to fresh tasks without retraining. Placing objects sensibly inside a scene was one such task. Captioning a motion in words was the other. Both worked zero-shot through the shared geometry. Interaction models can now be grounded against scene context.
arxiv-2510-03300:
Bavalatti and colleagues wrote a 2025 arXiv review of adaptive cruise control in self driving cars. Such systems hold a set speed while keeping a safe gap from the car ahead. The review sorts the main designs and the sensors and control methods behind them. Earlier surveys, the authors argue, skipped a full account of the hard problems and the gaps that remain in the field.

The team builds a new taxonomy that sorts cruise control research and exposes where work is thin. Fault tolerance, bad weather, mixed traffic, and security all stand out as weak spots. The review then maps future directions meant to close those gaps. Its goal is cruise control that stays safe when parts fail or conditions turn rough. Students and engineers entering the field get a clear map of what is solved and what still blocks wide use on city roads.
arxiv-2510-03600:
Chorfi and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on forward and backward problems for a time fractional Schrödinger equation. The equation swaps the time derivative for a Caputo fractional one, which lets systems carry memory and spread in anomalous ways. The spatial part is a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space. The authors treat two versions, distinguished by how the imaginary unit enters the equation. They expand solutions along eigenvectors and lean on Mittag-Leffler functions.

For both versions they prove the forward problem is well posed, so solutions exist, are unique, and depend on the data. They tackle the backward problem of recovering an initial state from a later one. Uniqueness and stability estimates hold under conditions in each. The fractional setting breaks unitarity and time reversal, which makes the analysis hard. The paper ends with open problems, including a conjecture about where Mittag-Leffler functions vanish.
arxiv-2510-03700:
Lim and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper proposing a way to grade language models that list diagnoses. Top-k accuracy treats a near miss, like naming the disease family, as an error. Their framework, H-DDx, maps each text diagnosis to an ICD-10 code using retrieval and reranking. A hierarchical score then credits predictions that sit close to the diagnosis in the taxonomy. The team benchmarked twenty two models with it.

Flat metrics understated how coherent the models were, the study found. Models often identified the broader clinical context even when the diagnosis escaped them. Domain specialized open source models looked strong under the fairer scoring. The mapping pipeline reached about ninety three percent accuracy. Tests ran on a synthetic benchmark of a million cases, so real world validation remains due. Hospitals weighing diagnostic assistants need scores that reflect usefulness, and hierarchy aware grading is a step toward that.
arxiv-2510-03800:
Pal and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper reporting a charge density wave pattern in single layer vanadium disulfide, a two dimensional crystal with quantum phases. Charge density waves are periodic ripples of electron density that reshape electronic behavior. Using a liquid phase exfoliation and stamp transfer process, the team made monolayer flakes and imaged them with high resolution electron microscopy. Two crystal phases, 1T and 2H, coexist in the monolayers at room temperature, and only the 1T phase ripples.

In that phase they found an unreported incommensurate superstructure, a seven by seven pattern tied to clusters of seven vanadium atoms. Adding layers converts the pattern into a two by two order. Photoelectron measurements pin the change on vanadium atoms slipping between layers as ions and altering the electron count. Twisted bilayers hosted Moiré patterns that trapped the monolayer's wave. Thickness becomes a knob for tuning order in this material.
arxiv-2510-04200:
Kowalska and Sessolo present this 2025 arXiv paper deriving how much entanglement a scattering event creates between two particles. Colliders test quantum entanglement in scattered particles, but computing it usually requires the full final-state density matrix. For two-to-two scattering with a S-matrix, the authors find a shortcut. Starting from an unentangled product state, the entanglement measure called concurrence takes an analytic form.

At leading order, the concurrence depends only on the real part of the inelastic forward scattering amplitude and on the initial state. The authors also show the real part corrects that entropy at order, by an amount equal to the final state's entropy of coherence for basis states. Examples cover scalar scattering in the two-Higgs-doublet model and high-energy electron-positron annihilation. The formula lets phenomenologists estimate scattering entanglement from amplitudes they already compute.
arxiv-2510-04300:
Brusaschi and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper characterizing pulsed squeezed light generated inside a strongly driven silicon nitride microresonator. Squeezed light reduces noise in one field quadrature and is a key resource for continuous-variable quantum computation. Pulsed microresonators can concentrate squeezing into a dominant spectral-temporal mode, but high parametric gain brings self- and cross-phase modulation plus time-ordering effects that degrade the ideal state. The team experimentally maps performance from low gain to roughly sixteen photons per pulse.

They vary pulse energy, frequency detuning, and pulse duration while measuring average photon number and first- and second-order correlations in the marginal modes. The authors therefore propose and demonstrate a correction strategy based on the marginal distributions of multiphoton events. The work offers guidance for building brighter integrated squeezed-light sources without losing control of their temporal mode structure.
arxiv-2510-04400:
Marc Cavazza wrote this 2025 paper on whether AI written stories keep their meaning on track. Linguists use the idea of an isotopy, a thread of related meaning that runs through a text. Cavazza asked whether large language models keep such threads intact when they continue a story. He first checked that a top model could pull isotopies out of test texts with known answers. Then he ran a large story completion test.

The test used ten thousand short story prompts drawn from a public story collection. Five language models each finished the stories in their own way. The team measured how well each thread was covered, how dense it was, and how far it spread. Within the length limits used, the models kept the meaning threads largely intact across all measures. The result feeds a wider debate about what these models truly grasp.
arxiv-2510-04800:
Sangmin Bae and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on mixing building blocks inside language models. Transformers read with attention, which grows costly as texts lengthen. State space models like Mamba compress history into a state and scale more gently. Hybrid models interleave the two, and results looked strong on long texts. What nobody had mapped was which mixing choices matter. The authors compare hybrids built by stacking blocks in sequence and by fusing them per layer.

They judge designs on language quality, long context skill, and scaling behavior. Training speed and inference cost enter the scorecard. Digging into primitives, they name the elements that drive each fusion style. From that they propose recipes for hybrid families. The recipes tell builders where attention earns its cost and where state layers suffice. Such guidance saves the field from architecture search. Long context work, from books to code bases, is where hybrids promise.
arxiv-2510-04900:
Nick Janßen, Melanie Schaller, and Bodo Rosenhahn wrote this 2025 paper on stress testing forecasting models with synthetic data they control. Forecasting benchmarks hide their noise, so nobody knows why a model fails. The authors generate data sets with dials for signal shape, noise type, and frequency. Architectures for long forecasting face the testbed. The roster covers a state space model, a transformer, a linear model, and a decomposition based one.

Every model collapsed when its lookback window could not contain one seasonal period. Wave shape split the field: sawtooth patterns favored the state space models. Sine waves favored the linear models. Noise hurt everyone as it grew, but trend noise singled out a model and seasonal noise another. Two models rebuilt the frequency of signals. The lesson is to match the model to the signal, not the leaderboard. Controlled synthetic tests expose such matches that data hides.
arxiv-2510-05100:
Stefan Roiser, Robert Schöfbeck, and Zenny Wettersten speed up particle-physics simulations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Physicists generate huge samples of collision events to compare theory with data. Reusing one sample under different model parameters requires reweighting every event. On modern chips built for parallel data, the standard tools crawl.

The authors present two C++ libraries, Rex and teaRex, for fast event handling and generic reweighting. Rex reads standard event files into a layout designed for data parallelism. The teaRex layer then reweights events to arbitrary new conditions with minimal user code. Their MadGraph module built on both ran 30 to 60 times faster on plain CPUs. With vector instructions and GPUs, the speedup reached several hundredfold.
arxiv-2510-05700:
Ladghami and Ouali treat the boundary theory's size as a dial for black hole thermodynamics. In holographic thermodynamics, a black hole's dual field theory carries a central charge. That charge counts the boundary theory's degrees of freedom. Their 2025 paper varies it while holding Newton's constant fixed.

The framework lets the AdS radius vary instead of fixing it. Charged black holes in five and six dimensions form the test cases. Van der Waals-like phase transitions emerge, governed by the central charge. Stability and phase structure shift as the boundary theory changes. Higher-dimensional holes behave differently from the lower-dimensional BTZ case. Varying the charge means moving between genuinely different boundary theories. Mass plays the role of enthalpy in this extended thermodynamics. Critical phenomena follow the charge as the controlling parameter. The results show boundary degrees of freedom shaping bulk gravity directly.
arxiv-2510-06100:
Larkin and five co-authors track how winds from young massive clusters evolve in a 2025 astrophysics paper. In a cluster's first few million years, the winds of its stars push gas outward and shape the host galaxy. Those winds vary sharply as stars evolve, so one fixed speed misleads models.

Using the pySTARBURST99 code, the team computed average cluster wind speeds across metallicities from metal-poor dwarfs to the Galactic Centre. The speed falls steeply below the Large Magellanic Cloud's metallicity, and the authors recommend 500 to 1,000 kilometers per second there. Counting only Wolf-Rayet stars can overshoot the speed by up to 2,000 kilometers per second at higher metallicity. Uncertain red supergiant mass loss alone shifts answers by about 1,000 kilometers per second. The study tells galaxy modelers which shortcut to drop and which measurements to improve.
arxiv-2510-06200:
Li and eight co-authors introduce StarEmbed, a benchmark testing time series foundation models on variable star light curves. Such models train mostly on regularly sampled data, while stellar light curves arrive irregularly with uneven noise. Astronomy offers a hard, realistic test bed that training corpora largely omit.

StarEmbed holds real observations of roughly forty thousand stars, expert-labeled in seven classes. Models face clustering, classification, and out-of-distribution detection tasks. The team benchmarked foundation models of varied architecture and training strategy, plus domain-specific transformers. The Chronos family reached state-of-the-art clustering and detection results despite pretraining on regular, non-astronomical data. No foundation model strictly beat the established domain baseline at classification, though all generalized impressively. The public benchmark aims at universal light curve embeddings. It gives model builders a concrete target for irregular, noisy real-world time series.
arxiv-2510-06400:
van Dongen and three co-authors simulate how potassium carbonate doping improves activated carbons for direct air capture in a 2025 materials science paper. Capturing carbon dioxide from air is a leading climate mitigation strategy. Porous adsorbents work even in humid air, but improving them remains difficult.

The team ran atomistic simulations of carbon dioxide and water in realistic activated carbons. Surfaces carried functional groups to mimic experimental samples' chemistry. Potassium carbonate was introduced into the pores as a dopant. Both changes enhanced adsorption in the simulations. Their main effect was shifting uptake onset to lower pressures. The carbonate clusters serve as extra adsorption sites for both gases. They also nucleate water and promote a hydrogen bond network in the pores. The study explains atomistically why doped carbons grab dilute carbon dioxide earlier and more eagerly.
arxiv-2510-06600:
Zhaochun Ren and six co-authors work on fine-grained emotion recognition in text. Their 2025 paper, presented at the CIKM conference in Seoul, asks how models label the exact emotion in a query. Recent systems use in-context learning, showing the model similar examples first. Those systems explain their reasoning, but they pay less attention to the final decision step.

The authors analyze that decision step through prototype theory. They show the model matches a query against stored emotional prototypes. Semantically similar examples can mislead that matching and cause errors. Their improved method, called EICL, uses emotionally similar examples instead. It also applies dynamic soft labels and a two-stage exclusion step at decision time. Across four datasets, EICL beat standard in-context learning by a clear margin. The study shows that fixing how a model decides matters as much as fixing how it reasons.
arxiv-2510-06700:
Leonardo Bertolazzi, Sandro Pezzelle, and Raffaella Bernardi study a reasoning bias shared by people and language models. Their 2025 paper concerns content effects. A plausible-sounding claim feels more valid when the logic is flawed. An implausible claim feels wrong when the logic is sound. Humans show this bias, and so do the models.

The team probed how models store the ideas of validity and plausibility inside their networks. Both ideas turn out to be encoded in simple linear directions. Those directions point in strongly aligned ways, so the concepts blur together. Steering one concept with a vector shifted judgments of the other, in both directions. The degree of alignment predicted how strong the bias was in each model. The authors then built debiasing vectors that pull the concepts apart. Those vectors reduced content effects and improved reasoning accuracy. The work hints at fixes for a common logic failure.
arxiv-2510-07000:
Neel Rachamalla and colleagues at Krutrim AI build training data that teaches language models Indian languages and culture. Their 2025 paper presents the Pragyaan datasets for post-training. Open datasets often miss Indian languages, cultural grounding, and task variety. Models trained on them serve hundreds of millions of speakers poorly.

Their pipeline mixes translation with synthetic expansion, keeping humans in the loop throughout. Annotators fix language errors and adapt expressions to Indian cultural norms. Two collections came out of that effort. Pragyaan-IT holds twenty-two thousand teaching examples, and Pragyaan-Align holds one hundred thousand ranked examples. Together they span ten Indian languages and dozens of task groups. The source material draws on fifty-seven existing sources. Quality checks weigh instruction fidelity, safety, and keeping cultural nuance. Multi-turn dialogue gets special attention, since real use is chat-based. The collections give builders a base for more inclusive multilingual models.
arxiv-2510-07200:
Khatiwada and colleagues survey how people in Nepal lived through their government's ban on TikTok. Their 2025 study appeared in a journal on human-computer interaction. TikTok had become a key space for learning, culture, and community in the country. The team surveyed just over one hundred users online. They asked about values, habits, and the workarounds people used during the ban.

Most respondents doubted the ban's wisdom yet accepted it passively rather than protesting. Many moved to other platforms to stay connected. Some used virtual private networks to keep reaching TikTok itself. The authors argue that platform rules should be set with public debate, not by sudden decree. They call for shared governance models that give users a real voice. The case warns other governments weighing bans that users adapt quickly, while trust in institutions erodes.
arxiv-2510-07500:
Chen and Khisti present SurpMark, a detector that decides whether a passage was written by a machine by watching how its predictability flows. Their 2025 paper works under black-box constraints: the true source model is unknown, and the scoring model available may not match it. SurpMark summarizes a text by the sequence of token surprisals, measures of how unexpected each word is. Those values are quantized into interpretable states, and a transition matrix records how surprise evolves through the passage.

The method needs no per-input contrast samples, avoiding a heavy cost of rival detectors. Theory supplies a principled rule for the quantization and proves the decision statistic becomes normally distributed for long texts. Across datasets, source models, and scenarios, SurpMark matched or beat baseline detectors.
arxiv-2510-08000:
Steijn, Goli, and Antonini wrote this 2025 paper presenting DemandCast, a framework for forecasting electricity demand hour by hour across the globe. Planners facing the energy transition need demand paths for fifty-plus countries, not just one grid. The authors assembled a multi-year dataset joining past demand with weather and socioeconomic variables. Their model uses gradient boosting to predict normalized demand profiles for each region.

A time-based split keeps the evaluation honest, testing only on later data. Out-of-sample error averaged under ten percent in their tests. The pipeline runs end to end reproducibly and is released as open source. Coverage spans a quarter century of records, which lets the model learn long-run patterns. Data quality still varies sharply between countries, and the authors flag that openly. Transparent global demand forecasts help governments and utilities plan grids that can actually carry electrified transport and heating.
arxiv-2510-08300:
Bart Kuipers and co-authors explore metanetworks that respect scaling symmetry in a 2025 arXiv paper on faster optimization. Amortized optimization learns a map that solves many related problems at once, reusing shared structure. Their tool, the Scale Equivariant Graph Metanetwork, works directly on a neural network's weights. It can fine-tune a trained model in one shot, skipping long iterative retraining.

The team demonstrates the approach on experiments and adds a theoretical result. They prove that the gauge freedom from scaling symmetries is strictly smaller in convolutional networks than in plain multilayer perceptrons. Gauge freedom means redundant ways to write the same model with different weights. This gap helps explain performance differences seen between the two architectures. Their code is public, and they argue symmetry-aware metanetworks could make network tuning cheaper and more general.
arxiv-2510-08400:
James Bartusek, Aparna Gupte, Saachi Mutreja, and Omri Shmueli hide quantum circuits inside classical programs in a 2025 arXiv paper. An obfuscator rewrites a program so it still works but reveals as little as possible. For quantum circuits, a classical obfuscator outputs a scrambled classical description of an equal circuit. Prior results covered only trivial 'null' circuits that always reject.

Relative to a classical oracle, the team builds an obfuscator for all pseudo-deterministic quantum circuits. These circuits give the same answer with high probability on every run. Their main step is a compact quantum homomorphic encryption scheme with public verification. Such encryption lets others compute on encrypted quantum data and check the result openly. Earlier designs needed ciphertexts that were both quantum and bulky. Their improvement makes the scheme compact while keeping public checks for correct evaluation.
arxiv-2510-08500:
Daniel Stilck França and Tim Möbus, with Cambyse Rouzé and Albert Werner, show how to learn time-varying quantum dynamics from simple experiments in a 2025 arXiv paper. Hamiltonian learning helps benchmark quantum computers, but nearly all rigorous protocols assume fixed Hamiltonians. Real devices drift, and noise generators, called Lindbladians, also change with time. Their protocol learns both for locally interacting qubit systems.

The method needs only product Pauli eigenstate preparations, evolution for chosen times, and product Pauli basis measurements. It assumes the time-dependent parameters are well approximated in a known function space, like polynomials. Sample counts scale polynomially in that space's dimension, where naive extensions scale exponentially. Preprocessing and postprocessing also stay polynomial in system and basis size. The protocol outputs an expansion approximating the parameters up to a chosen error. High success probability is guaranteed with modest logarithmic overheads.
arxiv-2510-08600:
Devleena Das, Rajeev Patwari, and Ashish Sirasao recover accuracy in damaged language models without any real data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Deployment steps like quantization, pruning, format conversion, and serialization can silently degrade a model's task performance. Most recovery work targets quantization specifically. Their method, Recover-LoRA, repairs damage from any source that corrupts model weights.

Recover-LoRA trains low-rank adapters on selected layers using only synthetic data. Logit distillation aligns the degraded model's outputs with those of its full-precision original. The method is lightweight and agnostic to which dataset caused the concern. Tests covered diverse small language models with multi-head and group-query attention designs. Accuracy recovered by five to seventeen percentage points across those models, they report. Several evaluation data sets confirmed the recovery was broad, not tuned to one benchmark.
arxiv-2510-08700:
Zhuolun Li and co-authors ask voters themselves to guard ballot secrecy in a blockchain voting system in a 2025 arXiv paper. Electronic voting needs strong secrecy, but decentralized large-scale elections struggle to guarantee it. Their concept, collectively secure voting, lets voters opt in as secret holders protecting the tally. A practical blockchain system implements the idea end to end.

Threshold cryptography and smart contracts keep ballots confidential while every protocol step stays transparent and verifiable. Voters need no prior blockchain knowledge, thanks to an interface that hides the underlying complexity. User testing measured willingness to serve as secret holders and reliability in releasing shares afterward. Participants showed high willingness, dependable share release, and strong confidence in the system's security. The authors conclude voters can collectively maintain secrecy in a feasible real-world deployment.
arxiv-2510-08900:
Wang and co-authors survey methods that predict molecule traits from only a few labeled examples, in this 2025 arXiv review. Measuring a molecule's properties in a wet lab is slow and expensive, so drug and materials projects often hold just a handful of confirmed results. Learning from so little data is called few-shot learning. Work on it has grown quickly but in scattered pieces, with no shared map of the methods or their pitfalls.

The authors present what they describe as the first full survey of this field. They start by analyzing how the few-shot pattern shows up in real molecular datasets. Two core challenges stand out: methods must transfer across different traits, and they must cope with the special structure of molecules. The survey then organizes the known approaches against those challenges. It closes by charting where the field lacks evidence and which directions look most promising.
arxiv-2510-09000:
Ai, Huang, and Xie propose a fresh route to the universe's surplus of matter over antimatter, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their mechanism hangs on a phase transition in the infant universe, when the Higgs field changed state as space cooled. They extend the standard model with two generations of heavy partner leptons. The lighter partners make the transition run in reverse, briefly restoring a broken symmetry near two hundred giga-electronvolts and sending bubbles racing outward.

The heavier partners, meanwhile, give neutrinos their tiny masses through a seesaw-like mechanism. As bubble walls sweep through the hot plasma, they produce the heavy partners in abundance. Those particles then decay unevenly between matter and antimatter versions, a known bias called CP violation, and the imbalance survives as today's baryon surplus. Because the new particles sit near the tera-electronvolt scale, current and planned colliders can test the story.
arxiv-2510-09100:
de la Hamette, Kabel, and Brukner ask what observers inside a quantum system can ever learn about the whole, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum reference frame theory treats measuring sticks as physical quantum objects themselves. Earlier work mostly assumed the total momentum of everything, frames included, was zero. This paper removes that crutch and fixes the total momentum at an arbitrary value, treating every such global setting as equally fundamental.

A fixed global momentum leaves fingerprints: it becomes encoded in the quantum states, and switching between internal frames adds a phase that depends on it. The authors track how the main schools of the field describe this situation, then grant the internal observers gradually more tools and access. They identify exactly when those observers can deduce the total momentum from inside. The literature's differing conclusions, they show, trace to differing assumptions about what counts as observable from within.
arxiv-2510-09200:
Karuppasamy and co-authors build tools for a car to explain a driver's next maneuver before it happens, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Anticipating whether the driver will turn, brake, or change lanes matters for safety, and an explanation matters for trust. The team curated a new dataset, DAAD-X, of first-person driving video paired with layered written explanations. The explanations act as causal reasoning, drawn from the driver's eye gaze and the car's own road view.

On top of the data they propose a model, VCBM, built around a concept bottleneck, an intermediate layer of named concepts. Because explanations flow through that layer, the model's reasoning is visible by design rather than reconstructed afterward. The explanations stay coherent across space and time. In evaluations, transformer-based versions produced more interpretable behavior than convolutional ones. A new visualization further shows how the explanations disentangle and influence one another.
arxiv-2510-09500:
Shiyuan Luo and six co-authors present Geo-STARS in a 2025 arXiv paper, a model for predicting stream water temperature. Temperature governs water quality and river ecosystems, yet physics-based models and data-driven ones alike often fail when moved to new watersheds or scales. Sparse observations make the generalisation problem worse, since many streams are barely monitored.

The framework adds geo-aware embeddings, which feed geographic information into the model so it can learn principles shared across regions and scales. These embeddings sit inside a gated spatio-temporal graph neural network, a model that learns patterns across connected locations and over time. The geographic and hydrological context guides learning even where observations are thin or absent. On real data spanning thirty-seven years across watersheds along the United States' eastern coast, Geo-STARS beat leading baselines at generalising across both regions and scales.
arxiv-2510-09600:
T Mera, C Ashall, P Hoeflich, and many co-authors report telescope observations of a supernova in a 2025 arXiv paper. The James Webb Space Telescope observed SN 2024ggi, a nearby exploded star, at two late epochs, about two hundred eighty-five and three hundred eighty-five days after the blast. Its near-infrared spectra show lopsided emission lines from many elements, evidence of an aspherical explosion.

Strong bands of carbon monoxide also appear, modelled with a new data-driven approach using three-dimensional radiative transfer simulations. The gas had formed before the first epoch and then progressively evaporated. Its mass fell sharply while its average temperature dropped from about twenty-nine hundred to twenty-five hundred kelvin, and it clumped more strongly over time. The emitting region's minimum speed stayed near eleven hundred kilometres per second, well above the receding photosphere.
arxiv-2510-09800:
Lucas Wang, the sole author, pins down how large a planar point set can be while using few distinct distances, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Given a budget of k different distances between pairs of points, how many points can fit in the plane at all? The answer, captured by the function g of k, has been a question in discrete geometry because extremal sets tend to hide lattice structure.

Wang proves matching bounds that fix the growth rate. The maximum size grows like k times the square root of the logarithm of k, the constant made explicit from the hexagonal lattice. He also proves lower bounds for general arithmetic lattices. A stability result rounds out the paper. Unless a set hugs a line or has two popular non-parallel shifts, its pairs cluster below a high quantile of its distances, or align into one residue class of a doubled lattice.
arxiv-2510-09900:
Ramezani and Sumit Sharma compute hydration free energies of linear alkanes in this 2025 arXiv paper in computational chemistry. Hydration free energy measures how strongly a molecule resists or welcomes moving into water. Standard force fields tend to overestimate this value for water-fearing solutes, which inflates the hydrophobic effect.

The authors run free energy perturbation calculations for alkanes from methane up to eicosane, a twenty-carbon chain. They test three-site water models, SPC/E and OPC3, against four-site models, TIP4P/2005 and OPC, with the TraPPE-UA force field for the alkanes. Comparing all pairings shows which water model skews the energies most. The work then corrects the classical predictions against the pattern they find.
arxiv-2510-10100:
Guo and co-authors tackle unsupervised federated classification in this 2025 arXiv paper on distributed learning. Federated learning trains a shared model across many clients without moving their data. The unsupervised version has no labels either, and past work mostly stopped at representation learning and clustering.

The authors use cooperative pseudo labeling, where clients help assign working labels to unlabeled data. Vision-language models such as CLIP, with strong zero-shot predictions, support the scheme by giving initial label guesses. Clients then refine each other's pseudo labels rather than trusting one source. The goal is true classification across a federation that shares neither raw data nor ground-truth labels, a common real-world constraint.
arxiv-2510-10200:
Ze-Hua Zhang and Xiang Liu compute mass shifts of charmonium states in nuclear matter in this 2025 arXiv paper in particle physics. Charmonia are bound states of a charm quark and its antiquark. The study covers the 1P-wave family, three states labeled by total angular momentum zero, one, and two.

The authors use the quark-meson coupling model to place these states inside cold symmetric nuclear matter, the environment inside atomic nuclei. In-medium loop contributions, quantum corrections from the surrounding nucleons, shift the masses. Such shifts are a probe of how quark forces change in matter. Experiments that produce charmonia in nuclei can test the predictions against measured spectra.
arxiv-2510-10300:
Ruffini examines the algorithmic regulator in this 2025 arXiv theoretical paper on control and cognition. The regulator theorem says an optimal controller must embody an internal model of the system it regulates. The idea grounds predictive brain theories such as the free-energy principle and algorithmic agent theory.

But the theorem is proven only in limited settings. Ruffini asks how far it extends when the controller is viewed algorithmically, as a program trading off model complexity and performance. The analysis probes what any good regulator, biological or artificial, must internally represent. A sharper theorem would clarify claims that brains must model their world, separating proven necessity from suggestive analogy.
arxiv-2510-10800:
Davide Rolino, Paolo Perinotti, and Alessandro Tosini pin down a famous but slippery concept from the foundations of quantum physics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Complementarity, introduced by Niels Bohr, says that some properties of a system cannot be pinned down at the same time. The idea shaped quantum thought for a century, yet it lacked a precise operational definition. The authors supply one: two properties count as complementary when they cannot both be well defined at once.

They then prove a sharp equivalence inside quantum theory. Under their definition, complementarity amounts exactly to the incompatibility of operations, meaning the operations that would measure or realize the two properties cannot be performed simultaneously. This connects Bohr's philosophical notion to a concrete, testable feature of quantum operations. Debates about whether two properties are truly complementary can now be settled by checking operational compatibility.
arxiv-2510-10900:
Jyotiranjan Beuria maps the shape of allowed parameter space for two extensions of the Standard Model of particle physics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The two models studied are the Singlet Scalar Dark Matter model plus its partner, the Next-to-Two-Higgs Doublet Model, each at two values of a key parameter. Parameter points are classed as allowed or excluded by Higgs measurement constraints. Beuria combines topological data analysis with dimension reduction and discriminant analysis to characterize the global geometry of these landscapes.

He finds that the singlet model and the Type I doublet model show finely tuned islands of collider viability, small allowed regions in a sea of exclusion. Raising the parameter in Type I increases topological fragmentation, indicating richer structure. The chosen parameters exclude the entire Type II parameter space under current Higgs data. He also trains machine learning models on the topological features to classify regions faster.
arxiv-2510-11200:
Simulating an open quantum system on a classical computer gets hard fast: the state space grows exponentially, and environments with memory make the dynamics non-Markovian and harder still. Sujay Mondal and co-authors develop an efficient simulation algorithm in this 2025 arXiv quantum physics paper. Their target is large one-dimensional systems such as spin chains, in both memoryless and memory-carrying regimes.

The method extends the Tensor Jump Method, which evolves stochastic trajectories with tensor networks and a Trotter decomposition, by allowing time-dependent decay rates. Positive rates are handled as time-inhomogeneous Markovian processes. Negative rates, the signature of memory effects, are treated through the Influence Martingale formalism, which unravels the non-Markovian dynamics into trajectories a tensor network can follow. The authors demonstrate the framework on a transverse-field Ising chain of up to one hundred spin qubits.
arxiv-2510-11700:
Nagisa Hiroshima and three co-authors revisit how strongly observations limit the behavior of dark matter. Dark matter is the invisible material thought to outweigh ordinary matter in the universe. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses measured flows of electrons and positrons in cosmic rays. From those flows they bound two things. One is how often dark matter particles destroy each other. The other is how long unstable particles survive before decaying.

The team combined data from seven instruments, including CALET, DAMPE, AMS-02, and HAWC. They covered five annihilation and decay channels. The newest CALET data gave the tightest limits for lighter dark matter. For a particle of one TeV in mass, AMS-02 data exclude short lifetimes in the muon channel. The excluded lifetimes run below about ten to the twenty-seventh power seconds. HAWC and CASA-MIA set the strongest limits at the highest masses.
arxiv-2510-11800:
Akaxia Cruz and nine colleagues test whether the standard cosmology can explain the wild variety of dwarf galaxy rotation curves. Dwarf galaxies of the same mass spin in strikingly different ways, long a challenge for the cold dark matter model. Earlier simulations with gas and star physics never reproduced the full spread. The team's 2025 arXiv paper uses the Marvelous Massive Dwarf suite of high-resolution zoom-in simulations.

Their standard star formation and feedback recipes finally produce the observed breadth of curve shapes. Some simulated dwarfs develop dark matter cores, and their rotation curves rise slowly. Others stay compact, with curves rising steeply. The same runs match the observed size and stellar mass link, including its scatter. The authors conclude that earlier simulations likely used feedback that was too strong. With gentler feedback, cold dark matter plus ordinary gas physics needs no exotic replacement.
arxiv-2510-11900:
Guillermo Palma and Gabriel Gómez propose explaining both dark matter and cosmic acceleration with a single sticky fluid. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a unified dark matter model with bulk viscosity, an internal friction that resists expansion. The treatment extends the causal Israel-Stewart theory into a nonlinear regime. That lets the fluid stay far from equilibrium, which a consistent story of viscosity-driven acceleration requires.

The authors recast the cosmic equations as an autonomous dynamical system and map its phase space, mixing exact asymptotic solutions with numerics. Early on, the fluid mimics stiff matter; later it behaves like ordinary dark matter. Three kinds of late-time attractor appear, sorted by a single viscosity exponent. One gives quintessence-like expansion, one is an exact de Sitter state, and one turns phantom-like. Acceleration emerges regardless of the viscosity's size, loosening older bounds. Entropy production stays positive.
arxiv-2510-12000:
Jinchuan Tian and a large team from Carnegie Mellon and NVIDIA unify three audio skills in one model. Audio language models usually specialize: some understand sound, others generate it, and reasoning sits apart. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces UALM, a Unified Audio Language Model meant to do all three. The path starts with UALM-Gen, a text-to-audio model that predicts audio tokens directly.

With careful data blending, training recipes, and inference techniques, the single UALM matches state-of-the-art specialists at audio understanding and text-to-audio generation, and holds its own at text reasoning. Gen alone rivals leading diffusion-based generators. The team then builds UALM-Reason, which thinks through problems using both text and audio in its intermediate steps. They describe it as the first demonstration of cross-modal generative reasoning in audio research. Subjective listening evaluations confirmed the reasoning model's effectiveness on complex generation tasks.
arxiv-2510-12100:
Nadia Benakli, Nicole Froitzheim, and David Martinez ask how few landmarks a graph needs before every address is unique. In a resolving set, chosen vertices act as beacons: each vertex is identified by its list of distances to the beacons. The metric dimension is the smallest such set's size, with uses from navigation to chemistry. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies generalized theta graphs.

These graphs take two hub vertices and join them by many internally disjoint paths, like meridians between two poles. With exactly three paths they form theta graphs, the third and hardest family of bicyclic graphs. Cycles need only two beacons, and other bicyclic families were settled earlier. The authors provide exact metric dimensions and structural insights for several subclasses of the generalized family, mapping how the number and lengths of the parallel paths drive the beacon count. The results extend the classification of graph families by identifying dimension,
arxiv-2510-12200:
Ren and colleagues introduce HackWorld, a 2025 arXiv benchmark for testing whether computer use agents can exploit flaws in web applications. These agents operate software through a graphical interface, clicking and typing like a person. The paper asks whether such agents can find and use real security weaknesses when they act on their own.

HackWorld places agents inside thirty six real applications built with eleven frameworks and seven programming languages. The applications contain flaws such as injection attacks, broken login checks, and unsafe handling of user input. Using a capture the flag setup, the team measured how often agents completed an exploit. Leading agents succeeded less than twelve percent of the time and often showed weak security awareness, poor multi step planning, and clumsy use of security tools.
arxiv-2510-12300:
Urciuoli builds a machine checked formal theory of pure type systems, in a 2025 arXiv logic in computer science paper. Pure type systems are a family of logical frameworks that unify many typed lambda calculi, the formal languages behind proof assistants. Formalizing their metatheory is notoriously fiddly because variable binding and substitution are easy to get subtly wrong.

The development uses first order syntax with a single sort of variable names and Stoughton's multiple substitutions, which substitute for many variables at once. Urciuoli formalizes conversion for Church style terms with Pi types, then proves fundamental properties including weakening, syntactic validity, and closure under alpha conversion and substitution. The whole development was machine checked in the Agda system. He also compares the approach with related formalizations. The work shows that dependent type theory can be mechanized using conventional syntax, without identifying terms that differ only by renamed bound variables.
arxiv-2510-12400:
Torneiro and colleagues review whether vision language models can monitor city infrastructure the way residents perceive it, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Cities must track the condition of waste bins, road signs, vegetation, construction sites, and sidewalks. Sensors and manual inspections are costly and hard to scale.

Following the PRISMA method for systematic reviews, the authors reviewed thirty two peer reviewed papers published between 2021 and 2025. They ask which monitoring tasks these models handle, which architectures perform best, what datasets support the field, and how applications are evaluated. They sort the literature into seven application categories and analyze the eleven leading model architectures, noting strengths and limits of each.  The review closes with a research agenda identifying critical gaps, presented as the first comprehensive review devoted to vision language models in urban monitoring.
arxiv-2510-12500:
Harrington, Ignace, and Gayley calculate how polarized light can reveal whether massive stars spin close to breaking apart, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Rapid rotation and binary mass transfer are both common in massive stars. How angular momentum moves inside them shapes two classes of rotators: Be stars with disk like emission and Bn stars with widened absorption lines. How conservative mass transfer can be depends on how near critical rotation a star can reach.

The authors compute the continuum polarization produced by spin distortion and gravity darkening, the dimming of the faster spinning equator. Two estimates for gravity darkening give similar values that rise strongly in the far ultraviolet. Edge on stars near critical rotation reach about one percent polarization at the shortest wavelengths. Even moderate tilts show clear signals. They argue future far ultraviolet instruments could measure near critical rotation rates in B stars directly.
arxiv-2510-12600:
Gerencsér and Harangi improve lower bounds on how large an independent set a random regular graph must contain, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. In a random regular graph every vertex has the same number of neighbors. The independence ratio, the largest fraction of vertices with no edges among them, is a key open quantity for sparse random graphs. Strong upper bounds there are known to be sharp for large degrees.

The authors start from a second moment argument, a counting method that estimates the chance a random structure exists. They boost it by showing the independent set obtained has a spatial Markov property, meaning its local pieces behave almost independently. Local modifications can then enlarge the set greatly. The resulting explicit lower bounds beat the previous best for degrees of ten and above. The same approach proves existence of other objects, shown by decomposing random regular graphs into stars.
arxiv-2510-12900:
Elaçmaz, Martinez-Soler, and Perez-Gonzalez update limits on large extra dimensions in this 2025 arXiv paper. Extra dimensions beyond the familiar four are one proposed explanation for why neutrinos are so light. They would subtly change how antineutrinos from nuclear reactors change flavor as they travel. Reactor experiments can therefore bound how big a hidden dimension could be.

The authors analyzed the full datasets of five reactor experiments, including Daya Bay, RENO, and KamLAND. For a single extra dimension, they bounded its radius below roughly six tenths of a micrometer under one neutrino mass ordering. That improves earlier limits by about a fifth. A tighter bound holds under the other ordering. They also give the first combined limits for scenarios with two, three, and four extra dimensions, which grow stricter as dimensions are added.
arxiv-2510-13000:
Bastianel, Van Hertem, Ergun, and Roald hunt for the best places to split busbars in power grids in this 2025 arXiv paper. Splitting a busbar, an electrical node in a substation, is a topology change that can relieve congestion and cut generation costs as demand and renewables grow. But optimizing over every substation needs huge numbers of binary decisions and is computationally intractable on large grids.

The authors propose metrics that score and rank substations by their promise, focusing on buses where a split could reduce generation costs. They evaluate splits with a mixed-integer optimization model, then verify the chosen topologies remain feasible under full nonlinear alternating current power flow simulation. Across test cases of different sizes, the metrics reliably identified busbars whose optimized topology lowered total generation costs, avoiding the need to test every substation one at a time.
arxiv-2510-13900:
Julian Minder and co-authors ask whether narrow finetuning, meaning extra training on one small topic, leaves readable marks inside a large language model. Their 2025 arXiv paper examines activation patterns, the internal signals a model produces while processing text, before and after such training. The question is whether an outside observer can recover what the model was trained on.

The authors show that narrow finetuning leaves strong biases in the activations that point back to the training domain. Steering a model with the activation difference produced text resembling the finetuning data in format and content. An interpretability agent given these clues did more than twice as well on broad goals, and far better on specific details, than prompting baselines. Mixing pretraining data into finetuning largely removed the bias.
arxiv-2510-14200:
Zhichao Wang, Andy Wong, and Ruslan Belkin propose training models with reinforcement learning rewarded by similarity to human answers, instead of supervised fine-tuning, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Supervised fine-tuning teaches instruction following by next-token prediction on human-labeled responses, but it can memorize form rather than meaning.

Their method, RLSR, lets the base model generate responses per prompt. It scores each by cosine similarity, in a semantic embedding space, between the generated response and the human-labeled one. This turns the existing fine-tuning data set into a reward signal. Used as a replacement, RLSR beat fine-tuning on instruction-following benchmarks; one configuration lifted a seven-billion-parameter model's AlpacaEval win rate from twenty-one percent under fine-tuning to over twenty-six percent. Combining both methods did better still, pushing the win rate above thirty percent, and the authors report gains on other tasks.
arxiv-2510-14500:
Sergey Ivanov, Yaroslav Kartashov, and Vladimir Konotop develop a theory of wave oscillations in moiré lattices, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These are the aperiodic patterns formed when two periodic structures are overlaid at a twist, here under a weak gradient. Aperiodic lattices lack symmetry, so they have no band structure; instead they feature a mobility edge, beyond which all modes are localized.

When a gradient is applied, it enables energy transfer between localized modes whose energies and positions satisfy a selection rule. This produces Bloch-Landau-Zener oscillations: a tunneling in real space and in energy space. The gradient's strength and direction control which coupling pathways open. The authors derive a multimode model for these waves in the regime and analyze how attractive and repulsive nonlinearities reshape the dynamics. The framework extends to other aperiodic systems where localized modes couple through a tilt.
arxiv-2510-15500:
J. Ostmeyer and C. Urbach introduce a cleaner way to extract particle masses from lattice simulation data, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Physicists approximate Euclidean correlation functions, the raw output of such simulations, as sums of exponentials whose rates give the masses. Many existing algebraic methods attack that fitting problem, each with its own weaknesses around noisy data.

Their truncated Hankel correlator approach first assembles a Hankel matrix out of the recorded data, trims its spectrum to a low-rank core, and only then applies the Prony eigenvalue method. Classic techniques, including block Lanczos and the generalized eigenvalue problem, reappear as less optimal special cases of this route. Measurement weights can be folded in so the fit stays statistically sound. The authors prove that beating their approximation in general is exponentially hard, which certifies its near-optimality. The method is also robust against noise.
arxiv-2510-15600:
Writing exact laboratory protocols is slow, and language models often produce incomplete or jumbled versions. Haoran Sun and eleven colleagues tackle protocol generation in this 2025 arXiv paper. They first build SciRecipe, a dataset of over twelve thousand structured protocols from twenty-seven biological fields. Their Sketch-and-Fill approach splits writing into analysis, structuring, and expression, so each step stays checkable. A reward scheme scores step detail, action order, and meaning to guide model training.

Their model Thoth learns through stages, from knowledge to action, ending in runnable protocol writing. Across benchmarks, Thoth beats leading commercial and open models on step fit, ordering, and accuracy. The team plans to release the data, code, and models publicly.
arxiv-2510-15700:
Formal proofs from automated provers can run thousands of lines, too long for humans to follow. Alex Gu trains a language model to shorten Lean proofs in this 2025 arXiv paper. No human-written simplification examples exist, so the model learns from Lean's own verification feedback. Training uses expert iteration and reinforcement learning, rewarding shorter proofs that still check. At use time, the model shortens a proof step by step in repeated passes.

On standard benchmarks, ProofOptimizer cuts proof length by eighty-seven percent on miniF2F. It achieves fifty-seven percent on PutnamBench and forty-nine percent on IMO 2025 proofs. Shorter proofs also check faster and improve provers retrained on them.
arxiv-2510-15900:
Emmanuel Boadi, writing alone, forecasts Bitcoin prices by splitting the price series before learning from it. Bitcoin swings often and sharply, which makes direct forecasting hard. Variational Mode Decomposition first breaks the raw series into intrinsic mode functions, simpler waves that together rebuild the original signal.

Each mode is then modelled by its own long short-term memory network, a recurrent design suited to temporal patterns. Adding the separate forecasts gives the final prediction for the original series. Boadi compares the hybrid against a standard long short-term memory model used alone. Across root mean square error, mean absolute error, and the coefficient of determination, the hybrid wins on every metric. He also reports a reliable thirty-day forecast from the combined model.
arxiv-2510-16000:
Martin Ryzy leads eight co-authors in imaging nanometre layer thickness with laser ultrasound at gigahertz frequencies. Knowing thin layer thickness to the nanometre guides both basic research and the making of micro devices. Their microscope is contactless and opto-acoustic, reading zero-group-velocity elastic plate resonances whose energy stays localised, giving sharp spectral peaks.

For a demonstration they etched height patterns under ten nanometres into the top layer of bulk-acoustic resonators designed near the gigahertz range stated in the work. Raster scans recover the local resonance frequency as the imaging contrast, and a numerical calibration converts frequency shift into height change. Steps of a few nanometres resolve clearly, pointing to sub-nanometre depth sensitivity, while sideways resolution sits in the micrometre range. Atomic force microscopy checks confirm the images.
arxiv-2510-16100:
Leopoldo A Pando Zayas and Jingchao Zhang work on a deep theory question about black holes and fluids. In holography, hard fluid problems get mapped onto gravity problems. A famous result then links how thick a fluid flows, its viscosity, to a black hole's entropy. Near the coldest, near-extremal black holes, quantum ripples in a thin throat near the horizon can shift that link.

The authors compute the first such shift, called a one-loop correction, working in full four-dimensional space. They use a charged black hole model with its sideways space wrapped into a finite ring shape. The fix grows as the black hole gets colder, matched with a known log-shaped fix to the entropy. Their result gives other theorists a clean test case to check simpler two-dimensional treatments against.
arxiv-2510-16500:
Chen Min leads fourteen co-authors in a 2025 release of a big data set for off-road driving. Self-driving research off paved roads lacks large, clean data sets. Their set, ORAD-3D, covers woods, farms, grass, river banks, and gravel roads. It spans sun, rain, fog, and snow, plus day and night light.

Five benchmark suites come with the set for fair tests. They cover free-space scans, 3D filled-space guesses, rough path plans, and more. One suite tests models that drive from words and images. One tests world models that dream up off-road scenes. The set and code will be shared in public. Off-road teams gain a shared yardstick at last.
arxiv-2510-16900:
Maksym Luz and Mykhailo Moklyachuk study forecasting from past values alone in a 2025 paper. Their data are random sequences whose step-to-step changes settle into stable patterns. Such sequences are said to have stationary increments. The task is estimating weighted sums of unknown future values.

Only past observations, stretching backward without end, may be used. When the spectrum is known exactly, formulas give the best linear estimate. A spectrum describes how the sequence's energy spreads across frequencies. The formulas also give the estimate's mean square error. When the spectrum is uncertain, allowed sets replace the single spectrum. The authors then find worst-case spectra and robust minimax estimates. The work extends safe forecasting methods to this wider sequence family.
arxiv-2510-17000:
Masahiro Kaneko and Timothy Baldwin measure how much attacks leak per question in a 2025 paper. Attackers probe language models to uncover hidden target properties. A target might be a trigger flag or deleted information. Each reply, including reasoning tokens, can leak hints.

Their framework treats leaked information in strict mathematical terms. Mutual information measures how much one reply reveals about the target. They prove attackers need a minimum number of queries. That minimum grows as the allowed error shrinks. It shrinks as each reply leaks more bits. Auditors can now compare their attacks against this fundamental limit. Defenders gain a principled view of the transparency-risk tradeoff. The work replaces anecdotes about leakage with measurable bounds.
arxiv-2510-17100:
R. Bucik and five co-authors study an odd burst of particles from the Sun in this 2025 paper. The burst was seen in October 2023 by the Solar Orbiter craft. Light helium was far more common than in normal solar bursts. Heavy atoms also rose, but not in a smooth order by mass.

Images showed a tiny thread on the Sun burst and launch a thin jet. The jet sat at the edge of a dark patch with weak fields. Heat measures pointed to a cool source for such a burst. The authors argue that source heat helps pick which atoms get boosted. Past like events share the tiny burst and jet pattern.
arxiv-2510-17300:
Mao Shi disproves a guess on slope bounds for rational Bezier curves in this 2025 paper. Such curves shape fonts, car bodies, and CAD parts with weights. A 2013 guess capped the top slope of the curve by set terms. Shi builds a clean counter-case of degree seven that breaks the cap.

Shi also writes the slope curve in the same curve form. A lift trick then gives a true top bound that can be computed. More lifts push the bound toward the true top value. A rule sets how many lifts a set error bar needs. Tests back the counter-case and show the bound is fast and sharp.
arxiv-2510-17400:
Gromov-Witten invariants count curves inside a geometric space, and a supersymmetric version of those counts is harder to define and compute. Artan Sheshmani, Shing-Tung Yau, and Benjamin Zhou show that the genus zero version can be handled with tropical geometry, a method that replaces smooth spaces with simpler, graph like shapes. Their setting is a convex toric variety, a well understood class of spaces built from symmetry.

When the space shrinks to a single point, the tropical counts match known descendant invariants on a space of tropical curves. For a general space, Sheshmani and his co-authors give a step by step procedure for the key correction term, assuming part of the setup can be made tropical. They also compute one concrete invariant for the projective line as a check.
arxiv-2510-17500:
Material moving on a conveyor belt does not react only to what sits right beside it; each patch of load responds to a stretch of belt around it. Paola Goatin, Simone Göttlich, and Fabian Ziegler model that nonlocal behaviour for mixed, heterogeneous material flowing in two dimensions on a bounded domain. Their equations extend an earlier single material result to a system describing several materials at once, with the belt edges built into the nonlocal terms.

To solve the model, Goatin and her co-authors use a finite volume scheme that splits the two directions and follows a classic wave based method. They prove that the numerical solutions converge to the true solution, under a smoothed version of the flow law, and they establish the variation bounds the proof needs. Computer tests match the model well against detailed microscopic simulations.
arxiv-2510-17700:
Walter Simoncini, with Michael Dorkenwald and three co-authors, makes vision models adjustable after training in a 2025 arXiv paper. Vision foundation models ship in only a few fixed sizes. Real deployments face varied compute budgets, so a fixed size often wastes power or starves the task. Their method, called SnapViT, prunes a trained Vision Transformer in one shot. Pruning means removing unneeded network parts.

The pruning scores parts using gradient data plus structure links across the network. An evolutionary algorithm approximates those links cheaply. No labeled data and no retraining are required. The method even works for models without a classification head. Across four model families, it beat prior pruning methods at many sparsity levels. Building an adjustable model took under five minutes on one GPU.
arxiv-2510-17800:
Jiale Cheng and thirteen co-authors present Glyph, a way to give language models much longer context. Long context lets models read whole documents and reason across them. Scaling token windows toward a million tokens costs huge memory and compute. Glyph instead renders long text as images for vision models.

Images pack the same words into far fewer input units. A search procedure, guided by a language model, tunes the rendering settings. It balances compression against reading accuracy for each setup. Tests reached three to four times compression with accuracy near leading text models. Speed rose about fourfold for both reading and generation stages.
arxiv-2510-17900:
Kush Juvekar and three co-authors build the first exam-based test of whether language models are ready for Indian legal work. Their benchmark gathers real questions from top national and state law exams over several years. Models also face long written answers, graded blind by lawyers, from a Supreme Court exam.
