Frontier models cleared past cut-off marks on the objective tests and often matched top scorers. None beat the best human on long-form reasoning, though. Graders flagged weak rule following, shaky citations, and format slips. Courts and firms get a grounded yardstick for what these models can safely do.
arxiv-2510-18000:
Justin Kalloor, with six co-authors, compiles quantum circuits at the scale of hundreds of qubits while keeping error under control. Compiling must cut costly gates and rotations, yet stay close to the ideal circuit the algorithm defines. Their workflow splits circuits into parts and averages over sets of variants to hold that balance.

Benchmark circuits with up to several hundred qubits run through the system with firm error bounds. The trade between cost and accuracy is managed openly rather than by feel. For quantum software teams, the work shows a practical route to large circuits that can still be checked with care.
arxiv-2510-18900:
Alexius Wadell and twenty-eight co-authors describe MIST, a family of foundation models meant to search and explore chemical space. Predicting atomic, heat, and motion-related properties from molecular structure guides new materials, but older methods cannot scan the huge space of possible molecules fast enough.

Trained on large unlabeled data with a new tokenizer called Smirk, MIST models learn many kinds of molecules and their nuclear, electronic, and shape traits. After fine-tuning, they match or beat prior best results on more than four hundred structure-property tasks, from physiology to other applied areas.
arxiv-2510-19800:
B. Bale and six co-authors measure lithium and CNO abundances in RS CVn stars, a class of magnetically active binary stars. The aim is to see how activity stirs the stars' outer layers. High-resolution spectra came from the Moletai Astronomical Observatory. Lithium was read from a single spectral line. Carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen came from molecular bands and an oxygen line, and carbon isotope ratios from a labeled CN band.

Thirty-two stars were analyzed in detail, with thirteen more from archival spectra. Some stars show isotope ratios already altered by extra mixing, earlier in their lives than standard theory expects. The lithium patterns split by mass. Some match first dredge-up predictions, while others point to deeper mixing. One lithium-rich giant, OP And, remains puzzling.
arxiv-2510-19900:
Soubhik Kumar and Michael Nee show how a warped extra dimension of space could betray itself in the statistics of the early universe. Extra dimensions are staples of string theory but usually hide at unreachable energies. During inflation, though, heavy states tied to them, such as the radion and Kaluza-Klein gravitons, could have been produced directly.

The authors work through an explicit five-dimensional model with a stabilized warped dimension, computing the masses and couplings of those states. Because the states are gravitational, they inevitably couple to the field driving inflation and leave oscillatory, angle-dependent patterns in primordial non-Gaussianity. Some example cases are already testable with Planck satellite data, making cosmology a genuine probe of extra dimensions.
arxiv-2510-20000:
Minjun Kim, Seokhwan Moon, and Jinsu Kim classify the long-term behavior of continuous-time Markov chains that count upward from zero. Such chains model biological systems, populations, and queues, and birth-and-death chains are the best-known examples. Earlier criteria covered polynomial transition rates, while this work allows arbitrary rate functions.

The classification is written in terms of how the transition rates grow, and it decides properties such as explosivity, recurrence, and exponential ergodicity. For rates with certain expansion forms, including all rational functions, the authors give exact if-and-only-if conditions. Only three easy quantities are needed: the top degree and the mean and variance of the rates.
arxiv-2510-20500:
Hong-Li Zeng and three co-authors test if fitness rates and the rank of gene forms can be read from genome data of a whole group. Their groups grow by choice, change, and gene swaps, with all genomes known or a fair sample known. In place of real life forms first, they test the read in fake groups where truth is set.

The fake runs map zones where the read works and zones where it must fail. That map gives a frame to judge when a read is sound from full, time-sliced genome data. It also flags states where no read can work. A short scan ties the frame to model life forms and to germs that hit man.
arxiv-2510-20600:
Dildar Ali, Suman Banerjee, and Yamuna Prasad study a multi-product version of billboard slot selection where balance between products matters. An advertiser promotes several products with a separate budget for each, choosing slots so total influence is maximized while the influence gap between any two products stays below a given threshold. Influence is measured against traveler trajectories and a billboard database, and cost per product must respect its budget.

The authors prove the balanced popularity problem is NP-hard to solve optimally. They formulate it as a linear program and apply relaxation with randomized rounding, and they also propose a greedy heuristic with a balance correction step. A number of experiments with real-style data evaluate and compare the proposed solution approaches.
arxiv-2510-20800:
Shiva Sreeram, Alaa Maalouf, Pratyusha Sharma, and Daniela Rus make a rank cutting adaptation method for large language models fast enough for rapid use. The base method boosts accuracy by trimming parts of chosen weight matrices, but its exhaustive search needs full data passes for each matrix and is far too slow.

Four findings drive the speedup, only a few matrices need checks, gradient signals on singular values point to the right ones, splitting rows into clustered groups lifts accuracy further. Just one hundred samples suffice for both the search signals and final scoring. The last point holds because task adaptation turns mostly on prompt style. Together the cuts turn a heavy search into a single gradient step workflow.
arxiv-2510-21200:
Ashlesha Hota, Susobhan Bandopadhyay, and Palash Dey study bribery in elections where voters influence each other through a social network. In shift bribery, a briber pays voters to rank a favored candidate higher, and here a paid voter can also sway neighbors toward that candidate.

They model voters as nodes in a directed, weighted graph and ask whether a winning bribery plan exists within a fixed budget. The problem turns out to be hard in general, even with two candidates and equal costs. Still, they give fast algorithms for several special network shapes, including complete graphs, paths, and cluster graphs, and map out where the problem stays manageable.
arxiv-2510-21300:
Tobias Fuchs and Nadja Klein work on partial-label learning, where each training example carries a set of candidate labels and only one of them is right. Such data arise when human labelers disagree, as in crowdsourcing, and older methods that sort out the true labels can be slow and costly.

Their method treats the true label as a hidden quantity and estimates its probability distribution directly, using neural networks that output the needed parameters for each example at low cost. The design works with any network shape, keeping the rigor of probability models with the speed of deep learning. Theory plus tests on synthetic and real data place the method at the front on both accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2510-21600:
Thilo Maurer and six co-authors build a hardware decoder that keeps a quantum memory's errors in check in real time. Their target is a recently discovered quantum error-correcting code holding twelve logical qubits in one hundred forty-four physical ones, whose checks must be interpreted faster than errors pile up.

The prototype runs on an FPGA chip and implements a relay belief propagation algorithm tuned for the code. Each iteration takes twenty-four nanoseconds, and despite reduced-precision arithmetic the decoder matches the error performance of a full floating-point version. At realistic error rates the average decoding time per cycle stays under a microsecond, fast enough for live operation. The prototype marks a practical step toward decoders that can scale with fault-tolerant quantum computers.
arxiv-2510-21900:
Hongbo Zhang leads a nine-author team building a system that writes literature surveys the way a careful human researcher reads: in rounds, not in one gulp. Most automatic survey tools fetch a huge pile of papers at once, freeze an outline, and then draft, which invites noisy sources, broken structure, and overloaded context.

Their framework loops instead. A planning agent retrieves and reads in stages, updating the outline as understanding grows, so breadth and coherence build together. Each paper is distilled into a card recording its contribution, methods, and findings, keeping claims grounded, and a review-and-refine pass improves flow and weaves in figures and tables. On established and emerging topics alike, the surveys beat leading baselines on coverage, structure, and citation quality.
arxiv-2510-22200:
The Meituan LongCat Team, with Xunliang Cai, Qilong Huang, Zhuoliang Kang, Hongyu Li, Shijun Liang, Liya Ma, Siyu Ren. Three further colleagues, reports a video generation model built for length. LongCat-Video carries over thirteen billion parameters on a Diffusion Transformer backbone, and one model handles text-to-video, image-to-video, and continuing an existing clip.

Length is the headline feature. Pretraining on continuation tasks lets the model hold quality and temporal coherence across minutes of footage rather than seconds. A coarse-to-fine strategy over both time and space, helped by block sparse attention, produces high-definition thirty-frame-per-second video within minutes of computing. The team frames the system as a first step toward world models, systems that simulate how scenes unfold, where sustaining a plausible long video is the entry fee.
arxiv-2510-22500:
Judging a very strong artificial intelligence system gets hard when no single expert knows every field a task touches. Ren Yin, Takashi Ishida, and Masashi Sugiyama address that oversight problem in a 2025 paper, focusing on questions that need deep skill in several domains at once.

Their idea lets each expert rule out one wrong option, even when the right answer stays unknown. From those weaker labels, Yin and co-authors build a fair estimate of top answer accuracy and count how many labels are needed. They also mix scarce full labels with plentiful partial ones and prove error bounds for both settings.
arxiv-2510-22700:
Entropy is a measure of disorder in a system. R V Romanik wrote a 2025 paper on entropy in a fluid model. His co-authors are O A Dobush and M P Kozlovskii. I V Pylyuk and M A Shpot are co-authors too. In this model, each cell can hold many particles at once.

The team derive entropy in exact form. It is given as a function of heat and chemical potential. A second form uses density as the key variable. The model shows phase shifts at low heat, one after the next. Entropy per particle dips near whole number densities. Entropy per cell dips there too. The authors think this dip may be a trait of all such models.
arxiv-2510-22900:
A sky survey in hydrogen alpha light can map glowing gas across the sky. Noor Aftab leads a team with nine co-authors. In 2025 they present Data Release 1 of the MDW H alpha Sky Survey. Hydrogen alpha is a red spectral line. The survey runs autonomously with narrow band imaging.

This release covers the northern sky. Each field stacks twelve twenty minute exposures. Star removed mean fields are included. Point source catalogs match two other surveys. Early work measures filament widths in the Lyra region. Catalogs help find variable and excess H alpha sources. The survey was founded by amateur astronomers. Its data are now refined for academic use.
arxiv-2510-23000:
Julia Falcone leads a team of nine astronomers measuring gas flowing out of the Seyfert galaxy NGC 3227. Using Hubble slit spectra and imaging plus ground-based data, they mapped ionized and molecular gas near the bright center. Photoionization models helped turn line strengths into physical rates.

Ionized outflow peaked at about twenty solar masses per year at roughly forty seven parsecs from the central black hole. Archival data added the molecular side of the flow. Resolved rates like these show how a feeding black hole can push back on its host galaxy, a key part of galaxy growth models.
arxiv-2510-23500:
Oscar Thees, Roman Müller, and Matthias Templ study a practical problem in data privacy: how to judge whether protected data still stays useful. When records are anonymized or replaced with synthetic copies, analysts must weigh disclosure risk against data utility. Older checks often used one measure or a flat two-way chart, which misses how many linked measures behave at once.

The authors compare six ways to picture several risk and utility scores together, from heatmaps and dot plots to charts built with a method called PCA. They add two new PCA variants and use each display to find methods that no rival beats on every score. Their results show that viewing all measures at once leads to better, better-informed choices among anonymization methods.
arxiv-2510-23700:
Rebecca Diesing and two co-authors examine how shocks in merging galaxy clusters accelerate cosmic rays, and what small magnetic structures do to that process. Merging clusters glow with radio relics and halos from electrons boosted at shocks, a mechanism called diffusive shock acceleration. In the thin, weakly magnetized gas between galaxies, particles should wander too freely for shocks to push protons to high energies.

Recent transport work suggests the gas can police itself. Drifts from local equilibrium trigger the mirror instability, spawning plasma-scale magnetic bumps, or micromirrors, that scatter cosmic rays efficiently. The authors show micromirror confinement sets a floor on the top proton energy, around a hundred GeV, without needing cosmic-ray-driven field growth. A simulation of a Coma-like merger with micromirror-set diffusion stays consistent with gamma-ray observations, supporting the picture.
arxiv-2510-23800:
P. Sherpa and thirteen co-authors report a sharp Hebel-Slichter coherence peak in the superconductor LaNiGa2, and use it to test what kind of pairing the material hosts. This crystalline superconductor was thought to pair electrons in an internally antisymmetric non-unitary triplet state, with two gaps tied to different spins. Nuclear quadrupolar resonance measurements of the spin-lattice relaxation rate give a check.

The peak's temperature dependence fits the triplet model only if the two gaps are equal and the state is unitary. Slight non-unitarity with unequal gaps shrinks the peak fast and breaks the fit. By contrast, a two-band singlet BCS-like pairing with two gaps fits the data well and matches earlier measurements. The authors argue the result casts doubt on the claimed time-reversal-breaking triplet state in this material. Gap symmetry, it turns out, can be read from one peak.
arxiv-2510-24000:
Heethanjan Kanagalingam and three co-authors present AdvBlur, a method that makes diabetic retinopathy classifiers hold up across hospitals and cameras. Retinopathy grading from retinal photos saves sight when caught early, but deep learning models sag on new data because devices, imaging conditions, and patient populations shift. The authors attack that fragility during training rather than after it.

AdvBlur mixes adversarially blurred images into the training set and trains with a dual-loss framework aimed at domain generalization. Blurring forces the model to lean on features that survive changes in image quality and equipment. Evaluations span several datasets, with experiments isolating the effects of camera type, low-quality images, and dataset size. Ablations confirm both the blurred images and the loss design earn their keep. The model performs competitively against leading domain generalization methods on external datasets it never saw, a practical step toward screening tools that travel.
arxiv-2510-24200:
Alexander Bakarsky and three co-authors extend SPEAR, an attack that recovers private training data from shared gradients in federated learning. Federated learning trains models across clients without explicit data sharing, but gradient inversion attacks challenge that privacy promise. Most attacks rely on direct optimization with no formal guarantees, so real world risk stays disputed.

SPEAR stood out for its theory, based on gradients of linear layers with ReLU activations, but its practical reach was limited. The new version, SPEAR++, uses sparsely used dictionary learning to scale the attack. This gives a stronger test of whether a given federated deployment can leak data, helping teams judge privacy risk before release.
arxiv-2510-24500:
Yong Huang, Zhongqi Yang, and Amir Rahmani, three authors, build a sepsis data set. Sepsis is a body-wide response to infection that can kill fast. Intensive care units treat the sickest patients and log rich data. Past sepsis studies used old data and pipelines no one could rerun. The team draw a clean cohort from the MIMIC-IV hospital database.

The cohort holds 35,239 patients with time-aligned clinical records. Treatment data cover fluids, blood-pressure drugs, breathing machines, and antibiotics. Cases follow the Sepsis-3 rule, and gaps are filled in a stated way. Set tasks predict early death, stay length, and shock onset. Adding treatment data boosted scores, most for Transformer models. The open pipeline gives critical care research a shared test bed.
arxiv-2510-24600:
Kateryna Akbash, Ivan Matsak, and Oleg Zakusylo study a random process that renews itself in cycles. Their math work asks how likely such a process is to climb to a high level. They give bounds from both sides for that chance, not just one rough guess.

Two side results on sums with a delay play a key role in their proof. The authors then show how the bounds can be used in queue work. Such queues model lines of jobs or calls that wait for help, so the bounds help judge how long or how full a line may get.
arxiv-2510-24900:
Samane Raji, Ignacio Trujillo, Fernando Buitrago, Giulia Golini, and Ignacio Ruiz Cejudo recheck how disk galaxy edges are classed, with far deeper shots than in the past. New gear now lets teams see disks about two grades more faint than two decades back. That depth opens zones that old sky shots could not reach at all.

They trace mass maps for disk galaxies of like weight from a deep stripe survey. Three past edge types all showed edges at near the same faint light level and mass per patch. That level sat outside old shot range, so it went unseen. Hints say the main split among past types may just be how strong the core bulge is.
arxiv-2510-25200:
Philani Rodney Majozi, the sole author, studies a one sided form of space where range can shift with the way one goes. Such spaces stretch the usual modular metric frame in a one way way. To each, he ties two set forms of same reach, one fore and one back, with their own ways of how points draw near.

Marks such as end of a run, full reach, and tight pack are then split by way. Those split marks are not kept when the space is forced to be two way, he shows. Fore and back ends of runs can differ, and a tight pack two way can hide a loose one way. A rich class view frames the split.
arxiv-2511-00200:
Black holes between about one hundred and one hundred thousand solar masses are oddly scarce in observations, and Lavinia Paiella and three co-authors ask how such mid-weight holes could form at all. Two routes are on the table: stars crashing together in packed clusters, and pairs of black holes merging again and again. The team tests both routes in young, globular, and nuclear star clusters.

Using an updated population code called B-POP, they vary the starting seeds and the history of each cluster. Star collisions turn out to be the main route across most cluster types. The results also hint that lone mid-weight holes may drift inside galaxies like our own.
arxiv-2511-00500:
Anqi Dong, Karl Henrik Johansson, and Johan Karlsson bring traffic limits into optimal transport theory, the mathematics of moving mass at least cost. Classical transport ignores capacity, yet roads saturate: each street has a density beyond which flow chokes, a relation traffic engineers call the fundamental diagram. The authors build that relation into a dynamic, continuous-flow transport model on graphs.

Density lives on nodes, like intersections storing mass, while momentum lives on edges, like road segments carrying speed, mirroring how traffic engineers think. The constrained problem keeps mass conservation and admits a convex discretization, so congestion-aware optimal flows can actually be computed. The team proves an optimal flow exists and is unique, gives an efficient solver, and tests it from a single-lane line up to a city-scale network.
arxiv-2511-01000:
Hassan Ugail and Ismail Lujain Jaleel build a machine learning system for judging whether a painting is truly by Francisco Goya. Goya's style changed a lot over his career, and forgeries are common, so visual checks alone often fail. Their system also uses X-ray images, which reveal layers beneath the surface.

The same feature extraction is applied to both kinds of image: texture measures, local patterns, entropy, energy, and color distribution. A one class support vector machine, tuned carefully, then learns what authentic works look like from twenty four verified Goya paintings with matching X-rays. The framework reached high classification accuracy with a low false positive rate, and a case study of Un Gigante returned strong authentication confidence.
arxiv-2511-01200:
Mengyuan Liu and colleagues introduce MoSa, a system that generates three dimensional human motion from text descriptions. It builds on vector quantization guided generative transformers, where motion is compressed into discrete tokens and a transformer predicts them. Earlier systems predict one token at a time, which is slow.

MoSa generates coarse to fine instead. A hierarchical quantization scheme with a multi scale token preservation strategy keeps tokens at several scales. A scalable autoregressive model predicts whole scale levels per step, needing only as many steps as there are quantization layers. A lightweight convolution attention autoencoder guards reconstruction quality against the frequent interpolation used. On the Motion-X data set, MoSa beat a leading prior method on fidelity while cutting inference time by about a quarter.
arxiv-2511-01300:
Zong-Wei Wu and Jun-Hong An study giant atoms in a waveguide, superconducting artificial atoms that couple to light at several separated points along a one dimensional channel. Such systems are candidates for quantum interconnects. They behave in ways natural atoms do not. But the standard approximations used to describe them discard memory effects.

Going beyond the Born-Markov and Wigner-Weisskopf approximations, the authors follow the non-Markovian dynamics of one and two giant atoms in a waveguide made of coupled resonators. The behavior, they find, is governed by the energy spectrum of the combined atom and photon system. Whenever bound states exist in that spectrum, excited state populations settle to stable finite values or oscillate without loss. Their oscillation frequencies are set by the bound state energy gaps. The result is a guideline for fighting decoherence.
arxiv-2511-01500:
Thomas Le Corre, Adrien Séguret, and Ana Bušić look at a power-grid problem. The task is coordinating huge fleets of thermostatically controlled loads, such as water heaters. The aim is to help the grid without leaving anyone cold. Their approach models the fleet with piecewise deterministic Markov processes, systems that drift smoothly and then jump at random moments.

Rather than tracking every device, the mean-field method controls a single representative device against an average cost, which keeps the problem solvable. A comfort constraint is enforced by adding an extra switching push whenever a device nears the edge of its allowed temperature band. A decentralized algorithm, built on a dual formulation and stochastic gradient descent, is demonstrated on water heaters in signal-tracking and price-response tests.
arxiv-2511-01600:
Agnar Martin Bjørnstad, Elias Stenhede, and Arian Ranjbar present a lightweight model for outlining tumors in three-dimensional CT scans. Measuring whole tumor volume tracks treatment response better than the standard RECIST approach, which uses one diameter in one plane, but hand-drawing volumes is too slow for routine care.

Their model, Lite ENSAM, adapts the ENSAM architecture for efficiency and learns from scans annotated only with RECIST measurements. It was entered in the MICCAI FLARE 2025 pan-cancer segmentation task, where it scored a Dice similarity of about 60.7 percent and a normalized surface Dice of about 63.6 percent on the hidden test set. On public validation data it ran in about 14.4 seconds per scan on a plain CPU.
arxiv-2511-01700:
Abhi Savaliya builds a dark energy model out of a massive vector field. The prompt is the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's second data release. It hints that dark energy may evolve, rather than sit constant as in the standard Lambda-CDM cosmology. In his generalized Proca theory setup, the vector field couples non-minimally to the background curvature through marginal interactions.

Analyzing the effective equation of state, he finds only a narrow strip of parameter space fits the observations. The coupling must be extremely small. The field's mass is confined to a tight window around 10 to the minus 66 grams in scale. The present-day equation of state lands above the cosmological-constant value. Its deviation falls in the range suggested by combined DESI, microwave background, and Pantheon+ supernova data. The model thus offers a controlled, if tightly fenced, departure from the standard picture.
arxiv-2511-01800:
Prateek Chanda, Shrey Modi, and Ganesh Ramakrishnan slim down federated learning for personal devices. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model without surrendering raw data, but training on each client's full dataset every round is cumbersome. Their proposal lets each client forward updates computed from a small, weighted coreset, a representative sample of its data, instead of everything it holds.

The method is personalized, so each client's model can adapt to its own data. Theoretical analysis shows the average generalization error is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. It also gives a closed-form expression for the gap to vanilla federated learning. The gap is a function of the coreset weights and size. Experiments on benchmark datasets with several recent personalized architectures show significant gains over random sampling followed by federated training.
arxiv-2511-01900:
Boris Zilber rethinks the foundations of quantum mechanics with model theory. Physicists learn the subject through the Dirac-von Neumann axioms. Those axioms use operators and integrals. Standard logic handles them awkwardly, since the quantities are continuous, not discrete.

Zilber recasts the axioms in continuous model theory. He proves that the basic axiom system has approximate finite models of any large size. More than that, the canonical continuous model is isomorphic to an ultraproduct of finite ones. He also studies the continuous-logic quantifier that matches Dirac integration. In finite settings it splits into local and global versions. The two coincide on Gaussian wavefunctions. The work ties quantum theory to finite structures.
arxiv-2511-02100:
Rodrigo Mendoza-Smith proposes a cheaper way to judge which data points in a training set matter most. The principled Shapley approach values each point by its contribution across every possible subset, which is far too expensive at scale. His alternative uses statistical leverage scores, a geometric measure of how much each point stretches the span of the dataset and adds to its effective dimensionality.

These scores, he shows, satisfy three of the fairness axioms that make Shapley values attractive, and a ridge version connects to classical optimal design criteria. Training on a leverage-sampled subset gives a model close to the full-data optimum in both parameters and prediction risk. An active learning experiment shows the sampling beats standard baselines without needing gradients.
arxiv-2511-02400:
Yalda Zafari, Hongyi Pan, Gorkem Durak, Ulas Bagci, Essam Rashed, and Mohamed Mabrok build shared infrastructure for fairer AI in breast cancer screening. Public mammography datasets differ wildly in image quality, metadata habits, and patient populations, so models absorb dataset-specific biases and fail elsewhere, a core obstacle to clinical use. Their public framework, MammoClean, standardises case selection and image processing, including laterality and intensity correction, and unifies metadata into one consistent multi-view structure.

Alongside a review of breast anatomy, imaging traits, and the public datasets, the team applied the framework to three heterogeneous collections. They measured large shifts in breast density and abnormality rates between them. The sharpest demonstration was direct: models trained on corrupted versions of the data performed notably worse than those trained on curated versions. Clean, harmonised corpora built this way gave better generalisation across domains.
arxiv-2511-02800:
Vijay Ganesh Sadhasivam, Jan Rost, and Stuart Althorpe ask why operators in quantum systems can grow at an exponential rate. Operator growth, tracked by Krylov complexity, has known universal speed limits. Separately, thermalization research studies how operator entries look in the energy basis. Their 2025 paper joins the two lines of work into one picture.

They show that exponential growth happens exactly when the operator's off-diagonal entries fall off exponentially in the energy basis. If that falloff is slower, like a power law, the growth rate instead hits the universal bound. The result pins down a microscopic origin for operator growth. Strikingly, it holds regardless of chaos, dimension, or whether particles interact, which makes the criterion broadly useful.
arxiv-2511-02900:
Ryohei Kobayashi, Guanyu Zhu, and Po-Shen Hsin extend a family of quantum error-correcting codes past a famous limit. The Bravyi-Konig bound caps the gates that topological stabilizer codes in a given dimension can perform safely. Their 2025 paper builds Clifford hierarchy stabilizer codes, tied to Dijkgraaf-Witten gauge theories with non-Abelian order. It equips them with transversal non-Clifford gates.

In two dimensions, they obtain the first transversal T and CS gates for Clifford stabilizer codes, using a twisted gauge theory. They add a fast route to prepare a magic state by code switching. In three dimensions, they build a transversal square-root-of-T gate at the third level of the hierarchy. Both results pass the old bound by one level, in each dimension.
arxiv-2511-03000:
Alexander Gates unifies two families of scores that judge how alike two clusterings are. One family counts agreeing pairs of items. The other measures shared information across the full table of overlaps. The two camps often disagree, and earlier work patched the gap with empirical fixes. His 2025 paper seeks the analytic link underneath.

Gates writes both families as weighted sums over observed versus expected co-occurrences. Pair-counting scores appear as a low-order, quadratic approximation, while information scores add higher-order, frequency-weighted terms. Extending pair counting to triples and larger tuples shows the information family as the same idea carried further. Worked cases for the Rand index and mutual information show how other scores follow. The framework explains when the families diverge and helps users pick a score.
arxiv-2511-03500:
Yannick Hoyer and Kristoffer Rank Rasmussen build a new model structure for modules over curved differential graded algebras. Curvature twists the usual rule that applying the differential twice gives zero, and that twist breaks standard homological tools. Their injective Guan-Lazarev structure restores a workable homotopy theory for those modules.

The module category with that structure proves equivalent, in the Quillen sense, to contramodules over an extended bar construction. That bridge links two earlier duality theories that had covered separate cases, conilpotent and non-conilpotent. A payoff is that tensor products behave correctly as a Quillen bifunctor in this setting. The result gives algebraists a unified frame for curved Koszul triality arguments.
arxiv-2511-03600:
A A Gladkij and co-authors ask if a bright burst state in hybrid perovskite films can stand up to lattice shakes. Recent tests found superfluorescence in these films at warm room heat. In that burst, many excitons act as one and flash in step. Phonons, the shakes of the lattice, could help or harm that step.

Flat excitons are tied to two kinds of phonons in their model. That tie leads to a two-dimensional wave rule for the exciton. A lone wave form in that rule anchors the test of stability. Traits of the soft, polar crystal shape the terms used. If such states stay firm at room heat, they could serve as light sources for quantum tools with no deep cold.
arxiv-2511-03700:
Oleh E Omel'chenko and Georg A Gottwald derive exact statistics for the flicker that finite size causes in synchronized oscillator crowds. The Kuramoto-Sakaguchi model, a standard for coupled rhythms with phase lag, settles into partial synchrony in the infinite limit. Real crowds are finite, so their shared order parameter wobbles around that limit.

An explicit solution of a key single-oscillator equation unlocks covariance formulas for the wobble, plus the variance of its strength, all written purely in model parameters. No prior picture of the synchronized state is assumed. Simulations of the full model confirm the formulas on both sides of the sync threshold. Power grids and neural rhythms both lean on such models, so honest finite-size error bars matter.
arxiv-2511-04000:
Kyaw Hpone Myint, Zhe Wu, Alexandre G R Day, and Giri Iyengar propose a scalable way to meta-learn near-optimal decision trees, models valued in finance and healthcare because people can read them. Their trick is to generate the pretraining data synthetically by sampling near-optimal trees, creating large, realistic datasets cheaply.

Paired with the MetaTree transformer architecture, synthetic pretraining matched performance from pretraining on real data or on costly optimal trees. Costs drop, data generation gains flexibility, and the route scales better. The work points toward practical meta-learning for interpretable models, where a learned system proposes a good tree quickly instead of solving each case from scratch.
arxiv-2511-04100:
Kieran Flatt and Joonwoo Bae study contextual advantages in telling two quantum states apart, a task now also used to witness general contextuality. Catalog evidence carried a different title about unifying advantages; the arXiv record gives the title used here, and that record governs the framing.

Noncontextuality inequalities are derived for conclusive and inconclusive outcomes across guessing strategies. For minimum-error discrimination the advantage appears in outcome confidences, while for clear-cut discrimination it appears in average guessing probability. Maximum-confidence guessing shows edges in confidence, guessing rate, and inconclusive rate alike. Contextual edges, the pair conclude, appear across every two-state scheme and measure examined.
arxiv-2511-04300:
Ramy Aboushelbaya, Annika Moslein, Hadi Azar, Hamid Tanhaei, and Marko von der Leyen present a self-correcting, high-speed optoelectronic probabilistic computer built from quantum photonic p-bits with electronic control. Probabilistic computing needs huge numbers of fast, random binary units, and magnetic implementations set the current speed and energy benchmarks.

A prototype on photonic integrated circuits with FPGA control handles sixty-four thousand logical p-bits. Flip rates reached billions per second with energy per flip in single nanojoules, nearly a thousandfold better than magnetic tunnel junction systems on both measures in the reported comparison. A source-device independent protocol adds real-time self-certification and error correction as p-bit counts scale.
arxiv-2511-04600:
The SNO+ Collaboration reports how many neutrons cosmic muons create in water underground. Those neutrons form a major background for rare low-energy physics searches. SNO+ sees some of the highest average muon energies of any site, near three hundred sixty-four gigaelectronvolts.

Using ultra-pure water, the team measured the neutron yield at that energy. The result matches the FLUKA simulation model clearly. It disagrees with the widely used GEANT4 model, a notable gap for planners. The yield also came out lower than a comparable earlier observation, which tightens background estimates for future detectors.
arxiv-2511-04700:
Song Wang leads eight authors with WinnowRAG, a framework for cleaning retrieved documents before answering. Pulling more documents raises the odds of finding the right one. It also drags in noise, and misleading pages can drag accuracy down.

Winnowing, their name for the fix, filters junk while keeping valuable content. The framework runs in two stages to sort wheat from chaff at scale. The metaphor is literal: thresh out the husks, keep the grain. For retrieval systems that cast a wide net, a disciplined filter may matter as much as the retriever itself.
arxiv-2511-05000:
Hyunkyu Kim, Yeeun Yoo, and Youngjun Kwak build a way to make test queries for bank search tools without using real client data. Banks need strong search for language model services, but real user needs are complex, domain-bound, and barred by law from use as test data.

Their pipeline makes queries from one or many bank files, then checks if each query can in fact be answered from those files. The check matches human calls more closely than past methods. Their KoBankIR set holds 815 queries from 204 bank files, and top search models still fail on its multi-file queries.
arxiv-2511-05300:
Emmanuel Pio Pastore and co-authors coin the entropy-rank ratio, a new gauge of DNA sequence complexity. Shannon entropy is the standard gauge, but it saturates on long uniform stretches, so unlike sequences can score the same.

Their ratio places a sequence in the full spread of all sequences of the same length. It counts the share with entropy at or below the target, so ordered strings score near zero and rich ones score high. The gauge aims to sort and classify DNA with finer splits than entropy alone can give.
arxiv-2511-05600:
Soumyajit Maity and colleagues use a medical foundation model from Google to spot abnormalities in bone and joint X-rays. Their system builds on MedGemma, whose vision encoder was pretrained on many kinds of medical images. X-rays are first cleaned, then turned into rich feature vectors by that encoder.

A small neural classifier reads those vectors and labels each image normal or abnormal. In tests the system beat older convolutional and autoencoder pipelines. The authors credit the foundation model's transfer learning for stronger generalization and simpler feature work. They suggest such systems could speed up clinical triage of radiographs and extend to other medical image tasks.
arxiv-2511-05800:
Ziyue Yu, Xinyu Si, and Lei Fang challenge a basic belief about turbulence: that it needs fast flow. Turbulence is marked by energy passing between motion at different scales. Textbooks tie it to high Reynolds numbers, where inertial forces dominate friction. The team shows strong scale-to-scale energy flow even when that ratio is near one.

In a thin, flat flow driven by electromagnetic forcing, they added direction-biased disturbances. Those disturbances amplified the energy flux between scales by more than a hundredfold, with no strong inertia present. They recast the transfer as a mechanical interplay between turbulent stress and large-scale deformation. The result opens a new regime of two-dimensional turbulence, with ideas for moving fluids in microfluidic and biological settings.
arxiv-2511-06000:
Favour Yahdii Aghaebe and co-authors test whether language models keep track of patient age when summarizing medical studies. Age decides safety in medicine: drugs fine for adults can harm children or fail older patients. As models enter evidence synthesis, losing age distinctions is a real risk.

The team built DemogSummary, a data set of systematic review studies split into child, adult, and older adult groups. Three summarizers, two open and one commercial, were graded with standard scores plus a new Demographic Salience Score measuring kept and invented age details. Age fidelity ran lowest for adult-focused summaries, oddly enough. Under-represented groups drew more invented details. The authors call for fairness-aware scoring and pipelines in biomedical language tools.
arxiv-2511-06100:
Martin Ivanov, Mikhail Krastanov, and Nadezhda Ribarska prove that a broad class of differential inclusions always has a solution. A differential inclusion generalizes an equation: the rate of change may be any of a set of allowed values. Their right-hand sides are uniformly bounded and take nonempty closed sets, which need not be convex.

Nonconvex values are the hard case, since many standard existence proofs lean on convexity. Their sufficient condition handles it, and a classic Olech-type result falls out as a corollary. To show the theorem earns its keep, they give an example rooted in the Fuller problem from optimal control theory. That problem is famous for its chattering optimal controls, making it a fitting stress test for inclusion theory.
arxiv-2511-06300:
Bar Genossar, Sagi Dalyot, Roee Shraga, and Avigdor Gal address entity resolution for three-dimensional city data. Cities are mapped again and again by satellites, drones, and street cameras, and matching the same building or object across those sources is hard. Coordinate systems often clash, and names or identifiers may be missing or unreliable.

Their pipeline, 3dSAGER, compares objects by their intrinsic geometry instead of by position or labels. A featurization step captures shape in a way that ignores the spatial reference frame. A lightweight blocking method, BKAFI, quickly gathers high-recall candidate pairs for checking. Experiments on real urban datasets showed clear gains in accuracy and efficiency over strong baselines.
arxiv-2511-06400: Yağmur Bülbül, Ilmar Gahramanov, Ali Mert Yetkin, and Reyhan Yumuşak build a new structure in algebra called the lens hyperbolic modular double. In math physics, a modular double pairs two linked algebras. Doubles of this kind support exact solutions of key equations in the field. Here, the intertwining operator of the new double yields a lens hyperbolic hypergeometric solution of the Yang-Baxter equation. That equation sits at the heart of integrable systems and of models that can be solved in exact form.
arxiv-2511-06700:
Damian Curran, Vanessa Sporne, Lea Frermann, and Jeannie Paterson test whether chatbots give equally reliable legal information in different cities. Comparing legal knowledge across places is tricky because institutions differ, so the team borrowed functionalism from comparative law, matching scenarios rather than statutes. Real advice-seeking posts from Reddit supplied family, housing, work, crime, and traffic situations.

Each scenario was posed for Los Angeles, London, and Sydney, and the legal summaries returned were hand-checked for invented content. Hallucination rates differed significantly by place among leading closed models, so answer quality is unevenly spread across geography. A model's self-consistency across repeated samples tracked its error rate closely, offering a practical uncertainty signal.
arxiv-2511-06800:
Sathiyamoorthy Buvaneswaran, Trilochan Sahoo, and Saurabh Ghosh use computer calculations to propose two new substances for solar energy conversion. The compounds combine potassium or sodium with lanthanum, iron, and molybdenum, and are double perovskites, crystals with two kinds of metal sites in a regular pattern. Both are ferroelectric, meaning they carry a built-in electric polarization.

The results show strong polarization, band gaps near 1.8 electron volts that suit visible-light absorption, and light charge carriers that should move charge efficiently. Models further suggest the magnetization can be switched along with it above room temperature. That coupling of electric and magnetic behavior in a single light-absorbing substance makes the pair promising for future solar and memory devices.
arxiv-2511-06900:
Ricardo Suárez continues a program linking special geometric structures to the internal structure of Clifford algebras. In earlier work he matched SU(3), G2, and Spin(7) structures with minimal left ideals of certain Clifford algebras. Minimal left ideals are the smallest building blocks from which spinor representations are assembled, so the correspondence ties geometry to spinor algebra.

Here he treats U(n)-structures, which are defined by a symplectic form acting as a stabilizer inside the orthogonal group. Using the Kähler polynomial induced by that form, he identifies U(n)-structures with minimal left ideals for Clifford algebras of various signatures. The paper thereby extends the dictionary suggested by Berger's classification of holonomy groups, connecting another classic family of geometries to its algebraic counterpart.
arxiv-2511-07200:
Mi Feng, Liang Tian, and Changsong Zhou design vaccine prioritization plans that look at the end of an epidemic rather than the next week. Real outbreaks have memory: today's infections depend on a history that inflates the state space and defeats long-term optimization, so most plans chase short-term goals and miss the indirect protection vaccination confers. The authors build an age-stratified, non-Markovian epidemic model that captures memory through state aggregation and covers many epidemic models in one system.

A mapping converts the memory-laden final state into an equivalent Markovian one, making long-term outcomes predictable in real time under any vaccination plan. Their dynamic strategy continually allocates doses to minimize the predicted final burden, balancing indirect transmission blocking against direct protection. It beats static and short-term heuristic policies, and the analysis explains why priorities shift as coverage accumulates.
arxiv-2511-07600:
Swaroop Panda reimagines how people see their own heartbeats. Wearables record rich heart rate series, yet apps mostly show simple averages and zones. Patterns across hours and days, where stress and recovery live, stay hidden.

Five prototype views borrow proven methods from visualization research: variability heatmaps, recurrence plots, spectrograms, clustered maps, and Poincaré plots. Synthetic datasets shaped by physiology, drafted with language model help, stand in for personal data. Each view is checked for what pattern it reveals across time scales. The speculative study invites designers to treat heart data as a landscape worth exploring, not just a score.
arxiv-2511-07700:
Brandon Dominique, Prudence Lam, and Nicholas Kurtansky argue that fairness audits of skin cancer AI miss half the story. Models can match expert melanoma detection overall while scoring demographic groups unevenly. Most audits use ranking accuracy, which says nothing about whether risk estimates themselves are trustworthy.

Calibration, whether a stated risk matches real outcomes, enters the benchmark beside ranking metrics. A model can rank fairly yet quote biased probabilities to one group, misleading triage. Adding calibration exposes such gaps before clinic use. The proposal pushes medical AI evaluation toward the numbers doctors actually act on, not just leaderboards.
arxiv-2511-07900:
Arvid Siqveland focuses algebra: he builds ring versions of zooming in on a neighborhood. Earlier work built schemes of objects in categories with chosen basepoints and local representatives. Here the setting is rings with unit, and basepoints come from endomorphism rings of simple modules.

For any finite set of such points on a ring, the local ring exists. That theorem completes the construction for rings. Zooming in lets algebraists study a ring through its behavior near chosen points, much as geometry studies neighborhoods. Extending scheme tools beyond commutative algebra widens where geometric intuition can be applied.
arxiv-2511-08000:
Catherine Beneteau and five co-authors compute metric projections in Hardy spaces, a setting central to complex analysis on the disc. Beurling theorem describes shift unchanged subsets of the square integrable Hardy space through an orthogonal projection. Extensions to other powers usually reduce matters back to that case through factorization tricks.

Here the projection of the constant function is calculated directly for powers between one and infinity. Unlike the classic case, the best approximation can be zero or a nonconstant outer function. The authors find exact distances to shift unchanged subsets, raise open problems, and draw consequences for zeros of optimal polynomial approximants.
arxiv-2511-08100: Przemyslaw Koprowski examines polynomials that send a local field into the subset of its prime power values, where the prime is the residue characteristic of that field. A local field here is a completion of a number field at a non Archimedean place. Koprowski characterizes exactly which polynomials have this mapping property and shows the class is always much broader than simple prime powers of polynomials themselves.
arxiv-2511-08300:
Isaac Smith, Catherine Cerny, Keren Sharon, and Guillaume Mahler present the first strong gravitational lensing model of the galaxy cluster PSZ2 G118.46+39.32, at redshift near zero point four. New near infrared imaging from the JWST SLICE program reveals lensed galaxies, some invisible to Hubble, thanks to broad filter coverage. Those multiple images constrain how mass is spread through the cluster.

The model uses eleven multiply imaged systems, split into thirty images and sixty clumps, as constraints. The cluster shows two clear mass peaks, suggesting an ongoing merger. Predicted mass lines up with the X ray gas distribution, which points to a pre merger state before the gas and galaxies fully mix.
arxiv-2511-08500:
Berkcan Kapusuzoglu and co-authors present SPEAR-MM, a framework for adapting language models to finance without wiping out their general reasoning. Domain training often causes catastrophic forgetting of skills customers and analysts still need. Their method first measures, after the fact, how much each transformer layer matters for outside benchmarks, then selectively freezes or restores layers through spherical interpolation merging with the original model.

Applied to LLaMA-3.1-8B on financial tasks, the method retains over ninety percent of general capability, versus about seventy percent for standard continual pretraining. It also keeps almost all of the domain adaptation gains. Interpretable trade off control and a ninety percent cut in computing cost target resource limited financial institutions.
arxiv-2511-08600:
Yilan Liu tackles a practical teaching problem in speech-language pathology: writing realistic clinical case vignettes for students takes hours, and general chatbots invent details they should not. The proof-of-concept system pairs a language model with retrieval over curated knowledge bases and shaped prompt templates.

Seven test scenarios cover varied disorders and grade levels in pediatric care. Several commercial and open-source models generate the cases, and an automated rubric grades each one for completeness, consistency, clinical fit, and the quality of education-plan goals and session notes. Commercial models scored slightly higher, but open models were close enough to suit private, on-site use. The author stresses that expert review and student pilots must come before classroom use.
arxiv-2511-09000:
Jarin Tasnim and three co-authors audit the hidden cost of backporting, the everyday practice of carrying a bug fix from a new software version back into an older one still in service. Every backport risks planting fresh technical debt in code that was supposed to stay stable, and nobody had measured how often that happens at scale.

The study mines one hundred five thousand backport commits drawn from thirty-one thousand sources across eighty-seven repositories in the Apache, Eclipse, and Python ecosystems. About four point three percent of backports introduce new technical debt. Apache contributes the most cases in absolute terms, while Python and Eclipse run debt-to-commit ratios nearly three times Apache's. Feature migrations poison early Apache releases, whereas Python and Eclipse debt clusters mid-cycle. Inexperienced, overloaded, and non-owner developers introduce debt most often.
arxiv-2511-09200:
Philipp Dingfelder and Christian Riess show that a popular benchmark for detecting AI-generated text is contaminated by easy giveaway patterns. Their paper's own playful title copies the kind of leftover chatbot phrase found in the data. In the DetectRL benchmark, 98.5 percent of the Claude-generated texts carry simple generation patterns, such as stock openings or refusals.

Detectors trained on such data learn these shortcuts instead of real signs of machine writing. That makes the detectors easy to fool with spoofing attacks that hide the patterns. The authors reprocessed DetectRL with several cleansing steps and released the cleaned dataset publicly. Experiments show attacks become harder once the giveaway patterns are removed.
arxiv-2511-09300:
Yanbin Zhu, Xiaomeng Jiang, and Yong Li derive the Onsager-Machlup functional for equations driven by a special kind of random noise. That functional measures how likely a given path of a stochastic system is, which helps identify the most probable route between states. Their noise is fractional Brownian motion whose character changes over time.

The results cover Hurst parameters between one quarter and one, extending small-ball probability estimates and the Girsanov theorem to time-dependent coefficients. Different ranges of the parameter call for different norms, from supremum to Hölder norms, with admissible choices spelled out. Numerical simulations on a double-well system show how the time-varying noise shapes transitions between metastable states.
arxiv-2511-09400:
Philip Sosnin, Matthew Wicker, Josh Collyer, and Calvin Tsay unify three safety questions about training data under one certification framework. Models can be corrupted by poisoned training samples. They must sometimes forget removed data, and may need privacy guarantees when one person's data changes. Inference-time attacks already have certification tools; training-time perturbations largely did not.

Their method, Abstract Gradient Training, bounds the set of parameters a training run could possibly reach. Those parameter-space bounds then certify behavior under bounded perturbations, deleted points, or added samples. The framework applies to models trained by first-order optimization methods. One machinery thereby serves data poisoning defense, machine unlearning, and differential privacy alike.
arxiv-2511-09600:
Gustavo Bodanza writes a research note in abstract argumentation, the formal study of how arguments attack and defend one another. Argumentation frameworks evaluate sets of arguments, called extensions, under varied semantics that spell out which sets pass. This note compares two non-standard semantics: cogent and weakly admissible.

Bodanza proves that every cogent extension is also weakly admissible. The converse fails: some weakly admissible extensions are not cogent, so the cogent notion is strictly stronger. Pinning down such inclusion relations matters because argumentation systems must know exactly which standard they implement. A one-way link like this tells designers that choosing cogent semantics buys weak admissibility for free, but not the reverse.
arxiv-2511-09700:
Warren Li and three co-authors challenge a comfortable assumption about in-context learning. Choosing examples, it says, matters far more than ordering them. Language models learn new tasks from example sequences in the prompt, and research had concentrated almost entirely on selection. The authors run controlled comparisons of the two factors head to head.

Across classification and generation tasks, several open model families, and GPT-5, ordering variance rivals selection variance in size. Strong orderings can be found using only a development set, nearly matching an oracle that peeks at test labels. Selection and ordering are equally important and intertwined, they conclude. Prompt design practice should stop treating order as an afterthought.
arxiv-2511-09900:
Yaodong Yang and six co-authors propose AlphaDE, a framework for evolving proteins inside the computer with help from protein language models. Directed evolution improves proteins through mutation, and language models trained on sequences have absorbed rich evolutionary patterns. Earlier computational methods mostly used heuristic search and did not combine these models with strong optimization.

AlphaDE first fine-tunes a pretrained protein language model on relatives of the target protein, using masked language modeling to wake up family-specific plausibility. It then searches at test time with Monte Carlo tree search, guided by the fine-tuned model. Benchmarks showed clear gains over previous state-of-the-art methods even with few-shot fine-tuning, and a case study condensed the sequence space of the fluorescent protein avGFP.
arxiv-2511-10100:
Xiaofeng Cai, Yibing Chen, Kunkai Fu, and Liujun Pan built a scheme that solves transport equations on curved meshes made of triangles, the kind of grid that fits real, complex shapes. Their method is third-order, keeps mass exact, and pairs a semi-Lagrangian update with a discontinuous Galerkin frame. The hard part is moving data from one mesh to the next with no loss, which their remapping step does by tracking how curved cells overlap.

Two limiters keep the runs clean: one damps fake waves, and one keeps values from going below zero. The semi-Lagrangian step allows large time steps while the code stays explicit and fast. Error checks confirm third-order rates in space and time, and test flows, from stiff rotation to swirling fields with sharp fronts, held up well.
arxiv-2511-10400:
Lifan Zheng and five co-authors ask whether language model agents make multi-agent systems more reliable when some members fail or lie. They borrow their lens from Byzantine fault tolerance, the study of systems that must agree despite faulty members. Their pilot tests compare language model agents with traditional agents across different network shapes.

The language model agents showed stronger skepticism toward wrong messages and beat traditional agents in the comparisons. Building on that, the team designed CP-WBFT, a consensus method that probes each agent's confidence and weights messages accordingly. In tests with fault rates as high as 85.7 percent, the method kept accuracy high across topologies. It held up on both math reasoning and safety assessment tasks.
arxiv-2511-10700:
Sabrina DeSoto and nine co-authors track the changing shape of supernova 2012au through six rounds of optical spectropolarimetry spanning its first 295 days. This slow-evolving Type Ib supernova is thought to be powered by a magnetar, and polarization reveals asymmetries that ordinary spectra hide.

Its polarization levels exceed those of any Type Ib studied before, making it either the most asymmetric of the sample or the most favorably viewed. Early on, the photosphere departed from spherical symmetry by ten to forty percent along a steady axis, while helium-rich material near the poles traced its own rotated pattern. By day 295 a new elongated structure appeared along an axis perpendicular to the first, a dual-axis geometry the authors link to the magnetar engine.
arxiv-2511-11200:
Leonid Lantsman attempts a topological theory of superfluid helium-4, the liquid that flows without friction at very low temperatures. His frame is a rigid U(1) model, named for its circle symmetry, in which that starting symmetry is destroyed as the liquid orders. In its place, domains with distinct topological numbers appear, separated by domain walls.

The walls are treated as step voltages between domains, a picture the author uses to account for the liquid's superfluid behavior. The same picture explains why topologically distinct vortices, stable swirls that cannot be smoothed away, arise in a specimen of the liquid. The work is a theoretical construction rather than a measurement study.
arxiv-2511-11300:
Abrar Ahmed Naqash, Fardeen Ahmad Sofi, and their colleagues present a hybrid method for a nonlinear eigenvalue equation that arises when measuring entanglement, the quantum link between particles. Their target is the geometric measure, which rests on how close a state sits to its nearest unentangled match. Exact evaluation is hard because the defining problem couples several blocks at once.

The method mixes a fixed-point iteration with a controlled perturbative correction. They prove that at the optimum all block multipliers coincide with the squared fidelity to the closest separable state. A normalization-preserving linearization then gives a first-order correction, and each step provably raises the squared overlap toward its limit.
arxiv-2511-11500:
Mohamad Amin Mohamadi, Tianhao Wang, and Zhiyuan Li argue that trustworthy language models must learn when not to answer, and propose Reinforced Hesitation to teach that skill. Frontier models almost never abstain on math, medical, and science tests. That holds even when they are warned of severe penalties for wrong answers. Prompting, it seems, cannot undo training that rewards any answer over silence. Their fix changes the reward to three values: credit for a right answer, zero for abstaining, and a penalty scaled by a risk dial for an error.

Controlled tests on logic puzzles show each penalty setting yields the model that is optimal for its risk regime, from aggressive answerers to cautious abstainers. The same frontier appears on harder math and medical questions and transfers to unseen data.
arxiv-2511-11600:
Piyushkumar Patel presents CausalGuard, a system meant to catch false statements from large language models as they form, not after they are printed. Confident, plausible errors, often called hallucinations, block the use of these models wherever accuracy is critical.

CausalGuard pairs causal reasoning with symbolic logic to trace the chain that leads to a false claim and intervene early. Two complementary paths work together, one following causal structure and one checking logical consistency, without retraining the whole model. The aim is prevention at a reasonable computing cost. For high-stakes uses such as medicine, law, and finance, catching errors at their source is the difference that matters.
arxiv-2511-11700:
Jiahui Wang and five co-authors present EPSegFZ, a network that labels three-dimensional point clouds when only a few examples, or none, are available for the target classes. Standard few-shot methods first pretrain, then adapt, which makes them rigid, and they mostly ignore the text annotations sitting beside the support examples.

EPSegFZ drops the pretraining stage entirely and uses language guidance to exploit support information more fully, restoring zero-shot ability that earlier designs lost. Point cloud labeling matters for robotics and mapping, where new object types appear constantly and labeling budgets are tiny. A flexible, pretraining-free route widens where few-shot segmentation can be deployed.
arxiv-2511-11800:
T. Giang Nguyen and five co-authors model the skies of lava planets, worlds so hot their rock surfaces melt and vaporize into an atmosphere made of rock. Because that vapor comes straight from the mantle, reading the atmosphere could reveal the planet's interior, if observers know what to look for.

Their SonicVapour model simulates the dynamics of these chemically complex atmospheres. Above a surface temperature near twenty-seven hundred kelvin, rock vapor turns optically thick, the air becomes vertically uniform in temperature, convection stalls, and emission spectroscopy loses its grip. Cooler lava worlds stay more readable. The results tell telescope planners which molten planets can actually be characterized.
arxiv-2511-12000:
Hiroki Ohta, Aaron Merlin Müller, and Shunji Tsuchiya show that the ground state of a spin-one XXZ chain, inside its Haldane phase, can power measurement-based quantum computation. In that model of computing, a prepared entangled resource state is consumed by measurements that enact the gates, so finding good resource states in real materials matters.

Single-ion and Ising-like anisotropies tune the chain, and gate fidelities for elementary rotations and general single-qubit unitaries exceed ninety-nine percent at good settings. An analytic fidelity formula ties performance to the post-measurement spin-spin correlation function and failure probability within the symmetry-protected phase. Condensed matter and quantum information meet in the Haldane phase once again.
arxiv-2511-12100:
Yannan Chen and eight co-authors question whether vision models learn enough, or just lean on a few easy cues. A model that uses only a small set of visual clues can fail when data shifts or those clues vanish. Explanation tools can reveal that habit, but they are rarely fed back into training.

Their method, called SS-CA, masks the regions a model relies on most to build counterfactual examples, meaning altered images that push it toward another class. Careful mask choice and filling keep the image meaning intact. Training on these examples pushes the model to use wider evidence, and tests on five ImageNet variants show gains in accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2511-12300:
Naoya Sugiura and four co-authors compare what makes quiz questions hard for humans and for large language models, using Japanese quiz data from a buzzer format. Models now beat humans on many language tasks, but that does not mean the same items are hard for both. The dataset includes human correct rates for each question.

The team prompts models under several settings and compares their success with the human rates. Models struggle more than humans on questions whose answers are not covered by Wikipedia entries. They also find numerical answers especially hard. The study shows that human and model difficulty follow different patterns.
arxiv-2511-13000:
Lingxuan Kong and three co-authors help small clinical trials decide which variables actually matter. Trials for cell and gene therapies and ultra-rare diseases enroll few patients, so standard variable selection starves for data. Their adaptive posterior-informed shrinkage prior borrows strength from external studies, but adaptively: the data decide how much to borrow, through a mixture shrinkage prior, and decisions are calibrated against an empirical null. The aim is borrowing that helps when sources agree and backs off when they do not.

In simulations the method selected variables more efficiently than rival methods, while staying robust. The authors then applied it to a real islet transplantation study, identifying variables tied to peak C-peptide seventy-five days after transplant in one consortium trial by borrowing from a sister trial.
arxiv-2511-13300:
Xiaobin Rong and 4 co-authors present PASE, a generative speech cleaner designed to invent less false speech in heavy noise. Generative cleaners sound better than older filters, but in severe noise they can hallucinate wrong words or a wrong voice. The word-level error, tied to broken sound structure, is treated as the deeper problem.

PASE leans on the sound-pattern knowledge stored in the pretrained WavLM model, first tuning it into a denoising expert by distillation. A vocoder then joins a clean phonetic stream with a low-level stream that keeps voice and tone. Tests showed better quality than strong rivals and far fewer word and voice errors.
arxiv-2511-13400:
Jinkun Zhao and 3 co-authors introduce the Embedded Stroop benchmark for a failure where models read words inside an image instead of seeing the ink color. The test renders the question itself inside the picture and asks what color the text is, across many fine color shades. Variants include standard, flipped, and masked forms.

Testing sixteen major models, they split errors into true accuracy, Stroop hallucination, and other errors, with statistical checks that held in most conditions. Exact color accuracy was low, yet coarse color families were often right while the hallucination rate stayed high. Masking or flipping the text cut the effect, showing that readable meaning can override seen color.
arxiv-2511-13600:
Claire Y. Yin and Peter M. Kogge compare a Prolog program for subgraph isomorphism against several conventional implementations. The task searches a large graph for a vertex set whose edges match a fixed pattern graph. Their pattern is relatively complex, and parallel conventional versions already exist for it.

The study details how the pattern becomes logic statements in Prolog and how the two styles behave as graph size grows. Writing the search as logic rules proved an efficient way to attack a hard graph problem, in their analysis. The comparison clarifies where the complexity of each approach truly sits, a useful guide for programmers facing pattern search in large networks.
arxiv-2511-14100:
Yiqing Shen, Chenjia Li, and Mathias Unberath define reasoning video editing, where an edit request is indirect. Instead of naming a target with exact location and timing, a user might describe a relationship or property, and the system must infer what to change. Their model, RIVER, is a first attempt at the task.

RIVER first builds a digital twin of the video that records spatial relations, motion paths, and semantic attributes. A language model reasons over that twin in several hops and emits structured edit instructions for a diffusion-based editor. Training uses reinforcement learning with rewards for reasoning accuracy and output quality. The authors also introduce a benchmark, RVE, for this harder editing task.
arxiv-2511-14300:
R. A. Battye, S. J. Cotterill, and P. Millington find a hidden flaw in the string-like flaws of pseudo-Hermitian field theories. Such theories, PT-symmetric ones among them, allow effects that plain Hermitian theories cannot. The flaws at stake are vortices, and their fate matters for cosmology. In a stock model of this kind, the set values sit in what looks like a safe zone.

Yet the team shows, first by math and then by computer runs, that the vortex is only near-stable. The flaw itself breaks the theory's antilinear symmetry a bit. That makes the rules for waves on the vortex change from place to place. Odd points and complex tones then appear in the wave spectrum, a path to slow decay.
arxiv-2511-14400:
I-Ting Lee, Bao-Kai Wang, Liang-Chi Chen, and four co-authors benchmark two ways of computing inside memory. Classic processing-in-memory chips compute near the data but force explicit staging transfers because host and device live in separate address spaces. CXL-based designs offer one unified, cache-coherent address space at the price of higher access latency. Which wins depends on the workload in ways small studies miss.

Combining measurements on real PIM hardware with trace-driven CXL modeling, the team maps where unified addressing amortizes its latency and where tightly coupled memory still wins. The ranking between the architectures flips across workload phases and data set sizes, giving concrete guidance for near-memory system design.
arxiv-2511-14700:
Nan Liu, Yanbo Liu, Yuya Sasaki, and Yuanyuan Wan develop statistical methods for yes-or-no decisions where mistakes carry unequal costs. Such problems cover scoring rules, best-action prediction, and policy learning from data. They are known for slow convergence and odd limiting behavior, and flexible nonparametric versions can even fail to pin down an answer.

The authors introduce a smooth surrogate loss that does identify a clear representative policy from the data. Estimating that policy then allows standard Gaussian-style inference on both the best policy and its value. The simpler math should make careful policy evaluation far easier to carry out in practice.
arxiv-2511-14800:
Cong Li studies how background electromagnetic fields alter photon emission and lepton pair production at future electron ion colliders. A background field can modify the photon propagator in a non perturbative way. That change acts like a correction to the effective coupling. It shifts the spectrum of quasi real photons emitted in collisions.

Lepton pairs from photon photon fusion then serve as a clean probe of the effect. One photon comes from the electron and the other from the nuclear field. Estimates at realistic energies show corrections that are not negligible in some regions. The effect also matters for extracting small x gluon distributions. Photon gluon fusion shares the same initial photon dynamics.
arxiv-2511-15000:
Alexander J Root, Christophe Gyurgyik, and five co-authors present Bonsai, a compiler that turns database-style queries over tree data structures into fast pruned traversals. Trees speed up searching and summing over large collections because each node carries metadata about its subtree. When a query condition can rule a whole subtree in or out, the traversal skips it, but writing that pruning logic by hand for each query is slow and error-prone.

Bonsai derives the pruning conditions automatically from the metadata at each node, using symbolic interval analysis extended with rules for geometric tests such as overlap and containment. It also fuses combined queries, such as filtering followed by summing, into a single pass. The result is hand-tuned traversal speed without hand-written pruning code.
arxiv-2511-15100:
Fouad Chahrour, Şahin K. Ozdemir, and three co-authors show that ordinary classical light waves can push quantum light into thermal balance. Isolated quantum systems settling toward thermal distributions is a deep puzzle, and light offers a clean test bed. In their numerical experiments, single-photon and two-photon states travel through a multimode nonlinear optical system bathed in classical light.

The quantum light emerges with the classic Rayleigh-Jeans and Boltzmann distributions, the unmistakable marks of thermalization. The classical nonlinearity effectively mediates interactions between photons that would otherwise pass through each other. That trick opens a route to studying quantum many-body behavior on optical benches, without building fully quantum interacting systems.
arxiv-2511-15400:
Chukwuebuka J. Ugwu, James O. Chibueze, Willice Obonyo, and Mavis Seidu study a massive young star cluster called G358.46-0.39, using older data from the ALMA telescope. Their work maps where four kinds of gas molecules sit in the cluster and how the gas moves. The cluster was already known to hold four dense cores where stars can form.

Maps of one molecule show long, bent strands of gas that look squeezed by a nearby hot region. Another molecule traces two outflows that overlap and seem to come from a young star still hidden inside the brightest core. Signs of rotation appear there too, and the pattern points to more than one young star forming in that core.
arxiv-2511-16100:
Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Hirotaka Yoneda, and Masataka Yoneda break a nearly thirty-year barrier in online graph coloring. Online coloring assigns colors to vertices as they arrive, using as few colors as possible, for graphs guaranteed to be colorable with a given number of colors. The best deterministic bounds had stood since 1998, especially weak for large color budgets and for the four-colorable case.

For graphs needing at least five colors, their deterministic algorithm uses far fewer colors than the old bound, with an exponent depending on pairs of colors rather than factorials. For four-colorable graphs they improve the exponent further. For bipartite graphs, they pin down the randomized optimum within a small factor, giving matching upper and lower logarithmic bounds.
arxiv-2511-16900:
Jingzehua Xu and six co-authors build a control system for self-driving underwater vehicles that fuses three ingredients usually kept separate. Underwater robots face nonlinear water forces, shifting disturbances, and poor position fixes. Older controllers adapt weakly, and reinforcement learning is sample hungry, short sighted, and lacks stability guarantees.

A diffusion model proposes smooth actions of several kinds that tolerate disturbances. A Lyapunov critic filters them under dual constraints. Above both, a large language model outer loop picks and refines the Lyapunov functions to fit the mission and training feedback. In tests under complex ocean conditions, the loop tracked paths better, finished more tasks, used less energy, and converged faster than standard reinforcement learning and diffusion-augmented baselines.
arxiv-2511-17200:
Shubhranil Basak, Mada Hemanth, and Madhav Rao ask whether muscle activity signals can be synthesized from motion sensors alone. Surface electromyography, which reads electrical activity from skin electrodes, reveals muscle function but is noisy and awkward to collect. Inertial measurement units, the motion chips in wearables, are robust and easy to wear, so predicting the muscle signal from them would be valuable for prosthetics and rehabilitation feedback.

The team recorded both signals together, at high sampling rates, during varied arm movements. A neural network built on dilated causal convolutions, called Sliding-Window-Wave-Net, learned to map the motion data onto the muscle signal. It predicted the timing and general shape of muscle activations well, though it often understated peak amplitudes. The authors conclude the approach is feasible for detecting movement intent.
arxiv-2511-17400:
Sukwon Yun, Heming Yao, Burkhard Hoeckendorf, David Richmond, Aviv Regev, and Russell Littman ask whether vision models for multi-channel images really need to compare every channel with every other. In fields like cell painting and satellite imaging, each channel carries distinct information, but comparing all pairs makes the attention step grow steeply and training costly.

Their answer is a sparse mixture-of-experts design for vision transformers. Rather than full cross-channel attention, the model routes work through selected experts, keeping the useful channel links while cutting wasted computation. The team presents the design as an efficiency move: it keeps the strengths that made vision transformers the base of vision foundation models, while making multi-channel training cheaper to run.
arxiv-2511-17800:
