Ren Deng, Kaya Mori, Eric Miao, and five co-authors report X-ray observations of a periodic optical source first thought to be a white dwarf pulsar. Its period is only about twelve minutes and its visible light varies strongly, so three space telescopes observed it across a broad X-ray range.

The data show hard, bright emission and a clear spin period, ruling out a pulsar or a compact binary of another kind. Spectra point to an intermediate polar, a magnetic white dwarf pulling in gas, with a mass above the usual average for such systems. The case shows how X-ray follow up can classify sources found by sky surveys.
arxiv-2511-17900:
Mengqing Zhang, Shengbin Pei, Shan Chang, and Pengfei Zhang revisit gamma ray changes tied to the orbit of a redback millisecond pulsar, a fast spinning neutron star with a low mass companion. They analyze sixteen years of data from the Fermi space telescope.

A modulation with the known orbital period appears clearly, matching earlier reports, but the signal vanishes after a point in twenty twenty one. The authors suggest the system may be shifting from rotation powered to accretion powered behavior. Phase and spectral studies show an anti correlation between gamma ray and X-ray emission, as high energy models for such systems predict.
arxiv-2511-18000:
Radman Rakhshandehroo and Daniel Coombs present ContagionRL, a reinforcement learning platform for studying how reward design shapes behavior in spatial epidemic model runs. Traditional epidemic models set actions by rule, so they cannot show how people might learn on their own to survive an outbreak.

The platform couples a spatial disease model with adjustable settings for what agents can see, movement, and population mix. Testing five reward designs across several learning methods, they find that directional guidance and explicit rewards for following protective measures matter most. Agents trained with a potential field reward learn strong adherence and smart avoidance. Code is shared openly.
arxiv-2511-18200:
Haoming Wang, Qiyao Xue, and Wei Gao build InfiniBench, a tool that tests how well vision and language models judge space in a scene. Old tests fix the scene, so they cannot show why a model fails when a room gets more full or more hard to parse. A test that can change on demand fills that gap.

InfiniBench turns plain text scene notes into real looking videos of 3D rooms. A language model agent tunes the scene rules step by step, and the user sets how complex each scene should be. That lets testers stress one skill at a time and trace a fault to its cause. The tool can make a near endless range of scenes.
arxiv-2511-18300:
Ying-ying Sun, Da-jun Zhang, and Frank Nijhoff build exact solutions for a lattice equation in the CKP family. Lattice equations place their values on a grid, and exact wave like solutions help test both theory and code. Their route uses a direct method built on an elliptic kernel, a tool tied to curves of genus one.

The scheme yields a tidy elliptic form of the equation and a set of linked helper equations. Smooth limits then turn grid results into results for the smooth case. With apt choices of weight and range in the core integral, multi wave solutions drop out in elliptic form. The work adds a firm exact base for this lattice family.
arxiv-2511-19100:
Chih-Duo Hong and five co-authors study register automata, small machines that can remember data values while reading a sequence. Data streams such as sensor traces carry values from huge domains, and plain finite automata cannot compare values across positions. Register automata can, which makes them compact descriptions of patterns in ordered data.

The report gives a local-search method to learn such automata and an exact checker for robustness, working over ordered rational numbers. For a fixed number of registers the checker runs in polynomial time. As a use case, learned automata serve as readable stand-ins for neural sequence classifiers, with a validation loop that refines them or finds real failures.
arxiv-2511-19500:
Hou Hei Lam and seven co-authors hunt for better organic solar cell materials by modeling donor and acceptor molecules together. Organic photovoltaics promise clean energy, but strong pairs are rare and most design tools study only one side of the pair. Their framework, CycleChemist, joins prediction with molecule generation.

A curated data set, OPV2D, gathers two thousand tested donor-acceptor pairs, the largest of its kind. On top of it sit a classifier for solar behavior, a graph network that models how the two partners interact, and estimators for orbital energy levels and cell performance. The unified view aims to find high-efficiency pairs faster.
arxiv-2511-20300:
Feng, Jiao, Xu, and a large team test whether star birth ignores its violent neighborhood. Their 2025 paper studies six clouds in the Galactic center. The central molecular zone is extreme by any measure. Dense, hot, turbulent gas fills the region. Star formation there looks oddly suppressed overall.

The clouds include Sgr B2, Sgr C, and the Brick. Four telescopes supplied multi-band dust maps. Column density maps reached sharp 8.5 arcsecond detail. Density distributions were fitted cloud by cloud. Four clouds show log-normal plus power-law shapes. The power-law tail marks gravity-bound gas. Bound gas mass tracks the biggest core's mass. Star formation rates follow the same relation. Those links match quiet solar-neighborhood clouds closely. Self-gravity seems to regulate its own activity. Exterior chaos matters less than five-to-ten parsec scales suggest.
arxiv-2511-20800:
Dario Morle and Reid Zaffino unify in 2025 a scattered family of neural network tricks under one operator they call warping. Dynamic sampling methods let a network choose where to read its input instead of sampling a fixed grid. Deformable convolutions shift their kernel taps. Spatial transformer networks warp whole feature maps. Active convolutional units learn fixed offsets. Each was analysed in isolation.

Warping is the minimal common core. With it, they reconstruct all three architectures and analyse the operator's statistics under two input models. Two discoveries stand out. First, training is asymmetric: the forward and backward passes of a warping layer behave differently, a quirk absent from convolutions. Second, these operators form a different orthogonal class from the translation-invariant operators of standard convolution. From the analysis they extract conditions for stable training, study discretisation effects, and introduce a loss-landscape visualisation built from gradient updates.
arxiv-2511-21000:
Seoyoung Choi and colleagues introduce in 2025 PileUp, a way to make rugs and sleeves that sense touch through their fluff. Electronic textiles usually chase thin, flat forms. PileUp instead tufts conductive yarn into looped or cut piles, the shaggy construction of carpets. The resulting three-dimensional fabric senses pressure, bending, and strain through changes in its electrical response, and can even detect moisture. A design space maps how texture and form factor shape what a tufted sensor can feel.

The team characterised the yarns' behaviour under compression, bending, and strain in the lab. Three applications show the range: a meditation rug with multi-zone touch sensing, a fleece sleeve that reads arm motion at the elbow, and wall art that senses dampness. Tufting, a craft technique anyone can learn, becomes a fabrication route for soft, tactile, volumetric interfaces that invite squeezing and stroking, not just tapping.
arxiv-2511-21600:
Yizhou Zhao, Xiang Li, Peter Song, Qi Long, and Weijie Su watermark synthetic spreadsheets so their origin can be proven later, in 2025. Generative AI now produces realistic tabular data for healthcare, finance, and policy, and provenance matters when such data is misused. Existing watermarks are expensive, relying on large diffusion models, or break on mixed data types, or wash out under edits.

Their scheme, Tab-Drw, works after generation as a light edit. It normalizes each column with a Yeo-Johnson transformation, applies the discrete Fourier transform, and nudges the imaginary parts of adaptively chosen entries to encode pseudorandom bits. A rank-based trick generates those bits so any row's watermark can be retrieved without storing anything extra. On five benchmark tabular datasets, Tab-Drw stayed strongly detectable after common post-processing attacks, preserved data fidelity, and handled mixed discrete and continuous columns, a combination earlier methods struggled to deliver.
arxiv-2511-21700:
Yuhao Zhan and seven coauthors build an automatic judge for grammar corrections, in 2025. Grammar error correction systems are graded against reference corrections, but most datasets offer only one or two references per sentence, so valid alternative corrections get marked wrong and training stays narrow. Their framework, JELV, validates individual edits for grammar, faithfulness, and fluency.

JELV comes in two forms. A multi-turn LLM-as-judges pipeline reaches 90 percent agreement with human annotators on their hand-labeled benchmark. A distilled DeBERTa classifier hits 85 percent precision on valid edits, fast enough for large-scale use. Applied to evaluation, it reclassifies misjudged false positives and feeds a new metric with state-of-the-art correlation to human judgments. Applied to data, it filters machine-generated candidates to expand the BEA-19 dataset of 38,692 source sentences beyond its single references. Retrained systems gained measurably.
arxiv-2511-22300:
Yokoyama, Qiang, Zwicker, and Nikoubashman, soft-matter physicists, simulate why droplets inside polymer networks stop growing. When mixtures demix inside an elastic network, as biomolecular condensates do inside the cell's cytoskeleton, domains often halt at finite size instead of coarsening forever. Bulk elasticity was the suspected brake. With coarse-grained molecular dynamics in implicit solvent, the team varies chain contour length, chain rigidity, and network topology to find which microscopic feature actually sets the droplet size.

Finite domains emerge when intrinsic chain- or network-level length scales, the persistence length or entanglement length, locally constrain coarsening. The arrested domain size correlates strongly with those microscopic properties while depending surprisingly little on the network's bulk elasticity. The result relocates the explanation from continuum mechanics to molecular architecture, giving design principles for engineering patterned gels and a sharper lens for interpreting condensate sizes in living cells.
arxiv-2511-22500:
YM, Orfila, Chatellier, and Judalet make city-scale air pollution mapping work. Cheap sensors, fixed and mobile, now stream data across cities. Modelling it with a spatio-temporal Gaussian process, tracking how pollution varies smoothly over space and time, is too slow on large datasets. Their three-level model handles the pollution process and sensor errors together, speeding up the maths with the Vecchia approximation, conditioning each observation on a few neighbours.

The main question is how to order observations and choose neighbours for that approximation. Testing many configurations on simulated data built from real mobile sensor routes in Nantes, France, they find two winners: min-max distance ordering, and a random ordering needing no distance definition. Both beat four rival schemes by about 102 percent on average in log Kullback-Leibler divergence, a measure of approximation error. Applied to real Nantes data, it produced maps ready for practical monitoring.
arxiv-2511-22900:
Zhang, Luo, and Yin ask when a noisy, weakly damped Burgers equation still has solutions. The fractional rough Burgers equation drives a fluid-like field with space-time white noise while fractional dissipation smooths it; too weak, and the noise wins. Working in Sobolev spaces on the torus, the authors sort the dissipation exponent gamma into regimes and prove well-posedness in each.

For higher dissipation, gamma between four thirds and two, they establish local well-posedness, extended to global well-posedness when gamma exceeds three halves. The harder regime is lower dissipation, gamma between five quarters and four thirds, where products in the equation need reinterpretation. There they construct paracontrolled solutions, Gubinelli's machinery that tames singular stochastic equations by tracking the solution's dependence on the noise. A final section conjectures the sharp boundary relating noise roughness to dissipation; the results connect to shallow water models.
arxiv-2511-23000:
Wang and Stadler study intrusion prediction, software that watches an IT system during a cyberattack and estimates which stage of the attack is under way. So defenders can respond in time. Existing predictors are usually monolithic, built and trained for one specific attack. But the MITRE ATT&CK catalogue lists hundreds of attack types. So hand-building a separate predictor for each is not realistic.

They propose a modular framework in which predictors are assembled from reusable components, each consuming chosen streams of system events. And a complete predictor can be put together dynamically during training. In their examples, a chain of just 2 to 4 components was enough to build an effective predictor. The modular design lets operators tune the trade-off among accuracy, timeliness, computing overhead, and how much training data is needed, instead of accepting one fixed balance.
arxiv-2511-23100:
Auricchio and colleagues address a measurement gap in machine learning. It is how to score predictions when the answer is an ordered category, such as a credit rating or a satisfaction grade, rather than a number. Ordinal labels have an order but no distances, the gap between grades A and B is not defined, so ordinary accuracy distances and the R-squared statistic do not meaningfully apply.

They develop the Rank Graduation family, RGX metrics indexed by a parameter p. They are built from comparing the ranks of predictions and outcomes. They prove these metrics measure the share of the response's variability explained by the predictions, playing the role R-squared plays for continuous data. Experiments across datasets and tasks, including models of ESG pillar scores where a linear model's rankings stayed coherent at about 0.9 correlation across specifications, support the metrics as interpretable and robust tools for judging ordinal classifiers.
arxiv-2511-23200:
Phan and Le measure how much accuracy a daily stress-recognition system must give up to stop leaking where a person actually goes, using phone GPS traces from students. Instead of clustering raw coordinates, which can expose home and workplace, their framework converts locations into semantic features, what kind of place it is and how long was spent there. It uses a self-hosted OpenStreetMap engine and a language-model-bootstrapped static map.

Under leave-one-subject-out validation, the privacy-aware model performed statistically indistinguishably from a non-private model fed richer location data. So the expected utility cost of privacy did not materialize in this test in practice. The language model's place labels matched human ground truth with 90 percent zero-shot accuracy. The strongest stress signals were the times spent on recreational activities, working, and traveling, a ranking that held in their feature importance analysis across participants.
arxiv-2512-00400:
Embedded systems must do more every year while staying strictly predictable in time. Yifan Zhang and co-authors present TenonOS in 2025, a self-generating framework that stacks one library operating system on another. Monolithic designs and rigid layers bring resource bloat and unpredictable scheduling.

The framework targets time-critical embedded operating systems, where temporal determinism is as important as raw function. Generating the system in layers aims to keep functionality rich but timing behavior controlled. Such work matters for vehicles, medical devices, and industrial controllers, where a late answer can be as bad as a wrong one. A library operating system assembles system services like building blocks, per application. For folks who write code for cars, pumps, or plant gear, the gain is a base that can grow step by step. All the while, the clocks in the gear stay true.
arxiv-2512-00600:
Xinyuan Dou, Ming Jin, Guangbin Ren, and Irene Sabadini study pure math in a 2025 paper on sedenionic power series. Sedenions are a sixteen-part number system that extends the better known quaternions and octonions. The authors ask where a certain kind of series, built from star powers, settles down and converges.

Their work sits inside slice regular function theory. That field extends complex analysis, the study of functions of complex numbers, to larger number systems. It has already been pushed to Clifford algebras, octonions, and other settings. Mapping the convergence domains helps show how far the theory can safely reach.
arxiv-2512-00800:
Shawan Jha, Makoto Tsubota, and Pankaj Mishra study two-dimensional quantum turbulence in a 2025 paper. A quantum fluid can swirl through vortices, whirlpools whose spin comes in fixed steps. How a tangle of vortices settles down over time is a basic question about such fluids.

The team follows four starting patterns: dipole, plasma, cluster, and lattice arrangements of vortices. They evolve each with the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, the standard model for these fluids. The cluster pattern reaches equilibrium fastest, they find. The other three stay out of balance and drift toward non-thermal fixed points instead.
arxiv-2512-01100:
Fatemeh Khashami examines quantum features in nuclear magnetic resonance systems in a 2025 paper. NMR systems use the spins of atomic nuclei, and a pair of spin one-half nuclei is a clean test bed for quantum effects. At thermal equilibrium under strong magnetic fields, such systems hold subtle quantum correlations.

Using suitable quantifiers, Khashami analyzes quantum coherence, mixedness, and entanglement in these two-spin systems. She also examines witnessing tests, which certify that such links are present without a full rebuilding of the state. The results clarify how much genuine quantumness survives in warm, everyday NMR settings used by chemists.
arxiv-2512-01200:
Chang-geun Oh, Haruki Watanabe, and Naoto Tsuji study a light-based probe of superconductors in a 2025 paper. Superconductors host collective modes, shared vibrations of the whole condensate, such as the Higgs mode. That mode is named for its likeness to the Higgs particle's role in its own field.

Third-harmonic generation, where a material emits light at triple the input frequency, is a primary tool for probing the Higgs mode. Its signal competes with quasiparticle excitations, and impurity scattering rates decide which dominates. The authors examine the role of quantum geometry in that competition, clarifying when the Higgs signal can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-01400:
Paula Harder and co-authors test if rain models trained in one place work in others. Deep learning can sharpen coarse rain forecasts to fine detail. That skill is called downscaling. Most models are built for one region only.

Whether they hold up in new terrain and climate is not clear. The team checks broad models across many regions. They score how well fine rain patterns move to unseen places. The results show where one global model can serve and where local training is still needed for safe flood and farm plans.
arxiv-2512-01500:
Alfredo Reichlin, Miguel Vasco, and Danica Kragic offer a simpler way to gauge doubt in neural nets. Bayesian nets model doubt by a spread over weights. Exact sums for that spread cannot be done. Common shortcuts scale poorly and miss the true spread in big nets.

Their method walks along a fiber, a curved path in weight space. That walk gives a geometric guess of the spread. A simpler path could make doubt scores cheap for large models. Cheap, sound doubt scores matter for safe use in robots, clinics, and self-driving cars.
arxiv-2512-01800:
Zhe Chen gives conservative forms for the Standard Enskog and Povzner equations. Both extend the Boltzmann equation by adding particle volume in collisions. Dense gases need that volume term. Non-conservative forms can break mass or energy bookkeeping in simulations.

Chen's main result writes each collision integral as a divergence in velocity space. That form makes conservation manifest. Manifest conservation steadies numeric solvers for dense gases. It also clarifies how the two classic extensions relate to each other. Divergence form also aids boundary treatment in codes, since fluxes at cell faces can be balanced exactly in the new variables.
arxiv-2512-02100:
Watching a quantum system changes it, and frequent local measurements can tip a spin chain between very different behaviors. Yicheng Tang and four co-authors study this measurement-induced phase transition in 2025, in spin chains burdened by strong disorder.

They examine the transverse-field Ising model with a random field at each site, alongside a many-body localized Hamiltonian written in localized bits. Their finding is stark: both the prethermal and the localized regimes fall apart under local measurements, whichever direction the measurements point. The result limits how well disorder can protect quantum order once an observer keeps looking.
arxiv-2512-02200:
The Doughnut framework pictures a safe economy: a social floor below which no one should fall, and planetary boundaries that must not be crossed. Stefano Vrizzi and Daniel O'Neill show in 2025 how frugal machine learning can be applied to a simple macroeconomic model of that Doughnut.

Their analysis is a proof of concept, deliberately small, testing whether learning methods can track many social and environmental indicators at once. Frugal methods matter here because sustainability modeling must stay transparent and cheap enough for wide use. If the approach scales, it could help policymakers see which economies sit inside the Doughnut and which spill outside it.
arxiv-2512-02400:
A robot told to find an object it has never seen, in a building it has never entered, must reason openly about language and space. Wentao Xiang and a large team present Nav-R2 in 2025, a navigation system built on dual-relation reasoning for open-vocabulary object-goal navigation.

Existing approaches suffered from opaque decision-making and low success at locating novel objects in unseen environments. Reasoning over two kinds of relations aims to make the agent's choices both better and more legible. Robots that can hunt for arbitrary named objects are a step toward household and warehouse helpers that take instructions in plain words.
arxiv-2512-03100:
Adding outside knowledge to language models brings a privacy risk. Haowei Fu, Kunpeng Liu, Dan Lin, and Tyler Derr study that risk in this 2025 work. Two common ways to add knowledge are search-based retrieval and fine-tuning on new data.

Attackers can probe a model to guess if a given item was in its training data. Such membership attacks threaten trust in fields with private records. The authors propose a team-based defense that guards the model. Strong guards matter as firms add client files and records to their AI tools. The defense focus fits real deployments, where private files sit close to the model's core knowledge.
arxiv-2512-03500:
Long videos hide key moments in hours of footage. Te Yang and co-authors present an exploration-exploitation agent for that task in this 2025 work. Current methods either preprocess densely at high cost or balance search poorly.

Dense methods waste compute, while weak search misses sparse but critical information. Their agent, EEA, navigates long visual data more efficiently. It balances exploring new segments with exploiting promising ones. Better long video understanding helps surveillance review, sports analysis, and meeting archives. Exploration choices decide coverage, since a fixed scan of long footage wastes most frames.
arxiv-2512-03800:
Exotic particles made of four quarks, rather than the usual two or three, are a live frontier in particle physics. Bing-Dong Wan and colleagues compute the masses of such tetraquarks in a 2025 preprint. These states hide a charm or bottom quark pair inside. They carry spin and parity labels that ordinary mesons cannot have.

The calculations use QCD sum rules, a standard technique that connects quark-level theory to particle masses through an expansion including condensates up to dimension eight. The method predicts four hidden-charm states with masses just under five gigaelectronvolts. Their hidden-bottom partners come out near eleven gigaelectronvolts. Wan and colleagues also map the likely decay routes for these states. Those maps tell experimenters at BESIII, Belle II, and LHCb where to look, turning theory into a concrete search target.
arxiv-2512-03900:
Lasers that must hold an exact frequency, for clocks and precision spectroscopy, are commonly steadied with the Pound-Drever-Hall technique. Roame Hildebrand and colleagues expose a routinely underestimated error in that method in a 2025 optics preprint. The trouble starts when leftover optical sidebands meet higher-order spatial modes inside a slightly misaligned cavity.

In offset locking, that interaction shifts the lock point away from the intended frequency. The shift can reach half the cavity linewidth when the offset comes from a sinusoidally driven modulator. The team measures the deviation in the laboratory and matches it with a simple model. Swapping in a spectrally pure frequency offset shrinks the error by about tenfold. Their warning matters for optical clocks, precision spectroscopy, and quantum information experiments, where a silent frequency shift of this size can corrupt results.
arxiv-2512-04000:
Asking a multimodal model about a long video is expensive, because it can only swallow so many frames at once. Jialuo Li, Bin Li, Jiahao Li, and Yan Lu show in a 2025 preprint that the right frame selection strategy depends on the question. Global questions about a whole video behave differently from localised ones about one moment.

For global queries, plain uniform sampling already works well and cheaply, and elaborate search adds little. Localised queries genuinely need frames chosen with the query in mind. Their framework, DIG, routes each question accordingly: uniform sampling for global queries, and a specialised grounding pipeline for localised ones, all without training. On three long-video benchmarks, DIG beat existing baselines and kept improving performance as frame counts scaled into the hundreds. The lesson is restraint: spend computation only where the query demands it.
arxiv-2512-04100:
Sharing radio spectrum fairly requires a map: which frequencies are busy, where, and how strongly. Mukaram Shahid and colleagues build such maps with a physics-informed neural network in a 2025 preprint. Their system, ReVeal-MT, extends an earlier single-transmitter design to the messy case where many transmitters overlap and interfere.

The authors first write a partial differential equation for received signal strength from multiple sources. They fold its residual into the network's loss, so physics disciplines the fit to sparse sensor readings. Validation uses real measurements from the ARA living lab, a wireless testbed spanning rural and suburban terrain. Against standard channel models and their own single-transmitter baseline, ReVeal-MT reconstructed hundreds of square kilometres from fewer than fifty samples, with errors of a few decibels. The authors aim the tool at fine-grained spectrum management between primary and secondary users.
arxiv-2512-04200:
The Magellanic Clouds are an interacting galaxy pair close to the Milky Way, yet their three-dimensional geometry is still poorly pinned down. Slater J. Oden and a large team map them in a 2025 galactic astronomy preprint. Their rulers are red clump stars, standard candles once age and metal content are corrected for.

The sample combines about two million stars from Gaia's third data release. Median distances come out near fifty-one kiloparsecs for the Large Cloud and sixty-one for the Small. The maps refresh structures from the northern arm and southern hooks to the Magellanic Bridge and outlying overdensities. Fitting the disk yields its tilt and orientation. The striking find is a U-shaped warp around the periphery, reaching seven kiloparsecs vertically. The authors read it as a tidal scar from the Small Cloud's close passage three hundred million years ago.
arxiv-2512-04300:
Michael Barz builds a new object in algebraic geometry, the logarithmic de Rham stack, in work posted on arXiv in 2025. The setting is a smooth variety over a field of positive characteristic, paired with a boundary divisor whose parts cross in a tidy way. Stacks let geometers track spaces together with their symmetries. A logarithmic version also keeps track of behavior near the boundary.

With this stack in hand, Barz proves a fresh form of logarithmic Cartier descent. He also proves a logarithmic non-abelian Hodge theorem for curves. Both results run through a logarithmic twist of the Frobenius map. The Hodge result links two worlds: flat connections on one side, and certain sheaves on the other. It also yields, as a direct payoff, an earlier theorem by de Cataldo and Zhang. The stack looks set to become a standard tool for boundary-aware geometry.
arxiv-2512-04400:
Dror Shvadron asks why firms publish science for all to read, rivals included. Company labs have long shared findings in journals, at the risk that competitors copy them. Past accounts stress that tension, plus scientists' own wish to publish. His 2025 arXiv paper adds a managerial motive: the value of follow-on research that outside scientists build on a firm's papers.

Using data on United States public firms from 1990 to 2012, Shvadron exploits a near-random quirk in how journals assign papers to issues. That quirk lets him trace cause rather than mere correlation. He finds that when follow-on work piles up, the source firm invests more in science later. Its patenting improves, and it keeps staff longer. Gains run larger for firms with assets that complement research and for those in young fields. Openness, in short, can pay the firm that shares.
arxiv-2512-04500:
Edervaldo Melo presents the Nemosine Framework, a modular design for helping people reason through hard problems in an orderly way. The design splits thinking into functional units, called personas, each with a clear job. One unit plans, one weighs options, one cross-checks claims, and one weaves results into a story. His 2025 arXiv paper grounds the design in metacognition, distributed cognition, and modular system theory.

The paper lays out a formal specification for the modules. It gives internal consistency rules that keep the units from clashing. It also describes structural parts that others can rebuild and test. No software run is claimed; the aim is a clear conceptual base. Future builders can turn the spec into working tools for decision support. The work adds to study of symbolic, modular designs for reasoning, a path that prizes clarity over black-box guesses.
arxiv-2512-04600:
Giuseppe Viterbo and Tobias Buck build a framework that reads the Milky Way's gravity from the wreckage of a torn star cluster. Stellar streams are ribbons of stars ripped from a parent body by tides. Their shape in space and motion encodes both the host galaxy's pull and the parent's inner makeup. The team studies GD-1, the best-known such stream. Their 2025 arXiv paper infers both sides at once.

The method pairs flow matching with simulation-based inference, a fully Bayesian route that needs no tidy likelihood formula. A fast, differentiable N-body code spins up large suites of fake GD-1-like streams. The inference then weighs which mix of galaxy traits and parent traits best matches the real stream. Older tools fit orbits or angles and split the two jobs apart. Joint inference respects how stripping and gravity shape each other, promising cleaner maps of the dark matter halo.
arxiv-2512-04700:
Leah Albrow, Michele Bannister, and John Forbes ask what the speeds of interstellar objects reveal about the planetary systems that threw them out. Visitors like 'Oumuamua carry the imprint of their birth systems in their ejection velocities. Those velocities govern how the objects spread through the galaxy. Their 2025 arXiv paper runs N-body simulations of thousands of made-up systems as they turn unstable after their gas discs fade.

The team built thousands of random systems with varied total mass and planet counts, then let them evolve for millions of years amid a disc of test particles. Systems split into two broad classes by their starting layout. Catastrophic systems, crowded or holding heavy planets in tight orbits, ejected their debris in distinct patterns from calmer systems. Reading an interstellar object's speed may thus hint at the architecture it escaped, linking lone wanderers to the families that made them.
arxiv-2512-04800:
Gianmarco Del Sarto, Matthias Hieber, and Filippo Palma prove that a climate model of Sellers type, coupled to an active fluid, always admits a rhythm that repeats in time. Energy balance models track a planet's temperature from the tug between sunlight, radiation, and heat transport. Here a two-dimensional surface model couples through a dynamic boundary to the three-dimensional primitive equations of the ocean-atmosphere fluid below. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks whether steady periodic solutions exist when the forcing itself is periodic.

The answer is yes, with a strength worth noting. At least one strong time-periodic solution exists whenever the forcing repeats in time. The forcing needs no smallness condition at all; it may be arbitrarily large. Large forcing is where many existence proofs collapse, since estimates blow up. A result with no size cap gives climate theorists firmer ground for studying seasonal cycles in coupled models.
arxiv-2512-05300:
Yonggang Jiang, Yaowei Long, Thatchaphol Saranurak, and Benyu Wang give near-linear-time algorithms for two intertwined problems on directed graphs. One is finding the smallest cut that separates a root from the rest. The other is packing as many root-anchored branching trees as possible. The two are dual — each bounds the other — and both matter for network robustness. Exact algorithms existed but ran well beyond linear time, which hurts on the huge graphs modern applications produce.

The new algorithms settle for near-optimal answers at far greater speed. One computes a rooted cut within a modest factor of the minimum, even for weighted graphs. The other packs the trees with only slight congestion, certifying a lower bound on the cut in the process. Both run in almost linear time, resting on directed expander hierarchies the authors adapt from a toolkit that had mostly served undirected graphs.
arxiv-2512-05500:
Taketo Akama, Akima Connelly, Shun Minamikawa, and Natalia Polouliakh generate fake brain-wave data so that real brain-wave cleaning can be learned. Brain-wave recordings are contaminated by eye blinks, muscle noise, and outside interference. Classifiers that flag these artifacts are a clear alternative to blind separation methods. But classifiers need examples with labels, and adding labels by hand can never cover the variety of real data.

Their framework, SSDLabeler, makes partly fake data from real recordings. It breaks genuine EEG into independent components and checks which epochs are artifacts using signal criteria. It then reinjects several artifact types at once into clean data — matching how artifacts actually co-occur. A classifier trained on this data beats ones trained on earlier partly fake data or raw data, across conditions. The authors offer it as a scalable base for artifact handling in brain-computer interfaces and clinical pipelines.
arxiv-2512-05600:
Takeshi Sato, Souta Miyamoto, and Shota Kato test whether a data driven method can discover the rules of flow. Rheology needs such rules, called constitutive models, to predict how soft fluids deform. A recent framework named Rheo-SINDy learns a sparse, readable equation from simulation data. Yet it had only been tried on shear flow. This study asks whether it works when material is pulled apart, in extensional flow.

The team runs two checks. First, they feed the method data made by the well known Giesekus model, and it recovers that model's exact equation. Next, they give it data from a dumbbell model whose springs stretch only so far. With a library of terms shaped by rheology know-how, it finds a compact equation that matches well, even beyond the range it was trained on. The results suggest the approach can turn flow data into usable models more generally.
arxiv-2512-05700:
Ben Malin, Tatiana Kalganova, and Nikolaos Boulgouris work on a practical question: how faithfully does a language model's answer stick to its source? Judging faithfulness by hand is slow, so automatic metrics do the work. Their 2025 paper combines many simple faithfulness metrics into one fused score. A tree based model learns how much weight each metric deserves.

The learning is guided by human judgments of real model answers. To make the test fair across fields, the team unified datasets from question answering and dialogue into one collection. It carries both the model responses and the human faithfulness ratings. Across all domains tested, the fused score tracked human judgment more closely than any single metric did. Better measurement matters beyond research scores. Trust in a model grows when its faithfulness can be checked well, and that trust decides where such systems may safely be put to work.
arxiv-2512-06600:
Tomas Tapia, Agustin Castellano, Enrique Mallada, and Yury Dvorkin teach batteries on the power grid to save charge for the hours that matter. Storage can soak up swings in weather driven power, but its energy is limited, and chasing prices alone can drain a battery just before a critical stretch. The value of stored energy depends on choices made across time under prices no one can know in advance.

Their design adds a stopping time reward that pays the battery for holding a healthy charge before critical hours, plus a penalty when its charge strays from a target band. The problem is framed as online optimization with a chance based promise on the final charge. Price forecasting and the control policy are then trained together, end to end. The result keeps target charge ranges within reach more often, earns more under wild prices, and swings less in profit.
arxiv-2512-06800:
Deepa Gurung, S M Zia Ur Rashid, Zain ul Abdeen, and Suman Rath trace how cloud computing grew from early ideas into a global system. Their history starts with old dreams of sharing computer power the way people share electric power. It then moves through virtual machines, linked computer systems, and fast networks. The story ends with today's huge data centers run by a few giant firms.

Along the way, the authors weigh what the cloud changed for the groups that use it. Renting power over the internet lowered the cost of starting heavy computing projects. Yet wide use also brought weak security settings, strict local rules, and deep reliance on single vendors. The closing sections look at edge computing placed closer to users, systems built for artificial intelligence, and early quantum services, and ask how scale can grow without losing trust.
arxiv-2512-07300:
Kai-Yang Lin and co-authors describe the back end of BURSTT, a wide-angle radio telescope in Taiwan built to catch fast radio bursts, the millisecond flashes whose sources remain unknown. The telescope watches an enormous swath of sky at once and must beamform, search, and react in real time. Expecting to log dozens of bursts a year and pinpoint them to sub-arcsecond precision with outrigger stations.

The signal chain is staged for speed. A radio-frequency system-on-chip performs the first beamforming, then server processors using wide vector instructions handle the second stage and channelization. A heavily optimized de-dispersion program sweeps hundreds of beams for pulses, and on a trigger it orders the distant outriggers to save their raw voltages for interferometric localization. The team validated the pipeline on bright radio sources and by detecting known pulsars live.
arxiv-2512-07400:
Giulia Lanzillotta, Damiano Meier, and Thomas Hofmann wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on a puzzle in continual learning. A network can keep clear inner features for old tasks while its final answers for them fail. They name the split deep forgetting and shallow forgetting.

Their tool is experience replay, where stored old examples are shown again during new training. Small replay buffers, they show, are enough to anchor the inner feature layout. Saving the final answers, though, takes far larger buffers. To explain why, they extend the neural collapse framework to learning in sequence. Small buffers can warp class averages and blind the final classifier to real boundaries. Fixing those warped statistics, they argue, could give strong results with little replay. That claim pushes against the habit of relying on large buffers.
arxiv-2512-07900:
Beatrice Crippa, Anna Scotti, and Andrea Villa, researchers in applied mathematics and engineering, posted a modeling study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is electrical treeing, the branching damage that grows inside insulating materials under strong electric fields. Plasma models describe such discharges well, but the tangled shape of a tree makes full simulations very costly.

The team builds a reduced model that works in one dimension along the tree. It tracks charge concentrations inside the branches and on the surface of the dielectric, plus equations for the dipole moment. Their numerical scheme uses finite volumes and Patankar type methods, keeping key physical properties intact. Tests run from a straight line up to a realistic tree shape.
arxiv-2512-08300:
Sijia Chen, Baochun Li, and Di Niu, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about turning ordinary language models into reasoning models. Reasoning models show telling moments where they pause, reflect, and rethink inside their chain of thought. The authors ask whether a small external planner can inject those strategies into a model on the fly.

Their mechanism, called rSIM, trains a planner agent and the language model together with multi agent reinforcement learning and simple rule based rewards. The planner guides the chain of thought by inserting strategies such as self reflection at the right moments. A tiny half billion parameter model trained this way became a reasoning model that beat a model many times its size. The planner also transfers: trained once, it plugs into other models and lifts their reasoning, and it keeps learning across tasks.
arxiv-2512-08400:
Samitha Nuwan Thilakarathna, Ercan Avsar, and colleagues, computer vision researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their task is re identifying individual fish on video from electronic monitoring systems now used in fisheries. Boats generate more footage than anyone can review by hand, yet managers need accurate counts for sustainable quotas.

The team built a deep learning pipeline tested on a new dataset that mimics a monitoring conveyor belt with six similar looking species. Hard triplet mining, which trains on the toughest look alike examples, plus a custom image preparation pipeline, lifted the key scores sharply. A vision transformer design beat a standard convolutional network, reaching strong top rank accuracy. Their error analysis found the hardest problem is telling apart individuals of the same species. Changing viewpoints hurt far more than partial blocking of the fish. The findings guide where monitoring systems should improve next.
arxiv-2512-08500:
Jianan Li, Xiao Chen, Tao Huang, and Tien Tsin Wong, computer graphics researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their framework, Mimic2DM, teaches physically simulated characters to move by watching ordinary videos. Motion capture is costly, and rebuilding three dimensional motion from video often fails outside narrow settings or produces poses no body could hold.

Instead of reconstructing in three dimensions at all, the tracker learns from two dimensional keypoint paths pulled straight from video. It follows those paths inside a physics simulation by minimizing how far the simulated body projects from the reference points. Trained across many viewpoints, the same policy gains true three dimensional tracking skill. A transformer based generator then invents fresh two dimensional reference motions, which the tracker performs. The system learned dancing, soccer dribbling, and animal movement, all physically plausible, with no three dimensional motion data anywhere in the loop.
arxiv-2512-08600:
V Arvind, Srijan Chakraborty, Samir Datta, and Asif Khan, computer scientists in India, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Counting paths and matchings in graphs is a classic hard problem family, and the known fast exact algorithms for Hamiltonian paths look very different in undirected and in bipartite directed graphs. The team unifies them with one elegant tool, the Matrix Tree theorem, combined with sieving by roots of unity.

Their algorithms are simpler, while matching the best known running times. The same framework counts perfect matchings at a speed rivaling the classic Ryser method. It also counts ways to split a graph into star shaped pieces, faster as the stars grow. A side result counts maximum matchings in general graphs. Every algorithm uses only polynomial memory.
arxiv-2512-08800:
Christof Kuelske and Niklas Schubert study a thinned Bernoulli field on a one dimensional lattice, where occupied sites that stand isolated are removed from a random configuration. Earlier work covered higher dimensions and trees. This study focuses on detailed behavior on the line, especially as the occupation density approaches full.

Three views are developed. First, the field on the line is always quasilocally Gibbs, yet it grows more sensitive to boundary conditions as density rises, echoing a loss of quasilocality seen in higher dimensions. Precise asymptotics quantify that effect. Second, from a one sided view, the field is a g measure in dynamical systems, with a g function that is quasilocal but long range at high density. Third, the authors give a transparent construction driven by a Markov chain of a generalized house of cards type. Together, the views clarify a subtle borderline case in statistical mechanics.
arxiv-2512-08900:
Pablo Tikas Pueyo, Tomas Fernandez Martos, and Gabriel Senno study deterministic extraction of randomness from quantum sources when only partial trust in the devices is available. In classical theory, no deterministic method can extract near ideal randomness from an arbitrary source. With extra knowledge about the source structure, such as independent trials, deterministic extractors do exist.

The authors extend a recent device independent construction to prepare and measure settings with partial trust. They prove the same functions work as extractors for memoryless devices when either preparation or measurement is trusted. A semi device independent setting with an overlap assumption on prepared states is also covered. Simulations on a new, experimentally relevant family of behaviors show positive randomness rates already at a modest number of rounds. The work widens the range where certified quantum randomness can be extracted without randomized hashing steps.
arxiv-2512-09400:
Krzysztof Burdzy, Ilias Ftouhi, and Phanuel Mariano study shape optimization for the torsion function, a classic object in partial differential equations. It describes, for example, the twisting of an elastic bar or flow through a tube. For a planar convex region, they look at the largest gradient of its torsion function, scaled either by the region's area or by its perimeter.

The authors prove that regions maximizing each of these two functionals actually exist among planar convex domains. Moreover, any maximizer has a smooth boundary of the best basic kind, and that boundary must contain a straight line segment. On that segment, the gradient of the torsion function attains its maximum value. The result identifies a distinctive geometric feature that optimal shapes for this problem are forced to have, combining existence theory with a precise statement about where the extremal behavior sits.
arxiv-2512-09500:
Preethi M, Parameshwaran A, and Bhaskar Sen Gupta simulate how phase separation unfolds inside porous materials, and how activity changes the story. When a fluid mixture separates into vapor-rich and liquid-rich regions, the domains normally grow by a power law. Confinement inside pores, relevant to geology, filtration, emulsions, and cells, disrupts that growth in ways that were poorly understood.

Using large molecular dynamics simulations with porous hosts made by a freeze-quench protocol, they control the average pore size. In passive fluids, confinement slows growth from the classic power law to a logarithmic crawl and finally arrests it, leaving rough, fractal interfaces. Adding self-propelled particles reverses the picture: activity restores smooth interfaces, breaks the confinement scaling laws, and at high activity drives growth to a fast, ballistic regime. The authors present activity as a control knob that can unlock coarsening in crowded, structured environments.
arxiv-2512-09800:
Zhaolan Huang, Kaspar Schleiser, Gyungmin Myung, and Emmanuel Baccelli introduce Ariel-ML, a toolkit for running small neural networks on low power microcontrollers. These chips are shifting from one core to many cores, and embedded code is increasingly written in Rust rather than C or C++. Yet no Rust platform automated the splitting of network inference across several cores. Ariel-ML fills that gap, pairing a general TinyML pipeline with an embedded Rust platform.

The toolkit targets several common thirty-two bit chip families, including Arm Cortex-M, RISC-V, and ESP-32 parts. The authors released the full code as open source. They benchmarked it on a varied set of small models, called a zoo. Ariel-ML beat earlier tools on inference speed, as expected, and matched the memory footprint of existing toolkits built in embedded C and C++. It offers a working base for TinyML practice on tight hardware.
arxiv-2512-10100:
Apostol Vassilev argues that making artificial intelligence truly secure and aligned faces basic limits, not just engineering difficulty. The draft sets out information theoretic limits for AI robustness by extending Gödel's incompleteness theorem to AI systems. Incompleteness says sufficiently rich formal systems cannot prove all truths about themselves. His extension is meant to show that similar self reference barriers cap what can be promised about an AI's behavior. Knowing these limits, he argues, is key to wise use of the technology.

The paper also offers practical approaches for working despite the limits, and it proves broader implications for how AI systems reason. The title's question, whether robust security and alignment are a Sisyphean endeavor, is answered with limits plus coping plans rather than despair. The piece will appear in IEEE Security and Privacy magazine.
arxiv-2512-10200:
Alex Colling proves a rigidity theorem for the most extreme black holes in general relativity. Extremal horizons spin or charge as much as physics allows. Hawking's classic theorem says a rotating horizon must hide a symmetry, a Killing vector field generating rotation. Colling proves an intrinsic analogue, working from the horizon's own shape, in any dimension, for spacetimes obeying the null energy condition. Any compact cross section of a rotating extremal horizon must admit such a Killing field. With a slightly stronger energy condition, more follows: the near horizon geometry extends to one with a larger symmetry group.

In the Poincaré case, a known instability of fields near extremal horizons, the Aretakis instability, shifts by one order in transverse derivatives, a concrete physical upshot. Colling verifies the picture across a broad class of theories, including charged matter and Yang-Mills fields, and shows the matter inherits the symmetries.
arxiv-2512-10300:
Yanbei Jiang leads a team opening up vision language models to ask which of their attention heads do the reasoning. These models ace multimodal benchmarks while remaining black boxes. The authors build CogVision, a dataset that breaks complex picture questions into step by step subquestions. Each is tied to a specific mental function, such as high level visual reception or inference, mimicking human chain of thought. Probing the models, they find attention heads that specialize in these functions. They call them functional heads, and they chart how the heads interact and organize in layers.

Across several model families, functional heads are always sparse: few heads carry each function, and their counts and locations vary by function. Intervention experiments prove the heads matter causally. Removing functional heads degrades reasoning performance; boosting them improves accuracy.
arxiv-2512-10400:
Max Downing and co-authors study boundaries in critical loop models, systems of random loops used to describe phase transitions. A boundary is called sticky if loops may attach to it, and reflecting if they may not. Their paper asks what mathematical data pins down a reflecting boundary, using analytic bootstrap methods that build answers from consistency conditions alone.

They show a reflecting boundary is fixed by a single complex parameter, playing a role much like the boundary cosmological constant in Liouville theory. From that they determine the disc one-point functions and give an explicit formula for disc two-point functions as an endless sum of conformal blocks. A sketch of how reflecting boundaries look on the underlying lattice rounds out the picture for physicists who simulate these models.
arxiv-2512-10700:
Mohamed Elobaid, Shinkyu Park, and Eric Feron stabilise a team of agents in a rigid formation that rides along a curve. The target arrangement is an equilateral polygon, a regular ring. It must settle onto a closed, smooth planar curve and sweep along it. Think of a formation of drones tracing a boundary before locking into shape.

Finding where a regular polygon can sit inscribed in the curve is itself a search problem. The authors solve it with a randomised multi-start Newton-like algorithm. That algorithm can certify a minimiser exists. They then design a continuous feedback law that first guarantees the formation converges and sweeps the curve sufficiently, then settles each agent onto its vertex while keeping agents from colliding. Simulations across several curve families and formation sizes confirm the approach, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-11000:
Francesco Lässig asks whether a neural state can carry its meaning in itself, without needing an outside decoder. Everyday codes, like letters for sounds, mean nothing without shared rules, yet a conscious sight of a red square does not seem free to mean a green triangle instead. He formalises that difference using information theory and a measure of representational ambiguity.

Experiments on networks trained to classify handwritten digits show that wiring patterns alone can reveal what an output neuron stands for. Networks trained with dropout allowed perfect identification from structure alone, while standard training allowed much less, even though both performed the task equally well. Input position could also be decoded from connections. The work offers a quantitative way to study ambiguity in neural systems.
arxiv-2512-11300:
Thinh Le, Shiqian Guo, and Jianqing Liu propose navigating by Earth's magnetic field using quantum sensors, as a backup when satellite navigation is jammed, spoofed, or blocked. Magnetic patterns over the ground encode location, a trick many animals exploit, but reading them precisely needs an extremely sensitive magnetometer. Diamond based quantum sensors are candidates for that job.

The team derives the theoretical error limit for location estimates from such sensors and proves they beat standard magnetometers. A distributed sensing protocol reaches that limit in principle. Position is then found by matching measured fields against a magnetic map. A two stage search uses field gradients where the landscape is varied, and raw samples where it is smooth. Model runs over four North American cities reached sub kilometre typical errors in varied regions, with the smoother area strategy also cutting search time several fold.
arxiv-2512-12000:
Y Alipour Fakhri builds a theory of exotic superconductivity on spaces with weakened geometric rules. Finsler geometry lets distance depend on direction. The Tonelli conditions keep that geometry tame; dropping them global uniformity while keeping local good behavior opens odd energy landscapes that shift with temperature.

On such Weakly Non-Tonelli manifolds, the author couples a Ginzburg-Landau theory of superconductors to heat. The work builds the needed Legendre map, metric, and Laplacian, and proves sharp behavior for the Green kernel. Energy limits then reveal metastable vortex filaments that minimize a renormalized energy. A dynamic limit yields filament flow driven by curvature and heat forces, with a phase split at a critical temperature.
arxiv-2512-12300:
Kartik Gaur and fourteen co-authors report a scalable quantum light platform in a 2025 paper. Quantum photonics needs tiny light sources placed exactly inside light guiding structures. Self assembled quantum dots form at random spots, so aligning them with resonators has needed slow, complex patterning steps.

Their dots grow at controlled sites, using a buried stressor method, and line up with circular Bragg grating resonators. A 6 by 6 array reached 100 percent device yield, with 35 devices in the range where photon extraction should top 20 percent. The best device reached an extraction efficiency of 47.1 percent, plus or minus 3.8. Its single photon purity was 99.58 percent.
arxiv-2512-12700:
Xiaolei Yang proposes a new method for a special class of integrals in a 2025 math paper. The method rests on a series decomposition, breaking a hard integral into a sum of simpler pieces. Such tools matter because integrals of this class appear in the study of nonlocal evolution equations, where effects spread across space and time rather than acting at a point.

As an application, Yang uses the method to derive optimal pointwise temporal estimates for a class of those equations. Optimal means the bounds cannot be tightened in general. Unlike rival methods, this approach yields an upper bound and a lower bound at the same time. Getting both sides at once pins the true behavior of solutions from above and below.
arxiv-2512-13100:
Guanhua Ji and co-authors present OXE-AugE, a much larger version of a well-known robot training data set. General robot policies need data from many robot bodies, but collecting fresh demonstrations for each new arm and gripper is too costly. The base data set is also heavily skewed toward a few robot types.

Their toolkit augments the old data with nine new robot embodiments, yielding over 4.4 million trajectories, more than triple the original size. Policies fine-tuned on the enlarged set did better on new robots, on shifted settings, and even on the original robots. Success rates rose by 24 to 45 percent on unseen robot-gripper pairs.
arxiv-2512-13300:
Qinglin Jia and co-authors tackle conversion rate prediction for online advertising, where advertisers chase many different customer actions at once. Models are trained on post-click data across those goals. In practice, many advertisers report only some actions, so training labels come out incomplete and skewed.

Their framework, KAML, transfers knowledge carefully across the asymmetric label sets. A masking strategy driven by attribution makes better use of partial labels, while a hierarchy based extraction step handles the noise that looser masking admits. A ranking loss exploits unlabeled samples too. Offline tests and online A/B trials showed clear gains over multi-task baselines.
arxiv-2512-13900:
Dragomir Davidovic studies long-time failures of time-convolutionless master equations for the spin-boson model. Such equations can break down at late times, as small-step generators grow without bound in correlation-dominated regimes. His regulated reconstruction rebuilds the dynamic map around a Davies reference semigroup.

The reconstruction uses a non-Markovian density-matrix correlator that stays bounded at late times. An exactly solvable rotating-wave benchmark links generator growth to interference-driven near-zeros of coherence, and shows how the method regulates the map. Applied to the unbiased spin-boson model, it reveals an emergent transverse probe effect: bath memory locks phase and erases relative phase between the sigma-x states in finite time. The effect vanishes in standard shortcuts, marking its non-Markovian origin.
arxiv-2512-14700:
Most research on online harassment studies public social media, leaving abuse in private messaging comparatively neglected. One team turns to Instagram's private messages and asks how large language models can help detect harassment there and respond to it effectively.

Private platforms pose distinct problems: messages are not public, context is personal, and any intervention must respect that privacy. Using language models for detection and response offers a scalable way to support targets in spaces where human review cannot read everything. The work speaks to platform safety teams weighing automated help in private messaging, and to researchers studying harm beyond public feeds.
arxiv-2512-15100:
Samuel Cogan and two coauthors fix a well known flaw in Grover's quantum search algorithm. Grover's method beats classical search with a quadratic speedup, but its success swings up and down like a soufflé rising and falling. Landing at the peak requires knowing in advance how many solutions exist, which users often do not.

The fix couples the solution states to an engineered ancilla reservoir, so the starting state is absorbed into the solution space without bouncing back. The swinging motion becomes near exponential convergence onto the answer. Turning the continuous design into a circuit by Trotter steps keeps the same performance and the same quadratic speedup. The result removes a practical headache for quantum search, without giving up its edge or demanding delicate control.
arxiv-2512-15200:
Paritosh Verma and a coauthor compute the gravitational waves from a spinning neutron star that is lumpy, not smooth. A deformed pulsar should radiate continuous gravitational waves, not yet detected, which would probe both gravity and extreme matter. Most estimates assume one overall ellipticity for the star.

Real crusts can hold several mountains at once, bumps the star's gravity cannot flatten. The authors use astronomically motivated distributions of such mountains. They compute the wave strain, power, torque, and the pulsar's spin down rate from the whole set. The work is done in Brans-Dicke gravity, which adds a scalar wave mode driven by the dipole moment to the two tensor modes of general relativity. Limiting results for pure general relativity are included, so readers can compare theories.
arxiv-2512-15400:
Yiming Pan and five coauthors watch electrons sort themselves between valleys in tin selenide, on timescales under a trillionth of a second. Valleytronics aims to store and process data in which valley of a band structure an electron sits in. Tin selenide has strong direction based traits, so polarized light can address its distinct valleys one at a time.

The team pairs ultrafast photoemission with Boltzmann equation models to track valley balance after light excites the sample. Exciting valleys at the lowest conduction minima gives near perfect valley balance that does not decay. Exciting the other valley channel leads to fast decay and even a flip of the balance within a picosecond. Strong coupling between electrons and one optical phonon mode drives the scattering between valleys. The results show valley physics in this material unlike that of the common two dimensional valley systems.
arxiv-2512-15500:
Benedicte Haas and Gregory Miermont study ancestral diversity in fragmentation trees in a 2025 probability paper. Take a tree, sample many groups of k leaves, and count how many distinct most recent common ancestors those groups have. How that count grows reveals the shape and branching habits of the tree.

Earlier work by Chapuy covered pairs of leaves in the Brownian continuum random tree, motivated by edge density in a random graph model. Haas and Miermont extend the study to general group sizes and general fragmentation trees, including stable Levy trees and idealized family trees of species. They find a phase transition: the growth regime changes when the group size passes a model dependent critical value.
arxiv-2512-15600:
Alexandre Dussolle and Pietro Lio introduce N-simplicial attention in a 2025 paper. Attention in transformers compares tokens in pairs. Simplicial attention goes further, letting groups of tokens interact at once, which may capture richer structure at extra computing cost.

The authors adapt the idea for rotary position embeddings and add a cost effective simplex selection step, so the model spends effort on the most task sensitive groups. They then ask how smoothing this attention is, deriving a Lipschitz upper bound on its output change. The analysis shows N-simplicial attention also suffers from over smoothing on its own, despite the higher order interactions. The paper weighs that trade off for future architectures.
arxiv-2512-16100:
Xurong Chen and three co-authors study rare particle decays in a 2025 paper on arXiv. Pseudoscalar mesons, light particles like the pion and eta, can decay into photons or into neutrino pairs. The authors compute these decays with a dispersive method built on anomaly sum rules, a framework tying the decays to quantum chromodynamics.

A new ingredient is a non-perturbative gluon form factor for the virtual photon, whose shape they pin down from data. Near a photon virtuality of about 1 GeV squared, it shows structure that may signal a pseudoscalar glueball, a particle made mostly of gluons, with mass around 1.5 to 2 GeV. Including mixing effects triples the predicted pion decay rate to neutrinos, and raises the eta rate by several orders of magnitude. The authors discuss what this means for a planned detector in China.
arxiv-2512-16200:
Haishan Ye pins down the cost of a popular optimization style in a paper released on arXiv in 2025. Zeroth-order methods tune a system using only function values, never gradients. Rank-based versions care only about the ordering of values, which makes them robust to noise, and they power well-known algorithms like CMA-ES.

Theory for these methods was mostly asymptotic, giving no explicit price tag for top-k selection variants. Ye analyzes a simple rank-based algorithm and proves the first explicit, non-asymptotic query counts. For smooth, strongly convex problems, the cost grows with dimension times a condition number factor and log terms in the target accuracy. For smooth nonconvex problems, a simpler bound holds. The proofs avoid the usual drift and information geometry tools, offering a fresh view of why ranking works so well.
arxiv-2512-16500:
S. S. Podkorytov works in homotopy theory, the branch of math that studies how maps between spaces can be bent into each other. For pointed cell spaces X and Y, with X compact, he defines a new link between maps, written with a level r that counts how close two maps must be.

For each whole number r of zero or more, the new link sits next to an older notion called r-similarity. The note argues for the guess that the two notions always agree. Settling that guess would clarify how fine a scale homotopy classes can be sorted on, and where two maps that look alike at a coarse level must in fact match.
arxiv-2512-16600:
Sun-Sig Byun, Jeongmin Han, and Mikyoung Lee prove a sharp regularity result for a class of fully nonlinear elliptic equations. They look at the Dirichlet problem, where values are fixed on the edge of a region, and allow the equation to be nonconvex in the second derivatives.

Their main claim is a global Calderon-Zygmund type bound: the second derivatives of the solution are just as integrable as the given input term. The bound holds in a general Orlicz space, a flexible scale for measuring size. It holds even when the equation is only convex in a far-out, limiting sense, which widens the class of equations covered.
arxiv-2512-16700:
John M. Statheros, Hairong Wang, and Richard Klein present CLARiTy, a vision transformer that reads chest X-rays. It must name all diseases present and point to where each one sits, yet training data rarely mark exact zones, only image-level labels.

CLARiTy uses one token per disease class to build attention maps, plus a SegmentCAM part that cuts background using body-shape priors. It learns from image labels alone on the NIH ChestX-ray14 set, with help from a ConvNeXtV2 teacher. On the standard split it matched top scores across 14 diseases and beat past tools on placing 8 diseases by over 50 percent, with the largest gains on small spots like nodules.
arxiv-2512-17300:
Guangjun Shen, Jiangpeng Wang, and Xuekang Zhang study how to simulate a crowd of particles that each follow the group's overall spread. Equations of this kind, where each path depends on the whole distribution, model flocks, markets, and cells. Here the random kicks come from fractional Brownian motion, a noise with memory, scaled by the state itself.

The team proves two things for a stated range of the memory strength, set by the Hurst parameter. First, a large crowd of linked particles behaves like a set of independent copies, an effect called propagation of chaos. Second, the step-by-step Euler-Maruyama simulation stays within a proven error bound. Careful computer runs back up both claims.
arxiv-2512-17600:
Steve Barrett and four co-authors borrow a safety method from aviation and nuclear plants to chart how humans could lose control of advanced AI. Loss-of-control fears range from a model copying itself off a server to slow shifts that leave people powerless. The debate, they note, lacks a shared map of the failure routes.

Their tool, STAMP with its STPA hazard method, treats any workplace system as loops of control: who senses what, who can act, and what feedback flows back. Walking those loops reveals where control can quietly snap. The team adapts the method to AI systems and shows how operators can list concrete causal factors for each route. Regulators and labs gain a checklist grounded in decades of safety practice.
arxiv-2512-17800:
Gurinder Singh, Thaddeus Pellegrini, and Kenneth M Merz teach a quantum circuit to read images the way eyes do: locally first. Quantum machine learning circuits usually scramble all pixels together at once, which breeds noise and untrainable flat spots. Their Domain-Aware Quantum Circuit instead encodes pixels in zigzag windows, borrowing the scan pattern of image compression, and entangles only neighbors.

Encode, entangle, train, repeat: the circuit's view widens in stages while staying shallow and hardware-friendly. On three image sets, handwritten digits, fashion items, and chest X-rays, it ran on real quantum hardware. With only a simple linear readout on top, it matched strong classical networks like ResNet and beat rival quantum designs. The authors claim the best result yet for image classification on actual quantum machines.
arxiv-2512-17900:
Vongani H. Maluleke and five coauthors built MAGNet, a system that makes up motion for groups of people. Past motion tools were made for one narrow task and fixed group sizes. Groups are hard to fake because people react to each other over long stretches.

MAGNet handles two person and larger scenes in one model, and can fill in a missing partner or extend a scene for hundreds of steps. It keeps partners in sync while it cleans up each new frame, so dances and boxing look matched while loose social scenes stay natural. On two person tests it matched tools built just for that job.
arxiv-2512-18000:
M. Grant Roberts, Aarna Garg, Tesla Jeltema, and Stefano Profumo make a testable call about Little Red Dots, the compact red sources the Webb telescope found in the early universe. Their model seeds the dots from dark matter that collides strongly with itself. From that model they predict how strongly the dots should cluster on the sky.

The clustering strength comes out near 3.6, which points to home halos of about 6.3 times ten to the tenth solar masses. That value sets the dots apart from bright quasars of the same era. The call barely moves when the dark matter details change, so near term Webb surveys can test the idea head on.
arxiv-2512-18200:
Hyeonjin Lee, Jun-Hyuk Kim, and Jong-Seok Lee note that most image compression is tuned for human eyes, keeping detail that machines never use. Their 2025 paper proposes SLIM, a framework built for machine vision on a pretrained latent diffusion model. The compressor spends bits only on the regions of interest that matter for the task. It compresses those areas tightly in latent space.

A pretrained U-Net then enhances the result, guided by a text caption focused on those regions. Denoising steps refine the result, so the rebuilt image serves the machine task while still looking acceptable to people. No guide mask is needed when the system runs. Experiments show SLIM reaches higher classification accuracy than conventional machine oriented compression at the same bits per pixel. The work matters because more images now feed algorithms than humans, and bandwidth spent on invisible detail is wasted.
arxiv-2512-18300:
Suhas Vittal and Moinuddin Qureshi speed up computer memory by making its writes cheaper. In DDR5 memory, a burst of writes blocks reads. The cost of a write also swings wildly by address. It takes one unit of time for some banks, six for banks in one group, and 24 for a clash on the same bank. Cache rules that pick what to write back ignore that spread.

Their BARD policy favors flushing data whose bank is free. It comes in two flavors. One acts at eviction time, and the other cleans early. A hybrid of the two lifted speed by 4.3 percent on average and up to 8.5 percent across standard and server workloads. The added hardware cost is a mere 8 bytes per cache slice.
arxiv-2512-18600:
Juha Park and colleagues turn a flaw of wideband links into a feature. Low Earth orbit satellites promise fast global connectivity, but beam hopping serves only a small patch of ground in each time slot. That switching creates uplink bottlenecks and latency as user density grows. Wideband systems also suffer beam squint, where beams at different frequencies point in different directions.

Their 2025 design, called 3D rainbow beamforming, deliberately widens the squint. A joint phase time array with true time delay steers each frequency's beam toward a different direction. One satellite can then cover its whole service area in one slot, receiving uplink signals from huge numbers of users. They solve the resulting non convex optimization problem with a joint alternating and decomposition framework. In realistic 3D simulations, uplink throughput rises up to 2.8 fold over conventional beam hopping. The authors frame the result as a breakthrough path for 6G satellite networks.
arxiv-2512-18800:
Ranjeet Dwivedi and six co-authors design a better light switch for photonic chips. Phase shifters made from phase-change materials hold their setting without power, which suits programmable photonics. The challenge is dialing in many evenly spaced phase levels. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, studies a GeSe phase-change layer on a silicon waveguide, heated electrically.

A plain rectangular heater gives levels, but they bunch up unevenly because heating is uniform along the light's path. Their fix is a segmented heater that widens step by step along the propagation direction, smoothing how the material amorphizes. The design encodes hundreds of well-spaced levels between zero and pi, with worst-case insertion loss of only 0.6 dB. Tests under both pulse-width and pulse-amplitude control confirm the segmented design wins.
arxiv-2512-19200:
Maryem Jemri rebuilds charged black hole physics with Dunkl derivatives, a deformed kind of calculus that carries reflection data. Starting from the Christoffel symbols, she computes the curvature pieces and inserts them into Einstein's equations as modified by the Dunkl scheme. A new metric for charged Dunkl black holes follows.

Jemri then works through the thermodynamics: charge effects, heat capacity, and thermal stability. Pressure-volume criticality gives critical values shaped by charge and two Dunkl parameters, with one universal ratio. Turning one parameter off recovers Van der Waals fluid behavior. Joule-Thomson expansion shows both echoes of, and departures from, that classic fluid.
arxiv-2512-19400:
Yacouba Diarra, Panga Azazia Kamate, Nouhoum Souleymane Coulibaly, and Michael Leventhal release Kunkado, a speech dataset for Bambara, the main language of Mali. Speech tools for mostly oral languages starve for realistic data. Their one hundred sixty hours come from Malian radio archives, with all the mess of live speech.

Code-switching, disfluencies, noise, and overlapping voices are kept in, not cleaned away. Models based on Parakeet were fine-tuned on a human-reviewed thirty-three hour slice, with pragmatic transcript cleanup. Word error rates fell clearly on two real-world test sets. Human judges also preferred the system over one trained on far more, but cleaner, speech.
arxiv-2512-19500:
Peter Müller answers a question from the Kourovka Notebook, posed by John Thompson, for one large family of groups. Take a finite primitive permutation group and two distinct points. Must some element carry the first point to the second while fixing nothing at all? A single known counterexample, a huge triality group action, says not always.

Müller shows that almost simple primitive groups whose socle is a projective special linear group in two dimensions never give such counterexamples. For every pair of points in those actions, a fixed-point-free element does the required transport. The note narrows where a second counterexample could possibly hide.
arxiv-2512-19600:
Rafael Miyazaki, Cosmin Pohoata, and Michael Zheng work on a counting question in graph theory built around the chromatic polynomial. That polynomial counts proper colorings of a graph, ways to color vertices so neighbors differ. About ten years ago, Agol and Krushkal showed such polynomials grow exponentially varied, using a related flow polynomial on planar cubic graphs.

The new result widens the claim sharply. For every fixed real value except zero, one, and two, the number of distinct chromatic polynomial values across graphs on n vertices grows exponentially with n.
