Restricting to planar graphs alone still gives exponentially many values. The value three case also settles a conjecture of Agol, one rooted in the hardness of planar three-colorability.
arxiv-2512-19700:
Anton Alyakin turns a bibliometric eye on a naming fad his own field cannot quit. The 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer carried the title Attention Is All You Need, and researchers have been borrowing the formula ever since. Alyakin gathered 717 arXiv preprints whose titles contain the phrase All You Need, spanning 2009 to 2025, and charted the meme's spread.

Counts grew exponentially after the original paper, with 200 such titles in 2025 alone, and Attention remains the most frequently declared sole necessity among canonical uses. Read through memetics, the pattern's success is credited to competitive pressure favoring memorable titles over precise ones. Whether the habit is harmless whimsy or creeping sensationalism is left, self-awarely, to the reader.
arxiv-2512-20300:
Marjolein de Jager, Antoine Castagnède, Frank Smallenburg, and Laura Filion revisit how size variation affects crystal nucleation in hard spheres. Hard spheres are the simplest model of a freezing liquid. When the spheres come in a range of sizes, textbook mappings to an effective packing fraction predict nucleation should follow the uniform-size trend.

Event-driven molecular dynamics simulations say otherwise: measured nucleation rates depart from that trend even after the mapping is applied. The authors then look at where crystals are born. Nuclei tend to start in regions that happen to hold more larger-than-average particles. Those local composition fluctuations act as precursors, giving polydisperse systems a nucleation pathway that uniform spheres do not have.
arxiv-2512-20600:
Coen Hutters and Max B Mendel borrow a modelling language from electrical engineering and lend it to economics. Multiport network theory describes components by ports where flows and efforts meet. In their mapping, the flow of goods plays the role of current, and an agent's incentive plays the role of voltage.

Networks of agents connected through ports then model an economy at several abstraction levels at once, macro behaviour emerging from micro interactions. The authors implement the models in LTSpice, an ordinary circuit simulator, and build a ladder of examples. The sequence runs from a one-person Robinson Crusoe economy to a model of an entire economy. The exercise shows circuit intuition and circuit software can carry real economic dynamics.
arxiv-2512-20700:
Ping Gao and Hong Liu read the horizon of a stringy black hole through a diagnostic called pole-skipping. In quantum chaotic systems, certain response functions skip their poles at special frequency-momentum points tied to chaos. The authors study systems that are chaotic but not maximally so, using Rindler conformal field theories and the large-q SYK chain as examples.

Pole-skipping points of few-body operators organize into trajectories in the complex frequency-momentum plane. The leading trajectory encodes the quantum Lyapunov exponent, chaos's growth rate. Gao and Liu propose these trajectories are the Regge trajectories of stringy excitations in a dual black hole geometry. Each operator's pole-skipping then tracks the stringy horizon individually. Chaos, in this view, reflects intrinsic horizon structure in the stringy regime.
arxiv-2512-21100:
Dongchao Yang, Shi-Ming Zhou, and five co-authors show that in spintronics the neighbor chooses the physics. Ruthenium dioxide, a leading d-wave altermagnet candidate, converts spin current to charge current. But spin-pumping experiments find the effective conversion angle flips sign depending on which ferromagnet sits on top. One bilayer uses insulating YIG, the other metallic permalloy. The reversal persists whether the oxide layer is crystalline or polycrystalline, ruling out bulk quality as the explanation.

A hair-thin gold spacer flips the YIG signal again, exposing an interfacial Rashba-Edelstein mechanism there, while the permalloy stack follows the bulk inverse spin Hall effect. First-principles calculations pin the difference on interface-selective band hybridization: Rashba surface states survive at the insulating contact and are quenched by the metal. Device designers gain a deterministic knob for building field-free, low-dissipation memory.
arxiv-2512-21200:
Yasaman Hakiminejad and Arash Tavakoli measure how walking actually feels, in real time, on real streets. Cities usually judge pedestrian environments with static infrastructure scores or after-the-fact surveys, tools blind to the moment-by-moment stress and pleasure of a walk. Their framework triangulates three streams. Wearable sensors track heart-rate variability and skin conductance. GPS traces show where participants actually went. Phone prompts ask about stress, mood, and perceived street conditions as they happen.

A field study around Greater Philadelphia, with volunteers wearing research-grade sensors through ordinary days, shows how far experience diverges from the indices. Responses vary widely between people and within the same person across contexts, shifting with traffic exposure, pavement quality, and how enclosed a street feels, and standard walkability scores miss much of it. Planners gain a transferable method for designing streets around lived experience rather than checklists.
arxiv-2512-21300:
Sequential data demands error bars that stay valid at every peek, not just at a fixed sample size. Ben Chugg and Aaditya Ramdas derive a confidence sequence for bounded random variables that adapts to the observed variance and comes in closed form. It is centered on the plain sample mean, and its scaled limiting width does not depend on the significance level.

In experiments up to a million observations, theirs is the tightest closed-form sequence they found for tracking means that drift over time. When the mean is actually constant, it beats the recent Waudby-Smith and Ramdas sequence asymptotically. Everything extends to random matrices with bounded eigenvalues, widening the audience to covariance-style estimation.
arxiv-2512-21400:
B. Amghar, A. Slaoui, and their co-authors build a geometric picture of many spin one-half particles that all interact with each other. The interaction is an Ising coupling, where each spin responds to the alignment of the others. They use the Fubini-Study formalism, a way of measuring distances between quantum states.

From that formalism they derive the metric and curvature of the space of quantum states. The space turns out to be a smooth, compact two-dimensional surface. It has the topology of a sphere and a dumbbell-like shape. They then study geometric phases and the quantum brachistochrone problem, which asks for the shortest possible time for the system to evolve between states. Entanglement speeds up the evolution up to a threshold, after which the geometry begins to slow it down. The results offer guidance for designing fast, well-controlled quantum circuits.
arxiv-2512-21600:
Qiang Ren constructs special solutions to an Ambrosetti-Prodi type problem, a nonlinear elliptic equation posed on a two-dimensional domain. In this equation, a forcing term tied to the first eigenfunction competes with a superlinear power term. Ambrosetti-Prodi problems raise fine questions about how many solutions exist as the forcing parameter varies.

Let a closed curve inside the domain be a non-degenerate critical point of a certain weighted length functional, built from the first eigenfunction and the coefficient matrix. Ren proves there are forcing values growing without bound for which the problem has solutions concentrating along that curve. The solutions form clustering layers: their mass piles up in thin sheets following the curve rather than spreading through the domain. Such constructions reveal how geometry organizes the extreme behavior of such equations.
arxiv-2512-21800:
Alexander Engström connects graph coloring to commutative algebra. The chromatic number of a graph is the fewest colors needed so adjacent vertices differ; it is at least the size of the largest clique, but can be much larger. A class of graphs is called chi-bounded when some function of the clique number caps the chromatic number, and polynomially bounded when that function can be a polynomial.

Engström studies graph classes defined by requiring one bigraded Betti number of the graph's edge ideal to vanish. Betti numbers are invariants from the ideal's syzygies, its relations among relations. He proves such classes are polynomially chi-bounded, with an explicit polynomial. One special case improves a classical result of Wagon about graphs with no large matching. Triangle-free graphs in these classes need only boundedly many colors, computable by an efficient algorithm.
arxiv-2512-22100:
Duygu Altinok introduces TrGLUE, a benchmark for testing how well language models understand Turkish. English has long had the GLUE benchmark, and Chinese, French, and Japanese have versions of their own, but Turkish had none. Alongside TrGLUE, Altinok presents SentiTurca, a companion benchmark devoted to sentiment analysis, plus code for fine-tuning and scoring transformer models.

TrGLUE is built from Turkish-native texts rather than translations, so the test material sounds natural. Its labels come from a semi-automated pipeline that combines annotation by strong language models, agreement checks across models, and final human validation. The design aims to give Turkish language research a shared, reproducible yardstick and a worked example of building quality datasets with partial automation.
arxiv-2512-22500:
Jin Lei replaces slow nuclear scattering runs with a neural network that can be differentiated. Optical model calculations describe how nucleons scatter off nuclei, and modern data evaluation needs uncertainty estimates and parameter fitting that gradient methods would accelerate. The emulator, built on two-way liquid neural networks, maps optical potential settings directly to scattering wave functions.

A phase-space coordinate trick normalizes how long each wave cycle runs at any energy, letting one network span projectile energies from 1 to 200 MeV. Trained on Numerov solutions for twelve nuclei, protons and neutrons alike, it reached an overall relative error near one percent. It also stayed accurate on three nuclei never seen in training, suggesting it learned the physics rather than memorizing targets.
arxiv-2512-22600:
Igor Filikhin, Roman Ya. Kezerashvili, and Branislav Vlahovic ask whether omega baryons, heavy particles made of three strange or three charm quarks, can bind inside light nuclei. Their starting point is an omega-nucleon potential recently developed by the HAL QCD collaboration. That potential has a deeply attractive core at very short range, which they remove and replace: the long-range part is refit with a two-range Gaussian while preserving the two-body bound state energy.

From the regularized interaction they build an effective omega-alpha-particle potential and compute binding in systems with one or two alpha particles and up to two omegas. Regularization substantially reduced the predicted binding energies. Extending the analysis to charm-omega clusters, several parametrizations still predict bound states, and a contact-style treatment covers the omega-omega interaction.
arxiv-2512-23000:
Mohammed Salah and co-authors improve how hidden defects are visualized in materials inspected with active infrared thermography. In that technique, a part is heated and filmed as it cools, and flaws show up as subtle thermal patterns, a method used heavily in aerospace testing. Autoencoders already clean up such thermal movies, but they often blur the faint defect signal together with the strong background response.

Their network, a masked CNN-attention autoencoder, learns by hiding parts of the thermal sequence and forcing itself to infer the missing responses from context, which suppresses background redundancy. Convolutional layers catch local patterns while attention tracks wider context. Because training needs only a subset of each sequence, training time falls by a factor of thirty. On PVC, carbon-fiber composite, and PLA specimens, the method beat leading autoencoders on contrast, signal-to-noise ratio, and neural-network-based quality metrics.
arxiv-2512-23100:
Joon-Hwi Kim recasts scattering theory in phase space terms, the arena combining position and momentum where classical mechanics lives. The central object linking quantum scattering to classical dynamics is the S-matrix and its classical twin, a symplectomorphism, a canonical transformation of phase space made by the scattering process. Kim proves an exact relation between the two.

The bridge is phase space quantum mechanics itself. The S-matrix, acting on phase space functions, defines a fuzzy diffeomorphism, a slightly blurred remapping, whose classical limit recovers the S-symplectomorphism exactly. The relation between classical and quantum eikonals, the phase functions behind high-energy scattering, then falls out by deforming each Poisson bracket in the Magnus formula with Planck's constant. Diagram computations of the quantum eikonal are shown for both symmetric and normal operator orderings, showing how the method works in practice.
arxiv-2512-23200:
Ziru Niu, Hai Dong, A. K. Qin, Tao Gu, and Pengcheng Zhang make federated learning cheaper for the small devices of the Internet of Things. Federated training keeps data on device and preserves privacy, but deep networks strain the compute, memory, and bandwidth of edge hardware. Earlier economies like dropout and layer freezing often cost accuracy or ignore memory limits entirely.

Their method, FedOLF, freezes layers in a fixed, predefined order before training begins, so every round of updates touches only part of the network, cutting computation and memory together. A lightweight tensor operation approximation replaces conventional quantization for communication, preserving accuracy while shrinking traffic and energy use. On non-identically distributed data across handwritten characters and three image benchmarks, FedOLF beat existing approaches on accuracy while using less energy and memory. The authors pitch ordered freezing as a simple discipline that resource-starved federations can actually sustain.
arxiv-2512-23300:
Minjiang Huang and co-authors built AI4Reading, a multi-agent system that produces podcast-style audiobook interpretations in Chinese. A good interpretation does more than read a book aloud. It analyzes themes, pulls in real-world cases, and organizes ideas so listeners learn. Making one by hand is slow and expensive. The system's three stated goals are faithful content, better comprehensibility, and a logical narrative structure.

Eleven specialized agents share the work, including topic analysts, case analysts, editors, a narrator, and proofreaders, passing drafts among themselves before speech synthesis voices the result. The team compared its output against expert-made interpretations. The honest verdict is split: a gap remains in the quality of the generated speech, while the interpretive scripts came out simpler and more accurate than the experts'. The study offers a template for how far multi-agent pipelines can go in producing educational audio content.
arxiv-2512-23400:
Abd Ullah Khan, Uman Khalid, Trung Duong, and Hyundong Shin survey beyond-diagonal reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, a new kind of radio surface for future wireless networks. A standard reconfigurable surface uses separate elements that each tweak a wave's phase. The beyond-diagonal design wires elements together. That gains freedom to shape both amplitude and phase of waves with cheap, simple connections. The idea is billed as a step change in shaping waves.

The article introduces the design, covering working principles, advantages, and types, then reviews recent advances and the challenges blocking rollout. A case study designs beamforming for ambient backscatter communication with four different algorithms and compares their data rates against compute cost. The authors also test hybrid quantum-classical machine learning models for beam forecasts on a real-world channel dataset. Their insights target 6G networks, where intelligent surfaces are expected to be standard gear.
arxiv-2512-23900:
Hesam Khoshkbari and four co-authors coordinate a fleet of flying base stations. High-altitude platforms and balloons are set to extend next-generation wireless coverage to remote areas and relieve dense cities. With massive antenna arrays they must jointly aim their beams, a task called distributed beamforming. Sharing perfect channel knowledge among platforms cannot be done, so each station must act on its own imperfect information.

Their framework casts every airborne platform as an independent agent in an entropy-based multi-agent deep reinforcement learning system, trained and tested with imperfect channel state information and no channel sharing between agents. That cuts overhead sharply. In simulations the method beat zero-forcing and maximum-ratio transmission baselines, especially where interference was heavy, stayed robust when channel estimates degraded, and scaled steadily as user counts and cluster layouts changed. The authors pitch it for dynamic, interference-rich non-terrestrial networks.
arxiv-2512-24400:
Biagio Montaruli and three colleagues audit a reputation score for software packages. SourceRank grades open-source packages on eighteen metrics of popularity and quality. Researchers use it to judge trust. Nobody had stress-tested it against evasion. Bad packages might inflate their scores and pass as benign.

The team first builds a threat model. Each metric gets its candidate evasion routes. One trick, URL confusion, points a package at an unrelated but legitimate repository. It alone can sway five of the eighteen metrics. Real data then test the score in practice. A benchmark malware set and a huge PyPI sample were analyzed. Past data showed a clear split between benign and bad packages. Real-world score ranges overlapped heavily, though. Slow reflection of removals is a main cause. The verdict is blunt: the score cannot reliably separate benign from malicious packages in the wild.
arxiv-2512-24600:
Yuanyuan Cheng and four colleagues drive a quantum spin chain periodically and watch for dynamical phase transitions. The system is a one-dimensional Ising model with a modulated transverse field. Sudden quenches are the usual route to such transitions. Periodic driving offers two other routes, the authors show.

Within one phase, a resonant drive can trigger the transition. The drive frequency must match a level transition of the system. Floquet topological phases emerge alongside. A scaling law sets the transition time from the drive strength and the critical mode's gap. Across the critical point, the rules change. Low frequencies always induce the transition, resonant or not. Level degeneracy at criticality guarantees excitation. High frequencies suppress it strongly. The study deepens the picture of nonequilibrium quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2512-24700:
Evagoras Makridis, Gabriele Oliva, Apostolos Rikos, and Themistoklis Charalambous design a distributed algorithm that lets a network of agents agree on their exact average while sending only a few bits per message. Directed links may be unbalanced, which makes averaging hard. Their method mixes push-pull consensus dynamics with a moving quantization frame that zooms and shifts.

Agents keep the true average while steadily refining precision, and a shared stopping rule ends the process in finite time once they are close enough. Proofs cover strongly connected directed graphs. Readers in control and networks get exact averaging under strict bandwidth limits, with formal guarantees.
arxiv-2512-24800:
Amaresh Mahato, Sampad Das, and Manasi Mandal study primary ideals in commutative semirings, algebraic systems where subtraction may not exist. They define irreducible and maximal variants relative to a multiplicative set, then develop decomposition theory for primary ideals in that relative setting. Localization, a tool that inverts chosen elements, supports existence and uniqueness results.

The radical of a primary ideal in their sense is shown to be prime. In principal ideal semidomains, each such ideal takes an explicit factored form. Algebra readers get the familiar primary decomposition story carried into semirings, where many ring arguments fail and must be rebuilt carefully.
arxiv-2601-00400:
Weng Ding, Yi Han, and Mu-Jiang-Shan Wang tackle coordinated fake behavior on social media, where linked accounts act together to mislead. Older detectors lean on surface correlation, fixed settings, and heavy hand labeling. Their 2026 paper presents a three-stage framework, called ACCD, that remembers which detection settings worked well and reuses them in new situations.

First, a cross-mapping technique looks for real causal links between accounts. Next, active learning inside a semi-supervised scheme cuts the labeling burden by asking about the most uncertain cases. A final stage checks results against past detection experience. On real datasets, including the Twitter IRA set, the framework scores well above the strongest baseline. It also cuts hand labeling sharply and runs faster.
arxiv-2601-01000:
Noemí Lubomirsky and two co-authors wrote a 2026 math paper that widens a classic bridge between two kinds of algebra. One kind, Heyting algebras, codes the logic of constructive proof. The other, Nelson algebras, codes a logic that can hold gaps in truth. In the late 1970s, Fidel and Vakarelov showed the two kinds mirror each other. The bridge was built for a narrower class of lattices, though.

The authors work in a wider class, lattices with a halved form of implication. They define a new family, the hemi-Nelson algebras, to serve as the mirror image there. They describe the congruence classes of such an algebra through special filters. A congruence says which elements the algebra treats as the same. Last, they prove the two categories match: each side can be rebuilt from the other. The result carries a fifty-year-old bridge onto broader ground.
arxiv-2601-02300:
Gordon Baym and Glennys Farrar resolve a puzzle about the hydrogen atom. The magnetic interaction between electron and proton, called the hyperfine interaction, grows sharply as the atom is squeezed smaller. Taken at face value, that suggests the atom should collapse to tiny size, yet real hydrogen is stable, and so is positronium, its electron and positron cousin.

Their calculation uses the exact Dirac equation solution for the ground state inside a variational estimate. As the trial atom shrinks below a key length, the effective magnetic moment of the electron itself shrinks, softening the interaction. The proton moment is suppressed the same way, so the magnetic energy stays bounded by the kinetic energy and no collapse occurs. They extend the same treatment to positronium and other simple atoms.
arxiv-2601-02500:
Brian Tekmen, Jason Yin, and Qianqian Tong make continual learning cheaper for large language models that adapt through small LoRA modules instead of full retraining. The classic safeguard against forgetting, gradient episodic memory, projects each new gradient so it does not hurt past tasks, but its quadratic projection step is far too slow at this scale. Their version, I-GEM, applies the same non interference rule only inside the adapter parameters.

A fixed budget, GPU resident dual projection approximates the original step at roughly a thousand times lower projection cost. On a three task news classification split with induced domain drift, using a mid sized GPT-2 with rank eight adapters. I-GEM matched the original method's average accuracy almost exactly and beat a cheaper averaged variant. The result suggests GEM style protection is practical at language model scale when confined to the adapter subspace.
arxiv-2601-02900:
Taisei Takano and Ryoya Yoshida describe their entry to the first XACLE Challenge, a contest for systems that judge how well a sound matches a text description. Such automatic scores are useful only if they track human perception. Their system builds on CLAPScore, which compares audio and text in a shared embedding space, and adds a new training method called Standardized Preference Optimization.

The method rescales each listener's raw scores before training, so the model learns relative preferences instead of one rater's habits. The team also screens out listeners whose ratings are inconsistent. Both steps improved agreement with human judgment, and the system placed sixth in the challenge, close behind the top entries.
arxiv-2601-03000:
Zhouxiang Huang, Dekui Peng, and Gao Zhang settle an open question about a class of topological groups called d-independent. A group has this property when every small subgroup can be dodged by some countable dense subgroup that meets it only at the identity. Márquez and Tkachenko introduced the notion and characterized it for well-behaved abelian groups, then asked whether the same answer holds for all separable locally compact groups.

Huang, Peng, and Zhang answer yes: every separable locally compact abelian M-group is d-independent, with no metrizability assumption needed. They also study how the property behaves under taking powers of groups and extend the notion to non-abelian groups. Finally, they prove every separable connected compact group is d-independent, answering a second question from the same source.
arxiv-2601-03100:
Chenchen Lin and six co-authors reduce hallucination in multimodal language models by making better use of the vision encoder's many layers. Such models usually read only one late-layer feature from a frozen image encoder, wasting the hierarchy of visual cues stored across layers, so the model leans on language habits and invents details. Their module, TGIF, treats the encoder's layers as depth-wise experts.

TGIF predicts a prompt-dependent blend of those layer features, so the visual input adapts to what the user actually asked. It needs no updates to the vision encoder and adds little overhead. Plugged into LLaVA-1.5-7B, it improved results across hallucination, text-recognition, and visual question answering benchmarks, while holding or improving performance on several general benchmarks as well.
arxiv-2601-03200:
Ziyang Sun and four co-authors build high-fidelity digital twins for robot manipulation using 3D Gaussian splatting, a fast photorealistic scene representation. Good twins matter because they let robots plan motions in simulation and execute them reliably in the real world. Older approaches suffer from slow reconstruction, limited visual quality, and trouble turning pretty models into collision geometry a planner can use.

Their framework constructs a twin within minutes from sparse ordinary photos. Visibility-aware semantic fusion adds accurate three-dimensional labels, and a filter-based conversion produces collision-ready geometry that plugs into a Unity, ROS2, and MoveIt physics setup. In trials, a Franka Emika Panda arm performed pick-and-place tasks against the twin, and the improved geometric accuracy supported robust manipulation in the real world.
arxiv-2601-03400:
Ali Najar and seven co-authors introduce Eye-Q, a multilingual benchmark of visual word puzzles for testing whether vision-language models truly reason about images. Standard benchmarks reward surface recognition, but these puzzles demand more: spotting implicit visual cues, forming and revising hypotheses, and mapping what is seen to a non-literal word or phrase. Shortcuts through literal grounding, text recognition, or retrieval matching are deliberately blocked.

Eye-Q contains 1,343 puzzles, each a conceptually dense scene with a brief description and a specific target word or phrase to infer. Distractors and contextual relationships force selective attention, abstraction, and associative inference. The set spans English, Persian, and Arabic puzzles, plus cross-lingual ones. The authors evaluate leading vision-language models with an open-ended protocol aligned to human judgment.
arxiv-2601-03700:
Sangmin Yoo and four co-authors present ADEPT, a method for letting transformer models stop computing early on easy tokens. Skipping layers saves effort, but earlier early-exit schemes worked only at limited points, and the memory cache for skipped layers still burdened later tokens. ADEPT enables dynamic early exit during both the prompt-reading phase and the generation phase.

Its token-level mechanism adjusts computation to each token's difficulty, aiming to save effort without hurting output quality. The method also reworks how the key-value cache is generated for skipped layers, loosening the step-by-step dependencies that made token-level exits impractical. For providers serving billions of tokens, such savings translate directly into lower cost and faster replies, provided quality truly holds.
arxiv-2601-04000:
Stefano Campanaro, Luca Bussi, Stefano Curtarolo, and Arrigo Calzolari examine how layered semiconductor stacks can shape terahertz light. Metals work poorly in that range because their electron density is too high. Stacks made only of dielectrics, shaped by added charge carriers, offer a tunable alternative.

The four authors use a multi-scale theory approach that links physics at different levels. They vary doping, layer thickness, makeup, and grating shape to see how each choice shifts high-momentum plasmon-polariton modes. Those modes are waves that mix light with charge motion across the stack. The findings guide how such hyperbolic materials could be tuned for terahertz devices without relying on standard metals.
arxiv-2601-04100:
Christian L. Camacho-Villalón and five co-authors ask which parts of a modular swarm optimiser matter most. The PSO-X framework holds dozens of modules for particle swarm methods on single-goal continuous problems. More modules mean more freedom, but also a harder search for a good setup.

The team builds well over a thousand swarm algorithms from the framework and runs them on the twenty-five functions of the CEC benchmark suite, at two sizes. Functional analysis of variance then splits performance by module and by module pairs, grouped by problem traits such as many peaks or changed shape. A cluster step groups problem classes with like patterns. Across classes, module importance varies little, which suggests a few key modules drive most swarm performance.
arxiv-2601-06700:
Zhiyao Zhang, Yazan Mash'Al, and Yuhan Wu characterize toxicity in generative models in 2026. Their paper explores linguistic factors that might cause toxic output. Models can produce harmful text even from ordinary-looking prompts.

They aim to identify how prone large language models are to toxicity. They also study lexical and syntactic structures that trigger toxic generation. Certain words and sentence shapes may reliably provoke bad outputs. Knowing the triggers helps builders filter and steer models better. The work treats toxicity as a linguistic phenomenon with structure. Safety researchers get factors they can measure, not just examples. Findings could guide training data curation and prompt design alike. It adds precision to a debate often run on anecdotes.
arxiv-2601-06900:
Issey Sukeda and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers minimum information markov model. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. The analysis of high-dimensional time series data has become increasingly important across a wide range of fields.

Recently, a method for constructing the minimum information Markov kernel on finite state spaces was established. The authors propose a statistical model based on a parametrization of its dependence function, which we call the Minimum Information Markov Model . The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07300:
R. Arun and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers self-oscillations induced by self-induced torque in magnetic double tunnel junction. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Self-oscillations of the magnetization due to self-induced torque (SIT) in a magnetic double tunnel junction that consists of perpendicularly polarized.

Pinned and free layers is investigated along with the field-like torque (FLT). The associated Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski equation is numerically analysed to exhibit the oscillations of magnetization driven by the current. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07600:
Juan José Martín, José Flich, and Carles Hernández test how well modern NVIDIA GPUs can isolate competing inference jobs. Safety-critical systems need predictable inference times, even when several deep learning models share one chip. The authors compare three isolation tools: MPS, MIG, and the newer Green Contexts. Their 2026 preprint reports performance tests on two platforms.

Experiments run on both the NVIDIA A100 and the Jetson Orin, covering data center and edge hardware. The team measures how partitioning affects speed and how strong the time isolation between processes really is. Weak isolation means one job can slow another without warning. The results speak to engineers placing AI models in cars, robots, and medical devices, where late answers can be unsafe.
arxiv-2601-08000:
Can Jin and colleagues strengthen language model safety by reasoning over legal precedents as well as rules. Ensuring models follow safety principles without refusing harmless requests is a standing challenge. Deliberative alignment teaches models to reason over detailed, code-like safety rules. Its success in open-source models, which usually reason less strongly, is understudied. Their 2026 preprint adds case augmentation to the approach. Precedents sit alongside statutes in the model's deliberation.

Lawyers reason from both written rules and past cases. The authors borrow that habit for model safety. Cases show how abstract principles land on concrete situations. That grounding may help smaller open models apply rules more faithfully. The paper serves AI alignment scholars. It tests whether richer deliberation material closes the gap with proprietary systems.
arxiv-2601-08100: Xinping Yi, Gaojie Jin, Xiaowei Huang, and Shi Jin work toward one PAC-Bayesian framework for norm-based generalization bounds. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that why deep networks generalize remains a core open question. PAC-Bayesian norm-based bounds stand out because they depend on the data at hand. They can also capture properties of both the algorithm and the geometry of learned models. A unified framework could replace scattered bounds with one clear account. That would help theorists compare methods and guide safer model design.
arxiv-2601-08400:
E. Rodriguez and G. Plunk wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a large bank of magnetic field forms for fusion. A stellarator is a ring-shaped device that holds hot plasma with magnets. A good field form for it is quasi-isodynamic, a trait that keeps the plasma held in well. The authors work close to the axis of the ring. There, the field can be summed by a short-cut rule called the near-axis expansion.

With that rule, the team built a bank of more than 800,000 field forms. Each form is stable and close to quasi-isodynamic, in a vacuum with no plasma yet. The forms span a range of field period counts and shape controls. Those controls cover the shape of the magnetic axis and how stretched the plasma is. Teams can mine the bank for strong designs, which beats shaping each one from scratch.
arxiv-2601-08500: Cristian Santini, Marieke van Erp, and Mehwish Alam wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on linking names in old texts to who they mean. The task is called entity linking. It stays hard for old texts, in spite of gains from large language models. Old texts vary in tongue, hold noisy input, and use words in ways that shift over time. Past tools need much training data, or field-bound rules that cap their scale. The authors set out a way with no training phase, based on trust in each link.
arxiv-2601-08600: Rodrigo de Medeiros and Francisco Queiroz wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on models for data that can not go below zero. Such data is nonnegative continuous data. The team works with Box-Cox symmetric distributions, a broad class for data above zero. The class can bend to fit skew and tail weight. Its values can be read by quantiles, which helps when the model is used in regression. Few members of the class had been used in regression work. The team adds a zero-adjusted form, for data with true zeros.
arxiv-2601-08700: Nam Van Tran studies a class of hard math tasks where one must find a point that meets a set of mixed rules. Such tasks show up in game play, traffic flow, and price balance work. The rules mix a map, a cost term, and a set that the answer must stay in. Plain step by step methods can be slow to settle.
arxiv-2601-08900:
Anush Lakshman S, Adam Haroon, and Beiwen Li build a test set for a 3D scan method that uses striped light. The method shines stripe lines on a thing and reads how they bend to get its shape. Learn tools for it lack large, rich train sets. Real scans are slow to make, so progress has limped.

The team makes a fake set with true to life light and shade in a sim tool. It holds a vast set of stripe shots and depth maps for scores of things. They also give a full test plan so labs can grade tools the same way. A reader in 3D sight gets both data and a scale. New tools can now be trained and ranked with less guess work.
arxiv-2601-09000:
Annalisa Belloni, Lorenzo Noci, and Antonio Orvieto ask if a fav train pace plan works past chat models. The plan warms up, holds a flat pace, then drops the pace late. It trains large chat models well, and it bends with ease to new run lengths. But is its gain a quirk of that one model type, or a broad law of train work.

The team tests the plan on more than one model form and task. They track how loss falls in each phase of the plan. A broad gain would hint at a deep rule in how nets learn. A narrow gain would tie it to chat nets. A reader who trains nets gets a test that can guide pace picks for new work.
arxiv-2601-09200:
SK Telecom gives a tech report on a vast tongue model called A.X K1. The model has a huge count of set values, split by a mix of experts plan. In that plan, just a few experts wake for each word, so run cost stays far below full size. It was trained from scratch, not tuned from a past model.

Train used a vast text set, near ten trillion tokens, sifted in more than one stage. Scale laws set the train shape and word list size for a fixed power bill. The aim is step thought skill at a lean run cost. A reader gets the build facts for a top tier model from a phone firm.
arxiv-2601-09400:
Olgierd Unold and Stanisław Franczyk test a learning system that builds maps of its world from experience. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins the Anticipatory Classifier System, ACS2, with Hindsight Experience Replay, known as HER. ACS2 learns by anticipating what each action will do next.

That style of learning, called latent learning, makes ACS2 strong at building cognitive maps. Its weakness shows in sparse-reward settings, where success signals are rare and progress stalls. HER replays past attempts, treating reached states as if they were the goal. The authors report preliminary tests of whether the pairing lifts the stall.
arxiv-2601-09500:
Yichen Wang and five co-authors study when a hypergraph is forced to contain a forbidden pattern. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at graphs appearing as traces inside uniform hypergraphs. A trace arises when the edges of a hypergraph, cut down to a chosen vertex set, reproduce the graph.

The forbidden graphs here are edge-critical ones, graphs where removing any edge drops the chromatic number. Asking which hypergraphs avoid them as traces is an extremal problem. Results of this type extend classic Turán-style questions from graphs to hypergraphs. They show how much structure a hypergraph can have before a sharp pattern must appear.
arxiv-2601-10600:
Joshua Caiata, Carter Blair, and Kate Larson study fairness in multi-agent bandit problems. In these problems, several agents learn by trial and error which option pays off best. Fairness is often judged by outcomes alone, such as total welfare or equal shares. The authors argue that this view is too narrow.

Work in psychology, economics, and Rawlsian theory shows that process matters too. People care about who gets a say in the choices made. The paper brings that idea of procedural fairness into bandit models. It asks how learning rules should share voice, not just rewards. The shift matters for systems that split tasks or goods among many users.
arxiv-2601-10800:
John D. Roberts, Marc H. Pinsonneault, Jennifer A. Johnson, and Madeline Howell use two mass measures to study red giant stars. Red giants shed mass as they age, but the mechanism is poorly understood. The surface carbon-to-nitrogen ratio tracks a star's birth mass and is not directly changed by mass loss. Asteroseismology, reading a star's quakes, gives its current mass.

By comparing giants with the same carbon-to-nitrogen ratio but different evolutionary states, the team can spot mass lost or gained along the way. Transfer between companion stars also leaves a trace. The method turns two routine measures into a diagnostic of a star's hidden history. It sharpens the story of how Sun-like stars end their lives.
arxiv-2601-11000:
Zhongxiang Sun and co-authors study hallucinations in personalized language models. Personalized models adapt to each user to raise satisfaction. That adaptation can distort factual reasoning: a model may bend facts toward what a user seems to believe. The authors work to understand this failure and to mitigate it.

Personalization is spreading into assistants, tutors, and search. If it quietly trades truth for agreement, users get flattered and misled at once. The study maps when the distortion appears and what fuels it. Fixes that keep the personal touch while guarding facts would help every product that tailors a model to its user.
arxiv-2601-11100:
Zhezheng Hao and co-authors present ReCreate, a system that builds domain agents from experience. Language model agents are reshaping industry. Yet most working agents are still designed by hand, because tasks differ so widely. Building each one is labor-intensive. The authors ask the central question directly: can agents be created and adapted automatically in the wild?

ReCreate drives both reasoning and creation with accumulated experience. Past runs become the material for better agents. If the loop holds, agent design shifts from craft to cultivation. The work speaks to teams that deploy agents across many niches and cannot hand-tune each one.
arxiv-2601-11400:
Shuai Yuan and nine coauthors map wetlands from sparse labels in this work. Their 2026 preprint joins satellite time series with a SAM variant. Wetland maps are vital for ecosystem tracking and care. Dense pixel labels for training are too costly to make.

In practice, only sparse point labels are at hand. Deep models trained on so little tend to struggle. Wetlands also shift with seasons and across years. One date of imagery misses much of that change. Errors of omission and commission then pile up. The team adds a temporal-aware segment anything model. Time series plus that model aim at maps from few labels. The goal is sound wetland maps at a sane labeling cost.
arxiv-2601-11800:
Huy Q. Nguyen and Noah Stevenson study large waves that travel on a fluid in a porous layer. The fluid is two dimensional and sits at a set depth. Gravity holds it to a flat, hard base, and air at fixed pressure sits on top.

The top is a free surface with no surface tension in their setup. Flow in the layer obeys Darcy's law, used for flow through stone and soil. Large waves are hard to treat, since small wave maths fail. Their work adds proof on how such big surface waves behave in this porous case.
arxiv-2601-11900:
Shiheng Zhang and Jingwei Hu present a fast method for a hard flow system that mixes free flight, fields, and crashes. The system is the Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck set. It models charged parts in plasma and gas.

Their low-rank method splits the crash term into parts that act on speed alone and space alone. That split makes the low-rank steps cheap. Their time steps also cope with stiff crash terms. Fast, sound tools for this system aid fusion and plasma design.  Plain forms help users test code for this flow case.  Such forms also aid tests of disk and flow code.
arxiv-2601-12200:
Mingyang Gong, Adiesha Liyanage, Braeden Sopp, and Binhai Zhu start the study of maximal repeating patterns in a single string. A maximal pattern is one that cannot be grown, though it may not be the longest. Like tasks on two or more strings were studied from 2019 by Hirota and Sakai.

The one-string case is new ground in their work. Repeating patterns help compress text and find motifs in bio data. Algorithms for the maximal case can be faster than for the maximum. The team set out the problem and its first results.
arxiv-2601-12700:
Haolin Chen works on audio question answering, where a model hears a sound clip and answers questions about it. He uses a method from statistics called variational inference. It treats the weights of a model as ranges, not fixed points. That way, the model can show how sure it is as it trains.

Chen applies a recent tool for this task, called IVON. He fine tunes a large model that works with both sound and text. A model that knows its own doubt gives answers users can trust more. Its stated trust in an answer is more likely to match how often it is right. The study tests if this gain holds for hard tasks that mix sound with words.
arxiv-2601-13300:
Yow-Fu Liou, Yu-Chien Tang, Yu-Hsiang Liu, and An-Zi Yen test how extra choices sway large language models. Test sets for such models are key to map skill, caps, and calm. Past work showed that cues past the core task can sway a model's pick. Social cues, frame, and stray orders all count.

Their bench is called OI-Bench, for option injection. It adds a directive laden choice to a task and checks if the model takes the bait. A model that flips for a stray choice is weak where it counts. For teams that grade models, the bench adds a test of nerve that plain skill tests miss.
arxiv-2601-13400:
Nhat Thanh Tran, Kevin Bui, and Jack Xin smooth pics with a deep prior plus a sharp edge guard. Pic smoothing keeps big forms, such as strong edges and rims, and wipes fine grain and texture. Old tools use local stats or solve an opt task. New deep tools score well but need a hand picked train set.

Their tool needs no train set. It uses a deep image prior, the bias of a net's own plan toward true pic forms. It adds an L0 gradient guard, a term that counts edge jumps and keeps the count low. That guard holds strong edges while grain is wiped. For pic teams, a train free smoother that keeps edges is a handy base tool.
arxiv-2601-13500:
Ashwani Anand and co-authors grant plan templates that let two foes move at once in graph games. Two player games on graphs are a firm base to model a system next to its world. In concurrent play both sides pick a move at the same step. That form fits the sync acts of cyber physical systems.

Yet such games see thin use in real system design. One block is how plans are stated. A plan template states a class of good plans in brief form. The team treats permissive templates, which keep all moves that stay in the class. Such templates may make concurrent games apt for design teams to use.
arxiv-2601-13600:
Paul He, Elke Kirschbaum, and Shiva Kasiviswanathan study how to check if a large set of facts fits together in 2026. Tasks like fact checks, short summaries, and knowledge bases all need facts that do not clash. Large language models can judge small groups of facts for clashes. But their calls are noisy, and pair-by-pair checks can miss clashes that span the whole set.

The team lays the base math for global checks with such flawed judges. They ask what can still be known when each small check may err. The work maps the limits of trust in model-based checks. It also points to where extra care or proof is a must.
arxiv-2601-13800:
Mukul Dwivedi, Ruben Gutendorf, and Andreas Rupp build a numeric method for a nonlocal wave equation in 2026. The equation blends Camassa-Holm and Kadomtsev-Petviashvili models in two dimensions. It holds a nonlocal operator that links far points, which is hard to compute. Their method is a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme.

Cartesian meshes with tensor-product polynomial spaces split x and y work apart. An auxiliary variable turns the nonlocal term into a local one. That trick allows efficient element-by-element computation. Fast solvers help model shallow water waves and plasma flows. The method keeps the hard part of the work in small local steps. Teams that model waves can use it to cut cost and time in their codes.
arxiv-2601-13900:
Michal Parnas surveys two rank measures for matrices and their link to a classic one in 2026. Binary rank and Boolean rank count how a matrix splits into simple parts. Real rank is the standard version taught in linear algebra. The survey covers both the math and the computational sides of the topic.

Parnas reviews the basic definitions and main alternative formulations. Computational complexity of these ranks gets full treatment. Their deep connection to communication complexity is also covered. Such ranks matter for data compression, logic, and network coding. The text is a good first stop for new students of these ranks. It pulls math and code views into one clear map.
arxiv-2601-14100:
Guilherme Inacio and co-authors propose a light-based probe for a subtle break in relativity in 2026. Some materials lack a center of symmetry, and their optical response can reveal hidden effects. The team targets emergent Lorentz symmetry violation in such noncentrosymmetric materials. Lorentz symmetry is a core pillar of modern physics.

Their protocol is electrically controlled and uses the second-order shift photocurrent. In a spinful Rice-Mele model, a stationary violating background changes the Bloch Hamiltonian. That change adds an odd-in-field term to the shift current. A tabletop probe could test physics once thought to need huge machines. The test uses light that a lab can make and read with care. A clear odd-in-field mark would be hard to fake with plain effects.
arxiv-2601-14900: A French text in the file states the theorem long known as Catalan's conjecture. It says that no two whole numbers next to each other, apart from 8 and 9, can both be exact powers. The entry is credited to the theorem proved by Mihăilescu. The text gives the claim in its classic short form, with a note that the words come from a letter by E. Catalan.
arxiv-2601-15000:
Christos Petridis and Konstantinos Pelechrinis rate basketball lineups, the groups of five players who share the court. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a stat called adjusted plus-minus. It tries to credit each lineup for how the team scores while it plays.

The hard part is sparse data. Players swap in and out all game long. Many lineups share the court for only a few plays. The authors add informed priors, prior beliefs built from known facts, to steady the ratings. Their method is named Lineup Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus, or L-RAPM for short.
arxiv-2601-15100:
Yanwei Huang and Arpit Narechania design help for people who make decisions on the web. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with web AI agents such as ChatGPT Agent and GenSpark. People use them for routine tasks, but the agents wait for typed prompts.

They also miss chances to act first, and they give no support for hands-on data study. The authors present WebSeek, a design probe. It aims to guide users in two modes: proactive hints before they ask, and reactive help once they do. The probe tests how such guidance could feel in use.
arxiv-2601-15300:
Weiwei Wang, Jiyong Min, and Weijie Zou find the point where long inputs start to break a language model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with intelligence degradation: performance falls off a cliff as context nears a critical length. The drop exceeds thirty percent on a composite of tasks.

The fall happens even when the long input stays relevant. That limits real uses that need long-context understanding. The authors pin down the critical threshold. They use the natural length distribution of texts to find where the break begins, rather than testing at round numbers alone.
arxiv-2601-15500:
Saptarshi Roy, Alessandro Rinaldo, and Purnamrita Sarkar study a popular image-generation method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The method is rectified flow, prized for fast, high-quality sampling. Real data often lie near a low-dimensional structure inside a large space. A good sampler should exploit that fact to run faster. The authors ask how well rectified flow does so on its own.

Their lens joins two viewpoints, per the title. One comes from diffusion methods. The other comes from stochastic localization, a tool from probability theory. Together they frame how the method adapts to low-dimensional support. The question matters for practice, not just theory. If adaptation is automatic, users get speed without extra tuning. If not, the paper points to where help is needed.
arxiv-2601-15700:
Anthony Lee classifies subgroups of the Bianchi group in a 2026 arXiv paper. The group in view is PSL(2, Z[sqrt(-2)]), built from matrices over a ring of algebraic integers. Inside it sit Fuchsian subgroups, which act on the hyperbolic plane. Lee describes the maximal nonelementary ones. Maximal means they cannot be enlarged within the class. Nonelementary marks the rich, non-degenerate cases.

His description is explicit, per the abstract. Each conjugacy class of such subgroups appears as integral orders of certain quaternion algebras. Those algebras are indefinite and defined over the rationals. Classification results like this give a complete map of a group's large pieces. Geometers and number theorists both use Bianchi groups, so the map serves two audiences.
arxiv-2601-16000:
Hao-Hsuan Chen and Ching-Ming Lee reframe the theory of a spin-based device in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their devices are non-collinear antiferromagnetic spin-torque oscillators. Such oscillators could serve as fast, compact signal sources. The authors unify spin dynamics under the Poisson bracket formalism. They move away from the usual torque-based accounts. Their new view rests on continuous operational symmetry. Two linked viewpoints follow from it.

A vector view reveals special states of the system. Infinitely many degenerate rigid body precession states arise. The exchange energy depends only on the rotational change involved, they note. The title adds hysteretic excitation and a terminal velocity view of the motion. A symmetry-first account can simplify how engineers think about these oscillators and their switching.
arxiv-2601-16100:
Rogelio Orozco-Duarte and coauthors model hot bubbles blown by dying stars. Their 2026 preprint is the third in a chain on such nebulae. A hot bubble forms when a fast wind hits slow gas shed by the star. The glow in X rays tells of the heat and mix in the bubble. This part adds winds of the Wolf Rayet type.

The team runs wind and glow models with the new wind type. They ask how the strong wind shifts bubble shape and X ray glow. Clear shifts would help read real nebulae with such stars at heart. The work links wind force to what space scopes see. It builds on the past two parts of the chain.
arxiv-2601-16200:
Song Xia and four coauthors give proof bounds for attacks on models that join sight and words. Their 2026 preprint deals with large models that take pics and text. Small tweaks to a pic can bend the deep code of the model. Bent code then leads to wrong picks by the model. Past guards oft lack firm proof that they hold.

The team smooths the deep code space to gain such proof. Smooth code gives a zone where no tweak can flip the pick. Proof zones tell users when a pick can be trusted. That trust counts for high stakes use of such models. The work adds a guard with maths to back it.
arxiv-2601-16300:
Alexander Savin shows that graphene bubbles can hold in more than one firm state. His 2026 preprint deals with tiny bubbles of graphene on flat bases. Gas atoms sit in the bubble, drawn from argon, krypton and xenon. Each bubble can rest in a set of firm states. Each state has its own count of atom layers in the clump.

More than one rest state makes the bubble a multi firm system. The state in use rests on how the bubble was formed. Such traits could serve in tiny stores or sense gear. They also warn that one bubble need not act the same twice. The work maps the states for three gases.
arxiv-2601-16600:
T. M. Shneidman and R. G. Nazmitdinov study a strange form of atomic nucleus. In their picture, two heavy nuclei join like parts of one molecule. The pair spins and shakes as a linked pair. Their 2026 preprint builds the math for this pair. They call the joined form a nuclear molecule.

The authors first write the energy rules for the two-part system. They then solve those rules with a set of round math tools. From that work they get clear formulas. The formulas tell how the joined nucleus can be stirred up. Such states are stretched far from a round shape. The study aids our grasp of how heavy nuclei fuse and split.
arxiv-2601-16700:
Ludwig Felder, Tobias Eisenreich, Mahsa Fischer, Stefan Wagner, and Chunyang Chen survey German software firms. Their 2026 preprint asks how deep AI tools have spread in that trade. Such tools now write, test, and fix code in many shops. Use rates climb month by month. Yet raw rates hide how well the tools are used.

The team probes what drives firm, deep use of the tools. They weigh skill, firm rules, and years on the job. Their poll shows where use is broad but thin. It also shows where use is deep and sound. Firms can use these facts to train staff. They can also set rules that help, not block, good use.
arxiv-2601-16800:
Gaurav Negi, M. A. Waskow, and Paul Buitelaar test if chatbots can tag fine views in text. Fine tags mark who a view aims at, not just its tone. Such tags take long hours of human work. Crowds must tag each view by hand. Their 2026 preprint asks if big models can take that load.

The team tries models as the first tag hands. They also try models as judges when hands clash. Sound tags would cut the cost of view polls. Brands and states track views to shape their acts. The tests show where bots help and where they slip.
arxiv-2601-16900:
Madeline Lisaius, Srinivasan Keshav, Andrew Blake, and Clement Atzberger map crops in Senegal from space shots. Crop maps back food plans and aid for small farms. Yet most space-based maps fail on small farm plots. Plots there are tiny, mixed, and shift oft. Their 2026 preprint works in the Groundnut Basin of Senegal. It builds maps from learned shot codes, called embeddings.

Codes pack each shot's traits in a compact form. The team tests how well codes sort crop types. Small farm zones need maps that fit their scale. Sound maps can guide seed, water, and aid plans. They also track how rains shift farm health.
arxiv-2601-17000:
Jie Gao, Shasha Li, Jianhua Zhang, Shan Li, and Tingting Wang track how students pace their own study with AI tutors. AI tutors now guide study in many schools. Self-paced study skill drives gains in such halls. That skill shifts step by step as students work. Their 2026 preprint reads those shift chains in tutor logs.

Chains show which study moves tend to follow which. Some chains end in deep work, some in drift. The team reads chains from a GenAI tutor's logs. Clear chain maps can help tutors nudge good moves. They can also flag students who drift to poor chains.
arxiv-2601-17100:
Arash Azizi shows how a split path can mute or wake a heat sense in quantum bits. A lone sense bit, flown on sped paths, feels heat from its rush. That feel is called the Unruh response. His 2026 preprint puts the bit's core in two sped paths at once. The paths stay apart in space the whole way.

At read-out, the path mark is wiped by the read choice. That wipe can mute the heat feel to nil. Or it can bring the feel back in full. Such tricks test deep links of heat, speed, and chance. They may aid fine sensors in years ahead.
arxiv-2601-17400:
Zhe Li, Mélanie Prague, Rodolphe Thiébaut, and Quentin Clairon present a new way to fit drug and disease models. Their models are nonlinear mixed-effects models built on ordinary differential equations. Data come from many subjects over time. The standard fit tool is likelihood-based and leans on Monte Carlo steps. It can be slow and fragile in mid-size problems.

The team uses a variational autoencoder instead. Their design is identifiability-aware, so it flags traits the data cannot pin down. That honesty matters in health research. Wrong certainty can mislead dose and care choices. A faster, aware fit tool could widen use of rich models in clinics and trials.
arxiv-2601-17500:
Emmanouil Georgios Lionis and five co-authors ask a small question with big search effects. Should learned sparse retrieval use cased or uncased models? Sparse methods build word-based vectors for queries and texts. Inverted indexes then search them fast. Past work used uncased backbones near by default. Uncased text drops case marks, which cuts word mismatch.

New top language models, though, keep case. The team tests the choice in learned sparse search. Case can split names and terms that lowercasing merges. It can also split one word into rare shards. Their study gives builders proof for a base choice. Search quality can hinge on such quiet details.
arxiv-2601-17600:
Mikheil Amaglobeli and Alexey Myasnikov study tensor completions of nilpotent groups. The groups are finitely generated, torsion-free, and of class two. Completions are taken in a quasivariety of R-exponential groups. R is a binomial integral domain. Tensor completion extends a group's scalars in a controlled way. It is a base step in model theory of groups.

Such completions let algebraists move groups into richer settings. Results here pin down the class-two case in full. Nilpotent groups model systems with layered commutators. Their theory feeds cryptography and geometry as well. A firm completion theory makes those uses safer. The work closes a clear gap in the theory.
arxiv-2601-17800:
Thanawat Sornwanee argues that a recent claim in optimization rests on a math error. His 2026 preprint examines a 2025 paper on differentiable integer linear programming. Integer programs choose whole-number values, and making them smooth enough for gradient methods is a prized trick. The earlier paper claimed such a method in its fifth theorem. Sornwanee shows that the proof of that claim is wrong.

The stakes go past one paper. Later work has already built on the same flawed step, so the error spreads. A clear notice of the fault helps others avoid building on sand. Work of this kind is part of how a field keeps its results sound. Readers get a warning plus a close look at where the proof fails.
arxiv-2601-18400:
Andrei Lebedev and Vincent Gramoli ask a plain question that had not been put to a test: how much net traffic does each blockchain plan burn? New plans for shared ledgers have grown fast in the past few years. Each plan asks home nodes to swap notes with peers, and that swap has a cost in data flow.

No past study had set the plans side by side on that cost. The pair run the first such test, with the same yard stick for each plan. Home users who host a node pay for the flow in time and in fees, so the count counts for them. A clear chart of flow cost could help teams pick a ledger that small hosts can still afford to run.
arxiv-2601-18500:
Chen Liang and eleven colleagues tackle a kind of missing data that breaks the usual fix. In most sets, a blank cell can be filled by a guess from the rest. Here some cells are blank by rule: the value cannot exist at all, given the facts of the case. A child with no job has no wage to fill in. The blank can also hinge on facts that are hid or on blanks in the next cells.

Plain fill-in tools treat such blanks as if the value were just lost. That misread can bend all that comes from the set. The team build a way to learn from such sets that is close to the best one could do. Their work serves fields like health and law, where blanks by rule are the norm. Sound tools for such sets could stop false claims built on bad fills.
arxiv-2601-18800:
Yoontae Hwang and six colleagues build NavFormer, a tool that reads where a craft points from the Earth's field while the craft turns. A cheap chip feels the field on three lines. As the craft turns, the read on each line shifts, though the full strength of the field stays the same. Tools that chase the line reads chase that turn noise. The true mark to chase is the full strength, set by a world chart of the field.

NavFormer chases that full mark. It builds its traits so that turns can't shift them, and it firms the spread of each batch of reads. A firm read of the field could guide craft with no need for sky marks. That serves subs, drones, and craft deep in mines or seas. The work ties a world chart to a learn tool in a new way.
arxiv-2601-19100:
Md Rayhanul Masud and three co-authors survey how to pay software agents for good work. Reinforcement learning now trains models for coding tasks: writing, fixing, testing, and speeding up code. In many classic settings the reward is one clear number, but software quality is not one number.

A reward that is easy to count may miss what makes code good, like clarity or safety. The team reviews how rewards for software tasks are built and where they mislead. Sound reward design is the hinge of the whole field, since agents grow into whatever the reward truly measures.
arxiv-2601-20300:
Jing Xu and four colleagues extend self-supervised speech models to new languages without losing the old ones. Such models learn strong speech representations, but they are limited to the languages seen in pretraining. Retraining from scratch for new languages is costly, while training in sequence often erases earlier skill, a failure called catastrophic forgetting.

Their method, MiLorE-SSL, scales multilingual ability while guarding past languages. The balance matters for speech tools in regions whose languages were absent from the first training run. Adding a language without breaking others makes voice technology fairer across the world.
arxiv-2601-20600:
Junmin An, Ji-Hoon Hong, Jon-Lark Kim, and Haeun Lim study the shortest embeddings of linear codes into LCD codes. LCD codes, whose hull is trivial, are counterparts of self-orthogonal codes and are prized in coding theory. Recent work on self-orthogonal embeddings produced some optimal codes, which raises the natural question for LCD codes.

The authors ask how short an LCD code can be while still containing a given binary, ternary, or quaternary linear code. Short embeddings matter because code length is cost: every extra symbol is bandwidth. Optimal LCD embeddings would extend a fruitful line of code design.
arxiv-2601-20800:
Kaito Baba, Yoshihiko Ozaki, and Shuhei Watanabe tackle a bookkeeping problem in machine learning tuning. Their 2026 paper concerns hyperparameter importance: which settings of a model matter most. Tools like PED-ANOVA estimate that importance fast, inside the best regions of the search space. But they assume every setting is always present. Real search spaces are conditional.

In a conditional space, one setting can switch another on or off. It can also change the range a setting may take. The original tool cannot handle such cases in a sound way. The authors propose conditional PED-ANOVA to fill that gap. It estimates importance while respecting which settings are active. The work helps tuners spend effort on the knobs that truly drive results.
arxiv-2601-20900:
Sergio Burdisso and a large team of co-authors adapt speech recognition using text alone. Their 2026 paper studies LLM-based automatic speech recognition in new domains. Text-only adaptation is a significant yet underexplored challenge. New domains offer plenty of text but little transcribed speech. Standard fine-tuning trains the language model on that target text. The risk is real, though.

Such tuning can disrupt the alignment between speech and text. That alignment is learned by the projector that joins the two. Once it degrades, recognition gets worse, not better. The authors turn to text denoising as the adaptation signal. Denoising teaches domain language while respecting the speech link. The method promises domain gains without new audio data. It suits call centers and clinics where text is plentiful but recordings are scarce.
arxiv-2601-21000:
Muhammad Ali Shafique and four co-authors build a reasoning test for a language with few such tools. Their 2026 paper introduces UrduBench. Large language models now reason well in English. Evaluating them in low-resource languages remains challenging. Urdu reasoning tests have been limited by fragile machine translation. They also favored general language tasks over true reasoning. UrduBench aims to fix both flaws.

The team built contextually ensembled translations. Multiple translation passes are combined for fidelity. A human-in-the-loop step checks the results. The benchmark then probes reasoning, not just fluency. Such tools matter for the hundreds of millions who speak low-resource languages. UrduBench gives model builders a fair scoreboard for Urdu. It also offers a recipe other languages can copy.
arxiv-2601-21500:
Tim Tomov, Dominik Fuchsgruber, and Stephan Günnemann make language model answers respect the hidden structure of the task. Many replies carry an inner form, such as a label, a number, or a graph. Standard decoding and uncertainty tools work only on the text and ignore that form.

The authors model outputs directly in a latent space shaped by the task. Knowing the task in advance improves both the answers and the model's sense of its own doubt. A model that knows it is choosing a label can weigh options more sanely. The gain is better calibration where answers feed real decisions.
arxiv-2601-21600:
Kshitij Mishra, Mirat Aubakirov, Martin Takac, Nils Lukas, and Salem Lahlou let language models teach each other during training. Models make different reasoning mistakes: on one problem, one model's split of the task works while another's fails. That spread is usually wasted.

Their framework, CoRe, turns a peer's success into a learning signal through cross teaching. When one model solves a case, its path becomes a lesson for the others. Training together this way spreads strengths across the group. The method aims at model teams that end up individually stronger, not just collectively lucky.
arxiv-2601-21800:
Dionizije Fa and co-authors introduce a test suite for artificial intelligence agents that do bioinformatics work. Modern agents promise to run whole analyses on request. But the field lacks shared ways to measure how well they perform and how robust they are. BioAgent Bench, presented in this 2026 preprint, is built to fill that gap.

The benchmark holds curated end-to-end tasks, including RNA sequencing analysis, variant calling, and metagenomics. Each prompt names the concrete output files the agent must produce, which allows automated checking of results. The suite also stress-tests agents under controlled disturbances. Shared benchmarks like this let labs compare agents fairly and spot failures before the tools reach real research pipelines.
arxiv-2601-21900:
Large foundation models can be manipulated by adversarial inputs, and most defenses rest on a locality idea. Find the isolated neurons or features that carry the harmful behavior, and suppress them. The 2026 preprint behind this entry argues that this picture is wrong in a way that matters.

Harmful meanings, the author contends, act as distributed circuits spread across layers, not as single switches. Interventions aimed at one spot are therefore brittle, and they tend to damage the model's usefulness as well. A defense that respects how meaning is actually spread through a network would need to work at the level of those circuits. The argument speaks to anyone deploying large models in settings where attacks are a real threat.
arxiv-2601-22500:
R. Elliott and a large team map the gas that floats above the discs of nine star-forming galaxies. Their 2026 preprint comes from GECKOS, a large program on the Very Large Telescope that targets edge-on galaxies much like the Milky Way. The MUSE tool reads the gas at fine scale.

The team trace a layer of charged gas above each disc, and winds that blow clear of the galaxy. That gas tells how stars feed energy back into space. It also shows how galaxies lose or recycle their fuel. The maps give a close look at a key life process of galaxies.
arxiv-2601-22600:
Shoma Nameki, Atsuyoshi Nakamura, Junpei Komiyama, and Koji Tabata give an efficient method for a threshold form of Monte Carlo tree search. Tree search guides game and planning agents by sampling paths. Their 2026 preprint asks a yes-no form: is the root value at least a set threshold?

Answering just that, rather than the full value, can save much work. Their method spends samples where the verdict is in doubt. The trick suits any setting with a pass bar, from games to verification. It is a leaner question, sharply answered.
arxiv-2601-22900:
Xuancheng Li and four co-authors improve how language models learn from feedback given in words. Reward-based training often gives only a single score, which is sparse and vague. On failed tries, a low score says the answer was wrong but not why it failed.

Their loop, MulFeRL, feeds verbal feedback back into training over several turns. Detailed comments can point at the exact step that went astray. Richer feedback should teach reasoning skills faster than scores alone, especially on hard problems where most first tries fail. Verbal feedback shines exactly on failed samples, where a plain score carries almost no usable teaching signal at all.
arxiv-2601-23100:
Manuel Houzet, Julia S. Meyer, and Yuli V. Nazarov study a superconducting qubit in an unusual state. The Josephson effect, supercurrent through a weak link, is the core of superconducting quantum circuits. A recent prediction says its quantum mechanics change fundamentally when a quasiparticle sits trapped in an Andreev bound state.

That trapped case is the odd parity sector, unlike the well-known even one. The authors work out the bound states there in detail. Odd-parity physics could open new qubit designs, or reveal error channels to avoid. The odd parity sector was predicted to differ fundamentally from the even one, and the authors develop that sector's mechanics.
arxiv-2601-23200:
Lorenzo Emer, Marco Lippi, Andrea Mina, and Andrea Vandin test language models on patent classification. Assigning CPC codes to patents underpins large studies of technological change. The task is hierarchical, multi-label, and heavily imbalanced, with many rare categories.

Encoder models from before generative AI remain the standard for this job. The authors weigh the strengths and trade-offs of newer language models, focusing on the long tail of rare classes. Better classification of rare technologies improves how we track emerging fields. Rare and weakly represented categories are where language models are tested hardest, since encoders trained on frequency dominate there.
arxiv-2603-01900:
Antal Jakovac shows how a weak interaction can turn strong at low energies when a singularity appears. His 2026 work studies renormalization group flow, the math that tracks how couplings change with energy scale. An operator classed as irrelevant at high energy should fade in the infrared, the low-energy end.

An infrared Landau pole, a blow-up in the flow, can flip that verdict entirely. His example is the four-fermion interaction, which can bind particles into composite states. The pole here does not come from a single singular loop, as in plain perturbation theory. Instead it comes from the endless tower of modes that enter the flow itself. The result warns that relevance labels from perturbation theory can mislead when collective modes pile up at low energy.
arxiv-2603-02100:
Arun Verma, Manjesh Kumar Hanawal, and Arun Rajkumar work on choice under doubt in this 2026 paper. The setting is the multi-armed bandit, where a learner picks among options and learns from rewards. Extra side data, called control variates, can sharpen reward guesses. Past work assumed that side data arrives in every round.

Real networks rarely give help that often, so the team built UCB-LCV for patchy help. Their method blends reward data and side data into tighter bounds. With no side data at all, a spin-off method beats older ones for normal rewards. Versions for other reward shapes are also given. Tests show the new method beats rival bandit methods overall.
arxiv-2603-02200:
Moru Liu, Hao Dong, Olga Fink, and Mario Trapp work on catching model failures in this 2026 paper. Models that mix image, text, and sound now serve in cars and clinics. When such a model fails, users need a warning, not just a wrong answer. The authors spot a clue: in most failures, the joint answer is less sure than one single-source answer.

Their method trains models to avoid that surety drop, which they call confidence loss. A loss term punishes any drop during training. They also swap features across sources to fake hard failure cases for practice. Across four data sets and three source types, the method gave steady, strong gains. It helps high-stakes systems flag and reject doubtful calls.
arxiv-2603-02300:
Zhong-Bo Kang, Robert Kao, Meijian Li, and Jani Penttala derive a new probe of dense gluon matter in this 2026 paper. Deep inelastic scattering knocks electrons off protons to reveal their inner parts. At very high energy, gluons crowd so densely that they saturate. The authors study a one-point energy correlator, which tracks energy flow at one angle.

Working inside the Color Glass Condensate frame, they give formulas for that correlator. A sum rule cancels messy fragmentation effects, leaving one clean input. That input is the dipole amplitude, a direct window on gluon saturation. Sample calculations for the future Electron-Ion Collider show sizable nuclear suppression. The observable looks highly sensitive to saturation, making it a sharp tool for the new machine.
arxiv-2603-03300:
Mohamed Afane and three colleagues benchmark artificial intelligence tools that survey state laws for lawyers. Their 2026 paper uses LaborBench, built from a slow manual count of every state's unemployment insurance rules by Department of Labor attorneys. Earlier tests found standard retrieval-augmented generation right only about seven times in ten on yes-or-no questions.

Three newer tools face the same test here. A custom research assistant, STARA, does far better, while the Westlaw and LexisNexis products score worse than the older standard method. Close error analysis then surprises everyone: many supposed machine errors were omissions by the human attorneys, lifting STARA's true score further.
