A vital force in the body runs through the talks as the first key idea. Kent adds how a person becomes open to illness, and the rule of one remedy at a time. He also explains potentization, the step-by-step dilution said to free a drug's power. Doctors trained in his school shaped homeopathic practice for decades.
king-henry-vi-part-1-pg1500:
This edition of Shakespeare's Henry the Sixth, Part One prints a full cast and a scene plan for the five acts. Henry the Sixth heads the list, with the dukes of Gloucester, Bedford, and Exeter among his uncles. The French side names King Charles, his bastard son, and Joan la Pucelle. Talbot, England's captain, stands among the soldiers.

The contents move from Westminster Abbey and London streets to Orleans and the Tower. Rouen, Paris, and Bordeaux carry the French war to its close. The plan shows two stories at once: England losing France town by town, and English lords quarreling at home. The Temple Garden rose-plucking scene sits in act two, planting the civil war to come.
knopf-aspects-of-birth-control-1900:
S. Adolphus Knopf wrote Aspects of Birth Control, issued as a cheap ten-cent pamphlet. The sample shows his paper on the moral aspects of birth control. He wrote while war in Europe was killing many young men.

Knopf says birth control does not have to mean race suicide, as critics claimed. He argues it should raise the health and vigor of the next generation. His plea aims at fewer children born with serious weakness. The pamphlet preserves an early medical voice in a heated public debate. Knopf frames his case as a moral duty, not a scandal. That framing shows how reformers argued inside a hostile climate.
kuyper-work-of-holy-spirit-1900:
Abraham Kuyper was a Dutch theologian who also served as prime minister of the Netherlands. His Work of the Holy Spirit, in this 1900 English edition, is his Reformed pneumatology, the doctrine of the Spirit's work. Kuyper writes as statesman and churchman at once.

He traces the Spirit's work in creation, in the church's common life, and in the individual heart's rebirth and growth. Against both cold orthodoxy and shallow revivalism, he stresses the Spirit's quiet, sovereign, and thorough action. Reformed readers still treat the book as the fullest classic treatment of its theme. English readers met in Kuyper a mind at home in pulpit, press, and parliament.
l-initiation-alchimique-treize-lettres-i:
Albert Poisson wrote L'Initiation Alchimique, printed in Paris in 1900. Its subtitle promises thirteen unpublished letters. Those letters concern the practice of the Great Work, the central aim of alchemy.

The book appeared under the imprint of Édition de l'Initiation. It even carries a portrait of its author. Poisson wrote for readers drawn to France's occult revival. His letters offer guidance in the old art, presented as direct personal teaching rather than dry history. Letters let Poisson speak as a guide rather than a historian. The unpublished claim adds a sense of private doctrine shared openly.
larmor-aether-and-matter-1900:
Joseph Larmor, an Irish sage who worked at Cambridge, built his most deep ether scheme in this book of 1900. It came out just five years before Einstein changed the field for good. Larmor sought a scheme in which the ether could bear all the new finds.

At its heart stand electrons, tiny charged parts that strain the ether round them. From their moves he draws light, magnetism, and the drag of fast bodies through space. The book is the most fine spun ether scheme ever made, and a peak of the old physics.
le-petit-rosaire-extract-on-alchemy-from: Le Petit Rosaire is an extract on alchemy drawn from the Roman de la Rose. Its record dates it to 1600. The hosted sample survives only as garbled scan marks. The title still identifies the piece and its source. It shows how later readers mined a famous love poem for alchemical teaching. Such extracts treated the Rose as a coded book of secrets.
leechbook-no-1-1400: Leechbook, no. 1, 1400. The medieval medical book. This book preserves that manuscript. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
london-son-of-the-wolf-1900:
Jack London published The Son of the Wolf in 1900, his first book, after struggling through years of rejections. London had rushed to the Klondike gold fields in 1897 and come home sick and empty-handed, but rich in material. These stories were the first Klondike tales to reach a wide public.

The tales follow miners, prospectors, and Native people through a frozen world ruled by what London called the White Silence. Malemute Kid, his recurring hero, settles disputes and saves lives with rough frontier justice. Greed, cold, and dog teams drive the plots. London's terse, muscular style made the far North vivid to readers who would never see snow like it. The book made his name.
love-and-life-an-old-story-in-eighteenth:

mark-twain-s-letters-volume-4-1886-1900:

maspero-passing-of-empires-1900:
Gaston Maspero ends his grand tale in The Passing of the Empires, in English from 1900. The tome spans from 850 years ere Christ to 330, the age of Alexander. One realm past the next takes the lead of the old East, then fades: Assyria, Babylon, Persia, and at last the Greeks at the gate.

mermaid-wonderful-prophecy-whitehaven-18:

morris-man-and-his-ancestor-1900:

mother-shipton-prophecies-1700:
Mother Shipton was a famed English folk seer, said to have lived in Yorkshire in the days of Henry VIII. This set of her life and forecasts came out as a cheap chapbook in 1700. Chapbooks were small, cheap books sold by men who walked from town to town.

novalis-hymns-to-the-night-1800:

plaw-106-173-2000:

plaw-106-174-2000:

plaw-106-175-2000:

The findings trace a career that moved between church and military. Born in Philadelphia in 1920, O'Connor joined the Navy Chaplains Corps in 1952 and saw combat action in Vietnam. He rose to Chief of Chaplains of the Navy, with the rank of rear admiral. Pope John Paul II made him a bishop in 1979, archbishop of New York in 1984, and cardinal in 1985. plaw-106-176-2000: Fixing small errors in park law is the whole content of Public Law 106-176, the Omnibus Parks Technical Corrections Act of 2000. Sample fixes in the Presidio of San Francisco sections change one verb's tense, repair a misspelling of administered, and correct a cross-reference. Another added sentence lets federal agencies sign agreements and leases with the Presidio Trust. The act was approved on March 10, 2000.

Those records inform risk checks and foster care placements, including protection against child sexual abuse. Byrne grant money is also opened to enforcing child abuse laws. Another use supports joint programs between police and media groups to gather and share useful information.
plaw-106-178-2000:

The President must report every foreign person credibly shown to have made such a transfer on or after January 1, 1999. The lists cover nuclear supplier guidelines and missile technology controls. They also cover chemical and biological weapons lists and dual-use goods. Reports go to the House International Relations Committee and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
plaw-106-179-2000:
Contracts that tie up tribal land for years need a federal check under the Indian Tribal Economic Development and Contract Encouragement Act of 2000, Public Law 106-179. The act rewrites an old Revised Statutes section on agreements with Indian tribes. Its preamble also points to disclosing tribal sovereign immunity in contracts.

No agreement encumbering Indian lands for seven years or more is valid without the approval of the Secretary of the Interior, or the secretary's designee. The secretary must refuse approval when a deal violates federal law. Refusal also follows when the contract lacks a provision for remedies in case of breach. Some agreements the secretary finds outside the rule are exempt from the approval demand.
plaw-106-180-2000:
Satellite communications were pushed toward private markets by the ORBIT Act, Public Law 106-180, in 2000. Its full name is the Open-market Reorganization for the Betterment of International Telecommunications Act. The act amends the Communications Satellite Act of 1962. Its stated purpose is a fully open world market for satellite services.

The path there runs through fully selling off the satellite bodies owned jointly by many nations, INTELSAT and Inmarsat. The act adds a new title on rivalry and sell-offs to the 1962 law. Under it, the Federal Communications Commission may license split-off firms only after deciding the license will not harm competition. The same test covers renewals, transfers, and use of their space segment by American firms.
plaw-106-181-2000:
Airports and the Federal Aviation Administration were funded anew by Public Law 106-181, the Wendell H. Ford Aviation Investment and Reform Act for the 21st Century. The act amends title 49 of the United States Code. Its first title is called Airport and Airway Improvements.

Funding parts cover the airport improvement program, airway sites, and the agency's running costs. Formula changes and fees on travelers get their own parts. Airport building parts follow, naming runway safety devices and emergency call boxes. Wind shear tools, paving upkeep, and better pilot vision tools also appear in the contents.
plaw-106-182-2000:
Retirees who keep working won relief from Public Law 106-182, the Senior Citizens' Freedom to Work Act of 2000. The act amends title II of the Social Security Act to eliminate the earnings test for people who have reached retirement age. Until then, the test's key age in the statute was seventy.

The amendments move through section 203 of the Social Security Act replacing that age, phrase by phrase. Seventy becomes retirement age, as a separate section of the act defines it. A following section turns off the rules for computing the exempt amount for people at retirement age. The change took effect with approval on April 7, 2000.
plaw-106-183-2000: Hamilton, New Jersey, lends its name to the post office renamed by Public Law 106-183. The post office building at 680 U.S. Highway 130 became the John K. Rafferty Hamilton Post Office Building. The House passed the act in October 1999, the Senate followed in April 2000, and it was approved on April 13, 2000. Under its references section, federal records mentioning the building use the Rafferty name.
plaw-106-184-2000: A California post office was designated for Joseph Ileto under Public Law 106-184, approved on April 14, 2000. The post office at 14071 Peyton Drive in Chino Hills became the Joseph Ileto Post Office. The bill passed the House in November 1999 and the Senate the following April. Any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is treated as a reference to the Joseph Ileto Post Office.
plaw-106-185-2000:
Property owners facing federal seizure gained new protections under the Civil Asset Forfeiture Reform Act of 2000, Public Law 106-185. Congress promised a more just and uniform procedure for federal civil forfeitures. The act begins by creating general rules for those proceedings.

Its contents list compensation for damage to seized property and payment of attorney fees, costs, and interest. A seizure warrant requirement appears, along with use of forfeited funds to pay restitution to crime victims. Other sections handle real property, stays, restraining orders, and a time limit for bringing actions. Fugitive disentitlement and encouraging criminal forfeiture as an alternative close out the major themes.
plaw-106-186-2000:
Peru's approaching elections troubled Congress enough to pass Public Law 106-186, a joint resolution approved on April 25, 2000. Presidential and congressional elections in Peru were set for April 9, 2000. Monitors from the Organization of American States, the National Democratic Institute, and the Carter Center had voiced grave doubts about fairness.

The resolution lists government control of electoral agencies, limits on press freedom, and harassment of opposition politicians. It states the sense of Congress that the President should warn Peru's president directly. If the world judged the elections not free and fair, the United States would review its political, economic, and military relations with Peru. It would also work with other democracies toward restoring democracy there.
plaw-106-187-2000: A small Nevada cemetery stayed in local hands through Public Law 106-187, approved on April 28, 2000. The Secretary of Agriculture must convey National Forest land to Elko County, free of charge, for continued use as a cemetery. The parcel, known as Jarbidge Cemetery, covers about two acres. The transfer also includes the bridge over the Jarbidge River that reaches it, and the road from the bridge. Elko County pays for the survey. Unusually, the United States may keep no right to take the land back.
plaw-106-188-2000: Money moved to the people of Bikini Atoll under the Bikini Resettlement and Relocation Act of 2000, Public Law 106-188. The act amends the terms of the Resettlement Trust Fund for the People of Bikini, set up under an earlier law. Three percent of the fund's market value on June 1, 1999, becomes available for an immediate payment to the Bikini people. The payment must not cut into the fund's corpus, its principal. Whatever is paid is deducted from any further such payments Congress later adds to the fund.
plaw-106-189-2000: Utah land paperwork was cleared by Public Law 106-189, approved on April 28, 2000. The Secretary of the Interior must release, without charge, the United States' reversionary interests in certain parcels in Washington County. Those leftover federal claims are shown on a 1999 map of exchange parcels. Releasing them clears the way for a land exchange the State of Utah planned to carry out. The secretary carries out the release by filing a deed of release or similar instrument.
plaw-106-190-2000: Fifteen acres of former landfill in Utah's Red Cliffs Desert Reserve are the subject of Public Law 106-190. The parcel, in Washington County, had been used as a landfill by the City of St. George. Its transfer from the city to the United States supports Washington County's habitat conservation plan for the desert tortoise. The act clarifies that the transfer gives the United States no liability it did not already hold on the transfer date. Congress approved it on April 28, 2000.
plaw-106-191-2000:
A mineral called trona, and the soda ash made from it, sits behind Public Law 106-191, an amendment to the Mineral Leasing Act. Congress found the world's largest trona body on federal land in southwestern Wyoming. Soda ash goes into glass, baking soda, detergents, and medicines. The act raises the most federal sodium lease acreage one company may hold in a single state.

The old cap, about fifteen thousand acres per state, dated to 1948 and was the act's oldest limit. It stood at a third of the coal cap and a small fraction of the oil and gas cap. Three of Wyoming's four trona producers were already near the ceiling. Congress cited modern mining technology and global competition as reasons existing mines needed more acreage to avoid closing early.
plaw-106-192-2000: New Hampshire's Lamprey River gained protected miles under Public Law 106-192, approved on May 2, 2000. The Lamprey Wild and Scenic River Extension Act amends the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. The designated recreational segment more than doubles, from eleven and a half miles to twenty-three and a half miles. It now starts at the Bunker Pond Dam in Epping rather than at the southern Lee town line. Epping joins the towns named in the river's management provisions as well.
plaw-106-193-2000: Methane hydrate, an unusual fuel source, got a federal research push from Public Law 106-193 in 2000. The Methane Hydrate Research and Development Act aims to promote finding, assessing, exploring, and developing methane hydrate resources. Its opening sections mostly build the program vocabulary. They define contracts, cooperative agreements, and grants, and they name the officials involved, including the Secretary of Energy acting through the assistant secretary for fossil energy, and the National Science Foundation's director. Universities and private industrial firms with matching skill count as partners.
plaw-106-194-2000:
Land taken from an Alaska Native community generations earlier is the grievance inside Public Law 106-194. The act amends the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act for the Elim Native Corporation. Congress found that about three hundred fifty thousand acres were withdrawn in 1917 for the Bureau of Education and Alaska Natives. Those lands formed the Norton Bay Reservation, set aside for the Native village of Elim.

In 1929, fifty thousand of those acres were removed from the reservation by executive order, for the benefit of others. The loss still frustrated Elim's shareholders and their descendants, Congress said. The act withdraws the mapped lands again for two years, barring mining claims and other disposal. During that window the land waits for selection by the Elim Native Corporation.
plaw-106-195-2000:
Fifty years after the Korean War began, Congress marked the anniversary with Public Law 106-195, a joint resolution approved on May 2, 2000. North Korea invaded South Korea on June 25, 1950, with about ninety thousand troops. President Harry S Truman ordered American intervention two days later. About five million seven hundred twenty thousand service members served during the war.

The resolution recites the cost: over fifty-four thousand American dead, more than ninety-two thousand wounded, and thousands missing or taken prisoner. Congress recognizes the anniversary's historic weight and thanks those who served. It honors members who died, including the unaccounted for. It also asks the President to proclaim the anniversary and call Americans to observe it with ceremonies.
plaw-106-196-2000: Albany, Georgia, is home to the courthouse named by Public Law 106-196 in 2000. The courthouse at 223 Broad Avenue became the C.B. King United States Courthouse. The Senate first passed the bill in October 1999; the House amended and passed it in April 2000, and the Senate agreed to the changes. Approved on May 2, 2000, the act makes the King name the one used in all federal references to the courthouse.
plaw-106-197-2000: Dozens of federal reports were saved from automatic death by Public Law 106-197, approved on May 2, 2000. A 1995 law, the Federal Reports Elimination and Sunset Act, had set many required reports to expire on their own. The 2000 act exempts a long list of report provisions from that fate. The spared provisions run through criminal law, the courts, immigration, civil rights in institutions, and war claims. Child protection and Aleutian and Pribilof Islands restitution reports also stay alive under the exemption.
plaw-106-198-2000: A new face joined the Smithsonian Institution's Board of Regents through Public Law 106-198, a joint resolution approved on May 5, 2000. Louis Gerstner of New York had resigned his citizen regent seat, leaving a vacancy in the class of regents who are not members of Congress. The resolution appoints Alan G. Spoon of Maryland to fill it. His six-year term takes effect on the day the resolution became law.
plaw-106-199-2000: Public Law 106-199 kept a Texan on the Smithsonian Institution's Board of Regents in May 2000. Manuel L. Ibanez served as a citizen regent, one of the regents who are not members of Congress. His term expired on May 4, 2000. The joint resolution reappoints him for six years, effective May 5, 2000. The Senate passed it in April and the House in early May, with approval following on May 5.
plaw-106-200-2000:
Africa and the Caribbean anchor the Trade and Development Act of 2000, Public Law 106-200. The act sets a new trade and investment policy for sub-Saharan Africa and expands trade benefits for Caribbean Basin countries. It also renews the generalized system of preferences and reauthorizes trade adjustment assistance programs.

The African title lays out eligibility requirements for the new benefits and creates a United States and sub-Saharan Africa trade and economic cooperation forum. Textiles and apparel get detailed treatment, with protections against transshipment. The contents also provide for free trade agreements with African countries. A new Assistant United States Trade Representative for African Affairs is created to run the policy.
plaw-106-201-2000: A sunset that nearly ended species reports was undone by Public Law 106-201, approved on May 18, 2000. The act amends the Endangered Species Act of 1973. Its change inserts a notwithstanding clause into the act's annual cost analysis section. The effect is that certain species conservation reports keep being required, despite the 1995 reports elimination law cited in the amendment. The fix reaches back, taking effect on December 19, 1999, if that came before the act itself.
plaw-106-202-2000:
Stock options and overtime pay meet in the Worker Economic Opportunity Act, Public Law 106-202, passed in 2000. The act amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. It clarifies how value from employer stock programs counts when figuring a worker's regular rate of pay.

The new paragraph keeps stock option value, stock appreciation rights, and employee stock purchase gains out of the regular rate, under conditions. Workers must learn the program's terms when they join or receive a grant. Options generally cannot be exercised for at least six months, with exceptions such as death or retirement. The exercise price must reach at least eighty-five percent of the stock's market value, and exercising stays voluntary.
plaw-106-203-2000: Fort Wayne, Indiana, gained a doubly named building under Public Law 106-203, approved on May 22, 2000. The federal building and courthouse at 1300 South Harrison Street became the E. Ross Adair Federal Building and United States Courthouse. The House passed the measure in March 2000 and the Senate in May. Its references section makes federal records use the full Adair name for the building.
plaw-106-204-2000: New York City's courthouse at 500 Pearl Street took a senator's name under Public Law 106-204. The federal building there became the Daniel Patrick Moynihan United States Courthouse. The Senate passed the bill on May 4, 2000, the House on May 15, and approval came on May 23. From then on, references to the building in federal laws, maps, and records meant the Moynihan courthouse.
plaw-106-205-2000:
Minority veterans of World War II were honored by Public Law 106-205, a joint resolution backing the Day of Honor 2000. Congress described the war as the event that preserved American democracy. It noted the country called on all its citizens, including its most oppressed, to serve against Nazism and fascism.

The numbers in the resolution are large: more than one million two hundred thousand African Americans served. So did more than three hundred thousand Hispanic Americans and more than fifty thousand Asian Americans. Native Americans, Native Hawaiians, Pacific Islanders, and Native Alaskans added tens of thousands more. Discrimination kept much of their service unreported for decades. Congress commends these veterans, honors those who died, and asks the President to proclaim the day.
plaw-106-206-2000:
Filming on federal land acquired a price tag under Public Law 106-206, approved on May 26, 2000. The Secretaries of the Interior and of Agriculture must require a permit for commercial filming on lands they administer. They must also set a reasonable fee that gives the United States a fair return.

The fee rests on how many days the filming lasts, how large the crew is, and how much equipment it brings. The agencies also recover their own costs, such as staff time, on top of the fee. Still photography is treated more lightly: no permit or fee where the public is generally allowed. Fees return for photography using models or props that are not part of the site itself.
plaw-106-207-2000:
Laotian fighters who served beside American forces received a path to citizenship in the Hmong Veterans' Naturalization Act of 2000, Public Law 106-207. The act eases naturalization for people admitted as refugees from Laos. It targets those who served with special guerrilla units or irregular forces based in Laos.

For those veterans, the usual English language requirement in naturalization law does not apply. Their service must have supported the United States military between February 28, 1961, and September 18, 1978. The exemption also reaches a veteran's spouse, judged by the marriage on the day the veteran applied for admission. The act further directs special consideration on the civics requirement for the same group.
plaw-106-208-2000: Old buildings and historic places gained more time under Public Law 106-208, the National Historic Preservation Act Amendments of 2000. Two terms move to the same year, 2005. The Historic Preservation Fund's term had run to 1997, and the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation's to 2000. A second rule ties where agencies place federal facilities on historic sites to a 1996 presidential order. The rest is small fixes to the old act, plus grant wording for the National Trust for Historic Preservation. It became law on May 26, 2000.
plaw-106-209-2000: Chicago appears again in Public Law 106-209, another postal designation approved on May 26, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 9308 South Chicago Avenue, zip code 60617, became the John J. Buchanan Post Office Building. The bill's path was longer than most: the House passed it in May 1999, the Senate amended it that November, and the House agreed to the changes in May 2000. Federal records referencing the facility now use the Buchanan name.
plaw-106-210-2000:
Professional boxing's business side was reformed by the Muhammad Ali Boxing Reform Act, Public Law 106-210, in 2000. Congress set out to end unfair and anticompetitive practices in the industry. Its findings describe a sport unlike other major American sports. Boxing has no league or central body setting uniform business and ethical standards.

Without that structure, Congress found repeated coercive practices harming boxers nationwide. State commissions are the proper regulators, but they lack the contract information needed to police abuses. Promoters can shop for states with weak oversight. Sanctioning organizations rate fighters without credible, objective criteria, the findings charge, leaving ratings open to manipulation. The act answers by reforming those business practices across the industry.
plaw-106-211-2000: Grant paperwork for tribal colleges was simplified under Public Law 106-211, amending the Higher Education Act of 1965. The Secretary of Education must use a simplified, streamlined application format for the tribal colleges program, sized for the small number of eligible schools. New award rules bar a funded tribal college from also drawing money under neighboring provisions. Awards should spread as widely and fairly as possible among eligible institutions. Matching special rules cover Alaska Native-serving and Native Hawaiian-serving institutions. The act was approved on May 26, 2000.
plaw-106-212-2000:
America's unofficial mission in Taiwan needed a safer home, and Public Law 106-212 authorizes money to build one. The American Institute in Taiwan Facilities Enhancement Act funds construction of a facility in Taipei suited to the institute's mission. Congress created the institute in the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 to carry on relations with Taiwan.

The findings are blunt about the old quarters. The Taipei office sat in buildings never designed for its work, in a location that gave employees poor security. At nearly fifty years old, the buildings cost more and more to maintain. The institute had saved toward a new building, but not enough for one large and secure enough. Congress claimed a special duty to close that gap.
plaw-106-213-2000: An Alabama hydroelectric license received years of extra time under Public Law 106-213, approved on May 26, 2000. The act covers Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 7115. At the licensee's request, the commission shall extend the deadline to begin construction by three straight two-year periods. The extension follows the Federal Power Act's tests of good faith, due diligence, and public interest. If the license already expired, the act orders it reinstated as of its expiration date, with the same extensions running from there.
plaw-106-214-2000:
Some Vietnam veterans died after coming home, from wounds and effects of their service, and Public Law 106-214 honors them at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. Their names cannot go on the memorial wall under its rules. The act authorizes a plaque inside the memorial site for them instead.

The American Battle Monuments Commission designs and places the plaque, at least six square feet and no more than eighteen. It consults the memorial's architects, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund, and the Vietnam Women's Memorial group. The inscription is the commission's to write. One firm limit applies: no federal funds may pay to design, buy, or install the plaque.
plaw-106-215-2000:
Tracking who enters and leaves the country was rebuilt by the Immigration and Naturalization Service Data Management Improvement Act of 2000, Public Law 106-215. The act rewrites a section of the 1996 immigration reform law. It orders the Attorney General to implement an integrated entry and exit data system.

That system is electronic. It pulls together arrival and departure records held in Justice Department and State Department databases, including records from ports of entry and consular offices. From those records it produces reports on arriving and departing visitors by nationality and by immigrant or nonimmigrant class. It also matches each person's arrival record against the departure record, closing the loop on a trip.
plaw-106-216-2000: Long leases on tribal trust land were widened by Public Law 106-216, approved on June 20, 2000. The act amends a 1955 leasing law by adding three names to its list. They are the Torres Martinez Desert Cahuilla Indians, the Guidiville Band of Pomo Indians, and the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation. Their trust lands can now carry leases of up to ninety-nine years, for leases signed or renewed after the act. A second section revokes the Stockbridge-Munsee Community's 1938 federal charter, at its request.
plaw-106-217-2000: Minnesota's Lower Sioux Indian Community gained free control of its non-trust land under Public Law 106-217. Land the community owns, but which the United States does not hold in trust for it, may be leased, sold, conveyed, or otherwise transferred by the community. No further approval, ratification, or authorization from the United States is needed. The act is careful to leave trust land untouched: nothing in it allows transfer of trust property or changes the laws governing such land. It was approved on June 20, 2000.
plaw-106-218-2000: The State Department's headquarters received a presidential name under Public Law 106-218, approved on June 20, 2000. The federal building at 2201 C Street, Northwest, in Washington became the Harry S Truman Federal Building. The act notes the building was the department's headquarters at the time. Following the standard pattern, any reference to the building in a federal law, map, regulation, or record counts as a reference to the Harry S Truman Federal Building.
plaw-106-219-2000: Opera gained an official national title in Public Law 106-219, a two-section act approved on June 20, 2000. The Washington Opera, organized under the laws of the District of Columbia, is designated as the National Opera. The second section directs that references to the Washington Opera in any federal law, map, regulation, document, or record be deemed references to the National Opera. The bill moved fast: the House passed it on June 6, 2000, and the Senate the next day.
plaw-106-220-2000:
An irrigation district in New Mexico took over federal project property under the Carlsbad Irrigation Project Acquired Land Transfer Act, Public Law 106-220. The Secretary of the Interior may convey the Carlsbad Project's acquired lands in Eddy County to the Carlsbad Irrigation District. The transfer includes the irrigation and drainage system and related sites, down to ditch rider houses, the maintenance shop, and the Pecos River Flume.

Two reservations limit the gift. The United States keeps the surface land under Brantley and Avalon dams and other project structures, though not the minerals beneath. It also keeps storage and flow easements on tracts lying under the reservoirs' highest spillway levels. The district itself is a quasi-municipal corporation under New Mexico law.
plaw-106-221-2000: Arizona water facilities changed hands under Public Law 106-221, the Wellton-Mohawk Transfer Act. The Secretary of the Interior may carry out a 1998 agreement with the Wellton-Mohawk Irrigation and Drainage District. Works, facilities, and titles of the Gila Project pass to the district, along with designated lands. Water and power deliveries continue under existing contracts: Colorado River water and Parker-Davis Project power. Nothing changes duties under the Colorado River salinity law. If the transfer lagged past July 1, 2000, a status report was owed.
plaw-106-222-2000:
Farmers were promised paperwork by computer under the Freedom to E-File Act, Public Law 106-222, passed in 2000. The Secretary of Agriculture had one hundred eighty days to build an internet-based filing and retrieval system, as far as practicable. Producers would use it to reach forms and public information from selected department agencies.

The covered agencies include the Farm Service Agency and the Natural Resources Conservation Service. Rural development offices in the department's service center network are included too. So is the Commodity Credit Corporation's producer programs work, run through the two named agencies. At minimum, the system lets producers download agency forms from the internet.
plaw-106-223-2000:
Three soldiers from three different wars were cleared for the Medal of Honor by Public Law 106-223, approved on June 20, 2000. The act waives the usual time limits for the award. It records that the Secretary of the Army had already judged each award warranted.

Ed W Freeman flew helicopters at landing zone X-Ray in Vietnam's Ia Drang Valley on November 14, 1965. James K Okubo served as a medic with the 442d Regimental Combat Team near Biffontaine, France, in the fall of 1944. Andrew J Smith fought as a corporal with the 55th Massachusetts regiment at Honey Hill, South Carolina, in 1864. Each citation speaks of gallantry beyond the call of duty, and the medal may go to them after death.
plaw-106-224-2000:
Farmers facing failed crops or lost income were promised a stronger safety net by the Agricultural Risk Protection Act of 2000, Public Law 106-224. The act amends the Federal Crop Insurance Act. Its goals are wider access to cheaper risk management tools and better protection against production and income losses.

The first title rewrites crop insurance coverage. Sections set premium schedules for added coverage and other insurance plans, and address catastrophic risk protection. Fees, assigned yields, production history adjustments, and rating methods all follow. A second subtitle guards the program itself, with compliance, protection of private information, good farming practices, and record rules. Prevented planting and a disaster help program for uninsured crops also appear.
plaw-106-225-2000:
Congress voted a posthumous gold medal for the creator of Peanuts under Public Law 106-225 in 2000. Charles M Schulz was born on November 26, 1922, in St. Paul, Minnesota. He served in World War II, rising from infantryman to staff sergeant leading a machine gun squad. Even then he drew cartoons of barracks life on fellow soldiers' letters home.

His first weekly strip, L'il Folks, introduced Charlie Brown before becoming Peanuts in October 1950. Schulz drew every frame himself. The strip ran in about two thousand six hundred newspapers, reaching roughly three hundred thirty-five million readers daily in twenty languages. A Charlie Brown Christmas had aired for thirty-four straight years, alongside more than sixty animated specials, four films, and a Broadway musical.
plaw-106-226-2000: Washington's school governance charter change was sped up by Public Law 106-226, approved on June 27, 2000. Normally a District of Columbia charter act waits through a congressional review period under the Home Rule Act. This act waives that wait for the School Governance Charter Amendment Act of 2000. The charter act takes effect as soon as District voters ratify it. Ratification requires a majority of registered, qualified voters taking part in the referendum.
plaw-106-227-2000:
The United States Army turned two hundred twenty-five in 2000, and Public Law 106-227, a joint resolution, marked the birthday. On June 14, 1775, the Second Continental Congress authorized the Continental Army for thirteen colonies. Congress tied that act of self-defense to the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution that followed.

For two hundred twenty-five years, the resolution says, the Army's central mission has been to fight and win the nation's wars. Its flag carries one hundred seventy-two battle streamers. The place names run from Valley Forge, Gettysburg, and Normandy to Pusan, the Ia Drang Valley, and Kuwait. Living by the motto Duty, Honor, Country, soldiers earn the nation's appreciation, which the resolution formally expresses.
plaw-106-228-2000: Mississippi tribal land status was corrected by Public Law 106-228, approved on June 29, 2000. All land taken into trust for the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians on or after December 23, 1944, is part of the Mississippi Choctaw Indian Reservation. Land the band held in fee inside Mississippi, as listed in a September 1999 report, is declared held in trust for the band. Post-1944 additions do not count as the tribe's initial reservation under a gaming law provision. The act leaves the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act's application unchanged.
plaw-106-229-2000:
Signing contracts on a computer became safer in law under the Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act, Public Law 106-229. Congress meant to ease the use of electronic records and signatures in interstate and foreign commerce. The act's first title states a general rule of validity.

A signature, contract, or record cannot be denied legal effect only because it is electronic. A contract cannot be rejected only because an electronic signature or record helped form it. The act leaves other legal duties untouched, beyond requirements that records be written or signed on paper. It also does not force anyone to accept electronic records, outside a narrow government agency exception.
plaw-106-230-2000:
Shadowy political groups were pushed into the open by Public Law 106-230, approved on July 1, 2000. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code to require organizations under section 527 to disclose their political work. It starts with a simple gate: no notice, no section 527 status.

An organization must tell the Secretary of the Treasury, electronically and in writing, that it claims section 527 treatment. The notice is due within twenty-four hours of the organization being established. It must give the group's name, addresses, and email, plus its purpose. Officers, highly paid employees, a contact person, the records custodian, and board members must all be named, along with related entities.
plaw-106-231-2000: Compton, California, renamed its main post office under Public Law 106-231, approved on July 6, 2000. The federal building at 701 South Santa Fe Avenue, known as the Compton Main Post Office, became the Mervyn Malcolm Dymally Post Office Building. The House passed the redesignation in November 1999 and the Senate the following June. Federal references to the building now carry the Dymally name.
plaw-106-232-2000: Los Angeles gained a renamed postal building through Public Law 106-232, also approved on July 6, 2000. The federal building at 10301 South Compton Avenue had been known as the Watts Finance Office. The act redesignates it as the Augustus F. Hawkins Post Office Building. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, or other record is treated as a mention under the Hawkins name.
plaw-106-233-2000: Madison, Florida, is the town in Public Law 106-233, a postal naming act approved on July 6, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 200 East Pinckney Street became the Captain Colin P. Kelly, Jr. Post Office. The House acted in March 2000 and the Senate in June. References to the facility in federal laws and records are considered references to the Kelly post office.
plaw-106-234-2000: Five Cedar Street in Hopkinton, Massachusetts, is the address behind Public Law 106-234. The Postal Service building there became the Thomas J. Brown Post Office Building under the act. Congress passed it during 1999 and 2000, and it was approved on July 6, 2000. The standard references clause follows, carrying the Brown name into federal laws, maps, regulations, and records.
plaw-106-235-2000: Shaker Heights, Ohio, renamed its post office under Public Law 106-235, approved on July 6, 2000. The post office at 3675 Warrensville Center Road became the Louise Stokes Post Office. The measure passed the House in October 1999 and the Senate in June 2000. After the act, federal laws and records referring to that post office refer to it by the Stokes name.
plaw-106-236-2000: Wiggins, Mississippi, attached a baseball nickname to its post office in Public Law 106-236. The post office at 125 Border Avenue West became the Jay Hanna Dizzy Dean Post Office. Congress approved the designation on July 6, 2000, after House passage in 1999 and Senate passage that June. Mentions of the post office in federal records are read as mentions of the Dean post office.
plaw-106-237-2000: Kansas gets the postal naming in Public Law 106-237, approved on July 6, 2000. The United States Post Office at 713 Elm Street in Wakefield became the William H. Avery Post Office. The House passed the bill in October 1999 and the Senate in June 2000. Its references clause makes the Avery name official across federal laws, maps, and records.
plaw-106-238-2000: A South Carolina postal station changed names, not just honorifics, under Public Law 106-238. The Postal Service facility at 100 Orchard Park Drive in Greenville had been known as the Orchard Park Station. The act redesignates it as the Keith D. Oglesby Station. It passed the House in March 2000 and the Senate in June, with approval on July 6. Federal references to the facility now mean the Oglesby Station.
plaw-106-239-2000: Four South Carolina post offices were named in one act, Public Law 106-239, approved on July 6, 2000. In Eastover, the post office at 301 Main Street became the Layford R. Johnson Post Office. Charleston gained two: the Richard E. Fields Post Office on Sycamore Street and the Marybelle H. Howe Post Office on East Bay Street. Columbia's Eau Claire community post office, on Lamar Street, became the Mamie G. Floyd Post Office. Each section adds its own references clause.
plaw-106-240-2000: Merrifield, Virginia, supplies the address for Public Law 106-240, approved on July 6, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 8409 Lee Highway became the Joel T. Broyhill Postal Building. The House passed the designation in March 2000 and the Senate in June. Afterward, any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, or record counts as a reference to the Broyhill building.
plaw-106-241-2000: Arlington, Virginia's postal facility was named by Public Law 106-241, approved the same July day as its neighbors. The facility at 3118 Washington Boulevard became the Joseph L. Fisher Post Office Building. It passed the House in March 2000 and the Senate in June. The act's references section deems mentions of the facility in federal laws and records to be mentions of the Fisher building.
plaw-106-242-2000: Wisconsin closes this run of postal laws with Public Law 106-242. The Postal Service facility at 1818 Milton Avenue in Janesville became the Les Aspin Post Office Building. Both chambers moved quickly in June 2000, the House on June 6 and the Senate on June 23, and approval followed on July 6. Federal references to the Janesville facility now use the Aspin name.
plaw-106-243-2000:
Bad water on a New Mexico reservation drew a federal study order in Public Law 106-243, approved on July 10, 2000. Congress found major gaps in water supplies for residents of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation. The municipal system, owned by the Bureau of Indian Affairs, was outdated and dilapidated. It could not safely serve current or future growth.

The findings grow harsher: the system could not meet federal discharge rules and ran without a federal discharge permit. The Environmental Protection Agency had cited it for drinking water violations threatening health on and off the reservation. The tribe had already spent four and a half million dollars of its own money on repairs. The act directs the Bureau of Reclamation to conduct a feasibility study for the reservation.
plaw-106-244-2000: Church benefit plans and state insurance law are untangled by Public Law 106-244, approved on July 10, 2000. The act amends title I of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. Its stated purpose is narrow: clarify how state insurance laws on licensing, solvency, and single employer status apply to a church plan that is a welfare plan. For those state law questions, such a plan counts as a single employer plan. It either reimburses costs from general church assets, buys insurance with those assets, or does both.
plaw-106-245-2000:
Workers harmed by uranium mining and nuclear test fallout were promised fairer payment under Public Law 106-245, the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act Amendments of 2000. The first act accepted a federal duty to pay people harmed by mining radioactive material and by nuclear test fallout. Congress now found the system too hard for some people who deserved payment.

A Senate hearing showed red tape blocking fair and fast payment. Reports backed wider reach, to more states where the government backed uranium mining and milling from 1941 through 1971. Science also backed covering more radiation-linked diseases. The findings say above-ground miners, millers, and ore haulers should be paid much like underground miners. Their sickness followed a federal failure to warn and protect them.
plaw-106-246-2000:
Bases, barracks, and family housing were paid for by Public Law 106-246, the military construction appropriations act for fiscal year 2001. Its first division carries the short title Military Construction Appropriations Act, 2001. Money flows for the year ending September 30, 2001, covering base realignment and closure as well.

Army military construction receives about nine hundred nine million dollars, available until September 30, 2005. Of that, a capped share near one hundred nine million dollars covers study, planning, design, and engineering services. The Secretary of Defense can exceed the cap only after notifying the appropriations committees. Navy construction follows at about nine hundred twenty-eight million dollars, on similar terms.
plaw-106-247-2000:
Birds that winter in the tropics and breed in the north drew a conservation program from Public Law 106-247, the Neotropical Migratory Bird Conservation Act. The Secretary of the Interior must establish a program to help conserve neotropical migratory birds. Of nearly eight hundred bird species found in the United States, Congress found, about five hundred migrate between countries.

Most of those migrants winter in Latin America and the Caribbean. Many once-common populations are falling, some far enough to threaten their survival in the wild. Habitat loss and damage, including pollution, is the main cause Congress names. Because the birds cross many borders each year, saving them takes effort from every country along the route, and the act backs that shared work with federal assistance.
plaw-106-248-2000:
A great volcanic bowl in New Mexico was brought into public hands by Public Law 106-248, whose first title is the Valles Caldera Preservation Act. The act authorizes buying the Valles Caldera and running an effective land and wildlife program for it inside the Department of Agriculture. The Baca ranch covers most of the caldera.

Congress praised the ranch as a unique land mass with scientific, cultural, historic, and ecological value. The caldera is a large resurgent lava dome with possible geothermal activity. The land traces to an 1860 grant to the heirs of Don Luis Maria Cabeza de Vaca. Careful work by its owners, selective logging, limited grazing, and prescribed fire, kept range and timber healthy. Hiking, fishing, camping, skiing, and hunting all figure in its future.
plaw-106-249-2000:
Nevada's Griffith Project, a major water system, was ordered transferred by the Griffith Project Prepayment and Conveyance Act, Public Law 106-249. The Secretary of the Interior is directed to convey the project to the Southern Nevada Water Authority. The act's title adds prepayment to the handover.

What changes hands is the Robert B. Griffith Water Project, built under the Southern Nevada Water Project Act. Its parts include pipelines, conduits, pumping plants, and intake facilities. Aqueducts, laterals, water storage and regulatory works, and electric substations are listed as well. So are all the land interests the United States acquired for the project, from fee title to easements. The project file rests at the Bureau of Reclamation.
plaw-106-250-2000:
Pope John Paul II received a congressional gold medal authorization under Public Law 106-250, approved on July 27, 2000. The Speaker of the House and the Senate's President Pro Tempore would present the medal on Congress's behalf. Congress honored the pope for lasting contributions to peace and religious understanding.

The findings call him spiritual leader of more than one billion Catholics and a leading moral authority worldwide. He led the Catholic Church into its third millennium, traveling widely as an example of faith. Congress credited his moral authority with hastening the fall of totalitarian regimes, symbolized by the Berlin Wall's collapse. He also reached across Christian divisions and toward the world's other great religions, the findings say.
plaw-106-251-2000:
A joint gold medal for a former president and first lady was authorized by Public Law 106-251 on July 27, 2000. The medal honors Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan together, for their service to the nation. The House Speaker and the Senate President Pro Tempore would present it, and the Treasury Secretary would strike it.

Congress praised Ronald Reagan for restoring confident American progress and optimism. His leadership, the findings say, helped end the Cold War, and his presidency brought sustained prosperity and job growth. Nancy Reagan is honored as a gracious first lady who championed the Just Say No campaign. That campaign fought alcohol and drug use among the nation's youth. Together, Congress said, the Reagans promoted national pride and better lives at home and abroad.
plaw-106-252-2000:
Cell phone taxes needed one clear home jurisdiction, and the Mobile Telecommunications Sourcing Act, Public Law 106-252, supplied the rules. The act amends title 4 of the United States Code. It sets sourcing requirements for state and local taxation of mobile telecommunications services, deciding which place may treat the service as its own.

The new sections apply to taxes, charges, and fees set per customer or measured by what customers are charged. They apply whether the tax falls on the seller or the buyer, and whatever the tax is called. Clear exceptions follow. Taxes on a provider's net income, capital stock, net worth, or property value stay outside the rules. So do fairly apportioned charges not based on individual transactions.
plaw-106-253-2000:
Fundraising stamps were put on a general footing by the Semipostal Authorization Act, Public Law 106-253, in 2000. A semipostal is a postage stamp sold at a premium to fund a cause. The act grants the Postal Service authority to issue semipostals under title 39 of the United States Code.

The Postal Service may issue and sell such stamps for causes it judges to be in the national public interest. The stamp's price equals the regular postage rate plus a differential the Governors set by regulation. That extra amount may not exceed twenty-five percent of the regular rate. The act frees the pricing from the usual postal rate procedures. Money raised flows to the chosen causes rather than to ordinary postal operations.
plaw-106-254-2000:
Police dogs and horses gained federal protection under the Federal Law Enforcement Animal Protection Act of 2000, Public Law 106-254. The act adds a new section to title 18 of the United States Code. A police animal is a dog or horse employed by a federal agency mainly to detect crime, enforce laws, or catch offenders.

Whoever willfully and maliciously harms such an animal, or tries or conspires to, faces a fine and up to one year in prison. If the attack permanently disables or disfigures the animal, or kills it, the maximum rises to ten years. Serious bodily injury to the animal brings the same higher maximum.
plaw-106-255-2000:
Northern Europe's environment and borders were joined in Public Law 106-255, the Cross-Border Cooperation and Environmental Safety in Northern Europe Act of 2000. Congress called the region increasingly vital, with real chances for American investment. It also saw a path toward a secure, prosperous, and stable Europe.

The findings praise the region's tradition of cooperation and its long ties to the United States. The Baltic states were committing to western institutions, and Russia could be drawn into positive work with its western neighbors. Since 1997 the United States Northern Europe Initiative had framed policy there. Its network covered trade, law enforcement, environment, energy, civil society, and public health. The act fosters the cross-border cooperation and environmental cleanup named in its purpose.
plaw-106-256-2000:
Ocean policy gained a study commission under the Oceans Act of 2000, Public Law 106-256. The act establishes a Commission on Ocean Policy. Its job is to recommend a coordinated and comprehensive national ocean policy for the United States.

The objectives Congress lists run wide. They include protecting life and property from natural and manmade hazards, and careful stewardship of fisheries and other ocean resources. Protecting the marine environment and preventing pollution stand beside growing marine commerce and settling conflicts among ocean users. More knowledge of the oceans, including their role in climate change, is another aim. So is closing ranks among government agencies and private firms, so ocean rules stay coherent.
plaw-106-257-2000:
Scattered land ownership in northeastern Oregon was the problem behind the Oregon Land Exchange Act of 2000, Public Law 106-257. Congress found private parcels mixed in with federal land across the region. The federal side spans Bureau of Land Management districts in Prineville and Vale, plus three national forests: the Malheur, the Wallowa-Whitman, and the Umatilla.

Some private surface land touches parcels the United States wants for fish and wildlife habitat. Consolidating ownership, Congress said, makes management sounder and cheaper for both sides. Federal land programs already dispose of small isolated tracts with low public value inside larger blocks. Among the public gains Congress names are better access, scenery, and recreation near wild and scenic river corridors.
plaw-106-258-2000: One house in Waterloo, New York, is the whole subject of Public Law 106-258, approved on August 8, 2000. The act amends the law establishing Women's Rights National Historical Park. It permits the Secretary of the Interior to acquire full ownership, in fee simple, of the Hunt House in Waterloo. The amendment reshapes one long sentence of the park law and removes another. A technical correction elsewhere in the same section changes the word Williams to Main. The Senate passed the bill in April 2000 and the House in July.
plaw-106-259-2000:
Military paychecks dominate the opening of Public Law 106-259, the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2001. The act funds the Department of Defense for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001. Title I covers military personnel across the services.

The Army personnel account receives a little over twenty-two billion dollars. It pays for salaries, allowances, clothing, food, and travel when members change stations. Cadets and aviation cadets are included, along with payments into the military retirement fund. The Navy's personnel account follows at a little under eighteen billion dollars. It covers sailors on active duty, midshipmen, and aviation cadets on much the same terms.
plaw-106-260-2000:
Tribal governments were handed more control by the Tribal Self-Governance Amendments of 2000, Public Law 106-260. The act amends the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act. Congress found that the right of self-government flows from the tribes' own sovereignty. A special government-to-government relationship binds the United States and the tribes.

Federal bureaucracy, with its centralized rules, has eroded that self-governance, Congress said. An earlier demonstration project let tribes take fuller control of federal funding and program management. It was meant to strengthen the government-to-government relationship. Congress reviewed the project and endorsed transferring full control and funding to tribal governments on request. The findings also admit the government has failed to fully meet its trust duties, including on Indian health care.
plaw-106-261-2000:
Wilson Creek in North Carolina joined the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System under Public Law 106-261, approved on August 18, 2000. The protected stretch runs twenty-three and three-tenths miles. It flows from the creek's headwaters to its meeting with Johns River, through Avery and Caldwell Counties.

The Secretary of Agriculture administers the creek in three pieces. A short scenic segment runs below Calloway Peak. A wild segment of about four and a half miles follows, then a recreational segment of nearly sixteen miles. One clause bars condemnation to win access across the land of T. Henry Wilson, Jr. and his heirs in the wild stretch.
plaw-106-262-2000: Rome, New York, holds the veterans clinic named by Public Law 106-262, approved on August 18, 2000. The Department of Veterans Affairs outpatient clinic there became the Donald J. Mitchell Department of Veterans Affairs Outpatient Clinic. Both chambers passed the bill in late July 2000, the House on July 25 and the Senate on July 27. References to the clinic in federal laws and records are treated as references to the Mitchell clinic.
plaw-106-263-2000:
Another Utah tribal water claim was settled by Public Law 106-263, the Shivwits Band of the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Water Rights Settlement Act. Congress restated its policy: settle tribal water claims rather than fight them in court. Viable reservation economies in the dry West need settled water rights and working water facilities.

History fills the findings. An 1891 act supported the Shivwits in Washington County and bought improvements along the Santa Clara River. About twenty-six thousand eight hundred eighty acres became their reservation by executive order in 1916, with more land added in 1937. The Santa Clara River is fully claimed except at high flow. A 1922 court decision had awarded the United States a small flow for the band's irrigation.
plaw-106-264-2000:
Fighting AIDS and tuberculosis worldwide is the mission of the Global AIDS and Tuberculosis Relief Act of 2000, Public Law 106-264. The act provides for negotiating a trust fund to fight the AIDS epidemic. The fund would be run by the World Bank's lending arms, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development or the International Development Association.

The first title aids countries with large populations living with HIV and AIDS. It adds assistance authority and a voluntary contribution to vaccine groups, including the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunizations. A coordinated donor strategy supports orphans in sub-Saharan Africa. Military training programs are drawn in through the African Crisis Response Initiative. The World Bank AIDS trust fund then gets its own subtitle.
plaw-106-265-2000:
Long-term care insurance came to the federal workforce through Public Law 106-265, approved on September 19, 2000. Its first title, the Long-Term Care Security Act, amends title 5 of the United States Code. It establishes a program making long-term care insurance available to federal employees. Members of the uniformed services and civilian and military retirees are covered too.

The new chapter of title 5 lays out the machinery: definitions, who may buy the insurance, and contracting authority. Financing, preemption, and studies and audits all receive sections. Court jurisdiction and cost accounting standards close the list. The wider act also corrects retirement coverage errors under the federal retirement chapters, a separate housekeeping job.
plaw-106-266-2000: Charlottesville, Virginia, is home to the federal facility named by Public Law 106-266. The facility at 1301 Emmet Street became Pamela B. Gwin Hall under the act. It passed the House in May 2000 and the Senate in September, and was approved on September 22, 2000. The references section of the act treats any mention of the building in federal records as a mention of Pamela B. Gwin Hall.
plaw-106-267-2000: Texas border traffic passes through the station renamed by Public Law 106-267, approved on September 22, 2000. The United States border station in Pharr, Texas, became the Kika de la Garza United States Border Station. The House passed the designation in May 2000 and the Senate in September. Federal laws, maps, and records referring to the station now refer to it by the de la Garza name.
plaw-106-268-2000: San Antonio's federal building took a new role-name under Public Law 106-268. The building at 643 East Durango Boulevard became the Adrian A. Spears Judicial Training Center. The House passed the act in June 2000, the Senate in September, and approval came on September 22. Its references clause carries the Spears name into every federal law, map, regulation, and record that mentions the building.
plaw-106-269-2000: Greeneville, Tennessee, closes this batch of naming laws with Public Law 106-269. The United States courthouse at 220 West Depot Street became the James H. Quillen United States Courthouse. Congress passed the bill in the summer of 2000 and it was approved on September 22. From then on, federal references to the Greeneville courthouse use the Quillen name.
plaw-106-270-2000: An Oregon conservation partnership kept its federal partner under Public Law 106-270, the Deschutes Resources Conservancy Reauthorization Act of 2000. The act reauthorizes the Bureau of Reclamation's participation in the Deschutes Resources Conservancy. It does so by amending the Oregon Resource Conservation Act of 1996. The new language adds funding of up to two million dollars in each of fiscal years 2002 through 2006. Both a participation cap and an authorization line receive the same yearly figure. The act was approved on September 22, 2000.
plaw-106-271-2000:
A Civil War battlefield in Mississippi and Tennessee was preserved by Public Law 106-271, the Corinth Battlefield Preservation Act of 2000. The act establishes the Corinth Unit of Shiloh National Military Park, near the city of Corinth, Mississippi, and reaching into Tennessee.

Congress recalled that in 1996 it authorized a center to interpret the Siege and Battle of Corinth and other Civil War actions nearby. The Corinth Battlefield had been ranked a top priority site, in critical need of coordinated action by the year 2000, by the Civil War Sites Advisory Commission. Mississippi, Tennessee, and their local governments can act against damaging uses, Congress noted. Protecting such sites serves a national interest.
plaw-106-272-2000:
Federal, state, and local offices in one Wyoming town were gathered onto a single campus by the Jackson Multi-Agency Campus Act of 2000, Public Law 106-272. Congress found that managing public land around Jackson, Wyoming, is shared work. The sharers include the Forest Service, the National Park Service, and the Fish and Wildlife Service.

Wyoming's Game and Fish Commission, Teton County, the town of Jackson, the chamber of commerce, and the local historical society share the duty too. Putting several offices on one site would ease communication among them, Congress said. It would also cut costs for every level of government and serve the public better. The act authorizes the federal agencies to develop and maintain the shared campus.
plaw-106-273-2000: Northwest power sales gained a required buyer class under Public Law 106-273, approved on September 22, 2000. The Bonneville Power Administration must sell electric power at wholesale to a joint operating entity. Such an entity is a public body or cooperative, formed by two or more public bodies or cooperatives that were Bonneville customers before January 1, 1999. The power may serve only the firm loads of the entity's member utilities. Members may not resell it, except to retail customers, fellow members, or as other law permits.
plaw-106-274-2000:
Religious exercise in zoning and in prisons was protected by the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000, Public Law 106-274. Congress declared its aim plainly: to protect religious liberty. The act's land use section sets a strict test for government.

No government may apply a land use rule in a way that puts a substantial burden on the religious exercise of a person, a religious assembly, or an institution. There is an exception only when the government proves two things. The burden must serve a compelling government interest, and it must be the least restrictive way of serving that interest. The rule reaches cases involving federal money, effects on commerce, and zoning systems with individual assessments.
plaw-106-275-2000:
With no regular spending bills finished, Congress kept the government running through Public Law 106-275, a continuing appropriations resolution for fiscal year 2001. The resolution appropriates such amounts as may be necessary, under the terms of the fiscal year 2000 appropriations acts. It continues projects and activities run in 2000, including direct loans and loan guarantees.

The arrangement is a bridge toward a list of named 2001 appropriations acts. Agriculture, Commerce and Justice and State, and the District of Columbia appear early in that list. Energy and water, foreign operations, Interior, and Labor and health and education follow. Legislative branch, transportation, and Treasury funding round out the bridge until the real bills could pass.
plaw-106-276-2000: Families of officers killed long ago gained education help under Public Law 106-276, approved on October 2, 2000. The act amends the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968. It extends the retroactive eligibility dates for higher education assistance for spouses and dependent children of law enforcement officers killed in the line of duty. Two statutory dates, in 1992 and 1997, are both replaced by January 1, 1978. The change takes effect as of October 1, 1999, reaching federal, state, and local officers' families alike.
plaw-106-277-2000: Rewards for tips on Rwandan war crimes suspects were allowed by Public Law 106-277, signed on October 2, 2000. The act widens an older rewards program, written in a 1998 law, beyond Yugoslavia to Rwanda. Its changes add the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda where the Yugoslavia court appeared. A note defines that court's statute as the one in the annex to United Nations Security Council Resolution 955 of November 8, 1994. The rewards cover people giving information about persons indicted for grave breaches of the laws of war.
plaw-106-278-2000:
Pennsylvania's coal country past was honored in Public Law 106-278, signed on October 6, 2000. The act names two areas: the Lackawanna Valley National Heritage Area and the Schuylkill River National Heritage Area. Its first title carries the Lackawanna act's own name.

Congress found the industrial and cultural heritage of northeastern Pennsylvania to be of national weight. Four counties, Lackawanna, Luzerne, Wayne, and Susquehanna, hold that anthracite coal story. Linked trades include ironmaking, textiles, and rail transport. The story includes the living folkways of its people and the region's labor movement. Major unions such as the United Mine Workers of America formed there, and miners struck in 1900 and 1902 over pay and work terms.
plaw-106-279-2000:
Adoptions across national borders were given a treaty frame by the Intercountry Adoption Act of 2000, Public Law 106-279. The act puts the Hague Convention on Protection of Children and Co-operation in Respect of Intercountry Adoption into force for the United States. It builds the American setup the treaty requires.

A first title names the United States central authority and assigns duties to the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, with a yearly report on such adoptions. Vetting comes next: agencies must be accredited or approved to give adoption services in treaty cases. Standards, vetting bodies, and federal checks are all covered. A third title handles honoring treaty adoptions inside the United States.
plaw-106-280-2000:
American security aid was retooled by the Security Assistance Act of 2000, Public Law 106-280. The act amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 and the Arms Export Control Act. It also authorizes transferring naval vessels to certain foreign countries.

Military and related assistance leads the contents. Foreign military sales and financing come first, with funding and rules on licensing defense exports. Stockpiling follows: additions to American war reserve stockpiles kept for allies, and transfer of obsolete or surplus articles in those stockpiles to Israel. Drawdowns of defense articles and transport of excess defense goods round out the title, before international military education and training begins.
plaw-106-281-2000: Homebuyers kept a simpler downpayment option a little longer under Public Law 106-281, the FHA Downpayment Simplification Extension Act of 2000. The act amends the National Housing Act for the Federal Housing Administration's single family mortgage insurance program. The simplified downpayment rules had applied to loans insured in fiscal years 1998 through 2000. The amendment swaps that wording for loans closed on or before October 30, 2000. Congress approved the short extension on October 6, 2000.
plaw-106-282-2000: Government funding was stretched eight more days by Public Law 106-282, a joint resolution approved on October 6, 2000. The resolution amends the earlier continuing appropriations law for fiscal year 2001, Public Law 106-275. In one section of that law, the date October 6, 2000, is struck and October 14, 2000, is inserted. That single change is the whole text. The House passed it on October 3, and the Senate finished work on October 5.
plaw-106-283-2000:
Protecting a small Alaska town's drinking water drives the land swaps in Public Law 106-283, the Kake Tribal Corporation Land Transfer Act. Congress stated the purpose directly: reallocate lands and selection rights among the State of Alaska, Kake Tribal Corporation, and the City of Kake. The municipal watershed gains protection and management through the shuffle.

The exchange runs on conditions. Alaska must give up its statehood act selection rights to certain lands, and the Kake and Sealaska corporations must convey other lands to the city. Then the Secretary of Agriculture has one hundred eighty days to act. Surface title goes to Kake Tribal Corporation, while the subsurface estate goes to Sealaska Corporation.
plaw-106-284-2000:
Swimmers at America's beaches gained cleaner water rules under the Beaches Environmental Assessment and Coastal Health Act of 2000, Public Law 106-284. The act amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act. Its aim is better quality in coastal recreation waters.

States with coastal recreation waters must adopt water quality criteria and standards for disease-causing organisms and their indicators. The first set is due within forty-two months, covering every pathogen for which the Environmental Protection Agency has published criteria. When the agency issues new or revised criteria, states get thirty-six months to update their standards. The act then provides for states that fail to adopt them.
plaw-106-285-2000:
An Arizona tribal community won wider freedom over its water under Public Law 106-285, approved on October 10, 2000. The act clarifies leasing provisions in the law on the Ak-Chin Indian Community's water rights. The community may devote its permanent water supply to any use: farming, municipal, industrial, commercial, mining, recreational, or other beneficial uses.

That freedom works inside three groundwater management areas near Pinal, Phoenix, and Tucson, drawn under Arizona's 1980 groundwater law. The community may lease its water, grant and renew lease options, extend leases, and exchange or temporarily dispose of water there. Two limits hold: no lease may start with a term over one hundred years, and the community may never permanently give away a water right.
plaw-106-286-2000:
China's trade status with the United States was reset by Public Law 106-286, approved on October 10, 2000. The act authorizes extending normal trade relations treatment, meaning nondiscriminatory treatment, to the People's Republic of China. It also sets a framework for relations between the two countries. The act divides itself in two.

Division A handles normal trade relations. It ends the application of a Trade Act of 1974 chapter to China and sets an effective date. Relief from market disruption and compensation authority follow. Division B, titled United States-China Relations, carries findings and policy for the wider relationship. The structure pairs the trade opening with a standing framework for watching it.
plaw-106-287-2000:
Two states sharing one city culture received Congress's blessing in Public Law 106-287. The act grants consent to the Kansas and Missouri Metropolitan Culture District Compact. The two states pledge faithful cooperation in planning and developing a metropolitan culture district together.

The compact's policy is to fully use and improve the region's cultural facilities. It coordinates the services of cultural organizations and works to win solid financial support for them. Sharing brings savings in building costs and operations, the states declare. A metropolitan culture district is the tool created to carry the policy out. Each state holds the district's advantages in trust for its people and for the nation.
plaw-106-288-2000:
A river's south bank vegetation line became a state border under the Red River Boundary Compact, blessed by Public Law 106-288. The joint resolution grants Congress's consent to the compact between Texas and Oklahoma. Except around Lake Texoma, where the compact sets its own procedures, the boundary follows the vegetation line on the river's south bank.

Texas approved the deal in May 1999 and Oklahoma that June. Congress recognizes the pair of state acts as an interstate compact under the Constitution. Careful limits protect tribal interests. Nothing in the compact alters the rights of the Kiowa, Comanche, and Apache Tribes, the Chickasaw Nation, or the Choctaw Nation. Trust lands, allotted lands, and tribal sovereignty stay untouched.
plaw-106-289-2000: East Chicago, Indiana, renamed its post office under Public Law 106-289, approved on October 10, 2000. The post office at 3813 Main Street became the Lance Corporal Harold Gomez Post Office. The name carries a Marine rank into the building's title. The Senate passed the act in November 1999 and the House in September 2000. Any federal reference to the post office now uses the Gomez name.
plaw-106-290-2000: Gettysburg's famous Wills House joined the national military park under Public Law 106-290, approved on October 10, 2000. The act expands the boundaries of Gettysburg National Military Park in Pennsylvania. The Wills House property sits in the Borough of Gettysburg and is marked as Tract P02-1 on the park map, as revised in May 1999. A second section tidies the acquisition provisions of the park's boundary law, updating a subsection reference so the land rules point at the right place.
plaw-106-291-2000:
Public lands and parks received their yearly money from Public Law 106-291, the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2001. The act funds the department for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001. Title I opens with the Bureau of Land Management.

Management of lands and resources receives about seven hundred ten million dollars, available until spent. Set-asides inside that sum include money to assess the mineral potential of public lands in Alaska. Three million dollars is reserved for conservation projects on bureau lands, matched at least dollar for dollar by the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. A separate thirty-four million dollar line runs the mining law administration program, reduced by fees the bureau collects.
plaw-106-292-2000:
The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum received a rewritten charter and funding authority under Public Law 106-292, approved on October 12, 2000. The act replaces chapter 23 of title 36 of the United States Code. It states that the museum is an independent establishment of the United States government.

Its duties begin with remembrance: providing fitting ways for the nation to mark the Days of Remembrance, the annual civic commemoration of the Holocaust. The museum also operates a permanent living memorial museum to the victims, working with the Secretary of the Interior. The chapter then covers the governing council, staff, insurance, and gifts. Annual reports, audits of its finances, and an authorization of appropriations close the structure.
plaw-106-293-2000:
New presidential teams were given training money by the Presidential Transition Act of 2000, Public Law 106-293. The act amends the Presidential Transition Act of 1963. It concerns people the president intends to appoint to key posts during a handover of power.

Transition funds may now pay for briefings and workshops that show future appointees the problems new appointees often face. Those sessions can mix the newcomers with veterans of earlier teams. Budget office and watchdog experts, plus accounting office staff, may take part. Records training is named as well. The act also calls for a study and report on the papers certain nominees must file about their own money.
plaw-106-294-2000:
