Federal prisoners were made to share the cost of their clinic visits by the Federal Prisoner Health Care Copayment Act of 2000, Public Law 106-294. Congress aimed to fight overuse of prison health care and control its rising costs. The act adds a fees section to title 18 of the United States Code.

The fee attaches to a health care visit, a term the act defines carefully. A visit arranged through a staff referral does not count, and neither does staff-approved follow-up care for a chronic condition. Fees draw on the prisoner's trust fund account, as the act defines it. The Bureau of Prisons director decides what counts as a visit, and only providers the director authorizes may supply the care.
plaw-106-295-2000: A bridge, not a building, carries the name in Public Law 106-295, approved on October 13, 2000. The bridge on United States Route 231 crosses the Ohio River between Maceo, Kentucky, and Rockport, Indiana. The act designates it as the William H. Natcher Bridge. The House passed the bill in May 1999 and the Senate in October 2000. Federal references to the bridge in laws, maps, and records now use the Natcher name.
plaw-106-296-2000: Harrison, Arkansas, is the town named in Public Law 106-296, approved on October 13, 2000. The federal building and courthouse at 402 North Walnut Street became the J. Smith Henley Federal Building and United States Courthouse. The House passed the measure in April 2000 and the Senate in October. Its references clause makes federal records treat mentions of the building as mentions of the Henley building and courthouse.
plaw-106-297-2000:
Deaths behind bars must be counted and reported under the Death in Custody Reporting Act of 2000, Public Law 106-297. The act amends the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994. States assure the Attorney General they will report deaths every three months.

The duty covers anyone being arrested, being taken to incarceration, or held in a jail, prison, or other correctional facility, including juvenile facilities. Each report gives the dead person's name, gender, race, ethnicity, and age. It adds the date, time, and place of death and a brief account of the circumstances.
plaw-106-298-2000:
A Nevada county that is almost entirely federal land stands at the center of the Lincoln County Land Act of 2000, Public Law 106-298. Lincoln County spans more than ten thousand square miles, and the federal government owns about ninety-eight percent of it. The act directs the Secretary of the Interior to sell certain public land there by competition.

The City of Mesquite needs room to grow north in an organized way, Congress found. Selling land would widen the private tax base, improving county services and schools, and sale receipts would flow out at once. The federal government, Congress said, will be fairly paid. A planning framework and environmental study had already marked specific lands as suitable for disposal, with desert tortoise habitat in view.
plaw-106-299-2000:
Florida springs and creeks joined the national protected rivers under the Wekiva Wild and Scenic River Act of 2000, Public Law 106-299. An earlier law had ordered a study of the Wekiva River and its tributaries. The study found four waterways eligible: the Wekiva, Wekiwa Springs Run, Rock Springs Run, and Black Water Creek.

Florida had already acted to protect them through its own Wekiva River Protection Act. A water management district had drawn wildlife and water quality protection zones along the banks, and the state bought neighboring land for conservation. Lake, Seminole, and Orange counties wrote protection into their land use plans. With strong public support recorded, the act designates the rivers as components of the national wild and scenic rivers system.
plaw-106-300-2000:
Louisiana's Red River Valley gained a federal refuge under the Red River National Wildlife Refuge Act, Public Law 106-300, in 2000. Congress called the valley, in five parishes along the Red River Waterway, critical habitat. More than three hundred fifty bird species use it, along with rich aquatic life.

The valley's bottomland hardwood forests have been almost totally cleared, and restoring them would help many species. The valley forms part of a great migration corridor running from the Arctic Circle to South America. Yet no significant public sanctuary existed for over three hundred river miles, Congress found. New locks and dams up to Shreveport had improved chances to manage fish and wildlife. Hunting, fishing, research, and bird watching all figure in the refuge's promise.
plaw-106-301-2000:
Checkerboard state land inside Utah's West Desert was traded away from wilderness study areas by Public Law 106-301, the Utah West Desert Land Exchange Act of 2000. Utah owned about ninety-five thousand acres, plus mineral interests, inside existing or proposed wilderness study areas. An 1894 enabling act had granted the land in trust for public schools and other institutions.

Developing or selling those scattered inholdings could clash with protecting wilderness character, Congress found. The lands sit mixed among federal parcels that make up the rest of the study areas. The United States owns other land outside the study areas that it can give Utah in exchange. That swap frees federal management without hurting its goals, and frees the state trust lands to be used elsewhere.
plaw-106-302-2000: An Air Force memorial project received five more years of life from Public Law 106-302, approved on October 13, 2000. The Air Force Memorial Foundation holds authority to build a memorial in the District of Columbia or its surroundings, under a 1993 law. That authority was set to expire under the Commemorative Works Act. The 2000 act overrides the usual deadline and extends the foundation's legislative authority to December 2, 2005. The House passed the extension in September 2000 and the Senate in October.
plaw-106-303-2000:
Personnel flexibility for the government's auditors arrived in Public Law 106-303, approved on October 13, 2000. The act gives the General Accounting Office a voluntary early retirement authority. It runs from the act's passage through December 31, 2003, under both federal retirement systems.

To retire early under it, an employee must have worked at the office for at least the prior thirty-one days, in a post without a time limit. No pending involuntary separation for misconduct or poor performance may hang over the employee. The Comptroller General must find the departures serve a purpose: realigning the workforce under budget limits, fixing skill gaps, or trimming high-grade and supervisory ranks.
plaw-106-304-2000: Jasper, Alabama, supplies the building in Public Law 106-304, approved on October 13, 2000. The federal building at 1710 Alabama Avenue became the Carl Elliott Federal Building. The House passed the bill in July 2000 and the Senate in October. Following the usual second section, references to the building in any federal law, map, or record are deemed references to the Carl Elliott Federal Building.
plaw-106-305-2000: Norfolk, Virginia's customhouse was renamed by Public Law 106-305, with a delayed start. The United States customhouse at 101 East Main Street became the Owen B. Pickett United States Customhouse. Unusually, the act's third section sets its own effective date: January 3, 2001, months after approval on October 13, 2000. The House and Senate both passed the bill in the first days of October 2000. Federal references to the customhouse use the Pickett name once the act takes effect.
plaw-106-306-2000: Six more days of government funding came from Public Law 106-306, a joint resolution approved on October 13, 2000. It amends the continuing appropriations law for fiscal year 2001, Public Law 106-275, one more time. A cutoff date of October 14, 2000, in that law is struck and replaced with October 20, 2000. Both the House and the Senate passed the resolution on October 12. The measure is a single sentence long.
plaw-106-307-2000:
A colonial royal road became a national historic trail under Public Law 106-307, approved on October 13, 2000. El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior, was the main route between Mexico City and Spain's provincial capitals in New Mexico. Those capitals moved from San Juan de Los Caballeros to San Gabriel, then Santa Fe.

The American stretch ran four hundred four miles, from El Paso, Texas, to present-day San Juan Pueblo, New Mexico. Long before Europeans, Pueblo Indians of the Rio Grande had cut trade trails there. Juan de Onate's 1598 expedition followed them north to found the road's northern part. Congress calls the road a symbol of cultural mixing and trade that built the borderland.
plaw-106-308-2000: Jackson, Wyoming, appears once more in this set, in Public Law 106-308, a courthouse naming approved on October 13, 2000. The federal courthouse at 145 East Simpson Avenue became the Clifford P. Hansen Federal Courthouse. The Senate passed the act in March 2000 and the House in October. Any reference to the courthouse in a federal law, map, or other record is a reference to the Hansen courthouse.
plaw-106-309-2000:
Tiny loans for the world's poorest businesses anchor the Microenterprise for Self-Reliance and International Anti-Corruption Act of 2000, Public Law 106-309. The act establishes a program of help for credit and other financial services for microenterprises in developing countries.

Its first title, the Microenterprise for Self-Reliance Act of 2000, sets findings, policy, and purposes. Grant assistance for microenterprise development comes first. Micro and small enterprise development credits follow, along with a United States Microfinance Loan Facility. The Agency for International Development is named the global leader and coordinator of such aid, across governments and international bodies. A sense of Congress section marks Mexico as a key priority when the funding is divided.
plaw-106-310-2000:
Children's diseases structure the Children's Health Act of 2000, Public Law 106-310, which amends the Public Health Service Act on children's health. Division A of the act carries the children's health titles. Autism leads the list.

The autism title expands and coordinates National Institutes of Health research on autism. Developmental disabilities surveillance and research programs follow, with public information and education. An Inter-agency Autism Coordinating Committee is created, and a report to Congress is required. Fragile X research, run through the national institute for child health, takes the second title. Juvenile arthritis and related conditions come third, with research and an information clearinghouse.
plaw-106-311-2000: Employer fees for foreign workers doubled under Public Law 106-311, approved on October 17, 2000. The act amends the fee provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act for H-1B nonimmigrant workers. The fee charged to petitioning employers rises from five hundred dollars to one thousand dollars. The amendment also rewrites the exemption list: schools, colleges, related nonprofits, clinical training nonprofits, nonprofit research groups, and government research groups stay exempt for petitions filed before October 1, 2003. The higher fee applies to petitions filed two months or more after the act.
plaw-106-312-2000:
Big federal rules would face an outside check under the Truth in Regulating Act of 2000, Public Law 106-312. The act sets up a three-year pilot project. The General Accounting Office would report to Congress on economically significant rules issued by federal agencies.

Congress stated three purposes: clearer views of important regulatory decisions, stronger congressional oversight, and more accountability for Congress and the agencies alike. An economically significant rule is one that may affect the economy by one hundred million dollars or more in a year. Rules that materially harm jobs, competition, the environment, or public health also qualify. The office's review is an independent evaluation, testing the agency's data, methods, and assumptions behind each rule.
plaw-106-313-2000:
Skilled foreign workers received a much larger door into the United States under Public Law 106-313, approved on October 17, 2000. Its first title is the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-first Century Act of 2000. The act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act on H-1B nonimmigrant workers.

The temporary increase is plain: the yearly allotment rises to one hundred ninety-five thousand visas for each of fiscal years 2001, 2002, and 2003. Left-over problems from the prior two years are cleaned up in the same section. Workers whose petitions were filed before September 1, 2000, and later approved still count against the fiscal year 2000 ceiling, whenever approval came. Extra visas for 1999 cover those caught when that year's limit was hit.
plaw-106-314-2000:
Approved on October 17, 2000, Public Law 106-314 is the Strengthening Abuse and Neglect Courts Act of 2000. Congress wrote it to improve how the nation's abuse and neglect courts work, in line with the Adoption and Safe Families Act of 1997. Its findings stress that courts play a central role in keeping abused and neglected children safe.

The findings explain that a child's health and safety must come first in every decision. They note rules pushing timely choices about returning children home or moving them to adoptive or other permanent homes. They also note the push to end parental rights for children long in foster care. The law supports faster, more effective court action so children spend less time waiting.
plaw-106-315-2000: Public Law 106-315, approved October 19, 2000, gives one postal building a new name. The United States Postal Service building at 307 Main Street in Johnson City, New York, becomes the James W. McCabe, Sr. Post Office Building. Section two says any reference to that building in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record means the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-106-316-2000:
Congress used Public Law 106-316, approved October 19, 2000, to keep a youth conservation program going. It reauthorizes the Junior Duck Stamp Conservation and Design Program Act of 1994. The earlier law's funding years, 1995 through 2000, become 2001 through 2005.

The law also widens who can take part. It adds a definition of State that covers the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa, Guam, and the Virgin Islands, plus other territories. So the program, built around a student duck stamp design effort, now reaches the island areas as well as the fifty states.
plaw-106-317-2000: Public Law 106-317, approved October 19, 2000, makes only date changes to title X of the Energy Policy Act of 1992. In section 1001, a 2002 date becomes 2007. Wording about funds held in escrow gives way to costs a licensee incurs after December 31, 2007. A July 31, 2005 date becomes December 31, 2008. The House passed the bill in late September and the Senate in early October, as the history in the text shows. Nothing else in the law changes at all.
plaw-106-318-2000:
The Taunton River Wild and Scenic River Study Act of 2000 became Public Law 106-318 on October 19, 2000. It amends the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act for the Taunton River in Massachusetts. Congress found the river holds wildlife, ecological, and scenic value, plus historic sites tied to the nation's heritage.

Rather than protecting the river at once, the law designates segments for study for possible addition to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System. Congress noted strong support from state and local officials, residents, and river users for a joint study. It also noted long interest in managing the river together in a productive way.
plaw-106-319-2000:
Public Law 106-319, approved October 19, 2000, is the Yuma Crossing National Heritage Area Act of 2000. It establishes the Yuma Crossing National Heritage Area in Arizona. Congress tied the area to Yuma Crossing, a natural crossing place on the Colorado River. The findings call its role in westward expansion in the mid-1800s nationally important.

The law names a board of directors as the management entity and calls for a management plan for the heritage area. The Secretary of the Interior is the federal official named throughout. The act sets up the area's structure so its historic and cultural story can be managed and presented as one place.
plaw-106-320-2000: Under Public Law 106-320, approved October 19, 2000, the Postal Service facility at 424 South Michigan Street in South Bend, Indiana, takes a person's name. It becomes the John Brademas Post Office. A second section provides that any mention of the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records refers to the John Brademas Post Office. The short act changes the name only.
plaw-106-321-2000: Public Law 106-321, approved October 19, 2000, renames a post office in Ithaca, New York. The Postal Service facility at 757 Warren Road becomes the Matthew F. McHugh Post Office. Its second section makes the new name apply wherever the facility is referenced in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other United States record. No other provision is included.
plaw-106-322-2000: A Macon, Georgia, post office receives a new name under Public Law 106-322, approved October 19, 2000. The post office at 451 College Street becomes the Henry McNeal Turner Post Office. The law's references section ensures that federal laws, maps, regulations, and records using the old description are read as using the Turner name. That naming, and its effect on records, is the whole act.
plaw-106-323-2000:
Effigy Mounds National Monument in Iowa grows under Public Law 106-323, approved October 19, 2000. Called the Effigy Mounds National Monument Additions Act, the law lets the Secretary of the Interior add certain parcels shown on a May 1999 boundary map. Purchases may come only from willing sellers.

One named parcel, the Ferguson and Kistler tract, covers about one thousand fifty-four acres of undeveloped private land in Allamakee County. Another, the riverfront tract, covers about fifty acres of bottom land. By limiting buys to willing sellers, the law expands the monument's borders without forcing any landowner to sell.
plaw-106-324-2000:
Public Law 106-324, approved October 19, 2000, dedicates a Colorado trail to a lost child. Congress found that Jaryd Atadero, a three-year-old from Littleton, was last seen on October 2, 1999, near the Big South Trail in the Comanche Peak Wilderness Area of Roosevelt National Forest.

Congress dedicates that trail to Jaryd Atadero and to his legacy of promoting safe outdoor recreation for children. The Secretary of Agriculture must post a sign at the trailhead about safe outdoor activity with children. For at least one year the sign also carries a copy of the act and an image of Jaryd.
plaw-106-325-2000: Chicago gains a named post office building in Public Law 106-325, approved October 19, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 4601 South Cottage Grove Avenue becomes the Henry W. McGee Post Office Building. Section two directs that references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records count as references to the McGee building. The act contains no other change.
plaw-106-326-2000: Public Law 106-326, approved October 19, 2000, redesignates a Florida postal facility. The building at 14900 Southwest 30th Street in Miramar becomes the Vicki Coceano Post Office Building. Because it is a redesignation, the law replaces an earlier name rather than naming a new site. Its references section applies the Coceano name across federal laws, maps, and records. Nothing beyond the renaming is enacted.
plaw-106-327-2000: Pasadena's post office building at 600 Lincoln Avenue gets a new name from Public Law 106-327, approved October 19, 2000. It becomes the Matthew 'Mack' Robinson Post Office Building, using the name Matthew Robinson with his nickname Mack. The second section states that any reference to the facility in a United States law, map, regulation, or record means the Robinson building.
plaw-106-328-2000: Under Public Law 106-328, approved October 19, 2000, a Reno postal building honors a named person. The Postal Service facility at 2000 Vassar Street in Reno, Nevada, becomes the Barbara F. Vucanovich Post Office Building. The law also provides that references to that facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and other records are references to the Vucanovich building. The designation is its only action.
plaw-106-329-2000:
Public Law 106-329, approved October 19, 2000, deals with Forest Service land in South Dakota. Its short title is the Black Hills National Forest and Rocky Mountain Research Station Improvement Act. It authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to sell or exchange federal land in the Black Hills National Forest.

The opening land section covers about three hundred sixty-two acres across named parcels, including a small Spearfish dwelling tract. Money from a sale or exchange is meant to buy replacement sites and to acquire or build administrative improvements for the forest. The law thus trades scattered sites for facilities the forest can better use.
plaw-106-330-2000:
Texas forest land is the subject of Public Law 106-330, approved October 19, 2000, the Texas National Forests Improvement Act of 2000. The law authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to convey certain administrative sites for National Forest System lands in Texas. It also covers conveying forest land to the New Waverly Gulf Coast Trades Center.

The conveyance authority allows sale or exchange, on terms the Secretary sets, of listed parcels with their improvements. Named sites include ranger quarters in the Davy Crockett National Forest near Groveton, one on State Highway 94 and one on Devine Street. The act is a land-management measure, parcel by parcel.
plaw-106-331-2000:
Alabama's Cahaba River gains a federal refuge in Public Law 106-331, approved October 19, 2000. The Cahaba River National Wildlife Refuge Establishment Act provides for a refuge in Bibb County. Congress found the river nationally known for its rich variety of life. It hosts many fish species, more than any other river of its size in North America.

The findings count dozens of rare and imperiled aquatic species, including fish, turtles, mussels, and snails, plus listed endangered and threatened species. The river also holds the world's largest population of the shoals lily, called the Cahaba Lily locally. Creating the refuge protects that habitat under federal wildlife law.
plaw-106-332-2000:
Public Law 106-332, approved October 19, 2000, changes one map in a coastal protection system. It clarifies boundaries for Unit NC-01 of the Coastal Barrier Resources System in North Carolina. The law replaces an older map for Pine Island Unit NC-01, in Currituck and Dare Counties, with a map dated May 1, 2000.

The Secretary of the Interior must keep the replacement map on file and open for inspection, as the Coastal Barrier Resources Act requires. Because these maps decide which coastal land falls inside the system, a corrected boundary can affect how the Pine Island unit is treated. The act makes no other change.
plaw-106-333-2000: Baltimore's postal facility at 919 West 34th Street is renamed by Public Law 106-333, approved October 19, 2000. It becomes the Samuel H. Lacy, Sr. Post Office Building. The references section provides that mentions of the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other United States records are taken to mean the Lacy building. The law consists of that designation alone.
plaw-106-334-2000: Public Law 106-334, approved October 19, 2000, names a Baltimore post office building for a judge. The Postal Service facility at 3500 Dolfield Avenue becomes the Judge Robert Bernard Watts, Sr. Post Office Building. Any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the Watts building under section two. No further provisions follow.
plaw-106-335-2000: Another Baltimore facility is named in Public Law 106-335, approved October 19, 2000. The Postal Service site at 1908 North Ellamont Street becomes the Dr. Flossie McClain Dedmond Post Office Building. Its second section applies the Dedmond name to references in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other records of the United States. The act does only that naming.
plaw-106-336-2000: Rockville, Maryland, is the site named in Public Law 106-336, approved October 19, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 500 North Washington Street becomes the Everett Alvarez, Jr. Post Office Building. References to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or other records count as references to the Alvarez building, under the law's second section. That is the full content of the act.
plaw-106-337-2000: Public Law 106-337, approved October 19, 2000, designates a post office building in Derry, New Hampshire. The Postal Service facility at 24 Tsienneto Road becomes the Alan B. Shepard, Jr. Post Office Building. Section two states that references in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records to the facility mean the Shepard building. The law makes that single designation.
plaw-106-338-2000: Lenoir, North Carolina, has its postal facility renamed by Public Law 106-338, approved October 19, 2000. The building at 114 Ridge Street, N.W., becomes the James T. Broyhill Post Office Building. The law is styled a redesignation, and its second section makes federal laws, maps, regulations, and records read the facility's name as the Broyhill building. Nothing else is changed.
plaw-106-339-2000: Public Law 106-339, approved October 19, 2000, redesignates a Philadelphia postal facility known as Kensington Station. The building at 1602 Frankford Avenue becomes the Joseph F. Smith Post Office Building. Section two provides that any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record to the facility counts as a reference to the Smith building. The act is that renaming alone.
plaw-106-340-2000: Omaha's Ames Station is renamed by Public Law 106-340, approved October 19, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 3030 Meredith Avenue becomes the Reverend J.C. Wade Post Office. The redesignation section gives the new name, and the references section applies it in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, and other United States records. The law contains no other provision.
plaw-106-341-2000: Public Law 106-341, approved October 19, 2000, names a post office building in Fayetteville, North Carolina. The Postal Service facility at 301 Green Street becomes the J.L. Dawkins Post Office Building. Any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Dawkins building under section two. That designation is the whole law.
plaw-106-342-2000: The Royal Oak Post Office in Michigan is redesignated by Public Law 106-342, approved October 19, 2000. Its facility at 200 West 2nd Street becomes the William S. Broomfield Post Office Building. The law adds that references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or other records mean the Broomfield building. Apart from the new name, the act changes nothing.
plaw-106-343-2000:
Public Law 106-343, approved October 19, 2000, gives a stalled Idaho power project more time to start work. It extends the time limit under the Federal Power Act for building the Arrowrock Dam Hydroelectric Project. The project is Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project number 4656, as the text states in its first section.

In place of the normal span in section 13, the Commission may grant three two-year extensions in a row. The licensee must ask for the added time, and notice must be given first. The law takes effect when the prior grant of time runs out. It also deals with bringing back a license if the time to start had already run out before the act became law.
plaw-106-344-2000: Public Law 106-344, approved October 20, 2000, is a short joint measure that keeps the federal government funded for a few more days. It makes further stopgap funds for fiscal year 2001 by changing Public Law 106-275. The date October 20, 2000, in that law becomes October 25, 2000. It also lets funds be used and lets set payments due on or about November 1 go on being made, as the text states. Both houses passed it on October 19, the day before it was approved.
plaw-106-345-2000:
Programs for people with HIV and AIDS are revised and extended by Public Law 106-345, approved October 20, 2000. Its title is the Ryan White CARE Act Amendments of 2000. It amends the Public Health Service Act and the programs first set up under the Ryan White Comprehensive AIDS Resources Emergency Act of 1990.

Title I covers emergency relief for areas with substantial need, including HIV health services planning councils, their membership and duties, and open meetings. It also covers formula grants and supplemental grants, how grant money may be used, and applications. Title II begins the CARE grant program provisions that follow in the full text.
plaw-106-346-2000:
Federal transportation spending for a year is enacted in Public Law 106-346, approved October 23, 2000. The Department of Transportation and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2001, covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001. Rather than printing every line itself, the act takes an unusual route.

Section 101 enacts into law the provisions of another bill, H.R. 5394, as introduced on October 5, 2000. It directs the Archivist to publish that bill's text as an appendix when the act appears in slip form and in the Statutes at Large. So the money figures a reader seeks sit in the incorporated bill.
plaw-106-347-2000: Newark, New Jersey, gains a named federal building under Public Law 106-347, approved October 23, 2000. The post office and courthouse at 2 Federal Square becomes the Frank R. Lautenberg Post Office and Courthouse. Section two says references to that post office and courthouse in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records mean the Lautenberg building. The designation is the act's only action.
plaw-106-348-2000:
Public Law 106-348, approved October 24, 2000, lets a private group build a memorial for men and women hurt in war. The Disabled Veterans' LIFE Memorial Foundation may set it up on federal land in the District of Columbia or near it. The site honors those who became disabled while in the United States Armed Forces.

Work on the memorial must meet the rules of the Commemorative Works Act, a law that guides such sites in the capital area. The group alone takes in gifts of money and pays all costs to build the site. No funds from the United States may pay for the work. If gifts are left once bills are paid, the extra sum must be put on deposit, as the text goes on to state.
plaw-106-349-2000:
A study, not yet a historic site, is ordered by Public Law 106-349, approved October 24, 2000. The Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site Study Act of 2000 directs the Secretary of the Interior to study designating the Carter G. Woodson Home in the District of Columbia.

Congress recalled that Dr. Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History on September 9, 1915. It was created amid widespread ignorance about African American history and racist claims of Black inferiority. Its mission was teaching the public about Black Americans' contributions to the nation's history and culture. The study weighs the home as a site honoring that work.
plaw-106-350-2000:
San Francisco's Golden Gate National Recreation Area expands slightly under Public Law 106-350, approved October 24, 2000. The Golden Gate National Recreation Area Boundary Adjustment Act of 2000 revises the recreation area's boundaries. It does so by adding lands to the list in the law that first established the area.

The added lands are those generally shown on a map titled Additions to Golden Gate National Recreation Area, dated July 2000. Because the act works only through that map, a reader must consult the map to see exactly which ground joined the recreation area. No program or rule change accompanies the boundary move.
plaw-106-351-2000:
Public Law 106-351, approved October 24, 2000, sets up a new national monument in the south of California. The Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains National Monument Act of 2000 gives two ranges that joint name. Congress found the peaks hold great worth for the whole land in their wild life, old sites, and open views.

The act lays out how federal land in the monument is to be run, and it calls for a plan to guide that work. It deals with old and long-held uses of the land, with buying more land, and with a board of local people who advise on the site. It also lets Congress set aside funds for the work. Eight parts in all make up the act, as its list of contents shows.
plaw-106-352-2000:
Women's wartime work at home is preserved by Public Law 106-352, approved October 24, 2000. It establishes the Rosie the Riveter/World War II Home Front National Historical Park in Richmond, California. Congress created the park to preserve sites tied to the industrial, governmental, and citizen efforts that led to victory in World War II.

The park's boundaries follow a proposed boundary map named in the law. In naming the park for Rosie the Riveter, Congress centered the story on the home front rather than the battlefield. The sites covered are meant for the benefit and inspiration of the people of the United States.
plaw-106-353-2000:
Western Colorado canyon country receives two layers of protection in Public Law 106-353, approved October 24, 2000. The Colorado Canyons National Conservation Area and Black Ridge Canyons Wilderness Act of 2000 sets up both a conservation area and a wilderness. The land sits in the Grand Valley in Mesa County, Colorado, and Grand County, Utah.

Congress found the Black Ridge and Ruby Canyons and Rabbit Valley hold scenic, recreational, paleontological, natural, and wildlife value. It noted public use for hiking and camping, and multiple uses including grazing, in a rural western setting. The law aims to protect and enhance the area for present and future generations.
plaw-106-354-2000:
Medicaid coverage for some cancer patients opens under Public Law 106-354, approved October 24, 2000. The Breast and Cervical Cancer Prevention and Treatment Act of 2000 amends title XIX of the Social Security Act. It provides medical help for certain women screened and found to have breast or cervical cancer under a federally funded screening program.

The law creates the group as an optional category states may cover under Medicaid, described in a new subsection. It also amends the Public Health Service Act and the food and drug law on watching and sharing information about cervical cancer and the human papillomavirus, called HPV. Screening and treatment are linked in one statute.
plaw-106-355-2000:
Historic lighthouses gain a national program in Public Law 106-355, approved October 24, 2000. The National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act of 2000 amends the National Historic Preservation Act. It establishes a national historic lighthouse preservation program inside the historic preservation law.

The Secretary must collect and share information about historic light stations, including lighthouses and related structures. The program supports education about their history and contribution, sponsors research and study, and keeps a listing of historic light stations. It also must assess how well the program works regarding conveying light stations to new holders. Preservation, in this law, includes passing stations on under set rules.
plaw-106-356-2000:
Dayton's aviation park is clarified by Public Law 106-356, approved October 24, 2000. The Dayton Aviation Heritage Preservation Amendments Act of 2000 amends the 1992 law of the same name. It states which areas belong in the Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park in Ohio and authorizes money for the park.

A core parcel in Dayton includes the Wright Cycle Company building, the Hoover Block, and lands between them. Other listed sites include the Setzer building property, homes at 26 and 30 South Williams Street, and Huffman Prairie Flying Field. The sites follow a map dated September 1, 2000, named in the amendment.
plaw-106-357-2000:
White Clay Creek joins a national river system through Public Law 106-357, approved October 24, 2000. The White Clay Creek Wild and Scenic Rivers System Act designates segments and tributaries of the creek, in Delaware and Pennsylvania, as part of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System.

Congress noted an earlier 1991 law directed a study of the creek's eligibility and suitability, done with state and local governments and affected landowners. That study produced a watershed management plan in May 1998. The plan set goals to protect the creek's outstanding values over the long term while managing nearby land and water in a compatible way.
plaw-106-358-2000: Public Law 106-358, approved October 26, 2000, is a one-sentence joint resolution on federal funding. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date specified in section 106(c) of that earlier law is replaced with October 26, 2000. In effect it extends stopgap funding only to that date. The resolution contains nothing else.
plaw-106-359-2000: Stopgap federal funding moves by a single day in Public Law 106-359, approved October 26, 2000. This joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001. It amends Public Law 106-275 by striking the date in section 106(c) and inserting October 27, 2000. Approved the day before that date, it kept appropriations running briefly while Congress worked. No other provision appears.
plaw-106-360-2000: A coastal map correction is ordered by Public Law 106-360, approved October 27, 2000. The Secretary of the Interior must, within thirty days, correct a map in the Coastal Barrier Resources System. The map relates to unit P19-P and sits in a set dated November 2, 1994. Corrections must match a map titled Amendments to the Coastal Barrier Resources System, dated June 5, 2000. The corrected map stays on file for public inspection.
plaw-106-361-2000:
Federal workers' retirement savings change under Public Law 106-361, approved October 27, 2000. It amends title 5 to let people contribute certain rollover distributions to accounts in the Thrift Savings Plan. It also removes some waiting-period requirements for taking part in that plan.

An employee or Member of Congress may move an eligible rollover distribution into the Thrift Savings Fund, using terms drawn from the Internal Revenue Code. The amount moved cannot exceed what would otherwise count in gross income. The point is portability: retirement money from a prior qualified plan can follow the worker into the federal plan.
plaw-106-362-2000:
Nevada public land for an airport is transferred by Public Law 106-362, approved October 27, 2000. The Ivanpah Valley Airport Public Lands Transfer Act provides for conveying federal public lands in the Ivanpah Valley to Clark County. The land is for developing an airport facility and related infrastructure.

The Secretary must convey all federal right, title, and interest in lands shown on a map dated April 1999, titled Ivanpah Valley, Nevada-Airport Selections. The transfer happens despite normal land use planning rules in the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, but subject to conditions and valid existing rights. The map stays open for public inspection.
plaw-106-363-2000: Public Law 106-363, approved October 27, 2000, extends the Defense Production Act of 1950 by one year. Section 717(a) is amended by striking September 30, 2000, and inserting September 30, 2001, as the termination date. Section 711(b) is amended by striking 2000 and inserting 2001, extending the authorization. Those two date changes are the entire law. It keeps the older defense production law alive through the new date.
plaw-106-364-2000: Public Law 106-364, approved October 27, 2000, hands a decision to the Virgin Islands. It amends the Revised Organic Act of the Virgin Islands, which had set the legislature at fifteen senators. The word fifteen is struck, and the number of senators is to be determined by the laws of the Virgin Islands. A second section says the number of members needed for a quorum also shall be set by Virgin Islands law. Congress thus leaves the size of the territory's legislature, and its quorum, to local law.
plaw-106-365-2000:
A plaque at the Lincoln Memorial is provided for by Public Law 106-365, approved October 27, 2000. The Secretary of the Interior shall install a suitable plaque in the memorial area in the District of Columbia. It commemorates the speech by Martin Luther King, Jr., known as the I Have A Dream speech.

Design and placement of the plaque must follow the Commemorative Works Act. The Secretary may accept and spend contributions toward preparing and installing it, without further appropriation. Federal funds may also be used to design, procure, or install the plaque. The law marks the speech at the place where it was delivered.
plaw-106-366-2000:
Nebraska irrigation property changes hands under Public Law 106-366, approved October 27, 2000. The Secretary of the Interior, through the Bureau of Reclamation, must convey property forming the assets of the Middle Loup Division of the Missouri River Basin Project. The buyers are the Loup Basin Reclamation District, the Sargent River Irrigation District, and the Farwell Irrigation District.

Payment terms are stated in dollars in the sample. The Secretary accepts a sum in the two million range from the district, and a similar sum from power customers, as consideration. Part of the money comes from power receipts tied to the Pick-Sloan Missouri Basin Program in fiscal year 2001.
plaw-106-367-2000:
Youth programs run by police gain federal support in Public Law 106-367, approved October 27, 2000. The National Police Athletic League Youth Enrichment Act of 2000 aims to improve school and social outcomes for youth. It also aims to cut juvenile crime and the risk that youth become crime victims, by offering activities during nonschool hours.

Congress listed the league's goals: raise academic success, build trust between youth and law enforcement staff, and raise school attendance. Other goals include lowering juvenile crime in participating communities and giving youths alternatives to drugs, alcohol, tobacco, and gang activity. Positive contact with officers sits at the center of the model.
plaw-106-368-2000: Public Law 106-368, approved October 27, 2000, permits new contracts for a Utah water project. The Secretary of the Interior may contract with the Weber Basin Water Conservancy District, or its member unit contractors, to use Weber Basin Project facilities. The use is for holding, storing, and carrying nonproject water. That water may serve domestic, municipal, industrial, and other beneficial purposes. The contracts may also allow exchange of water among project contractors, using the same facilities, for those purposes. The single-section law grants authority; it does not itself move water.
plaw-106-369-2000:
Louisiana gains a refuge in Public Law 106-369, approved October 27, 2000. The Cat Island National Wildlife Refuge Establishment Act provides for a refuge in West Feliciana Parish. Congress described Cat Island as the southernmost unleveed part of the Mississippi River. It stays shaped by the river's natural movement.

The findings praise one of the densest stands of virgin bald cypress in the Mississippi River Valley, including the nation's champion cypress, seventeen feet wide. Cat Island is habitat for declining forest songbirds and thousands of wintering waterfowl, plus deer, turkey, and furbearers such as mink and bobcats. Refuge status is meant to conserve that ground.
plaw-106-370-2000:
Water rights for a Utah city are conveyed by Public Law 106-370, approved October 27, 2000. The Duchesne City Water Rights Conveyance Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey certain water rights to Duchesne City. Its findings trace the land's long federal history.

Congress recalled that President Lincoln established the Uintah Valley Reservation by executive order in 1861, confirmed in 1864. Later, reservation lands were allotted and unallotted lands returned to the public domain. In July 1905 President Theodore Roosevelt reserved a townsite for Duchesne. That same month the United States filed two Utah applications to appropriate certain waters, the background to the rights conveyed.
plaw-106-371-2000: Public Law 106-371, approved October 27, 2000, raises one funding ceiling for an Idaho water project. It amends a 1950 act authorizing appropriations for the north side pumping division of the Minidoka reclamation project. The old figure, eleven million three hundred ninety-five thousand dollars, is struck. In its place the law inserts fourteen million two hundred thousand dollars. That single substitution is the entire act, raising the amount Congress may appropriate for that division.
plaw-106-372-2000:
A Washington pumping plant study is broadened by Public Law 106-372, approved October 27, 2000. It amends an earlier law about electrification of the Chandler Pumping Plant at Prosser Diversion Dam. The heading gains the words or Water Exchange, and a new alternative is added.

As an alternative to electrification, the Secretary may use up to four million dollars of the appropriated sums to study the engineering feasibility of a water exchange. The exchange would swap Columbia River water for water historically diverted from the Yakima River. The study is done with the Kennewick Irrigation District and in consultation with the Bonneville Power Administration, with a report required.
plaw-106-373-2000:
American help against hunger abroad is revised by Public Law 106-373, approved October 27, 2000. The Famine Prevention and Freedom From Hunger Improvement Act of 2000 amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. It revises provisions on famine prevention and freedom from hunger.

New policy language says the United States should mobilize land-grant universities, other eligible universities, and public and private partners, here and abroad, toward shared goals. Those goals include food security, human health, agricultural growth, trade expansion, and wise, sustainable use of natural resources. The work named includes global research on problems affecting food, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries, and building human and institutional capacity.
plaw-106-374-2000:
Public Law 106-374, approved October 27, 2000, renews grants for centers that study water. The centers were set up under the Water Resources Research Act of 1984. For the main grants, the old sums are struck out and new sums are put in their place in the text of the law.

The new sums are nine million dollars for fiscal year 2001. They are ten million dollars for each of the next two years, then twelve million for each of the two years after that. A second part lifts grants for work on water woes that cross state lines. Those sums rise in the same years, from three million to six million dollars by the last year named.
plaw-106-375-2000:
A commemorative coin is ordered by Public Law 106-375, approved October 27, 2000. The law may be cited as the National Museum of the American Indian Commemorative Coin Act of 2000, or the American Buffalo Coin Commemorative Coin Act of 2000. It requires the Secretary of the Treasury to mint coins honoring that Smithsonian museum.

The findings recall that the Smithsonian Institution was established in 1846 with funds bequeathed by James Smithson for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. Congress called it the world's largest museum complex, with sixteen museums, four research centers, and the National Zoo. The National Museum of the American Indian is presented as part of that story.
plaw-106-376-2000:
Colorado water facilities are transferred by Public Law 106-376, approved October 27, 2000. The Secretary of the Interior must convey certain water distribution facilities to the Northern Colorado Water Conservancy District. The facilities belong to the Colorado-Big Thompson Project in Larimer County.

Named facilities include the North Poudre Supply Canal and Diversion Works, also called the Munroe Gravity Canal. They also include the Charles Hansen Supply Canal and Windsor Extension, and the Dixon Feeder Canal. The district's contract with the United States dates to July 5, 1938. The law moves these distribution works from federal hands to the district that uses them.
plaw-106-377-2000:
Spending for veterans and housing agencies is enacted in Public Law 106-377, approved October 27, 2000. It is the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Housing and Urban Development, and Independent Agencies Appropriations Act, 2001. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001, plus sundry independent agencies, boards, commissions, and corporations.

Like another 2000 appropriations act, it works by incorporation. Section one enacts into law two bills of the 106th Congress, H.R. 5482 and H.R. 5483, both introduced October 18, 2000. The Archivist must print both bill texts as appendixes in the slip law and the Statutes at Large. The dollar lines live in those appended bills.
plaw-106-378-2000:
Public Law 106-378, approved October 27, 2000, adjusts the immigration status of certain Syrian nationals. Congress found that Presidents Bush and Clinton negotiated with Syria to win release of members of the Syrian Jewish population and their immigration to the United States. To accommodate Syria, these people were admitted on temporary visas and later given asylum, rather than as refugees.

That route, Congress said, caused a long and needless delay in their adjustment to lawful permanent resident status. The delay hurt their ability to work in their professions, travel freely, and seek naturalization. The law directs the Attorney General to grant that permanent status without further delay, under its second section.
plaw-106-379-2000:
Copyright wording is corrected by Public Law 106-379, approved October 27, 2000. The Work Made For Hire and Copyright Corrections Act of 2000 makes certain corrections in copyright law. Its central change concerns the definition of a work made for hire in section 101 of title 17.

The words as a sound recording are struck from one paragraph of that definition. The law also says a 1999 amendment that had added those words, and the deletion now made, carry no legal significance. Courts and the Copyright Office must not read them as congressional approval or disapproval of any court decision. The paragraph is read as if neither change had happened.
plaw-106-380-2000:
Veterans' own voices are to be recorded under Public Law 106-380, approved October 27, 2000. The Veterans' Oral History Project Act directs the American Folklife Center at the Library of Congress to set up a program. It will collect video and audio recordings of personal histories and testimonials of American war veterans.

Congress found that wartime service is the highest sacrifice a citizen can make, and it counted service across the century's wars in the millions. It noted almost nineteen million living war veterans at the time, but very few World War I veterans left. The project races that loss, saving firsthand accounts before they disappear.
plaw-106-381-2000: Public Law 106-381, approved October 27, 2000, is a joint resolution extending stopgap federal funding. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date in section 106(c) of that law is replaced with October 28, 2000. It was passed and approved on October 27, one day before the new date. The resolution has no other provision.
plaw-106-382-2000:
Montana water systems are authorized by Public Law 106-382, approved October 27, 2000. The Fort Peck Reservation Rural Water System Act of 2000 authorizes construction of the Fort Peck Reservation Rural Water System. Its first purpose is a safe and adequate municipal, rural, and industrial water supply for residents of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation.

A second purpose helps citizens of Roosevelt, Sheridan, Daniels, and Valley Counties, outside the reservation, develop safe water supplies of the same kinds. The law defines two systems: the Assiniboine and Sioux Rural Water System inside the reservation, and the Dry Prairie Rural Water System in those four counties. One act covers both reservation and neighboring county needs.
plaw-106-383-2000: Public Law 106-383, approved October 27, 2000, authorizes a Smithsonian building project in Hawaii. The Board of Regents may plan, design, construct, and equip laboratory, administrative, and support space. The space houses base operations for the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory Submillimeter Array, located on Mauna Kea at Hilo. Appropriations are authorized of two million dollars for fiscal year 2001 and two million five hundred thousand dollars for fiscal year 2002, to remain available until expended.
plaw-106-384-2000:
Mail rates for cheaper classes of mail are changed by Public Law 106-384, approved October 27, 2000. It amends chapter 36 of title 39, the postal law, to modify rates tied to reduced rate mail matter. The heading in the text calls these reduced rate mail modification provisions.

One new rule says regular rates for a mail class that includes special rate categories must be set using the title's policies. The costs counted cover regular rate mail combined with mail in the matching special categories. A second part gives a residual rule for preferred periodical mail. The law works inside ratemaking formulas, not postage prices a reader pays directly.
plaw-106-385-2000: Public Law 106-385, approved October 27, 2000, renames a Smithsonian museum. The National Museum of American Art, designated under a 1980 law, shall be known as the Smithsonian American Art Museum. Any reference in a law, regulation, document, or paper to the old name counts as a reference to the new one. The change takes effect the day after enactment. The short act makes no change to the museum's collections or work, only to its name in federal usage.
plaw-106-386-2000:
Two large shields for the weak are joined in Public Law 106-386, approved October 28, 2000. The Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act of 2000 works to fight the trade in persons. That trade feeds the sex trade, forced work, and forms of slavery. The act also renews federal plans to stop harm to women.

The act falls in three parts. Part A, the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, sets up a task force drawn from more than one agency. It works on ways to stop the trade and to shield and help its victims. Part B is the Violence Against Women Act of 2000. Part C holds a mix of other rules that did not fit the first two parts.
plaw-106-387-2000:
Farm and food spending for fiscal year 2001 is enacted by Public Law 106-387, approved October 28, 2000. It is the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2001. It covers the year ending September 30, 2001.

The act itself is short because it enacts another bill by reference. Section one makes H.R. 5426, introduced October 6, 2000, into law. The Archivist must print that bill's full text as an appendix to the slip law and in the Statutes at Large. Readers seeking the program dollar amounts must turn to the appended bill, not the brief enacting text.
plaw-106-388-2000: Public Law 106-388, approved October 28, 2000, extends temporary federal funding by one day. This joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001. It amends Public Law 106-275 by striking the date in section 106(c) and inserting October 29, 2000. It was considered, passed, and approved on October 28. The text contains that single change and nothing more.
plaw-106-389-2000: Another one-day funding extension becomes Public Law 106-389, approved October 29, 2000. The joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date specified in section 106(c) is replaced with October 30, 2000. Passed and approved on October 29, it kept stopgap funding in place through the following day. No other section is included.
plaw-106-390-2000:
Work to stop harm before a storm or flood hits gains ground in Public Law 106-390, approved October 30, 2000. The Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 amends the Stafford Disaster Relief Act. Its aims are to set up a plan for work done before disaster strikes, to make relief run more smoothly, and to hold down what relief costs the nation.

Title I deals with work done before disaster. It sets up a task force from more than one agency and calls for plans and for least rules for public and private buildings. Title II cuts costs and red tape. It deals with the costs of running relief, with notice to the public, and with states running a grant plan for this kind of work. It also covers aid to fix or rebuild sites hit by disaster.
plaw-106-391-2000:
Funds for the space agency are set out in Public Law 106-391, approved October 30, 2000. The act bears the long name National Aeronautics and Space Administration Authorization Act of 2000. It lets Congress set aside funds for NASA for fiscal years 2000, 2001, and 2002, and for other ends named in the text.

Title I lists funds for flights by crews, for science, for flight craft and new tools, and for the day-to-day work that backs them. It also funds the office that watches the agency from inside. The same title sets caps and special rules on how funds may be used to build. It names set topics too, such as a craft part called Trans-Hab and a pact that joins space work in one deal.
plaw-106-392-2000:
Endangered fish in two western river basins are helped by Public Law 106-392, approved October 30, 2000. It authorizes the Bureau of Reclamation to provide cost sharing for recovery programs for the Upper Colorado and San Juan River Basins. The stated purpose is to keep those programs moving on their established schedule.

The recovery programs grew from intergovernmental cooperative agreements. One, dated in 1987 and agreed in 1988, covers endangered fish in the Upper Colorado River. A second, dated October 21, 1992, covers the San Juan River. The law defines Upper Division States as Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming, framing the effort as shared across governments.
plaw-106-393-2000:
Counties with large federal land holdings gain steadier payments under Public Law 106-393, approved October 30, 2000. The Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000 aims to restore stability and predictability to yearly payments to states and counties. The land involved is National Forest System land and public domain land managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

Title I sets how the full payment amount is figured, and covers payments meant for public education, transportation, public safety, law enforcement, and other public purposes. The money flows through states from forest land and directly for bureau land programs. Title II covers special projects on federal lands.
plaw-106-394-2000:
Children of federal workers gain health coverage protection in Public Law 106-394, approved October 30, 2000. The Federal Employees Health Benefits Children's Equity Act of 2000 amends the federal employees health benefits law in title 5. It addresses cases where a state court orders an employee to provide health insurance for a child, but the employee fails to do so.

A worker who is not enrolled, yet is under such a court or administrative order, may enroll for self and family coverage. If the worker still fails to enroll in a plan giving full benefits where the child lives, and shows no proof of other coverage, the government can enroll the employee and family. The child is not left uncovered by a parent's inaction.
plaw-106-395-2000:
Some children born abroad gain citizenship on their own, by law, under Public Law 106-395. Congress approved the Child Citizenship Act of 2000 on October 30 of that year. It changes the Immigration and Nationality Act. The change deals with how a child born outside the United States may gain citizenship through a parent who holds it.

Title I writes a new text for section 320 of that act. A child born abroad is a citizen at once when all the set terms are met. One term is that at least one parent is a citizen, by birth or by taking the oath. The child must be under the age of eighteen years. The child must also live in the United States with that parent, in the parent's legal and physical care, after a lawful grant of the right to live here for good.
plaw-106-396-2000:
The visa waiver program becomes permanent in Public Law 106-396, approved October 30, 2000. The Visa Waiver Permanent Program Act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act. It makes improvements to the visa waiver pilot program under section 217 and authorizes it permanently.

Title I is the clearest part: it eliminates pilot program status. Again and again the word pilot is struck from headings and text in section 217, and pilot program period becomes simply program. The change is mostly a series of word deletions, but their effect is large. A temporary travel program no longer depends on pilot authority to continue.
plaw-106-397-2000:
Men and women a court puts in charge of city offices in the capital face new rules in Public Law 106-397. Congress approved the District of Columbia Receivership Accountability Act of 2000 on October 30. The act sets rules for such court-picked chiefs, who run parts of the District of Columbia government for a time.

A chief counts under the act if a District court first picked him or her in 1995 or in any year since then. Each such chief must meet the rules set out in section three of the act. The first rule named there is to push for sound funds and for work run well in the office the chief heads. The act treats this kind of court rule as work that must itself be held to account.
plaw-106-398-2000:
The yearly defense authorization becomes law in an unusual form in Public Law 106-398, approved October 30, 2000. It is the Floyd D. Spence National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2001. It authorizes money for military activities, military construction, and defense work by the Department of Energy, and sets personnel strengths for the armed forces.

The enacting text does not print those provisions itself. Section one enacts into law H.R. 5408, introduced October 6, 2000. Section two orders the Archivist to publish that bill's text as an appendix in the slip law and Statutes at Large. A reader must use the appendix to find any specific program or dollar figure.
plaw-106-399-2000:
Two kinds of guard are laid on one Oregon peak area by Public Law 106-399, approved October 30, 2000. The Steens Mountain Cooperative Management and Protection Act of 2000 marks out the Steens Mountain Wilderness Area. It also marks out a Steens Mountain Cooperative Management and Protection Area in Harney County, Oregon.

The first aim named is to keep the area sound in its old ways of life, its trade, its wild life, and its ties among people. Other aims are to buy private land by swap for both tracts. The act also grows joint work by public and private land owners near the tracts. It lets the state buy land, and rights to build or not to build on land, as the list of aims goes on in the text.
plaw-106-400-2000: Public Law 106-400, approved October 30, 2000, renames a homeless assistance law. The Stewart B. McKinney Homeless Assistance Act becomes the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act. Section one replaces that act's short title subsection with the new name. Section two says any reference in a federal law, regulation, document, or other record to the old name is deemed a reference to the McKinney-Vento name. The act changes the citation only; it does not alter the programs the older law contains.
plaw-106-401-2000: Public Law 106-401, approved October 30, 2000, is a joint resolution continuing federal appropriations briefly. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date in section 106(c) is struck and October 31, 2000, is inserted. The measure was passed and approved on October 30, the day before that date. Like the other resolutions in this series, it contains only that date change.
plaw-106-402-2000:
Help for people with growth and learning limits is rebuilt by Public Law 106-402, approved October 30, 2000. The act is the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act of 2000. It aims to make the web of help for such people work better for them and for their kin.

Title I bears the name Programs for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities. Its first part deals with what Congress found, with aims, with word meanings, and with files and checks on funds. It deals with the duties of the head of the agency and with that head's reports to Congress. It also deals with state say over the work, with jobs for people with such limits, and with their rights. A later part gives federal aid to state groups that plan this work.
plaw-106-403-2000: Public Law 106-403, approved November 1, 2000, carries stopgap funding to its own approval date. The joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001. It amends Public Law 106-275 by replacing the date in section 106(c) with November 1, 2000. Congress passed it on October 31, and it was approved the next day. The resolution consists of that single amendment and no other language.
plaw-106-404-2000:
Federal inventions move toward private use more easily under Public Law 106-404, approved November 1, 2000. The Technology Transfer Commercialization Act of 2000 aims to improve how federal agencies license federally owned inventions. Congress linked that aim to the nation's network of more than seven hundred federal laboratories and its universities.

The findings praise the Bayh-Dole Act of 1980 as a landmark change in technology policy. They say its success gives a framework for removing bureaucratic barriers and simplifying licenses for inventions in the federal patent portfolio. Congress also noted two decades of support for technology transfer and public-private partnerships to sharpen American competitiveness.
plaw-106-405-2000:
Commercial space flight is promoted by Public Law 106-405, approved November 1, 2000. The Commercial Space Transportation Competitiveness Act of 2000 aims to develop the commercial space transportation industry. It authorizes money for the Office of the Associate Administrator for Commercial Space Transportation and for the Office of Space Commercialization.

Congress found a strong United States space transportation industry vital to economic well-being and national security. It said a five-year extension of rules on excess third party claims payments would help American firms compete abroad. It also noted space transportation may evolve into airplane-style operations, and called for study of the liability risk-sharing system over the next three years.
plaw-106-406-2000:
Medical visitors who need more time in the United States are addressed by Public Law 106-406, approved November 1, 2000. The International Patient Act of 2000 creates a three-year pilot program under the Immigration and Nationality Act. It concerns certain nonimmigrant visitors admitted under the visa waiver pilot program who require medical treatment here.

Normally permission for voluntary departure is capped at one hundred twenty days. From October 1, 2000, through September 30, 2003, the Attorney General may, for humanitarian purposes and at his discretion, waive that limit in these medical cases. The waiver sits inside set conditions stated in the amendment. The law is narrow: it lengthens time, it does not grant a new status.
plaw-106-407-2000:
A federal site in Washington is opened to redevelopment by Public Law 106-407, approved November 1, 2000. The Southeast Federal Center Public-Private Development Act of 2000 authorizes the Administrator of General Services to provide for redevelopment of the Southeast Federal Center in the District of Columbia.

The center is defined by streets and river: from Issac Hull Avenue east to 1st Street west, and from M Street north to the Anacostia River south, with two stated exclusions. The Administrator may enter agreements including leases, contracts, cooperative agreements, limited partnerships, joint ventures, and trusts. The name public-private signals that private partners, not only agencies, may rebuild the site.
plaw-106-408-2000:
Fish and wildlife grant money is increased by Public Law 106-408, approved November 1, 2000. Its long title is the Fish and Wildlife Programs Improvement and National Wildlife Refuge System Centennial Act of 2000. It amends the Pittman-Robertson Wildlife Restoration Act and the Dingell-Johnson Sport Fish Restoration Act.

Title I, on wildlife and sport fish restoration, covers administration expenses, firearm and bow hunter education and safety grant programs, and a multistate conservation grant program. The act also reauthorizes the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation law. And it commemorates the centennial of the first national wildlife refuge, established March 14, 1903. Funding and remembrance are paired in one statute.
plaw-106-409-2000: Public Law 106-409, approved November 1, 2000, extends a religious worker immigration program for three years. The Religious Workers Act of 2000 amends the Immigration and Nationality Act. In the special immigrant religious worker provision, the year 2000, each place it appears, is struck and 2003 is inserted. The amendment takes effect October 1, 2000. The brief act does only that extension, keeping the special immigrant religious worker program in force for three more years.
plaw-106-410-2000: Public Law 106-410, approved November 1, 2000, authorizes four years of money for a records commission. It amends title 44 to authorize appropriations for the National Historical Publications and Records Commission for fiscal years 2002 through 2005. New subparagraphs set ten million dollars for each of those four years. The punctuation of the prior list is adjusted so the new items can be added at the end. The short act is a funding authorization only; the yearly amount in the sample is given here in words.
plaw-106-411-2000:
Great apes receive American conservation help under Public Law 106-411, approved November 1, 2000. The Great Ape Conservation Act of 2000 supports conservation programs in countries within the apes' range. It also funds projects by people with demonstrated expertise in great ape conservation.

Congress found great ape populations had fallen so far that long-term survival in the wild was in serious jeopardy. It named the chimpanzee, gorilla, bonobo, orangutan, and gibbon as endangered under the Endangered Species Act and an international trade convention. It blamed habitat loss from human encroachment and logging, and said resources so far had not been enough to cope. Money and expertise are the law's answer.
plaw-106-412-2000:
Public Law 106-412, approved November 1, 2000, authorizes a small land exchange in McLean, Virginia. The Secretary of the Interior and the Director of Central Intelligence may swap land at the George Washington Memorial Parkway. Interior would give about one and three-quarter acres inside the parkway boundary. The Central Intelligence Agency would give about two and nine-tenths acres next to that boundary.

Both parcels are shown on National Park Service drawings dated August 6, 1998, which must stay open for public inspection at park service offices. Conditions on the exchange follow in section two, beginning in the sample. The swap adjusts two neighboring federal holdings at once.
plaw-106-413-2000:
Veterans' pay rates rise with living costs under Public Law 106-413, approved November 1, 2000. The Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2000 takes effect December 1, 2000. It raises compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities. It also raises dependency and indemnity compensation for survivors of certain disabled veterans.

The Secretary of Veterans Affairs must increase the dollar amounts in effect under listed parts of title 38. The amounts covered include basic compensation, added compensation for dependents, and the clothing allowance. The law names the categories rather than printing new figures, so the increase is applied to the amounts already in effect on that date.
plaw-106-414-2000:
Vehicle and tire defect reporting is tightened by Public Law 106-414, approved November 1, 2000. It is the Transportation Recall Enhancement, Accountability, and Documentation Act, shortened to TREAD Act. It amends title 49 and requires reports about defects in motor vehicles, tires, or other equipment in foreign countries.

First, the law restores an earlier section by repealing a change made in a 2001 transportation appropriations act, as if that change had never been enacted. Then new reporting duties begin: a maker that decides to conduct a safety campaign abroad must report within five working days, under the language shown. The act links foreign defect news to American recall decisions.
plaw-106-415-2000:
Public Law 106-415, approved November 1, 2000, widens a naturalization help law to surviving spouses. It amends the Hmong Veterans' Naturalization Act of 2000. A new paragraph extends coverage to a person who meets one stated requirement and is the surviving spouse of a covered person. That covered person must have been killed or died in Laos, Thailand, or Vietnam.

A conforming amendment updates a cross-reference to include the new paragraph. Section two sets a deadline for applications by people in the new group, adding a sentence to the earlier act. The law is short and targeted: it keeps a widow or widower of a Hmong veteran inside a benefit the veteran's death might otherwise have ended.
plaw-106-416-2000: Public Law 106-416, approved November 1, 2000, is a joint resolution extending stopgap appropriations. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date in section 106(c) is replaced with November 2, 2000. Congress considered and passed it on November 1, the day it was approved. The resolution makes that single date change and contains no other provision, continuing the pattern of very short funding extensions that fall.
plaw-106-417-2000:
Tribal clinics gain permanent direct billing rights under Public Law 106-417, approved November 1, 2000. The Alaska Native and American Indian Direct Reimbursement Act of 2000 amends the Indian Health Care Improvement Act. It makes permanent a demonstration program for direct billing of Medicare, Medicaid, and other third party payors, and expands eligibility to more tribes.

Congress recalled that a 1988 law set up a test for four tribally operated Indian Health Service hospitals or clinics. They tried direct billing and receipt of payment for care given to patients covered by those programs. The findings in the sample begin to report that the four participants started the demonstration. Permanence, in 2000, is Congress endorsing the test.
plaw-106-418-2000:
Part of the Delaware River is protected by Public Law 106-418, approved November 1, 2000. The Lower Delaware Wild and Scenic Rivers Act designates portions of the lower Delaware River and its tributaries as part of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System.

Congress noted a 1992 law directed a study of the river's eligibility, done with federal, state, regional, and local agencies. During that study a task force and the National Park Service wrote a river management plan dated August 1997. The plan set goals for long-term protection of the river's outstanding values. Congress also noted twenty-four municipalities along eligible segments passed resolutions supporting designation.
plaw-106-419-2000:
School aid and health care for those who served in war are both raised by Public Law 106-419. Congress approved the Veterans Benefits and Health Care Improvement Act of 2000 on November 1 of that year. The act amends title 38 of the code. It lifts the rates of school aid paid under the Montgomery GI Bill for study after service.

Title I deals with school aid, and its first part deals with the GI Bill itself. Part one lifts the base rates of that aid for those who claim it. It adds one rule for all: a high school diploma, or a like pass, is a must before a claim for the aid. It also starts to drop a rule that tied the aid to a first set term of active duty in the armed forces.
plaw-106-420-2000:
Students shopping for college help gain fraud protection from Public Law 106-420, approved November 1, 2000. The College Scholarship Fraud Prevention Act of 2000 aims to strengthen protections against fraud in offers of financial assistance for college education.

Congress found a substantial amount of fraud in that market. The fraud includes false claims about sources of scholarships, grants, loans, and other aid, and about portfolios tailored to a buyer's needs. Other false claims cover students supposedly preselected as eligible, aid promised to buyers of set services, and the business ties of the seller. The findings map the pitches a family might hear before the law's protections begin.
plaw-106-421-2000:
Idaho land near a national reserve is rearranged by Public Law 106-421, approved November 1, 2000. The Castle Rock Ranch Acquisition Act of 2000 directs the Secretary of the Interior to use land exchanges to acquire about one thousand two hundred forty acres. The land, Castle Rock Ranch, sits outside the City of Rocks National Reserve near Almo, Idaho, and would be conveyed to the State of Idaho through the exchanges.

Definitions in the law also name Hagerman Fossil Beds National Monument, shown on a park service map dated January 7, 1998. The ranch is shown on a map dated March 25, 1999. Acquisition begins in section three, subject to a condition the sample cuts off.
plaw-106-422-2000:
The Tennessee Valley Authority gains a full inspector general under Public Law 106-422, approved November 1, 2000. It amends the Inspector General Act of 1978 so certain designated federal entities count as establishments under that act. The first section is entirely about the Tennessee Valley Authority.

Congress found that inspectors general help prevent and eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse in the federal government, and that independence is vital for one to work well. The amendment moves the Authority out of one list in section 8G and adds its Board of Directors to the definition of establishment head in section eleven. Similar treatment for named entities gives their watchdogs the act's full standing.
plaw-106-423-2000:
A permanent homeland for a tribe is provided by Public Law 106-423, approved November 1, 2000. The Timbisha Shoshone Homeland Act gives the Timbisha Shoshone Tribe a permanent land base within its aboriginal homeland, in California and Nevada.

Congress found the tribe has lived since time immemorial in parts of both states, including land now in Death Valley National Park. Since 1936 the tribe has lived and governed on about forty acres near Furnace Creek in the park. It won federal recognition in 1983 but had no land base in its homeland.
