Congress noted growing membership and a need for housing, government, cultural facilities, and sustainable economic development.
plaw-106-424-2000:
The board that probes crashes gains funds and new terms in Public Law 106-424, approved November 1, 2000. The National Transportation Safety Board Amendments Act of 2000 lets Congress set aside funds for the board for fiscal years 2000, 2001, 2002, and 2003. It amends title 49 of the code in more than one place as it goes.

One early change writes the word meanings part of that title anew. The word accident is made to cover harm to, or loss of, craft in travel by land or air, and in pipe lines as well. It counts as an accident no matter how the first event came about. A later part deals with the board's power to make deals with other groups, as the text shows at the point where the sample ends.
plaw-106-425-2000:
Long-running land claims in New Mexico are settled by Public Law 106-425, approved November 1, 2000. The Santo Domingo Pueblo Claims Settlement Act of 2000 settles the land claims of the Pueblo of Santo Domingo. Congress found the pueblo had asserted claims to lands in its aboriginal use area in north central New Mexico for many years, through many lawsuits.

One dispute traces to December 1927, when the Pueblo Lands Board confirmed a survey of the Santo Domingo Grant. At the same time it purported to extinguish Indian title to about twenty-seven thousand acres inside three overlapping Spanish land grants. Congress noted a federal appeals court later held the board had ignored a clear congressional directive. Settlement replaces that litigation.
plaw-106-426-2000: Public Law 106-426, approved November 3, 2000, does two things in one joint resolution. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001, amending Public Law 106-275 to insert November 3, 2000, as the date in section 106(c). It also adds a new section making seven million one hundred thousand dollars available to the Administrator of General Services. That money is for expenses under the Presidential Transition Act of 1963. Unlike the other one-line extensions that fall, this one pairs its date change with transition funding.
plaw-106-427-2000: Public Law 106-427, approved November 4, 2000, extends temporary appropriations by one day. This joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001. It amends Public Law 106-275 by striking the date in section 106(c) and inserting November 4, 2000. Congress passed it on November 3, and it was approved the next day. The single sentence is the whole measure, continuing the run of daily stopgap extensions during the fall budget standoff.
plaw-106-428-2000: Public Law 106-428, approved November 4, 2000, gives stopgap funding a longer stretch than its neighbors. This joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date in section 106(c) becomes November 14, 2000. Its history is older than most in the series: the House first passed it in November 1999, the Senate amended and passed it November 1, 2000, and the House agreed November 3. The resolution still makes only that date change.
plaw-106-429-2000:
Foreign aid and export spending for fiscal year 2001 is enacted by Public Law 106-429, approved November 6, 2000. It is the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2001, for the year ending September 30, 2001.

The act works by incorporating another bill. Section 101 enacts into law H.R. 5526, introduced October 24, 2000. The Archivist must include that bill's text as an appendix in the slip law and in the Statutes at Large. As with the other incorporated appropriations acts of 2000, the operative amounts and conditions sit in the appendix, not in the short public law itself.
plaw-106-430-2000:
Health workers' needle injuries are targeted by Public Law 106-430, approved November 6, 2000. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act requires changes in the bloodborne pathogens standard under the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970.

Congress found many workers exposed to bloodborne pathogens had caught fatal and serious diseases, including HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C, from blood and other infectious materials at work. It noted a 1991 safety standard had greatly reduced that risk. Yet accidental sharps injuries in health care settings stayed a serious problem, the findings say, citing the Centers for Disease Control as the sample breaks off. Safer devices and practice are the direction of the law.
plaw-106-431-2000:
An island in Lake Michigan is set aside by Public Law 106-431, approved November 6, 2000. The Saint Helena Island National Scenic Area Act establishes the Saint Helena Island National Scenic Area in Michigan. Its purposes are to preserve the island's outstanding resources and values for present and future generations.

Other stated purposes cover conservation and enhancement of primitive recreation, fish and wildlife habitat, vegetation, and historical and cultural resources. Establishment takes effect only when satisfactory title to the whole island passes to the United States. One exception is land conveyed to the Great Lakes Lighthouse Keepers Association under a coast guard law named in the text.
plaw-106-432-2000:
Public Law 106-432, approved November 6, 2000, expands an Oregon county park with federal land. The Miwaleta Park Expansion Act provides for the Bureau of Land Management to convey a county park and adjacent land to Douglas County, Oregon. The Secretary of the Interior shall convey the parcel without consideration, meaning without payment.

The parcel includes Miwaleta Park itself, a county park run by agreement on federal land, plus an adjacent federal tract. Its legal description places it in section 27, township 31 south, range 4 west, in Douglas County. Ownership follows management: the county already ran the park, and the law gives it the ground.
plaw-106-433-2000:
Social Security numbers are hidden from government check envelopes by Public Law 106-433, approved November 6, 2000. The Social Security Number Confidentiality Act of 2000 amends title 31. It bars the appearance of Social Security account numbers on or through unopened mailings of checks or other drafts drawn on public money in the Treasury.

A new subsection orders the Secretary of the Treasury to take the actions needed so numbers, including derivatives of them, are not visible on or through those unopened mailings. A third section sets the effective date and a transitional rule for the change. The protection is practical: a number cannot be read through an envelope window.
plaw-106-434-2000:
A radio station receives a small forest parcel under Public Law 106-434, approved November 6, 2000. The Secretary of Agriculture shall convey to KATY 101.3 FM all federal interest in about one and six-hundredths acres in the San Bernardino National Forest in Riverside County, California. The parcel lies in the north half of section 23, township 5 south, range 2 east.

The conveyance is subject to valid existing rights and settlement of claims as the section provides. Secretary and station must agree on the legal description, drawn from an appraisal report dated August 26, 1999. Consideration equals the appraised fair market value, as the sample begins to state. Generously, Congress settled a tiny land question by statute.
plaw-106-435-2000:
Coins for the Salt Lake winter games are authorized by Public Law 106-435, approved November 6, 2000. The 2002 Winter Olympic Commemorative Coin Act provides for minting coins to support the 2002 Salt Lake Olympic Winter Games and programs of the United States Olympic Committee.

The Secretary of the Treasury shall mint up to eighty thousand five dollar gold coins, ninety percent gold, and up to four hundred thousand one dollar silver coins, ninety percent silver. Designs must show American athletes taking part in the 2002 Olympic Winter Games. Each coin carries its value, the year 2002, and the words Liberty, In God We Trust, and United States, as the sample continues.
plaw-106-436-2000: Beachwood, Ohio, receives a named post office building under Public Law 106-436, approved November 6, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 3695 Green Road becomes the Larry Small Post Office Building. Section two deems any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to be a reference to the Small building. The House passed it October 2 and the Senate October 24, per the history printed in the sample. The act is a designation only.
plaw-106-437-2000:
Park Police medical bills get a direct payment route in Public Law 106-437, approved November 6, 2000. The law permits payment of medical expenses incurred by the United States Park Police in the line of duty to be made directly by the National Park Service. Payment rests on a certificate from the Chief of the Park Police stating the need for the services and the injury or disease involved.

The law also authorizes money to reimburse the park service on the schedule stated. Its second aim, from the title, allows waiver and indemnification in mutual law enforcement agreements between the park service and a state or local government when state law requires it. Two administrative fixes share one short statute.
plaw-106-438-2000: Public Law 106-438, approved November 6, 2000, names a Baltimore postal facility for a judge. The building at 900 East Fayette Street becomes the Judge Harry Augustus Cole Post Office Building. Its references section says any mention of the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other United States record means the Cole building. The act consists of the designation and that reference rule, and nothing else.
plaw-106-439-2000: Another Baltimore post office building is named in Public Law 106-439, approved November 6, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 1001 Frederick Road becomes the Frederick L. Dewberry, Jr. Post Office Building. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or record to that facility is deemed a reference to the Dewberry building. That is the full substance of the law, a single naming with its records effect.
plaw-106-440-2000: Erie, Pennsylvania, gains a named post office building from Public Law 106-440, approved November 6, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 2108 East 38th Street becomes the Gertrude A. Barber Post Office Building. Section two provides that references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records are references to the Barber building. The designation, with that records rule, is the entire law.
plaw-106-441-2000: Public Law 106-441, approved November 6, 2000, designates a postal building in Carrollton, Georgia. The facility at 110 Postal Way becomes the Samuel P. Roberts Post Office Building. The law's second section deems references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, or other records to be references to the Roberts building. It passed the House September 19 and the Senate October 24, according to the history in the sample. No other provision is enacted.
plaw-106-442-2000: Public Law 106-442, approved November 6, 2000, extends a foundation's time to build a memorial. It amends the Omnibus Parks and Public Lands Management Act of 1996. That law's section 506 gave the Black Patriots Foundation legislative authority to establish a commemorative work. The amendment strikes the year 2000 in that section and inserts 2005. In one line, the foundation gains five more years of authority. The act states no reason and adds no condition; the sample is the whole amendment and its legislative history.
plaw-106-443-2000:
An elementary school stays on park land longer under Public Law 106-443, approved November 6, 2000. It extends the Los Angeles Unified School District's authority to use park lands in South Gate, California, for elementary school purposes. The land was bought with money from the land and water conservation fund.

Congress found Tweedy Elementary School was closed in 1988 over health risk concerns at its site, and moved to South Gate Park. The city's lease expired in March 1991 with no new school built. A 1992 law gave an eight-year extension, due to expire October 23, 2000, with little progress made, the findings continue. The 2000 law extends the arrangement again.
plaw-106-444-2000:
Records of freed people after slavery are ordered preserved by Public Law 106-444, approved November 6, 2000. The Freedmen's Bureau Records Preservation Act of 2000 amends title 44 to ensure preservation of the records of the Freedmen's Bureau, formally the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands.

A new section directs the Archivist to preserve those records using microfilm technology, so the documents last for future generations. It also builds on a pilot project with the University of Florida. Partnerships with Howard University and other institutions should index the records and make them easier for the public to use, including historians, genealogists, and students. Preservation and access are joined.
plaw-106-445-2000:
Public Law 106-445, approved November 6, 2000, clarifies the United States Mint's power to make collector coins. The United States Mint Numismatic Coin Clarification Act of 2000 makes word-level fixes in title 31. For silver proof coins, a cross-reference changes from paragraphs one to paragraphs two. For platinum coins, the word bullion becomes platinum bullion coins.

A third section adds a report requirement. A Mint report must contain, not merely reflect, certain items, and a new subparagraph requires a supplemental schedule. That schedule details costs and expenses for production, marketing, and distribution, as the sample begins to list. Small wording changes carry the clarification Congress intended.
plaw-106-446-2000:
Dogs that served in war may find homes at the end of their work under Public Law 106-446. Congress approved the act on November 6, 2000. It amends title 10 of the code. Its aim is to ease the path by which law officers, past handlers, and others fit to care for such dogs may take them in.

A new part of the code lets the head of the armed forces make a dog free for a new home. That step comes at the end of the dog's working life, or when the dog is no longer needed. A dog ruled unfit for a new home is the one case left out of the plan. The chief of the dog's last unit rules on that point. That chief must weigh what the unit's animal doctor says on the dog's health and mood.
plaw-106-447-2000:
Trade and new firms on tribal land gain a push from Public Law 106-447, approved November 6, 2000. The Indian Tribal Regulatory Reform and Business Development Act of 2000 cuts red tape with one aim in view. That aim is to draw funds, firms, and growth to work done on Indian lands by tribes and by those who deal with them.

Congress found a hard truth at the root of the act. Native Americans hold rich lands and a proud drive to rule their own lives. Yet they face worse rates of job loss, want, poor health, and poor homes than any other group in the land. Congress found too that tribes find it hard to draw in the towns near their lands, and funds from far off, for work on tribal soil. That wall is what the act aims to break.
plaw-106-448-2000: Public Law 106-448, approved November 6, 2000, lifts an oath rule for some who seek to become citizens. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Act. The Attorney General may drop the oath for a man or woman who can not grasp what the oath means. The bar is a flaw of body or mind, or a limit in growth, as the act states. One let off the oath counts as true to the base law of the land. The change holds for claims made at any time.
plaw-106-449-2000: Public Law 106-449, approved November 6, 2000, moves the due date of a yearly plan from the Mayor of the District of Columbia. The plan, on how well the city runs its work, used to be due by March 1 of each year. Now it is due when the city sends its budget to Congress, starting with the year 2001. The act also strikes lines about two grades of work, a pass grade and a top grade, from the plan rules. One more date, in a later part, moves from 1999 to 2001 to match.
plaw-106-450-2000:
Two fisheries topics share Public Law 106-450, approved November 7, 2000. Title I, the Fishermen's Protective Act Amendments of 2000, extends help for owners of United States fishing vessels seized and detained by a foreign country. In the 1967 act, the reimbursement period's end year changes from 2000 to 2003. A clerical edit also replaces Secretary of the Interior with Secretary of Commerce.

Title II is the Yukon River Salmon Act of 2000, marked for Alaska and Canada in the text. It begins with a Yukon River Salmon Panel section. The pairing is practical rather than thematic: an extension for seized vessels and a new salmon title travel in one law, as short titles inside the larger public law show.
plaw-106-451-2000:
A government report on wartime wrongs is ordered by Public Law 106-451, approved November 7, 2000. The Wartime Violation of Italian American Civil Liberties Act calls for a report detailing injustices suffered by Italian Americans during World War II. It also calls for a formal acknowledgment of those injustices by the President.

Congress found the freedom of more than six hundred thousand Italian-born immigrants and their families was restricted by measures branding them enemy aliens. Those measures included identification cards, travel restrictions, and seizure of property. More than ten thousand Italian Americans on the West Coast were forced from their homes, and more than fifty thousand faced curfews. Thousands were arrested, hundreds interned.
plaw-106-452-2000: Chicago's Logan Square Post Office is redesignated by Public Law 106-452, approved November 7, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 2339 North California Avenue becomes the Roberto Clemente Post Office. Its references section deems any mention of the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record a reference to the Clemente post office. The law makes that renaming only, replacing the Logan Square name in federal usage.
plaw-106-453-2000: Public Law 106-453, approved November 7, 2000, redesignates a postal station in South Euclid, Ohio. The facility at 1568 South Green Road, known as the South Euclid Station, becomes the Arnold C. D'Amico Station. Note that the new name ends in Station, not Post Office Building, matching the facility's prior style. References to it in federal laws, maps, and records are deemed references to the D'Amico Station under section two.
plaw-106-454-2000: Odum, Georgia, gains a named post office building in Public Law 106-454, approved November 7, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 219 South Church Street becomes the Ruth Harris Coleman Post Office Building. Section two says references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records mean the Coleman building. The act contains the designation and that rule, and no further provision.
plaw-106-455-2000:
Resource questions in an Alaska park are addressed by Public Law 106-455, approved November 7, 2000. The Glacier Bay National Park Resource Management Act of 2000 covers Glacier Bay National Park. Its definitions name local residents, including people in Hoonah who descend from those with a historic tradition of sea gull egg gathering inside the present park.

Outer waters are defined as all marine waters in the park outside Glacier Bay proper. Section three turns to commercial fishing, which the Secretary shall allow in those outer waters under a management plan named in the text. The law balances park protection with local traditions and fishing that predate or surround the park.
plaw-106-456-2000:
Colorado wilderness grows by one named area in Public Law 106-456, approved November 7, 2000. The Spanish Peaks Wilderness Act of 2000 designates land in the San Isabel National Forest as the Spanish Peaks Wilderness. It amends the Colorado Wilderness Act of 1993 to add the area as item twenty.

The new wilderness covers about eighteen thousand acres, as shown on a map titled Proposed Spanish Peaks Wilderness, dated February 10, 1999. The Secretary of Agriculture must file a map and boundary description with two congressional committees as soon as practicable after enactment. The next subsection gives that filing legal force, as the sample begins. Designation and paperwork together complete the act.
plaw-106-457-2000:
Work to heal the mouths of rivers gains a plan in Public Law 106-457, approved November 7, 2000. The Estuaries and Clean Waters Act of 2000 aims to spur that healing work. It does so by making funds for such work flow with less waste. It also aims to join the work of federal and non-federal groups in one shared push.

Title I sets up a plan to heal these shore lands, a council to guide it, and a broad approach for the work as a whole. It adds watch over each job, reports on how jobs fare, and funds to pay for them. Title II deals with Chesapeake Bay and its healing. Title III adds a shore site to the list of such sites that the nation aids, and gives grants and funds for that list.
plaw-106-458-2000:
Arizona forest sites may be sold or traded under Public Law 106-458, approved November 7, 2000. The Arizona National Forest Improvement Act of 2000 authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to convey administrative sites in Arizona national forests. It also authorizes conveying land to the City of Sedona for a wastewater treatment facility.

Section three lists sites the Secretary may sell or exchange on set terms. The Camp Verde Administrative Site covers about two hundred thirteen acres, shown on a 1997 map. A portion of the Cave Creek Administrative Site covers about sixteen acres. The list continues with the Fredonia site as the sample ends. Sedona is defined simply as the City in the act.
plaw-106-459-2000:
Public Law 106-459, approved November 7, 2000, raises a funding ceiling for cleaning salt from the Colorado River. It amends the Colorado River Basin Salinity Control Act to authorize more measures to control salinity upstream of Imperial Dam in a cost-effective way. One figure in section 208(c) changes from seventy-five million dollars to one hundred seventy-five million dollars, with wording updated to match new section references.

Section two orders a report from the Secretary of the Interior. It must cover the program for reducing salt contributions to the river from lands run by the Bureau of Land Management. The report must give specific information on individual projects and how funding was allocated, by a deadline stated in the text.
plaw-106-460-2000: Public Law 106-460, approved November 7, 2000, gives a Montana school district federal land for free. The Secretary of the Interior shall issue to the Landusky School District, without consideration, a patent for the surface and mineral estates of certain lots. The land totals about two and six-hundredths acres. It is described as township 25 north, range 24 east, Montana Prime Meridian, section 27, block 2, school reserve, and block 3, lot 13. The transfer is subject to valid existing rights. The one-paragraph act contains the direction, the land description, and nothing else.
plaw-106-461-2000:
Hoover Dam souvenirs gain a legal home in Public Law 106-461, approved November 7, 2000. The Hoover Dam Miscellaneous Sales Act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to produce and sell products and publications about the dam. Revenue from the sales goes into the Colorado River Dam fund.

Congress found that selling public information about recreation, fish, wildlife, and public land and water serves real public benefits. It noted that in 1997 more than a million visitors toured Hoover Dam, including three hundred thousand from foreign countries. Visitors often ask to buy maps and publications, and the Bureau of Reclamation is often the sole source. The act lets the bureau meet that demand.
plaw-106-462-2000:
Divided ownership of Indian land is the problem in Public Law 106-462, approved November 7, 2000. The Indian Land Consolidation Act Amendments of 2000 aim to reduce the fractionated ownership of Indian lands. Title I is called Indian Land Consolidation.

The findings recount allotment policy in the 1800s and early 1900s, when the United States allotted tribal lands to individual members to assimilate Indian people. More than ninety million acres passed from tribal ownership as a result. Many allotments were taken out of trust, often without the owner's consent. Owners without limits on sale faced exploitation and sold with no lasting benefit. Later inheritance rules split remaining trust allotments among ever more owners, as the findings continue.
plaw-106-463-2000:
Coal lease limits rise under Public Law 106-463, approved November 7, 2000. The Coal Market Competition Act of 2000 amends the Mineral Leasing Act to increase the most federal coal lease acreage one entity may hold in any one state.

Congress found the nation's largest coal deposits sit on federal land in Utah, Colorado, Montana, and the Powder River Basin of Wyoming. It noted federal coal is mined under leases from the 1920 Mineral Leasing Act, and that the sub-bituminous coal is low in sulfur, the cleanest burning for energy. The acreage limit had stood since 1976, at forty-six thousand eighty acres per state, less than the limit for other minerals, as the findings begin to argue.
plaw-106-464-2000:
Native American business and tourism are promoted by Public Law 106-464, approved November 7, 2000. The Native American Business Development, Trade Promotion, and Tourism Act of 2000 provides for business development and trade promotion for Native Americans.

Its findings start with the Constitution: the commerce clause recognizes a special relationship between the United States and Indian tribes. Since 1970, each President has reaffirmed a government-to-government relationship in the Indian self-determination era, Congress said. A 1994 Clinton memorandum told agencies, especially those affecting economic development, to weigh their actions' impact on tribes. The act builds its programs on that stated relationship, though the sample cuts off before the program sections.
plaw-106-465-2000:
A massacre site becomes a national historic site under Public Law 106-465, approved November 7, 2000. The Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site Establishment Act of 2000 authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to establish the site in Colorado.

Congress found that on November 29, 1864, a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village under Chief Black Kettle, along Sand Creek, was attacked by about seven hundred volunteer soldiers under Colonel John M. Chivington. More than one hundred fifty Cheyenne and Arapaho were killed, most of them women, children, or elderly. Soldiers committed atrocities on the dead. Congress called the site deeply significant to descendants and tribes for remembering ancestors there.
plaw-106-466-2000:
Idaho irrigation works pass to a local district under Public Law 106-466, approved November 7, 2000. The Nampa and Meridian Conveyance Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey certain irrigation facilities to the Nampa and Meridian Irrigation District. The transfer should happen as soon as practicable after enactment.

It follows a Memorandum of Agreement dated July 7, 1999, between the Secretary and the district. The conveyance includes all federal interest in canals, laterals, drains, and other parts of the water distribution and drainage system. Those works are already operated or maintained by the district for lands inside its boundaries. A liability section follows, effective on the conveyance date.
plaw-106-467-2000: Public Law 106-467, approved November 9, 2000, lets the federal water chief sign deals with a county water agency in California. The agency is the Solano County Water Agency. The deals let it use works of the Solano Project to hold, store, and move water that is not part of the project. That water may serve homes, towns, and trade. Users may swap water as well. The grant stops at Mile 26 of the Putah South Canal.
plaw-106-468-2000:
Lost grown-ups gain a search net in Public Law 106-468, approved November 9, 2000. The act bears the short name Kristen's Act. It lets the Attorney General give grants to groups that work to find missing adults. The grants may go to public bodies, to groups that work for no gain, or to teams made of both.

Work paid for by the grants can help police and kin find a lost man or woman. It can keep a shared list for the whole land, to track those put at risk by age or by a weak mind, or lost in ways no one can yet explain. The grants can pay for counts of the lost, for facts and leads for kin, for word to the public, and for a hub that clears facts on the lost for all.
plaw-106-469-2000:
Energy conservation programs are extended by Public Law 106-469, approved November 9, 2000. Despite its broad short title, the Energy Act of 2000 extends programs under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act through fiscal year 2003. Title I concerns the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and may be cited separately as the Energy Policy and Conservation Act Amendments of 2000.

Early amendments edit that older act's findings, striking words about standby rationing authority and energy conservation plans. Two numbered paragraphs are removed outright. Further edits strike whole sections, one on a topic the sample does not name in full. The law is a housekeeping extension of the 1970s energy framework, trimming old language while keeping the programs alive.
plaw-106-470-2000:
A New England valley is studied for heritage status in Public Law 106-470, approved November 9, 2000. The Upper Housatonic National Heritage Area Study Act of 2000 directs the Secretary of the Interior to study the Upper Housatonic Valley in Connecticut and Massachusetts. The question is whether establishing a national heritage area there is suitable and feasible.

The study must judge whether the area holds natural, historic, and cultural resources that together show distinctive parts of American heritage. It asks whether those resources are best managed through partnerships of public and private groups, using diverse and sometimes separated resources and active communities. It also asks whether the valley reflects traditions, customs, beliefs, and folklife of value to the national story.
plaw-106-471-2000:
Two Virginia wilderness areas are created by Public Law 106-471, approved November 9, 2000. It designates certain National Forest System lands in Virginia as wilderness. The law amends a 1988 act on Virginia and West Virginia wilderness to add two paragraphs at the end of its list.

The first addition is land in the George Washington National Forest of about five thousand nine hundred sixty-three acres, known as the Priest Wilderness Area. The second is about four thousand six hundred eight acres in the same forest, known as the Three Ridges Wilderness Area. Both follow maps titled as study areas and dated June 6, 2000. Together they add over ten thousand acres.
plaw-106-472-2000:
Grain grading and farm storage are updated by Public Law 106-472, approved November 9, 2000. The Grain Standards and Warehouse Improvement Act of 2000 amends the United States Grain Standards Act. It extends the Secretary of Agriculture's power to collect fees for services under that act, extends its funding, and improves its administration.

Title I, on grain standards, covers sampling for export grain, geographic boundaries for official agencies, fee collection, testing of equipment, and limits on administrative costs. The act also reenacts the United States Warehouse Act. That part requires licensing and inspection of warehouses storing farm products and provides for receipts, including electronic receipts, for products stored or handled there.
plaw-106-473-2000:
A war-time march of six hundred miles is put under study by Public Law 106-473, approved November 9, 2000. The Washington-Rochambeau Revolutionary Route National Heritage Act of 2000 tells the head of the land agency to make a full study of that route. The road runs through nine states, from Connecticut to Virginia, by way of seven more named in the act.

George Washington and the French chief Rochambeau led troops on that road in the war that made the United States free of Britain. The study must reach two groups in Congress in two years, once funds are in hand. The head of the agency must ask the views of others as the work goes on, as the next part of the act starts to say. A study, not yet a park or a mark of fame, is all the act grants.
plaw-106-474-2000:
Songs and sounds of the past gain a hall of fame of their own in Public Law 106-474. Congress approved the National Recording Preservation Act of 2000 on November 9 of that year. The act sets up the National Recording Registry at the Library of Congress. The list is meant to keep sound works that hold great worth for the land's past, its art, or its way of life.

The head of the Library must set the tests and the steps by which a work may join the list. No work may join the list till ten years have passed since it was made, as the rule starts to state in the text. The first title of the act deals with care of sound works by the Library, and the list is its first part. Sound, in this law, is kept as a part of the past.
plaw-106-475-2000:
Help owed to those who claim aid for war service is spelled out anew in Public Law 106-475. Congress approved the Veterans Claims Assistance Act of 2000 on November 9 of that year. The act amends title 38 of the code. It states once more, and makes more clear, the duty of the head of the aid agency to help each man or woman who claims aid under its laws.

Part two adds a word meaning to the code. A claimant is any man or woman who asks for, or puts in a claim for, any aid the agency runs. Part three strikes two parts of the code and puts new words in their place. The new words start with forms given on request, and with word to a claimant whose form is not yet whole. The point is plain: no claim should fail for want of a form.
plaw-106-476-2000:
Temporary tariff changes fill Public Law 106-476, approved November 9, 2000. The Tariff Suspension and Trade Act of 2000 amends the Harmonized Tariff Schedule to modify certain duty rates for a time. It also makes other technical amendments to the trade laws.

Title I, Tariff Provisions, starts with expired provisions, then a subtitle of new duty suspensions and reductions. Its first items are two entries for an HIV and AIDS drug, followed by single chemicals and goods: triacetoneamine, instant print film in rolls, color instant print film, and mixtures of sennosides. As in the 1999 corrections act, each line is a narrow product decision rather than general trade policy.
plaw-106-477-2000: Public Law 106-477, approved November 9, 2000, names a federal courthouse in Riverside, California. The courthouse at 3470 12th Street becomes the George E. Brown, Jr. United States Courthouse. Any reference to that courthouse in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the Brown courthouse under section two. The designation is the whole act, with no change to the court's work or building beyond its name.
plaw-106-478-2000: Seattle's federal courthouse receives a name in Public Law 106-478, approved November 9, 2000. The courthouse at 1010 Fifth Avenue becomes the William Kenzo Nakamura United States Courthouse. Section two states that references to the building in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records mean the Nakamura courthouse. The statute does only that naming, as its two short sections show.
plaw-106-479-2000:
Public Law 106-479, approved November 9, 2000, authorizes a memorial and gardens for Frederick Douglass. The Frederick Douglass Gardens, Inc., may establish them on Interior Department lands in the District of Columbia or its environs. The project honors and commemorates Douglass, in the law's words.

Building the memorial and gardens must follow the Commemorative Works Act. The organization is solely responsible for accepting contributions and paying all expenses. No federal funds may be used for establishing the memorial and gardens. A third section requires deposit of excess funds once expenses are paid, following the pattern of other commemorative works laws in this slice.
plaw-106-480-2000: Public Law 106-480, approved November 9, 2000, names a building that does not yet exist. A building proposed for the Chincoteague National Wildlife Refuge, on Assateague Island, Virginia, shall be known as the Herbert H. Bateman Education and Administrative Center. References to the building in federal laws, maps, regulations, or other records mean the Bateman center. Because the building is only proposed, the law names a future education and administration site inside the refuge, before construction. That prospective wording sets it apart from the usual renamings.
plaw-106-481-2000:
The Library of Congress gains business-like funds in Public Law 106-481, approved November 9, 2000. The Library of Congress Fiscal Operations Improvement Act of 2000 establishes revolving funds for running certain library programs and activities. Title I is devoted to those revolving funds.

Its first fund is for audio and video duplication and delivery services tied to the national audiovisual conservation center. That center was authorized by a 1997 law. The Librarian may charge fees for the duplication services and must deposit the fees into the revolving fund. A revolving fund, in plain terms, lets fee income pay for the service that earns it, rather than sending the money to general receipts.
plaw-106-482-2000:
Public Law 106-482, approved November 9, 2000, allows Alexander Hamilton's home to move. It authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to acquire, by donation, suitable land as a new location for the Hamilton Grange. The City of New York would donate a parcel, or interests in land, of not more than one acre.

The new site must sit close to the Grange's original location and will be added to the memorial and run as part of it. The law amends a 1962 statute, as already amended in 1988, to add this relocation power. Moving a historic house is drastic; Congress required donated land nearby before allowing it.
plaw-106-483-2000:
Congress praises a citizen pledge in Public Law 106-483, approved November 9, 2000. This joint resolution recognizes that the Birmingham Pledge has made a significant contribution to racial harmony and reconciliation in the United States and around the world.

The resolution recalls that Birmingham, Alabama, saw racial strife in the 1950s and 1960s, and that its people have since made substantial progress toward racial equality. A grassroots movement from that history produced the pledge, written by Birmingham attorney James E. Rotch. The pledge text quoted begins with belief that every person has worth and is entitled to dignity and respect, regardless of race or color. The resolution honors the pledge; it appropriates nothing.
plaw-106-484-2000:
A reward of refuge for rescuing missing Americans is created by Public Law 106-484, approved November 9, 2000. The Bring Them Home Alive Act of 2000 provides refugee status for nationals of certain countries where American Vietnam War or Korean War prisoners or missing men may be present. The condition is that those nationals help return such Americans alive.

The Attorney General shall grant refugee status, on application, to a qualifying person. For Vietnam, eligibility covers nationals of Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, China, or former Soviet states who personally deliver a living American Vietnam War POW or MIA into United States custody. Parents, spouses, and children of such a person are also covered. Definitions follow in the sample.
plaw-106-485-2000:
Wyoming irrigation land may be sold to its district under Public Law 106-485, approved November 9, 2000. The Secretary of the Interior, through the Bureau of Land Management, shall convey land in Washakie County and Big Horn County to the Westside Irrigation District. First, an environmental analysis under the National Environmental Policy Act must be completed.

The United States keeps its mineral interest; only the surface and other interests pass. Price equals the appraised value, as set by the Secretary. The district buys only the portions it agrees to purchase. The land described totals about sixteen thousand five hundred acres, shown on a map as the sample begins to state. Appraisal and environmental review guard the sale.
plaw-106-486-2000: Public Law 106-486, approved November 9, 2000, orders a study, and only a study, about costly mountain rescues. Within nine months, the Secretary of the Interior must report on whether recovering the costs of high altitude rescues on Mt. McKinley, in Denali National Park and Preserve, Alaska, is suitable and feasible. The report also covers requiring climbers to show proof of medical insurance before getting a climbing permit from the National Park Service. It must review climbing permit fees and recommend changes to the fee structure. Two congressional committees receive the finished report.
plaw-106-487-2000:
Civil War battlefields along a campaign route may be preserved after study, under Public Law 106-487, approved November 9, 2000. The Vicksburg Campaign Trail Battlefields Preservation Act of 2000 authorizes a feasibility study on preserving certain battlefields along the Vicksburg Campaign Trail.

Congress found key battle sites along the trail in Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Tennessee. It called those battlefields collectively of national significance in Civil War history. It said preserving them would greatly aid understanding of the nation's heritage. The study must decide what measures should be taken to preserve them. Definitions name each campaign trail state, beginning in the sample with the four states listed.
plaw-106-488-2000:
Native hiring in Alaska is examined by Public Law 106-488, approved November 9, 2000. The law aims to improve Native hiring and contracting by the federal government within Alaska. Its first section is a report, due within six months from the Secretary of the Interior.

The report must detail progress in carrying out parts of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act and the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act. It must include a detailed action plan for the next three fiscal years, with measures to be taken and results expected. It focuses on Interior lands in Alaska. It must also name any laws, rules, or policies that deter hiring Native Alaskans or contracting with them, as the sample continues.
plaw-106-489-2000:
Ship pilots and crews gain tax fairness from Public Law 106-489, approved November 9, 2000. It amends title 46 to give equitable treatment on state and local income taxes to certain people who work on vessels. A new subsection limits which state may tax their pay.

A covered worker is not subject to income tax in any state other than the state of residence, for pay earned in the covered duties. Coverage reaches pilots licensed under federal or state law who work in more than one state. It also reaches masters, officers, and crew members with regularly assigned duties on a vessel operating on navigable waters of more than one state. Withholding rules are labeled in the amendment as well.
plaw-106-490-2000:
A Wyoming land exchange keeps mining law alive on the traded land, under Public Law 106-490, approved November 9, 2000. It provides that when the Bureau of Land Management conveys the surface estate of certain Wyoming land for private land, the land is not removed from the mining laws. Two federal regulations are declared not to apply to this conveyance.

The trade is the Cow Creek and 60 Bar land exchange, for about nine thousand four hundred eighty acres in Campbell County. The federal land described includes the Bill Barlow Ranch, about two thousand nine hundred sixty acres, and the T-Chair Ranch, about two thousand three hundred fifteen acres. Two Christensen ranches are also listed. Land the United States acquires is segregated, as the text continues.
plaw-106-491-2000: Public Law 106-491, approved November 9, 2000, lifts the size cap on a New Hampshire site tied to a famed sculptor. It amends the act that set up the Saint-Gaudens National Historic Site. The cap on land at the site rises from sixty-four acres to two hundred seventy-nine acres. Two sums of funds in that act rise as well. One goes from the low millions to a sum past ten million. The last goes from a five-figure sum to two million. The three swaps are the whole act.
plaw-106-492-2000:
A museum for law officers killed or lost in the line of work gains its site in Public Law 106-492. Congress approved the National Law Enforcement Museum Act on November 9, 2000. The act sets up the museum on federal land in the District of Columbia. Congress found that such a museum should stand to mark the work and the loss of law officers in the United States.

The fund that keeps the roll of lost officers may build the museum on a tract named in the act. To the north of the site lies the roll's own stone mark. To the west lies a court house, to the east a court block, and to the south the Old City Hall of the District. To place the museum by the mark for the lost is the clear aim of the act, as the site lines in the text show.
plaw-106-493-2000:
Land swaps around an Idaho reservoir are allowed by Public Law 106-493, approved November 9, 2000. It provides for equal exchanges of land around the Cascade Reservoir. The law replaces a subsection of a 1959 public law about land excess to the Cascade Reservoir reclamation project.

The Secretary may exchange either class of that land for non-federal land of not less than about equal value, set by an appraisal under federal acquisition standards. If values differ, the Secretary or the grantor pays the difference to equalize them. Equal value, proven by appraisal, is the safeguard that lets reclamation land trade hands without a sale.
plaw-106-494-2000:
A county in Wyoming may receive federal land for growth under Public Law 106-494, approved November 9, 2000. It provides for conveying certain land to Park County, Wyoming. Congress found more than eighty-two percent of the county's land is owned by the federal government.

The parcel was withdrawn from the public domain for reclamation and is managed by the Bureau of Reclamation. It has passed a withdrawal review, a contaminant survey, and historical and archaeological surveys. Both the reclamation bureau and the Bureau of Land Management agreed it should be disposed of. The county wants the land for local economic development, Congress noted. In a county so largely federal, one parcel's release matters locally.
plaw-106-495-2000:
A Wyoming fire department may move from a dangerous corner under Public Law 106-495, approved November 9, 2000. It permits conveying certain land in Powell, Wyoming, by removing a public purpose condition. The land was patented to the town in 1934 to help establish a town near the Shoshone Irrigation Project.

The patent required the land be used forever for a public purpose. It houses the Powell Volunteer Fire Department, serving a five hundred seventy-seven square mile area. Heavy traffic at U.S. Highway 14 and the main street makes the site unsafe now, Congress found. New, larger fire equipment, bought under national standards and local growth, no longer fits the old hall, as the findings continue.
plaw-106-496-2000:
An Oregon canal becomes a pipeline project with federal help under Public Law 106-496, approved November 9, 2000. The Bend Feed Canal Pipeline Project Act of 2000 authorizes the Bureau of Reclamation to join in planning, designing, and building the Bend Feed Canal Pipeline Project in Oregon. The Secretary of the Interior works with the Tumalo Irrigation District.

The federal share may not exceed fifty percent of total cost and is nonreimbursable. The district gets credit toward its share for money it spent on design, planning, or construction before enactment. Title to facilities built under the act will be held by the district. Operations language follows as the sample ends. Cost sharing with local ownership is the model.
plaw-106-497-2000:
Fake Indian crafts face stronger lawsuits under Public Law 106-497, approved November 9, 2000. The Indian Arts and Crafts Enforcement Act of 2000 aims to improve the cause of action for misrepresentation of Indian arts and crafts. It amends civil action parts of a law promoting Indian arts and crafts.

One edit adds the words directly or indirectly to who may be sued for violations. Another states that damages include all gross profits the defendant gained from the violating activities. A further change adds a new plaintiff category in subsection (c), as the sample breaks off. By reaching indirect sellers and counting gross profits, the law strengthens cases against passing off goods as Indian-made.
plaw-106-498-2000:
More water for an Oregon and California basin is studied under Public Law 106-498, approved November 9, 2000. The Klamath Basin Water Supply Enhancement Act of 2000 authorizes the Bureau of Reclamation to conduct feasibility studies to augment water supplies for the Klamath Project.

Congress lists several aims: meet growing water needs in the Klamath River Basin, improve water quality, and help Oregon resolve water rights claims in the Upper Klamath Basin, including Klamath tribal claims. Another aim is reducing conflict between the upper and lower basins. The Secretary must consult affected state, local, and tribal interests, stakeholder groups, and the public. One proposal studied is increasing storage capacity or yield of project facilities while improving quality, as the sample ends.
plaw-106-499-2000:
A stream in the west is put under study by Public Law 106-499, approved November 9, 2000. The act lets the head of the land agency study how to run the water of Salmon Creek in a better way. The creek feeds the Upper Columbia River in Okanogan County, Washington, a name the text spells with an added syllable in its print.

The aim is two-fold, and the two aims pull in ways that must be held in check. The study should bring back and lift the fish of the creek, most of all two prized fish runs that face a risk of loss for good. At the same time it should keep, or lift, the flow of water for farms, on which the wealth of the county rests. The study rests on a past joint work by a tribe and a farm water group of the same county.
plaw-106-500-2000:
Fossil discoveries at a California lake gain a museum under Public Law 106-500, approved November 9, 2000. The law helps establish an interpretive center and museum near Diamond Valley Lake in southern California. Its aim is protecting and explaining the paleontology discoveries made at the lake.

The Secretary of the Interior shall make a cost-sharing agreement with an appropriate entity to design, build, furnish, and run the center. It will sit on land of the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California, near Hemet. The center will preserve, display, and interpret the lake finds and promote other historical and cultural resources. A second agreement helps build trails for pedestrians and nonmotorized vehicles around the lake.
plaw-106-501-2000:
Programs for older Americans are renewed and modernized by Public Law 106-501, approved November 13, 2000. The Older Americans Act Amendments of 2000 amend the Older Americans Act of 1965. They extend funding authorizations for its programs and aim to modernize services for older individuals.

The table of contents proceeds title by title through the older act. Title I covers definitions. Title II covers the Assistant Secretary's functions, federal agency consultation, evaluation, reports, and funding. A subtitle amending the 1987 amendments addresses a White House Conference. The act is a broad reauthorization, adjusting many aging programs at once rather than creating one new service.
plaw-106-502-2000:
Fish hurt by irrigation diversions gain help in the Northwest under Public Law 106-502, approved November 13, 2000. The Fisheries Restoration and Irrigation Mitigation Act of 2000 lets the Secretary of the Interior set up a program to plan, design, and build fish screens, fish passage devices, and related features.

The program targets harm from irrigation system water diversions by local governments. Its area is the Pacific Ocean drainage of Oregon, Washington, Montana, and Idaho, meaning land whose water drains to the Pacific. The Secretary acts through the director of the Fish and Wildlife Service. Section three establishes the program, as the sample reaches. Screens and passages let water flow to farms while letting fish pass.
plaw-106-503-2000:
Fire crews and quake work share one funds act in Public Law 106-503, approved November 13, 2000. The act lets Congress set aside funds for the United States Fire Administration. It does the same for work under the Earthquake Hazards Reduction Act of 1977. The years covered are fiscal years 2001, 2002, and 2003, three years in all.

Title I bears its own short name, the Fire Administration Authorization Act of 2000. It adds a new funds line for the first of those years, with sums set in the text in figures. Parts of that sum are marked for study work, for deals that fund close looks at fire data, and for drills that train fire crews to meet attacks on the land. The quake funds are dealt with in a later title of the act.
plaw-106-504-2000:
Guam gets first chance at surplus federal land in Public Law 106-504, approved November 13, 2000. The law amends the Organic Act of Guam. Its first section is headed opportunity for the Government of Guam to acquire excess real property in Guam.

Before excess federal property on Guam is screened for other federal use, the Administrator must notify Guam's government that it is available for transfer under this section. Guam has one hundred eighty days to say it intends to acquire the property. If it does, the Administrator shall transfer it under set conditions. Any transfer may be only for a public purpose, as the conditions begin. Otherwise the property follows the normal federal disposal route.
plaw-106-505-2000:
Heart emergency devices in federal buildings are promoted by Public Law 106-505, approved November 13, 2000. The Public Health Improvement Act amends the Public Health Service Act. It provides for recommendations on placing automatic external defibrillators in federal buildings, to improve survival for people who suffer cardiac arrest there. It also sets protections from civil liability for emergency use of the devices.

The broader act reaches further. Title I is called Emerging Threats to Public Health. Title II, Clinical Research Enhancement, covers more involvement by the National Institutes of Health in clinical research, general clinical research centers, and a loan repayment program for clinical researchers. A research laboratory title follows in the contents.
plaw-106-506-2000:
A famous lake's fading clarity drives Public Law 106-506, approved November 13, 2000. The Lake Tahoe Restoration Act promotes environmental restoration around the Lake Tahoe basin, in California and Nevada. Congress called Tahoe one of the largest, deepest, and clearest lakes in the world, with cobalt blue water and a unique alpine setting.

The findings note Tahoe draws millions of visitors for skiing, water sports, biking, camping, and hiking, supporting local economies. Yet the lake is in environmental crisis, Congress said. Water clarity fell from one hundred five feet of visibility in 1967 to only seventy feet in 1999, with worse estimates ahead in the text. Restoration protects both ecology and the visitor economy built on it.
plaw-106-507-2000: Public Law 106-507, approved November 13, 2000, promotes an explorer long after his death. William Clark, of Virginia and Kentucky, co-leader of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, is deemed to have held the grade of captain, rather than lieutenant, in the Regular Army. The promotion is effective March 26, 1804, and lasts until his separation on February 27, 1807. Section two bars any bonus, gratuity, pay, or allowance based on the promotion. The act corrects the historical record of the 1804 to 1806 expedition leader's rank without creating any payment claim.
plaw-106-508-2000: Public Law 106-508, approved November 13, 2000, is titled as raising penalties, but its sample text does something else. Its stated purpose is increased penalties for violations of the Export Administration Act of 1979. The operative sentence, however, only amends section 20 of that act. It strikes August 20, 1994, and inserts August 20, 2001, extending a date in the old export law. That date change is the entire enacted text shown in the sample, a useful warning that a law's title and its sample can point in different directions.
plaw-106-509-2000:
An ancient Hawaiian trail joins the national system in Public Law 106-509, approved November 13, 2000. The Ala Kahakai National Historic Trail Act amends the National Trails System Act to designate the Ala Kahakai Trail as a National Historic Trail, in Hawaii.

Congress found the Ala Kahakai, or Trail by the Sea, is part of the ancient Ala Loa, the long trail circling the island of Hawaii. The Ala Loa was the major land route linking six hundred or more communities of the island kingdom from 1400 to 1700. It connects prehistoric and historic housing areas, nearly all royal centers, and most major temples. Its use ties to rulers, battlefields, armies, and yearly taxation, the findings continue.
plaw-106-510-2000:
Public Law 106-510, approved November 13, 2000, frees land buying near a Hawaiian park. The Hawaii Volcanoes National Park Adjustment Act of 2000 removes restrictions on acquiring certain land next to Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. It amends a 1938 law that added lands on the island of Hawaii to the park.

The qualifying language after the word park is replaced. Land, including land shown on a map called NPS-PAC 1997HW, may now be acquired by donation, exchange, or purchase with donated or appropriated funds. Section three corrects park names in earlier laws, adding the Hawaiian spelling mark to Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park. References throughout federal records follow the corrected name.
plaw-106-511-2000:
Compensation for a tribe flooded by a federal dam program is provided by Public Law 106-511, approved November 13, 2000. Title I may be cited as the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe Equitable Compensation Act, for South Dakota. It aims to give equitable compensation to the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe.

The findings trace the Flood Control Act of 1944, which approved the Pick-Sloan Missouri River Basin program. That program sought economic development, irrigation above Sioux City, Iowa, and protection from Missouri River floods. The Oahe Dam and Reservoir is a major part of it, generating hydropower and storing much water. The reservoir overlies the eastern boundary of the Cheyenne River Sioux reservation, as the findings begin to explain the loss.
plaw-106-512-2000:
A Texas water project leaves federal hands under Public Law 106-512, approved November 13, 2000. The Palmetto Bend Conveyance Act provides for conveying the Palmetto Bend project to the State of Texas. The project is a reclamation project authorized under a 1968 law.

The Secretary of the Interior shall convey to the state all federal interest in the project, except the mineral estate, subject to conditions in sections four and five. The state acts through the Texas Water Development Board, the Lavaca-Navidad River Authority, or both. If the conveyance is not finished within one year and one hundred eighty days, the Secretary must report to a House committee, as the sample breaks off. Local control follows transfer.
plaw-106-513-2000:
Sea parks gain fresh terms in Public Law 106-513, approved November 13, 2000. The National Marine Sanctuaries Amendments Act of 2000 amends the National Marine Sanctuaries Act. A rule in the new act guides how to read it. Each change it makes counts as a change to that sea parks law. The one bar is where the act says a change is to some other law.

Part three deals with what Congress found, with the aims of the law, and with the start of the sea parks web. In one find, the worth named for such tracts of sea grows in scope. Where the old text spoke of worth for study and for looks, the new text adds worth for the ways of life of the past and for old sites in the sea. The head line for the part that set up the web is made anew as well.
plaw-106-514-2000:
Coastal barrier protection is renewed and tightened by Public Law 106-514, approved November 13, 2000. The Coastal Barrier Resources Reauthorization Act of 2000 reauthorizes and amends the Coastal Barrier Resources Act.

New guidelines govern recommendations to add areas to the system, and decisions on whether a coastal barrier was undeveloped when its unit entered the system. The Secretary must consider whether building density is less than one structure per five acres above mean high tide. The Secretary must also consider existing infrastructure, including a reinforced road to each lot and a wastewater system able to serve each lot, as the list continues. Numbers, here, define what undeveloped means.
plaw-106-515-2000:
Special courts for mentally ill offenders are funded by Public Law 106-515, approved November 13, 2000. Its cited name is America's Law Enforcement and Mental Health Project. The law provides grants to establish demonstration mental health courts.

Congress found, citing a July 1999 Bureau of Justice Statistics report, that sixteen percent of state prison and local jail inmates suffer from mental illness. It cited estimates that six hundred thousand to seven hundred thousand mentally ill persons are booked into jail each year. It also noted seventy-five percent of mentally ill inmates had served time or probation before. Broward County, Florida, and King County, Washington, had created mental health courts placing nonviolent offenders in monitored treatment, as the findings continue.
plaw-106-516-2000:
Sites tied to Harriet Tubman are studied under Public Law 106-516, approved November 13, 2000. The Harriet Tubman Special Resource Study Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a special resource study. It concerns preservation and public use of sites linked to Tubman in Auburn, New York.

Congress found Tubman was born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in 1821. In 1849 she escaped on foot, following the North Star through Maryland, Delaware, and Pennsylvania to freedom in Philadelphia. She became famous as a conductor on the Underground Railroad, helping hundreds escape. During the Civil War she served the Union Army as guide, spy, and nurse. Afterward she spoke for education of Black children, the findings add.
plaw-106-517-2000:
Body armor for police is funded more clearly by Public Law 106-517, approved November 13, 2000. The Bulletproof Vest Partnership Grant Act of 2000 amends the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968. It clarifies procedures and conditions for matching grants to buy armor vests.

Congress found deaths of officers would drop greatly if every officer had an armor vest. It cited studies counting seven hundred nine officers killed in the line of duty from 1985 to 1994. The Federal Bureau of Investigation estimated the risk of death without a vest at fourteen times the risk with one. Bullet-resistant materials had saved more than two thousand officers in that period, Congress added.
plaw-106-518-2000:
The day-to-day work of the federal courts is tuned by Public Law 106-518, approved November 13, 2000. The Federal Courts Improvement Act of 2000 aims to make the courts run in a better way. Title I deals with how the courts hold and use their funds, and with fees paid by those who use the courts.

Its parts stretch a fund that pays for the courts' new tools, and deal with where small fees end up once paid. They lift one fee paid to file a case by a town or town-like body that can not pay its debts. They lift the fee to switch such a case to a new form as well. Title II deals with how cases move, with part-time judges in Guam and in the Northern Mariana Islands, and with the reach of such judges.
plaw-106-519-2000:
An export tax scheme is repealed and replaced in Public Law 106-519, approved November 15, 2000. The FSC Repeal and Extraterritorial Income Exclusion Act of 2000 amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Section two repeals the rules on foreign sales corporations, called FSCs, a whole subpart of the tax code.

Section three treats extraterritorial income instead. It adds a new section 114, titled Extraterritorial Income, to the part listing items excluded from gross income. The sample breaks off as that exclusion begins. The structure is clear: one export benefit, built on separate corporations, ends, and a direct exclusion of foreign-earned income replaces it.
plaw-106-520-2000:
Public Law 106-520, approved November 15, 2000, is a longer continuing resolution than most in this series. It makes further appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275, inserting December 5, 2000, as the date in section 106(c). It also adds three new sections to that law.

The first new section appropriates one million dollars for construction, salaries, and other expenses of conducting the inaugural ceremonies for the President and Vice President on January 20, 2001. The money is disbursed by the Secretary of the Senate and stays available until September 30, 2001. It may pay costs incurred before or after October 1, 2000, for the joint committee program named in the text.
plaw-106-521-2000:
Local police may enforce some citizens band radio rules under Public Law 106-521, approved November 22, 2000. It authorizes state and local governments to enforce certain Federal Communications Commission regulations on citizens band radio equipment. The law amends section 302 of the Communications Act of 1934.

A state or local law may bar violating a commission rule against unauthorized use of citizens band equipment. It may also bar unauthorized operation on frequencies between twenty-four and thirty-five megahertz. Stations licensed by the commission for the operation at issue are exempt, and local laws must state that exemption. The commission also gains a duty beginning in subsection three, as the sample continues. Enforcement moves closer to the noise.
plaw-106-522-2000:
The capital city's budget for a year is funded by Public Law 106-522, approved November 22, 2000. The District of Columbia Appropriations Act, 2001, makes appropriations for the District government and other activities charged against District revenues. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001.

Under federal funds, the first item is a federal payment for resident tuition support, seventeen million dollars, to remain available until expended. The Mayor administers the nationwide program. It pays, for eligible District residents, an amount based on the difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition at public colleges. Awards may be used at public and private colleges and may be prioritized by academic merit and other factors, as the proviso continues.
plaw-106-523-2000:
Crimes by people tied to the military abroad gain a federal court route in Public Law 106-523, approved November 22, 2000. The Military Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Act of 2000 amends title 18. It establishes federal jurisdiction over offenses committed outside the United States by persons employed by or accompanying the armed forces. It also covers service members released or separated before being identified and prosecuted.

A new chapter 212 lists sections on the offenses, arrest and commitment, delivery to foreign authorities, limits on removal, initial proceedings, regulations, and definitions. Section 3261 begins the offense provision as the sample ends. The law closes a gap where neither military nor local courts might reach a case.
plaw-106-524-2000:
Public Law 106-524, approved November 22, 2000, moves the line of a Florida site that guards an old fort. The Fort Matanzas National Monument gains a tract of about seventy acres in all. The tract is shown on a map with a set name and count, dated in February of 1991, as the terms of the act state in their first part.

The map must be kept on file, where all may look at it, in the office of the head of the National Park Service. The head of the land agency may gain land, water, or rights in land in the new tract in four ways. The ways are by gift, by a buy with gift or set funds, by a shift from some other federal body, or by a swap of land. A fourth part deals with how land held by the United States in the new tract is to be run.
plaw-106-525-2000:
Minority health research gains a national center under Public Law 106-525, approved November 22, 2000. The Minority Health and Health Disparities Research and Education Act of 2000 amends the Public Health Service Act to improve the health of minority individuals.

Title I establishes a National Center on Minority Health and Health Disparities inside the National Institutes of Health. It also provides centers of excellence for research education and training, and a loan repayment program for researchers working outside the institutes on disparities research. The center's general provisions and a report on institutes resources follow. Title II assigns health disparities research to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. A third title begins as the contents end.
plaw-106-526-2000:
Oregon forest administrative land may be sold under Public Law 106-526, approved November 22, 2000. The Bend Pine Nursery Land Conveyance Act authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to sell or exchange all or part of certain sites and other National Forest System land in Oregon. Proceeds from a sale or exchange must be used for National Forest System purposes.

The first parcel, Tract A, Bend Pine Nursery, covers about two hundred ten acres on a site plan dated May 13, 1999. Tract B covers only federal buildings at Shelter Cove Resort in the Deschutes National Forest, as its site plan description begins. The Secretary may set the terms of any sale or exchange. Recycling surplus sites funds the forest system itself.
plaw-106-527-2000:
Public Law 106-527, approved November 22, 2000, adjusts the boundary of a Mississippi parkway. The Secretary of the Interior shall add about one hundred fifty acres to the Natchez Trace Parkway, shown on a map dated May 1998. The Secretary shall also add about eighty acres shown on an Emerald Mound development plan map dated August 1987.

Both maps must be kept on file for public inspection at the National Park Service director's office. The Secretary may acquire the land by donation, purchase with donated or appropriated funds, or exchange, including with Mississippi, local governments, and private persons. Land acquired is then administered as part of the parkway, as the next subsection begins. Emerald Mound gives the addition a named historic focus.
plaw-106-528-2000:
Airport worker screening is strengthened by Public Law 106-528, approved November 22, 2000. The Airport Security Improvement Act of 2000 amends title 49 to improve airport security. Its first topic is criminal history record checks.

Within two years, the Federal Aviation Administration head must develop an electronic fingerprint transmission pilot project into an aviation-wide program for individual criminal history checks. The work is done with the Office of Personnel Management and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. An airport, airline, or screening company that finds participation not cost effective, and says so, cannot be forced to join. Later subsections cover how the expanded program applies, beginning in the sample. Fingerprints, not paper, are the direction.
plaw-106-529-2000:
A Maine heritage center is planned with federal help under Public Law 106-529, approved November 22, 2000. The Saint Croix Island Heritage Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to assist in planning and building a regional heritage center in Calais, Maine.

Congress found Saint Croix Island sits in the Saint Croix River, the boundary between Maine and Canada, and is the only international historic site in the National Park System. In 1604 French nobleman Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Mons, with Samuel Champlain among his group, landed and began a settlement. Congress called the 1604 and 1605 settlement the first permanent settlement site in the New World, before Jamestown in 1607. Many see the expedition as the start of Acadian culture in North America.
plaw-106-530-2000:
Colorado's sand dunes rise in status under Public Law 106-530, approved November 22, 2000. The Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve Act of 2000 provides for establishing the Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve and the Baca National Wildlife Refuge in Colorado.

Congress found the Great Sand Dunes National Monument was established by presidential proclamation in 1932. It preserves federal land with spectacular, unique sand dunes and features of scenic, scientific, and educational interest. The dunes, sand sheet, and nearby wetlands and uplands hold rare ecological, geological, paleontological, archaeological, scenic, historical, and wildlife parts. Two creeks, Sand Creek and Medano Creek, pulse in ways vital to the dunes system, the findings add.
plaw-106-531-2000:
Reports that agencies owe to Congress may be joined in one by Public Law 106-531, approved November 22, 2000. The Reports Consolidation Act of 2000 amends title 31 of the code. It lets agencies join set reports on their funds and on how well their work has gone, in place of a stack of split reports.

Congress found that the law lays a great load of such reports on each agency in the land. Split reports can mean the same work is done twice by the same staff. They can reach Congress in a form that is not of full use to the lawmakers who get them. Test runs by some agencies gave a clear result. One joined report, with a close look at funds and at work done, is of more use. It is made with less waste of time and staff.
plaw-106-532-2000:
Dairy price information must be reported under Public Law 106-532, approved November 22, 2000. The Dairy Market Enhancement Act of 2000 amends the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 to enhance dairy markets through mandatory reporting on dairy products.

A new subtitle states its purpose: a program of information on marketing dairy products that producers and other market participants can readily understand. The information covers prices, quantities sold, and inventories. The program should improve the Agriculture Department's price and supply reporting services and encourage competition in the dairy marketplace. Definitions follow, starting with dairy products as manufactured products the Secretary uses to set minimum prices, as the sample breaks off.
plaw-106-533-2000:
Arts in school gain a mark of praise from Congress in Public Law 106-533, approved November 22, 2000. The act amends the Congressional Award Act to set up a board with a long name. The board is the Congressional Recognition for Excellence in Arts Education Board. A new title in the old act bears a name of its own, in much the same words.

What Congress found gives the act its heart. Skill in the arts is a base aim of school for each child, the act states in its list of finds. Arts in school build the mind and the power to make new things. They build sharp thought, a free sense of what might be, and the power to work with a team to reach a choice. They build the lead role, high skill with words, and the power to pose and solve hard tasks.
plaw-106-534-2000:
Older Americans targeted by scams are the focus of Public Law 106-534, approved November 22, 2000. Its title is the Protecting Seniors From Fraud Act, and its whole stated purpose is to protect seniors from fraud.

Congress found older Americans are among the fastest growing parts of society, yet are too often victims of violent crime, property crime, and consumer and telemarketing fraud. The elderly are targeted again and again in such schemes, the findings say. Congress praised the TRIAD program, sponsored by sheriffs, police chiefs, and the retired persons association, which unites law enforcement, senior volunteers, care providers, families, and seniors. It said Congress should keep supporting TRIAD and similar community partnerships.
plaw-106-535-2000: Millersville, Pennsylvania, gains a named post office in Public Law 106-535, approved November 22, 2000. The Postal Service facility at 431 North George Street becomes the Robert S. Walker Post Office. Unusually, the designation and the references rule sit in one section: any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record means the Walker post office. The act passed the Senate first, in October, then the House, per its history. That naming is its only content.
plaw-106-536-2000: Public Law 106-536, approved November 22, 2000, opens a door for some who broadcast for the United States abroad. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Act to grant a special class of entry to such staff. The clause covers a man or woman who comes to work on the air for the International Broadcasting Bureau, or for a group it funds. A spouse and children may come as well. The count is capped at one hundred in each fiscal year.
plaw-106-537-2000: Public Law 106-537, approved December 5, 2000, extends stopgap federal funding for two days beyond its approval. This joint resolution makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date in section 106(c) is replaced with December 7, 2000. It was considered, passed, and approved on December 5. By December the one and two day extensions in this series had stretched into a longer budget standoff, but the legal form stayed a single date substitution. Nothing else is enacted.
plaw-106-538-2000:
An Arizona conservation area is created by Public Law 106-538, approved December 6, 2000. The law establishes the Las Cienegas National Conservation Area in Arizona. Its definitions name the conservation area, a management plan, and the Secretary of the Interior.

Section two establishes a related body first: the Sonoita Valley Acquisition Planning District. Its purpose is to provide for future purchases of important conservation land in the Sonoita Valley region of Arizona. Public lands, in the act, excludes interests in land not owned by the United States. The planning district frames buying land around the conservation area before section four establishes the area itself, as the definitions note.
plaw-106-539-2000: Public Law 106-539, approved December 7, 2000, is the last daily continuing resolution in this sample run. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by amending Public Law 106-275. The date in section 106(c) becomes December 8, 2000. The measure passed and was approved on December 7, one day earlier. Like its December predecessor, it contains only that substitution, keeping the government funded while final appropriations remained unfinished. No added section accompanies the date change here.
