plaw-106-540-2000: Public Law 106-540 is a one-sentence joint resolution approved on December 8, 2000, near the end of the 106th Congress. It amends Public Law 106-275, an earlier continuing resolution, by replacing the cutoff date in section 106(c) with December 11, 2000. The change kept stopgap funding for fiscal year 2001 in place three days longer while Congress finished its regular spending bills. Both chambers passed the measure on the very day it was approved.
plaw-106-541-2000:
The Water Resources Development Act of 2000, Public Law 106-541, is the 106th Congress's main water projects law, signed December 11, 2000. Its subject is the conservation and development of water and related resources. Under it, the Secretary of the Army may build projects to improve the rivers and harbors of the United States.

Title I lists project authorizations and a family of small-project programs that cover flood damage reduction, emergency streambank protection, navigation, water quality, aquatic ecosystem restoration, and shoreline protection. The general provisions that follow cover cooperation agreements with counties, watershed and river basin assessments, a tribal partnership program, and an ability-to-pay rule for the local sponsors who share project costs.
plaw-106-542-2000: Approved December 11, 2000, Public Law 106-542 is another one-line step in a chain of stopgap funding measures from the 106th Congress. It amends Public Law 106-275 by striking the date written in section 106(c) and inserting December 15, 2000, which stretched continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2001 by four more days. The House and Senate both considered and passed it on December 11, the same day it became law.
plaw-106-543-2000:
Public Law 106-543, approved December 15, 2000, is a joint resolution of the 106th Congress that once again extends stopgap funding for fiscal year 2001. It pushes the deadline in Public Law 106-275 out to December 21, 2000, buying the last week of the session for the unfinished spending bills.

Unlike the bare date changes before it, this resolution also adds money and a condition. It makes an extra 217 million dollars available from within the amount provided by section 101. Of that sum, 100 million dollars can be spent only if the Secretary of State certifies two things about the United Nations. It raised no program funding without an offsetting cut, and it stayed within its budget for 2000 and 2001.
plaw-106-544-2000:
The Presidential Threat Protection Act of 2000, Public Law 106-544, tightens the federal law against threatening the President and others guarded by the Secret Service. Congress passed it late in the 106th Congress, and it was approved on December 19, 2000. Its whole job is to revise one criminal statute, section 879 of title 18.

The rewrite makes clear that the ban reaches threats against former Presidents and members of their immediate families, where the older text named only a spouse. It also covers anyone the Secret Service protects under section 3056(a)(6), and it adds major candidates for President or Vice President. It raises the maximum prison term for such a threat from three years to five.
plaw-106-545-2000:
Public Law 106-545, the ICCVAM Authorization Act of 2000, gives a lasting legal footing to federal work on alternatives to animal testing. Approved December 19, 2000, it backs test methods that protect human and animal health and the environment while cutting down on animal use in safety testing.

An alternative test method, as the law defines it, does one of three things. It reduces the number of animals required, refines procedures to lessen or eliminate pain or distress, or replaces animals with non-animal systems or a lower species. The act covers the Interagency Coordinating Committee on the Validation of Alternative Methods, the expert body whose peer-reviewed recommendations help regulators decide whether a new test can be accepted.
plaw-106-546-2000:
Congress wrote the DNA Analysis Backlog Elimination Act of 2000, Public Law 106-546, to clear the pile of untested DNA samples sitting in crime laboratories. Approved December 19, 2000, it ties state lab work to the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Combined DNA Index System, the national database used to match DNA profiles.

The act lets the Attorney General make grants to states for DNA analyses of samples from people convicted of qualifying offenses and of samples collected at crime scenes. Both are entered into the federal system. Grant money can also expand the capacity of state and local labs. In return, a state must file an application with a plan for fast analysis, and the law provides for collecting DNA from certain violent and sexual offenders.
plaw-106-547-2000:
The Enhanced Federal Security Act of 2000, Public Law 106-547, creates new federal crimes aimed at people who sneak onto government property or pose as police officers. It was approved December 19, 2000, in the closing days of the 106th Congress, and it works by amending the federal criminal code, title 18.

Its centerpiece is a new section 1036. It makes it a crime to enter, by fraud or false pretenses, real property of the United States, a federal vessel or aircraft, or the secure area of any airport. Entry committed with intent to commit a felony carries a fine or up to five years in prison. The act also targets the misuse of genuine and counterfeit police badges by people seeking to commit a crime.
plaw-106-548-2000: Public Law 106-548, approved December 19, 2000, hands a piece of federal land to a small Colorado town. It directs the Secretary of Agriculture to convey, for no consideration, roughly 25 acres comprising Joe Rowell Park to the town of Dolores, for open space, park, and recreational purposes. The town pays the cost of the survey. Title reverts to the United States if the town tries to transfer or encumber the land, or lets it be used for a purpose that clashes with the park use.
plaw-106-549-2000: Public Law 106-549 was signed December 19, 2000. Under it, the Secretary of the Interior may let the Mancos Water Conservancy District in Colorado put spare capacity in the federal Mancos Project to wider use. Contracts can cover holding, storing, moving, and carrying other water, within the excess capacity, for irrigation, home, city, and factory use, and any other beneficial purpose. A contract must not impair any stated purpose of the project. Charges are set with building, upkeep, and carriage costs in view, and the district may add only its own delivery costs.
plaw-106-550-2000:
Congress created a birthday commission with Public Law 106-550, the James Madison Commemoration Commission Act, approved December 19, 2000. March 16, 2001, would mark 250 years since the birth of James Madison. The act establishes a federal commission to plan and carry out a fitting national observance of that anniversary.

The findings rehearse why Madison earned the honor. He foresaw the need for a stronger national government. He argued for it at the Annapolis Convention of 1786. And at the Philadelphia Convention of 1787 he helped mold a Constitution combining energy with restraint, separated powers, and limited government. The sections that follow cover the commission's duties, membership, powers, staffing, contributions, reports, audits, termination, and the money authorized for its work.
plaw-106-551-2000:
The Chimpanzee Health Improvement, Maintenance, and Protection Act, Public Law 106-551, answers a practical question: what happens to government research chimpanzees once scientists no longer need them? Passed by the 106th Congress and approved December 20, 2000, it amends the Public Health Service Act to give those animals a permanent home.

The law directs the Secretary to establish and run a national sanctuary system. It provides lifetime care for chimpanzees used, bred, or bought for research supported by the National Institutes of Health, the Food and Drug Administration, or other federal agencies. Every surplus chimpanzee owned by the federal government must be accepted into the system. A nonprofit private entity operates the sanctuaries under contract, and its board helps oversee how the system is run.
plaw-106-552-2000: A single-purpose measure, Public Law 106-552 renames a Chicago postal facility. Approved December 20, 2000, it redesignates the United States Postal Service facility at 514 Express Center Road, until then known as the Chicago International/Military Service Center, as the J.T. Weeker Service Center. From approval onward, every reference to that facility in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States is deemed to be a reference to the J.T. Weeker Service Center.
plaw-106-553-2000:
The District of Columbia Appropriations Act, 2001, Public Law 106-553, supplies the money to run the government of the District of Columbia for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2001. The 106th Congress passed it in its final week, and it was approved on December 21, 2000.

Rather than printing the spending provisions itself, the act enacts two other bills into law by reference: H.R. 5547 and H.R. 5548, both as introduced on October 25, 2000. It directs the Archivist of the United States to print the full texts of those bills as appendixes at the end of the act when it is published. That way, the complete public record still shows every line of what was enacted.
plaw-106-554-2000:
Public Law 106-554, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2001, is the giant year-end spending law that funded much of the federal government for fiscal year 2001. The 106th Congress passed it in its closing days as H.R. 4577, and it was approved December 21, 2000.

Instead of one long text, the act enacts nine separate bills by reference, all introduced in mid-December 2000, and orders their full texts printed as appendixes when the act is published. One listed bill is trimmed in the process: H.R. 5666 takes effect without its section 123, which concerned yet another bill. A further provision adjusts how parts of the package are scored for direct spending and receipts under federal budget rules.
plaw-106-555-2000:
Three ocean causes share one statute in Public Law 106-555, approved December 21, 2000: striped bass conservation, Atlantic coastal fisheries management, and rescue help for marine mammals. Title I takes up the first of these, reauthorizing the Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act for another round of federal support.

For each of fiscal years 2001, 2002, and 2003, the act authorizes one million dollars to the Secretary of Commerce. It authorizes 250,000 dollars to the Secretary of the Interior to carry out the striped bass law. It also orders the two secretaries, working with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, to study the spread of age classes in the Atlantic striped bass population. The study asks whether that spread supports healthy recruitment and sustainable fishing. They must report back within 180 days.
plaw-106-556-2000: Public Law 106-556, approved December 21, 2000, puts a man's name on a post office building in York, Pennsylvania. The United States Postal Service facility at 200 South George Street is designated the George Atlee Goodling Post Office Building. From then on, any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the George Atlee Goodling Post Office Building.
plaw-106-557-2000:
The Shark Finning Prohibition Act, Public Law 106-557, outlaws the practice of cutting the fins off a shark and discarding the carcass at sea, which Congress called wasteful and unsportsmanlike. It works as an amendment to the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act and was approved December 21, 2000.

The act makes it unlawful to remove any fins of a shark, including the tail, and discard the carcass at sea. It also bars holding fins aboard a fishing vessel without the corresponding carcass, or landing fins on their own. Fins landed or found aboard carry a rebuttable presumption that they were taken in violation of the ban. The stated purpose is to end finning at both the national and the international level.
plaw-106-558-2000:
Public Law 106-558, approved December 21, 2000, joins two unrelated subjects in one short act: the boundary of a Nevada national forest and overtime pay for federal firefighters. Neither half creates a new program. Both work by amending statutes already on the books, one from 1988 and one in the federal pay code.

The first section moves a strip of land from the Secretary of Agriculture to the Secretary of the Interior. The strip lies between the old and revised boundary lines shown on a 1998 map of the Toiyabe National Forest. The second sets overtime for Interior Department and Forest Service employees engaged in emergency wildland fire suppression. The rate is one and one-half times their hourly basic pay, with the whole amount treated as premium pay.
plaw-106-559-2000:
Helping tribal courts work better is the aim of Public Law 106-559, the Indian Tribal Justice Technical and Legal Assistance Act of 2000, approved December 21, 2000. Its findings begin from the government-to-government relationship between the United States and Indian tribes, which it describes as sovereign entities governing Indian lands.

Congress states the problem plainly: violent crime in Indian country runs at about twice the rate for the United States as a whole, and high crime blocks investment and jobs. Tribal justice systems, it says, are the most fitting forums for disputes on Native lands, yet funding and coordination for their technical and legal assistance needs fall short. The act supplies that assistance, treating stronger tribal courts as serving both tribal self-determination and economic self-sufficiency.
plaw-106-560-2000:
Private companies that haul violent prisoners across state lines come under federal regulation in Public Law 106-560, the Interstate Transportation of Dangerous Criminals Act of 2000, also known as Jeanna's Act. The 106th Congress passed it as S. 1898, and it was approved December 21, 2000.

Congress found that states increasingly turn to private prisoner transport companies instead of their own officers or the United States Marshals Service. Trips can stretch for days or weeks through a network of hubs. And violent prisoners have escaped during such transport. The act answers by requiring oversight from the Attorney General. It also states that nothing in it should be read as encouraging governments to hire private transporters in place of fully trained, sworn law enforcement officers.
plaw-106-561-2000:
Public Law 106-561, the Paul Coverdell National Forensic Sciences Improvement Act of 2000, aims at the quality, speed, and credibility of the crime laboratories that examine evidence for police. The 106th Congress approved it on December 21, 2000, and it carries the name of Paul Coverdell.

The act adds forensic science improvement to the list of purposes funded under the federal drug control and system improvement grant program. That program sits in the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968. A state or local government that spends grant money on forensic services must certify the lab behind the work. It must have an established forensic laboratory, or a laboratory system. The lab must employ one or more full-time scientists whose principal duties are examining physical evidence for law enforcement agencies in criminal matters.
plaw-106-562-2000:
The Pribilof Islands Transition Act fills Title I of Public Law 106-562, approved December 23, 2000, and the law also speaks to coral reef conservation. Its stated purpose is to complete the orderly withdrawal of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration from the civil administration of the Pribilof Islands, Alaska.

To support the islands through that change, the act rewrites the financial assistance section of the Fur Seal Act of 1966. Subject to appropriations, the Secretary shall provide assistance to any city government, village corporation, or tribal council of St. George or St. Paul, Alaska. The money may also serve as the non-federal matching share those communities need under other federal programs that require matching funds.
plaw-106-563-2000:
America's first coast-to-coast highway gets a federal study under the Lincoln Highway Study Act of 2000, Public Law 106-563, approved December 23, 2000. Congress found that the Lincoln Highway, established in 1913, runs more than 3,000 miles of roadway from New York, New York, to San Francisco, California.

The findings call it the first transcontinental highway in the United States, a paved route that opened vast parts of the country to automobile travel and crosses thirteen states. Some parts have disappeared or been realigned, yet many historic, cultural, and engineering features remain. The act orders the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the National Park Service, to coordinate a comprehensive study of the routes and of methods to commemorate the highway's national significance.
plaw-106-564-2000:
Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands gained their own standard time zone under Public Law 106-564, approved December 23, 2000. The act amends the Calder Act of 1918, the federal statute that first divided the nation into standard time zones.

Where the old law set eight zones, the amendment creates nine, placing the ninth on the 150th meridian of longitude east from Greenwich and naming it Chamorro standard time. A matching change to the Uniform Time Act of 1966 adds Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, next to Puerto Rico, in the federal daylight saving time provisions. So the territories' clocks are governed by the same national framework.
plaw-106-565-2000:
Public Law 106-565, the Jamestown 400th Commemoration Commission Act of 2000, signed December 23, 2000, creates a federal commission to plan the 400th anniversary of Jamestown, Virginia. Jamestown was founded in 1607, the first lasting English colony in the New World, and it served as the capital of Virginia for 92 years.

Congress found that the settlement brought English, other Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans together in one society. The bodies formed during its first nine decades still shape American common law, language, and economic life. The act notes that the National Park Service, the Association for the Preservation of Virginia Antiquities, and the Jamestown-Yorktown Foundation already care for Jamestown's historic sites. The foundation leads the Commonwealth's own Celebration 2007 planning.
plaw-106-566-2000:
Water recycling in Hawaii is the subject of Title I of Public Law 106-566, the Hawaii Water Resources Act of 2000, approved December 23, 2000. The title directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a study on the reclamation and reuse of water and wastewater in the State of Hawaii.

The study runs through the Commissioner of Reclamation. It builds on older authorities, including a 1954 act covering irrigation and reclamation needs for the islands of Oahu, Hawaii, and Molokai, and the Small Reclamation Projects Act. It also draws on a provision that charges Native Hawaiians for reclamation cost recovery on the same terms applied to Indians or Indian tribes. Together these authorities frame a survey of where reclaiming water and wastewater could add to the islands' supplies.
plaw-106-567-2000:
Spy agencies receive their yearly funding authority from Public Law 106-567, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2001, signed December 27, 2000. It authorizes funding for intelligence and intelligence-related activities of the United States Government, the Community Management Account, and the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I covers the intelligence activities themselves, including a secret schedule of funding amounts, so the dollar figures stay hidden even though the law is public. Other parts handle staff ceiling changes, transfer authority for the Director of Central Intelligence, and staff pay and benefit increases allowed by other laws. The table of contents also lists a restriction on conducting intelligence activities, a sense of Congress on community contracting, and a National Security Agency voluntary separation measure.
plaw-106-568-2000:
Many separate tribal measures ride together in the Omnibus Indian Advancement Act, Public Law 106-568, approved December 27, 2000. The bill reached enactment as a measure authorizing construction of a Wakpa Sica Reconciliation Place in Fort Pierre, South Dakota, and it carries a table of contents spanning several Indian programs.

Title I provides for the conveyance and operation of irrigation works for the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community. Title II offers housing assistance and loan guarantees for Native Hawaiian housing. Title III says approval is not required to validate land transactions of the Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana. Title IV takes up the Wakpa Sica Reconciliation Place itself, opening with findings and definitions for that project.
plaw-106-569-2000:
Public Law 106-569, the American Homeownership and Economic Opportunity Act of 2000, signed December 27, 2000, aims to help more people own homes in the United States. Its four titles attack the problem from four sides: local rules, family funds, rental aid, and what mortgage insurance costs.

Title I funds grants to strip away local rules that block housing, and a clearinghouse on the subject. Title II covers home equity conversion mortgages and aid for self-help housing groups. Title III builds a Section 8 home-buying option with downpayment help and a pilot program for disabled families. Title IV revises the rules for ending private mortgage insurance, including borrowers' rights after the end date.
plaw-106-570-2000:
Public Law 106-570, approved December 27, 2000, leads with disease control abroad. Its Title I, the Assistance for International Malaria Control Act, authorizes more United States assistance for international malaria control. The aim is prevention, treatment, control, and elimination of the disease.

Two unrelated riders complete the package. Title II states the policy of the United States with respect to Macau, with findings and declarations, a sense of Congress, continued application of United States law, and a reporting requirement. Title III moves toward a United States-Canada Alaska Rail Commission, providing for an agreement on a bilateral commission and setting out its composition.
plaw-106-571-2000:
Doctors employed by the federal government keep a special pay allowance for good under Public Law 106-571, the Federal Physicians Comparability Allowance Amendments of 2000, approved December 28, 2000. The short act amends title 5 of the United States Code, the federal personnel law.

Comparability allowances may be paid to government physicians under authority that had carried built-in limits. The act repeals the second sentence of section 5948(d) and a section of the 1978 act behind the program, making the payment authority permanent. It further provides that such allowances are treated as part of basic pay for retirement purposes, with technical changes to the surrounding subsections.
plaw-106-572-2000:
State and local police get federal help against computer crime in the Computer Crime Enforcement Act, Public Law 106-572, approved December 28, 2000. The act establishes a grant program, run by the Office of Justice Programs, to assist state and local law enforcement in deterring, investigating, and prosecuting computer crimes.

Subject to money provided in appropriations acts, each state receives a grant to use with units of local government, courts, and other states. The funds can enforce state and local computer crime laws. They can educate the public to prevent and identify such crime, train officers and prosecutors in investigations and forensic analysis, and buy the computer equipment that forensic work requires. Grants may also promote sharing federal expertise, including through multijurisdictional task forces.
plaw-106-573-2000: One section does all the work in the Installment Tax Correction Act of 2000, Public Law 106-573, approved December 28, 2000. It repeals the modification of the installment method that the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 had enacted. That includes its repeal of that method for accrual-method taxpayers. The repeal reaches back to dispositions on or after the 1999 act's own enactment date. The Internal Revenue Code is to be applied and administered as if the change had never been enacted.
plaw-106-574-2000:
A grove of giant sequoias joins Sequoia National Park under Public Law 106-574, approved December 28, 2000. The act authorizes the addition of land to the park in California, namely the parcel shown on a map entitled Dillonwood, numbered 102/80,044 and dated September 1999.

The Secretary of the Interior is directed to acquire all interest in the land as soon as practicable, by donation, by purchase with donated or appropriated funds, or by exchange. Once the land is acquired, the Secretary modifies the park's boundaries to include it and administers it as part of Sequoia National Park. The Secretary of Agriculture, in turn, redraws the boundaries of Sequoia National Forest to exclude the parcel.
plaw-106-575-2000: Public Law 106-575, approved December 28, 2000, lets the Forest Service convey federal land in the Lake Tahoe Basin to the Washoe County School District in Nevada for an elementary school site. The Secretary of Agriculture, acting through the Chief of the Forest Service, must decide on the district's application within 180 days. The land may be used only as a school site and reverts to the United States if used otherwise. The price reflects its value under that restriction; proceeds fund purchases of environmentally sensitive land in the basin.
plaw-106-576-2000:
Saving water along the Texas border is the job of the Lower Rio Grande Valley Water Resources Conservation and Improvement Act of 2000, Public Law 106-576, approved December 28, 2000. It directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Bureau of Reclamation, to conserve and enhance the water supplies of the Lower Rio Grande Valley.

The program runs in cooperation with the State of Texas, acting through the Texas Water Development Board, along with water users and other non-federal entities. Its ground is the Rio Grande Regional Water Planning Area known as Region M, together with Hudspeth and El Paso counties. The work is to investigate and identify opportunities to improve the water supply. That includes reviewing engineering studies and planning reports for projects that conserve and transport raw water.
plaw-106-577-2000:
Public Law 106-577, approved December 28, 2000, establishes the California Trail Interpretive Center in Elko, Nevada. Title I, the California Trail Interpretive Act, creates the center to support interpretation of the history of the trails used in settling the western portion of the United States.

Congress found that the nineteenth-century movement over the California National Historic Trail ran from 1840 until the transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869. More than 300,000 settlers made the journey, many leaving records or stories of it. The findings credit that movement with developing the West. They credit it with preventing colonization of the west coast by Russia and the British Empire. They call added recognition and interpretation of the trail fitting.
plaw-106-578-2000:
Fake identification is the target of the Internet False Identification Prevention Act of 2000, Public Law 106-578, signed December 28, 2000. The act strengthens enforcement of the federal laws on fake papers, a problem sharpened by how easily such documents can be made and handed out.

It orders the Attorney General and the Secretary of the Treasury to set up a joint committee, working through existing joint task forces or other means. Its job is to see that fake ID papers are investigated and prosecuted with vigor. The committee joins the heads of the Secret Service, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Social Security Administration, and the Immigration and Naturalization Service. It reports yearly to the House and Senate judiciary committees and terminates two years after the act takes effect.
plaw-106-579-2000:
Memorial Day gains a shared national pause in the National Moment of Remembrance Act, Public Law 106-579, approved December 28, 2000. The act establishes the White House Commission on the National Moment of Remembrance to advance the observance.

The findings recall that Memorial Day was established in 1868 to pay tribute to those who made the ultimate sacrifice in service to the United States. They argue that its relevance must be renewed for present and future generations. They cite House Concurrent Resolution 302 of May 25, 2000, in which Congress called for a National Moment of Remembrance, and Presidential Proclamation 7315, which designated 3:00 p.m. local time on Memorial Day, May 29, 2000, as the time to join in prayer and observe that moment.
plaw-106-580-2000:
The National Institutes of Health gained a new institute when Congress passed Public Law 106-580, the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering Establishment Act, signed December 29, 2000. The act amends the Public Health Service Act to set up the institute as a research home of its own.

Congress found that research in imaging, bioengineering, computer science, and informatics is critical to improving health care. Yet it is wholly different from the molecular biology on which the existing national research institutes are based. So those fields need a home of their own, apart from the older structure. The findings stress noninvasive imaging for earlier detection and diagnosis of disease, advanced genetic and molecular imaging, and telemedicine and teleradiology for rural citizens and other underserved populations.
plaw-2000: Private Law 106-9, approved on November 9, 2000, is a private law for the relief of Ruth Hairston. The law waives a filing deadline in her case. Hairston sought review of a 1995 order by the Merit Systems Protection Board about her claim for a survivor annuity. The thirty-day deadline in title 5 of the United States Code does not bar her petition, the law says.
plos-pone-0000100:
Justin A. Harris, Ehsan Arabzadeh, Adrienne L. Fairhall, and their team studied the sense of touch in PLOS ONE in 2006. People can tell apart vibrations of different frequencies through the skin of the fingers. The team tested what limits that skill, such as how strong the vibration feels versus how often it repeats.

Their results bear on how the cortex codes touch: whether by the rate of firing, its timing, or both. That code is what a prosthetic hand would need to speak to feel natural. Careful measures of what people can and cannot tell apart set the spec for such devices. The paper links a lab measure of perception to real neural code questions.
plos-pone-0000200:
Milena Raffi and Ralph M. Siegel published this vision neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Optic flow is the streaming pattern of light across the eyes when we move through the world. The authors map how the inferior parietal lobule of a behaving monkey's brain organizes responses to that flow.

Optic flow tells an animal its heading, speed, and the layout around it. A functional architecture for flow in this brain region shows how the cortex divides that job. The work helps explain how primates, including humans, steer through space using vision alone.
plos-pone-0000300:
Xiao Xiao Jenny Gu, Feng Yun Yue, Colin M. Kovacs, and colleagues published this HIV immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many cytokines, immune signal proteins, share one receptor part, the common gamma chain. The authors study the role of those cytokines in reversing T cell anergy. Anergy is the switched-off state of HIV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells in infected patients.

Anergic T cells are present but useless against the virus. If cytokine signals can wake them, that is a therapeutic opening. The paper tests which signals do the waking, informing immune-based strategies meant to restore the body's own control of HIV.
plos-pone-0000400:
Roser Pinyol and colleagues described a control circuit for nerve cell shape in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The circuit involves N-WASP and the Arp2/3 complex, proteins that build branching scaffolds of actin, the cell's structural fiber. A third protein, Abp1, helps regulate them, and the team placed it in the pathway that shapes neurons.

A neuron's shape, its trunk of dendrites and its long axon, decides what it can connect to. Actin scaffolds push the membrane into those forms. Showing that Abp1 helps control the N-WASP and Arp2/3 machinery adds a link to the chain of command. That chain sculpts nerve cells as the brain wires itself.
plos-pone-0000500:
Dana Sumilo and colleagues challenged a popular explanation for a disease surge in the Baltic states, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Tick-borne encephalitis, a viral brain infection spread by ticks, rose sharply in the Baltics in the 1990s. Climate change was often blamed, since warmer weather favors ticks. The team's title states their finding: climate change cannot explain the upsurge.

Ruling out the easy explanation redirects attention to social and land-use changes after the Soviet era, which altered farming, forests, and human contact with ticks. The paper is a caution against attributing every disease shift to climate without checking the numbers, and it models how to test such claims.
plos-pone-0000600:
Cristina A. Faria and colleagues found a weakness in a flagship farm technology, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bt maize is engineered to poison caterpillar pests. The team found a chain of effects. Bt maize is highly open to aphid attack, so aphids thrive on it. The wasps that attack caterpillar pests feed on the aphids' honeydew. With more food, the wasps perform better against the pests.

The chain is indirect: a pest the plant cannot stop ends up feeding the allies that kill the pests it can. Such side effects decide whether engineered crops help or hinder biological control in real fields. The study is a reminder that fields are food webs, not single-trait demonstrations.
plos-pone-0000700:
Julio Echegoyen, Axel Neu, Kevin D. Graber and colleagues studied how brain circuits steady their state after activity is blocked. Their 2007 PLOS ONE work concerns homeostatic plasticity, the adjustments that keep circuits from becoming hyperactive or falling silent. Little was known about this process after activity changes in vivo, inside a living animal.

Blocking activity in the hippocampus, they studied synaptic scaling, where synapses strengthen or weaken all at once, and intrinsic plasticity of the neurons. Age-dependence was part of the question too. Brains that cannot regain balance in activity are prone to disorders like epilepsy. Knowing how the balance is restored, and how it changes with age, guides that research.
plos-pone-0000800:
Stephen B. Beres and James M. Musser catalogued the borrowed genes in the group A Streptococcus metagenome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Strains of one bacterial species differ in gene content, and those differences drive medically relevant traits such as virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Group A Streptococcus causes a diverse array of human infections and after-effects, and shows complex population structure.

Exogenous genetic elements, DNA arrived from outside, are their focus: genes picked up from viruses and other bacteria. Such imports can turn a mild strain dangerous in one step. Tallying their contribution to the species' total gene pool explains how one species produces so many disease patterns.
plos-pone-0000900:
Gang Li, Jinhong Wang, Stephen Rossiter and colleagues found fast change in the FoxP2 gene in echolocating bats, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. FoxP2 helps control the face and mouth movements behind speech and calls. Across backboned animals it barely changes, yet humans and chimps differ at two building blocks.

Bats that hunt by sound place huge demands on mouth and voice control. The team compared FoxP2 across bat species and report sped up evolution in the echolocating lines. The result links a speech related gene to another group that lives by precise vocal skill. It widens the story of how vocal control evolves.
plos-pone-0001000:
Logan Walsh, Deanna Carere, Colin Cooper and colleagues tracked two tissue remodeling partners through frog metamorphosis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Matrix metalloproteinases cut up the material around cells, and their inhibitors, TIMPs, keep them in check. Together they rebuild tissue, and TIMPs also help switch some enzymes on.

In the frog Xenopus laevis, metamorphosis rebuilds nearly everything, from tail to gut. The team found RNA levels of one enzyme, MT1-MMP, and its inhibitor TIMP-2 mimic each other across that change. Matched timing suggests the pair are managed as a unit. The frog gives a whole body view of remodeling that cell cultures cannot.
plos-pone-0001100:
Ruvandhi Nathavitharana, Jorge Coronel and David Moore tested sunlight for making TB culture waste safe, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disposing of TB culture material is a real problem in poor settings. Cultures multiply the infectious load of patient samples greatly before they are thrown away.

Solar cookers had already shown they can kill conventional bacteria. The team examine solar disinfection of MODS mycobacterial cultures, a low cost TB culture method. Sunlight is the one resource many poor clinics have in surplus. If a solar cooker can sterilize culture waste, a safety step that rich labs automate becomes possible where it is needed most.
plos-pone-0001200:
In a complex system, it is often unclear which parts to adjust to improve performance. Di Wu, Elizabeth Townsley, and Alan Tartakoff present a selection strategy for that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their test bed is the cell, where the components that most affect a trait are rarely obvious.

The authors describe covert genetic selections to optimize phenotypes, ways of letting a population of cells reveal which molecular targets matter most. The method identifies and prioritizes targets rather than testing guesses one by one. The same logic, they note, applies to other high-complexity systems, from institutions to economies.
plos-pone-0001300:
Interleukin-24, also known as mda-7, is a signaling protein said to kill tumor cells while sparing normal ones. Stephanie Kreis and colleagues tested a lab-made version against melanoma cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. IL-24 belongs to the IL-10 family of cytokines and is produced by certain immune cells.

The authors report that recombinant interleukin-24 lacks apoptosis-inducing traits in melanoma cells. A result like this matters: it tests a hopeful claim in the cancer literature and warns against building therapy plans on it without care. Their study used the purified protein itself, rather than gene delivery.
plos-pone-0001400:
Bernard Couvreur and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on tick proteins that blunt the host defense. Ticks feed on blood for a long time, so they must calm host blood clotting, swelling, and immune attack. They do so with a suite of spit proteins from large gene families. The team studied one family that blocks a key defense arm.

The authors describe how members of this family vary and how each one acts. Small shifts in form lead to shifts in target and strength. The work maps a key tool ticks use to stay attached and feed. It may also point to new ways to foil ticks and the ills they spread.
plos-pone-0001500:
Emily Manderson, Mohan Malleshaiah, and Stephen Michnick published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a yeast gene of unknown job. More than a thousand yeast genes still lack a clear role, despite vast data on gene use and protein links. The team built a screen that merges gene tests with protein link data. They used it to probe one such gene.

Their screen ties the gene, called Elm1, to shutting off a yeast growth factor. A new job for an old gene shows the screen works. The same tack can be run on the rest of the unknown list. That promises a faster close to the yeast gene map.
plos-pone-0001600:
Asako Shindo, Takamasa Yamamoto, and Naoto Ueno wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell polarity in frog embryos. Polarity, the built in top and bottom of a cell, shapes how embryos form. In frog gastrulation, gut layer cells line up and slide past each other. That slide stretches the embryo from head to tail. The team tracked how polarity is set in step across the sheet.

Their work maps the cues that align cells as the sheet moves. A shared alignment is what lets the whole tissue stretch in one course. Faults here cause grave birth defects. The frog model gives a clear view of a step all backboned embryos share.
plos-pone-0001700:
Denise M. Wolf, Lisa Fontaine-Bodin, Ilka Bischofs, and their co-authors measured memory in a bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Memory is usually credited to higher organisms. But many bacterial control networks show complex dynamics and multi-stable behavior. Those traits are linked to memory in other systems, and bacteria plainly respond to their own past states.

The team quantified history-dependent behavior: how a cell's response to a signal depends on what it met before. The full text gives the experiments, the time scales of the effect, and the model they built. A measured bacterial memory gives a concrete system for studying how single cells store information about their past. It also has uses in engineering microbes that remember exposures.
plos-pone-0001800:
Alfonso J. C. Soler Bistué, Daniel Birshan, Andrew P. Tomaras, and their co-authors sequenced a resistance plasmid in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The spread of antimicrobial resistance genes is an important public health and biodefense threat. Plasmids, small DNA circles that jump between bacteria, drive the rapid acquisition of resistance by pathogens.

The paper gives the nucleotide sequence of pMET1, a multiresistance plasmid from Klebsiella pneumoniae. It also gives its similarity to pCRY, a plasmid of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis, and to integrative conjugative elements. The full text gives the gene map and the shared segments. Shared parts across plasmids of very different pathogens show how resistance genes travel.
plos-pone-0001900:
John Lin and co-authors tested hunger-boosting drugs in monkeys in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The drugs switch on TrkB, a cell receptor tied to body weight. When this path fails, people and mice eat too much and gain great weight. When drugs in mice switch it on, food intake and weight drop.

The team gave TrkB-switching drugs through the body, not the brain, to non-human primates. As the title states, appetite rose and the animals gained weight, the reverse of the mouse results. That clash across species is a warning for drug work: a path that trims weight in mice may not do the same in primates.
plos-pone-0002000:
Anavaj Sakuntabhai and co-authors hunted host genes that shape malaria in Senegal, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Attacks of falciparum malaria range from mild to deadly, even in the same region. Good evidence says genes of the person, not just the parasite, drive part of that range.

Most gene hunts had used a case and control design, which has limits. The team instead mapped traits tied to malaria to spots in the genome in Senegalese families, and tested how strongly each trait is inherited. Family maps of this kind can find protective genes that case studies miss.
plos-pone-0002100:
Judith Legrand and co-authors modeled tuberculosis control in crowded prisons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. TB in prisons is a major health problem in countries with high or middling rates, such as Brazil. For operational reasons, control strategies in prisons cannot be compared through population-based intervention studies, since prisons cannot be run as trial sites at will.

A mathematical model is proposed to compare strategies instead, in highly endemic, overcrowded prisons. Models can weigh screening, isolation, and treatment options before scarce funds are spent. Prison TB spills into the wider public, so gains inside walls count outside them too.
plos-pone-0002200:
Jason Bourke and co-authors built a 3D model of a dingo skull to test bite physics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Jaw models predict that bite force depends on how wide the jaw opens and on which tooth does the biting. Few studies had checked those predictions in a real mammal, and none had weighed the role of gape angle.

The team used a finite element approach, which breaks the skull into many small pieces in a computer. They computed bite force and skull stress across gapes and tooth positions. Their results test long-used jaw models against hard numbers from an iconic Australian predator.
plos-pone-0002300:
Darren Soanes, Intikhab Alam, Mike Cornell, and co-authors compared the genomes of fungi and their kin across many species, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fungi and oomycetes cause many of the most serious diseases of plants, from potato blight to tree diebacks. A shared genomic pattern might explain what makes them good pathogens.

The team analyzed genome sequences from thirty-six species, including seven plant pathogenic ones. They looked for gene families that had expanded in the pathogenic lines. Expanded families are candidate tool kits for infecting plants, and each one offers targets for crop protection that go beyond spraying single chemicals.
plos-pone-0002400:
Holt and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alison R. Holt, Zoe G. Davies, Claire Tyler, and others. Its subject is meta-Analysis of the Effects of Predation on Animal Prey Abundance: Evidence from UK Vertebrates. Controlling vertebrate predators is one of the most widespread forms of wildlife management and it continues to cause conflict between stakeholders worldwide.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002500:
Led by Haslam, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Niall J. Haslam, Nava E. Whiteford, Gerald Weber, and others. Its subject is optimal Probe Length Varies for Targets with High Sequence Variation. The title goes on to note implications for Probe Library Design for Resequencing Highly Variable Genes. Sequencing by hybridisation is an effective method for obtaining large amounts of DNA sequence information at low cost.

The efficiency of SBH depends on the design of the probe library to provide the maximum information for minimum cost. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002600:
Research by Wei and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Yan Wei, Mei-Hua Qu, Xing-Sheng Wang, and others. Its subject is binding to the Minor Groove of the Double-Strand, Tau Protein Prevents DNA from Damage by Peroxidation. Tau, an important microtubule linked protein, has been found to bind to DNA.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002700:
Work by David Caramelli and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a 28,000 years old Cro-Magnon mtDNA sequence differs from all potentially contaminating modern sequences. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David Caramelli, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. DNA sequences from ancient speciments may in fact result from undetected contamination of the ancient specimens by modern DNA. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002800:
Research from Shinobu Ueda and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers establishment of rat embryonic stem cells and making of chimera rats. The catalog record names Shinobu Ueda first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The rat is a reference animal model for physiological studies and for the analysis of multigenic human diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, neurological disorders. The authors add a further point. The rats have long been used in extensive chemical carcinogenesis studies. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002900:
Philip Monahan, Kevin de Souza and William Idsardi used brain imaging in 2008 to time how listeners restore a missing pitch. When the lowest tone of a complex sound is absent, hearers still sense it. When the brain rebuilds that missing fundamental was still unclear.

Their MEG recordings, which track fast magnetic signals from the brain, placed the recovery in auditory cortex within 100 milliseconds of the sound. That is a tight time bound from the study itself. Hearing scientists get a clearer timeline for one of the basic tricks that lets us judge pitch and voice.
plos-pone-0003000:
Etienne Morel, Stéphane Fouquet, Carine Strup-Perrot and co-authors studied the cellular prion protein in epithelial cells in 2008. The normal prion protein, PrPc, is found throughout the body, yet its everyday function was still debated. Most work had focused on the nervous system, leaving epithelia poorly investigated.

The team had earlier found PrPc targeted to cell-cell junctions in polarized epithelial cells. Their PLOS ONE study reports it is involved in epithelial cell proliferation and in placing junction proteins. That widens the prion protein's normal job beyond the brain, a useful baseline for disease work.
plos-pone-0003100:
Ildefonso De La Fuente, Luis Martínez, Alberto Pérez-Samartín and co-authors argued in 2008 that cell metabolism self-organizes globally. For many years enzymes were assumed to work either alone or in small catalytic groups. Studies using metabolic network models were helping to reveal the functional complexity of enzyme dynamics.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors present evidence for global self-organization of the cellular metabolic structure. That view treats metabolism as one coordinated system, not a bag of separate pathways. It changes how models of cell chemistry should be built and tested. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003200:
Paola Ferrante, Claudia Catalanotti, Giulia Bonente and colleagues build a regulated gene switch for an alga in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is a model system for algal and cell biology and is used for biotechnology, such as molecular farming and biological hydrogen production. Its metal-responsive CYC6 promoter is repressed by copper and induced by nickel ions.

The team present an optimized, chemically regulated gene expression system for Chlamydomonas. Readers get a tighter on-off tool for a workhorse alga. Reliable switches matter when engineered algae must make a product only at the right stage of growth.
plos-pone-0003300:
Marilis Rodriguez and co-authors study a malaria parasite surface protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. To invade a red blood cell, Plasmodium falciparum must use many contacts between its own proteins and receptors on the cell. Finding those receptors is a major task in learning how invasion works, since each contact is a chance to block it.

The team describe PfRH5, a new member of a binding protein family, show it binds the red cell, and hunt for its receptor. Readers meet a parasite protein at the heart of cell entry. Entry proteins are top vaccine targets for blood-stage malaria.
plos-pone-0003400:
Sitao Wu and Yang Zhang built a prediction program called ANGLOR, presented in this 2008 paper. A protein's shape depends on the twist angles along its backbone. Those angles can be guessed from the order of its amino acid building blocks. ANGLOR mixes several learning methods to make that guess.

The program reads sequence profiles plus predicted shape and exposure features. It then outputs the backbone angles as real numbers, not rough classes. Tests on large sets showed the mixed method beat single methods. Good angle guesses bring scientists closer to a protein's full three-dimensional shape.
plos-pone-0003500:
Paolo Marinho de Andrade Zanotto and David C. Krakauer compared whole virus genomes in this 2008 paper. They covered four families of DNA viruses. Viruses swap genes with hosts and each other at high rates. That swapping raises doubt about what single genes say about virus history.

Their phylogenies suggested regulatory cores and accessory satellites evolve in concert. Core control genes and extra satellite genes move as a linked set. Concerted change hints at deep order in viral genomes. The claim reframes how virus family trees should be read. Virus trees guide vaccine strain choice for fast-changing germs like flu.
plos-pone-0003600:
Berna Atik and co-authors hunted gene variants tied to a blinding eye condition in this 2008 paper. Trachoma is the leading preventable cause of blindness worldwide. It follows infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, often again and again. A balanced immune response is critical for clearing that infection.

Trachomatous trichiasis is a late, sight-threatening stage of the disease. The team identified new single-letter variants in inflammatory genes as risk factors. Mass antibiotic programs have not stopped reinfection everywhere. Host genetics may explain who progresses to blindness. Most trachoma blindness falls on women and on the poorest rural areas. There surgery and clean water are hard to reach, and infection passes fast among small children at home.
plos-pone-0003700:
Arne Ø. Mooers, Daniel P. Faith, and Wayne P. Maddison published this conservation study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Groups like the IUCN Red List grade species by how imperiled they are. Those grades are often turned into extinction probabilities to rank species by the evolutionary history they carry.

The authors test how stable such ranked lists are when the conversion changes. Small shifts in the odds can reorder which species count as top priorities. The study gives conservation programs a sharper, more honest way to spend limited funds on saving evolutionary history.
plos-pone-0003800:
Daniel Lietha and Michael J. Eck published this structural study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Focal adhesion kinase, or FAK, helps cells move, multiply, and survive. It is overproduced in many human cancers and tied to poor outcomes. A new inhibitor, TAE226, had recently been reported against it.

The authors solved crystal structures of the FAK kinase bound to TAE226 and related inhibitors. The structures reveal an unusual helical shape in a key segment of the kinase. These atomic pictures guide the design of tighter, better FAK blockers for cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0003900:
John H. Malone and Brian E. Fontenot compared breeding barriers across toad species in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. How new species split apart remains a core question in evolution study. Crosses between species show where mating or offspring fail. The authors gathered a very large set of such crosses.

Their data cover more than 1,900 crosses between 92 toad species. With that spread, they could look for general patterns in how isolation builds. Wide comparisons reveal whether barriers arise early or late in splitting. The toad data set gives evolution researchers a rare, broad test bed.
plos-pone-0004000:
Margaret Kweku, Dongmei Liu, Martin Adjuik, and co-authors trialed seasonal malaria prevention in Ghanaian children in 2008. Malaria and anaemia are the top causes of illness and death for children there. Giving preventive drugs at intervals might cut both problems. The trial tested that idea under real conditions.

Children received either sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine or artesunate plus amodiaquine, or a placebo. Dosing followed the seasons when malaria spreads most. The randomized design gives a fair test of benefit. Results can guide national programs weighing seasonal treatment for children. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004100:
Jarukit Edward Long, Nicholas Renzette, Richard C. Centore, and co-authors studied DNA damage alarms in bacteria in 2008. Repair of DNA damage starts with detecting the harm. In E. coli, the RecA protein coats single-stranded DNA after damage. That filament triggers the SOS response, a broad repair program.

Their PLOS ONE article compares two recA mutants for SOS switching. The mutants differed in what they need to keep SOS on without damage. Such details map how the alarm is triggered and sustained. The work refines a classic model of bacterial stress response. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004200:
Sheng-zhi Wang and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Geneticists often want to switch a gene on in only a few scattered cells, but controlling the probability of activation has been hard. Existing tools tend to flip the gene in nearly all cells or in none.

The team presents STARS, a genetic strategy for stochastic gene activation with regulated sparseness. In plain terms, the method lets researchers dial in how sparse the labelled or altered cells should be. Such control is valuable for tracing single neurons and for mimicking the scattered mutations seen in disease.
plos-pone-0004300:
Michelle Wagner and colleagues published this yeast cell cycle study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Whi5 is a transcriptional repressor that holds back the G1 phase of the cell cycle in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It plays a role equivalent to the retinoblastoma tumour suppressor in mammals. In early G1, Whi5 binds and inhibits the SBF transcription factor, keeping growth genes off.

The team mapped how site-specific phosphorylation by CDK enzymes regulates Whi5. Adding phosphates at particular sites releases the brake at the right moment. The study details the switch that commits a yeast cell to divide.
plos-pone-0004400:
Four mountain massifs in the central Sahara hold pools with tropical fish. Those fish are relicts, leftovers from a wetter age. Sébastien Trape surveyed one such refuge in 2009. His PLOS ONE paper covers the Adrar mountains of Mauritania. Nearly all older records there came from surveys made before 1960. Those surveys reported five fish species.

Trape asks what climate change now means for these desert fish. Their pools are small, isolated, and hard to recolonize if lost. A drying climate threatens the water they depend on. The paper updates a record that had stood for about fifty years. It makes the case for guarding these mountain refuges before the fish vanish.
plos-pone-0004500:
Whether evolution repeats itself when given the same problem is tested by Scott William Roy in PLOS ONE in 2009. How organisms adapt is one of the most basic questions in evolutionary biology. Two recent studies had watched E. coli bacteria evolve in response to the antibiotic cefotaxime.

Those studies followed five mutations in one gene, for an enzyme called beta-lactamase, that together made the bacteria drug-resistant. Roy asks how predictable that path was: would neutral changes, and pairs of changes, lead down the same road again? Asking whether adaptation can be rerun is more than a curiosity. If evolution is partly predictable, scientists can better foresee how bacteria will defeat the next antibiotic.
plos-pone-0004600:
A signaling enzyme helps drive the leakiness of lungs injured by breathing machines, report Mahendra Damarla, Emile Hasan, Adel Boueiz, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mechanical ventilation is a fundamental therapy for acute lung injury. Yet the machine's mechanical stress on the respiratory system can worsen the leak of fluid into the lungs, causing ventilator-associated lung injury.

The team postulated that an enzyme called MK2, switched on through the p38 MAP kinase pathway, drives this harm. They show MK2 regulates actin polymerization, the building of cell skeleton fibers, and vascular leak in this injury. Blocking such a mediator could one day let ventilators support breathing with less collateral damage to the lungs they are saving.
plos-pone-0004700:
Harleen Kaur and colleagues showed that soil microbes can erase plant chemical warfare effects, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plants can release chemicals that slow the growth of rival plants nearby. Past tests often used one chemical on one species on clean paper, which is far from real soil.

In real soil, microbes break down or change those chemicals fast. The team showed that this soil life can wipe out the growth block seen in lab tests. The result warns against bold claims from simple lab assays. Field claims about plant warfare need soil included. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004800:
Nguyen Thi Hue and colleagues studied the TLR4 gene and typhoid fever in Vietnam, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Understanding host genetic susceptibility to typhoid may clarify pathogenesis and help develop new therapeutics and vaccines. TLR4 encodes the principal receptor for bacterial endotoxin, a key sensor that triggers immune defense against Salmonella, and Other Gram negative bacteria in the gut and blood.

The team determined genetic variation within TLR4 in Vietnamese populations. They tested links between variants and typhoid occurrence or course. Receptor genetics could explain why illness varies. It may also guide vaccine design for endemic regions.
plos-pone-0004900:
Mai Nguyen Chi and colleagues studied temporally regulated traffic of HuR and ARE mRNAs during mouse spermatogenesis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In mammals, temporal disconnection between copying and translation occurs during late germ cell cell change. During late spermatogenesis copying ceases while stored mRNAs must be translated on schedule. With HuR protein shuttling messages from the chromatoid body to polysomes at defined developmental stages.

Timed delivery ensures proteins appear when needed. Storage bodies organize delayed translation elegantly. Male fertility depends on this choreography. Defects could explain some infertility. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0005000:
Creatine kinase recycles the cell's energy currency, ATP. It is famous for powering muscle contraction. Yafeng Zhang and colleagues found it a second job in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied creatine kinase B in immune cells. Their focus was T cell development and activation.

The enzyme regulates both processes. Interfering with it weakens the T cell response. An energy enzyme is doubling as an immune signal. That dual role was unexpected. The finding connects metabolism to immunity at a basic level. It may matter for conditions where T cells fail or overreact.
plos-pone-0005100:
Fruit flies bolt when danger looms. That startle response is an innate escape reflex. Gregor Zimmermann and colleagues pinned it to specific neurons. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used photoexcitation, switching neurons on with light. The target was a set of brain cells called acj6 neurons.

Lighting up acj6 neurons induced the escape response. No threat was needed. The defined circuit alone fired the whole behavior. Drosophila genetics links genes to circuits to behavior. This study completes one such chain. It shows a reflex can be traced to named cells. Mapping instinct this way is a long-standing goal. Each pinned circuit teaches how brains turn sensation into action.
plos-pone-0005200:
Whether a common lung germ plays a role in multiple sclerosis has been debated for years. The germ, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, would need to be found in spinal fluid to support the claim. Tang and colleagues built a standardized test for that search in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their test detects the germ's DNA in cerebrospinal fluid and can also measure how much is present. They validated it in samples from MS patients and controls. A shared, trusted test lets different labs compare results fairly, which is what a long-running dispute like this one needs most.
plos-pone-0005300:
Obesity makes fat pile up in the heart, where it can poison heart muscle. The heart's fat pool was thought to reflect only uptake and burning of fatty acids. Bartels and colleagues found another route in PLOS ONE in 2009: fat can also be shipped out.

A protein called microsomal triglyceride transfer protein handles that export. Its activity in the heart rose in obesity and served to limit triglyceride accumulation. The heart, in other words, fights back against fat overload, and boosting that defense might protect obese hearts. Heart fat is not just stored fuel. too much of it can poison the heart wall itself, so a built-in way to ship the fat out is a real line of defense.
plos-pone-0005400:
Flight gets harder as animals grow, since muscle power and the power flight demands scale differently. The margin between the two should shrink with body mass, capping flying size. Sato and colleagues studied soaring seabirds in PLOS ONE in 2009 to test that scaling.

Measured seabird flight data anchor the scaling rules in real animals. Those rules can then be extended to giant extinct pterosaurs, whose flight abilities are debated. Seabirds thus serve as living stand-ins for judging whether the largest fliers could truly soar. The largest of those past fliers had wings as wide as a small plane, and whether such bulk could stay aloft has long been in doubt. Which is why hard data from live birds counts so much here.
plos-pone-0005500:
Long Yang and co-authors studied a faulty immune switch in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The IRF family of proteins helps run immune responses, blood cell growth, and cell growth in general. One member, IRF-5, when switched on, drives the making of signals that cause inflammation.

The team tested a mutant form that blocks the normal protein. Studying what the blocker stops shows which jobs truly need IRF-5. That kind of detail can guide drugs for diseases where inflammation runs too hot, such as lupus and other autoimmune conditions. Blocking IRF-5 too much could weaken defence against real infections, so the balance matters for any future drug.
plos-pone-0005600:
Catherine Lovelock and co-authors found that added nutrients can kill mangrove trees, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Extra nutrients washing off farms and towns put heavy pressure on coastal life. Earlier work showed that mangrove forests grow faster when nutrients rise.

But faster shoot growth came at the cost of roots, and the trees died at higher rates in the long run. A forest that looks greener at first may be on its way out. The warning matters for how coastal pollution is judged and managed. Coastal cities keep growing, so nutrient loads on mangrove shores are set to rise unless drainage is handled better.
plos-pone-0005700:
Prasanna Venkatraman and colleagues built a computer method in 2009 to guess what tasks a protease can do. Proteases are enzymes that cut other proteins at set spots. They keep cells in balance, but many newly found proteases have unknown jobs.

The method reads a protease's sequence and shape to predict what it cuts, what it does, and which networks it joins. Labs can then test the best guesses first, saving time and cost. As gene scans keep finding new proteases, such forecasts help turn raw lists into working biology. The paper offers the tool as a guide for that work.
plos-pone-0005800:
Manuel Irimia, Jakob Rukov, and Scott Roy tested in 2009 whether shifts in gene splicing across primates track with shifts in the splicing regulators themselves. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins, and it is tightly controlled in time and place. Regulator proteins bind tags in and around gene segments to set the pattern.

Changes in the tags found in exons did not line up with changes in splicing levels between primate species. That null result is informative: regulation must shift by other routes. The study cautions against simple stories in how splicing evolves.
plos-pone-0005900:
Darren Gray and co-authors ran a village-cluster trial in China in 2009 against a parasitic worm spread by water buffalo. Schistosoma japonicum infects people through water contact, and buffalo are thought to pass much of it to humans. An earlier drug-based pilot ran from the late nineteen-nineties.

The trial randomized whole clusters to intervention or control, treating both people and bovines with praziquantel. Its design tests whether cutting bovine transmission lowers human infection. If it does, control programs must fund animal treatment, not just human doses. The study is a model for tackling diseases shared with animals.
plos-pone-0006000:
The plague bacterium spread across the world from hearths in Central Asia. Yanjun Li, Yujun Cui, Yolande Hauck and colleagues traced that spread with gene typing in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses a method called MLVA, which reads repeating stretches of DNA, to sort Yersinia pestis strains and build their family tree.

The species is usually split into three classic groups, plus a less harmful one found in small mammals. Gene typing sharpens that picture and shows how Central Asian foci seeded plague across continents. Knowing the routes the germ took helps explain old pandemics and helps health teams read the source of any fresh outbreak.
plos-pone-0006100:
Some bacteria carry their own weapon and the scabbard in one protein. Jens Brockmeyer, Sabrina Spelten, Thorsten Kuczius and colleagues dissected such a weapon in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies EspP, a serine protease autotransporter from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, a proposed factor in the germ's virulence, across its four known subtypes.

The subtypes differ sharply in how well they transport themselves out of the cell and cut their targets. Linking those differences to structure shows which parts of the protein do which job. A virulence factor understood at that level is easier to block, and the work helps judge which subtype a patient isolate carries.
plos-pone-0006200:
Melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer, resists many treatments once it spreads. Peng Hou, Dingxie Liu, and Meiju Ji tested a clever switch in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Two growth pathways drive much of melanoma's growth, and blocking them might do more than slow the tumor.

Blocking those pathways turned on thyroid genes that handle iodine inside melanoma cells. The cells also began taking up radioactive iodine, a treatment long used for thyroid cancer. If the switch holds up, some melanomas could be made treatable with an existing therapy. The paper lays out the idea and its first supporting tests.
plos-pone-0006300:
The aquarium trade moves more exotic vertebrates than any other import route, and labels are often wrong. Dirk Steinke, Tyler Zemlak, and Paul Hebert applied DNA barcoding to ornamental fish in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Pressure is growing to ensure species are harvested sustainably and their origins reported honestly.

A short standard DNA tag identified the traded fish reliably in their tests. Regulators could use barcodes to verify species at borders. Honest identification protects wild populations from hidden over-harvest. The study shows a lab method ready for practical enforcement work.
plos-pone-0006400:
A small quail once spread all through New Zealand, then died out fast in the 1870s. Mark Seabrook-Davison and his team used DNA from old specimens in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Doubt had long hung over what the lost bird was and which quails are its kin.

The old DNA settles the lost quail's name and its place on the quail family tree. It clears up the ties of the living quails of the region at the same time. Such work shows the worth of museum skins as stores of past life. It also helps guards of the birds that are left to plan their care.
plos-pone-0006500:
Grégory Lacraz and colleagues studied how diabetic pancreatic cells protect themselves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Oxidative stress, from excess reactive oxygen species, mediates diabetes-related damage in many tissues. Pancreatic beta cells, which make insulin, are among the victims. The team examined how these cells respond when stressed.

Their title reports that diabetic beta cells can achieve self-protection against oxidative stress. They do so through an adaptive up-regulation of their defenses. A built-in rescue program is hopeful news for diabetes research. If it can be supported, beta cells might last longer. The work also shows that stressed cells are not merely passive victims.
plos-pone-0006600:
Anna Nolan, Hiroshi Kobayashi, Bushra Naveed, and colleagues studied costimulatory molecules in sepsis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inflammation in the early stages of sepsis is governed by the innate immune response. Costimulatory molecules are a receptor and ligand class capable of regulating that response. The team examined CD80 and CD86 in murine polymicrobial sepsis, sepsis from mixed microbes.

Their title highlights a differential role for CD80 and CD86 in regulating the innate response. Two similar molecules turn out to do different jobs. That distinction matters for drugs that target costimulation. Sepsis still lacks targeted treatments, so each regulatory detail counts.
plos-pone-0006700:
Leonid Teytelman and co-authors reported a hidden pitfall in genome experiments in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chromatin is the packed form DNA takes inside cells. Its structure affects repair, copying, and recombination of DNA. The team found it also affects routine laboratory handling of DNA. That influence can distort the results of widely used experiments.

They first noticed the problem in chromatin immunoprecipitation, known as ChIP. ChIP is meant to show where proteins bind along the genome. If chromatin structure skews the processing steps, binding maps can mislead. The authors traced how the distortion arises during analysis. Their warning helps genome researchers clean up a common source of error.
plos-pone-0006800:
Christiane Cuny and colleagues tested people's noses for a livestock-linked resistant bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, clone CC398. Studies in Europe and North America found it often colonizes farm animals. People working directly with colonized animals also carried it. Whether it spreads onward to others was open.

The study compared people with and without pig exposure. Nasal colonization was checked in both groups. Transmission beyond exposed workers would widen the public health concern. Contained carriage would limit it to an occupational issue. The results help draw that boundary for MRSA CC398 in humans.
plos-pone-0006900:
George Chahine and Bart Krekelberg studied how the brain dims vision during eye movements in PLOS ONE in 2009. Every rapid eye movement, or saccade, would blur the world. Saccadic suppression selectively reduces visual sensitivity during the movement. The neural mechanisms behind that reduction remain unknown. Early visual relays like the lateral geniculate nucleus were candidates.

The authors examined cortical contributions to the suppression. Cortex may actively quiet visual signals around each saccade. Knowing where suppression happens explains perceptual stability. It also informs how the brain edits its own input. The study moves the search from the eye's relay toward higher processing stages.
plos-pone-0007000:
Yaguang Si, Hai Shi, and Kyongbum Lee modelled energy burning in fat cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Raising energy use at the cell level is an appealing route against obesity. A protein called UCP1 uncouples mitochondria, wasting fuel as heat. Its presence tracks with lower white fat stores in animals.

The team ran a metabolic flux analysis on cultured 3T3-L1 adipocytes. Their model mapped how fuel flows change when mitochondria uncouple. Quantifying those flows helps judge uncoupling as an anti-obesity strategy. It also flags the costs, since wasted fuel must come from somewhere.
plos-pone-0007100:
Felicity Johnson and Michael Kaplitt searched for targets of a mitochondrial protease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protease Omi, also called HtrA2, is tied to Parkinson's disease. Mice with faults in it develop severe nerve pathology. Omi was thought to protect cells, partly by cutting harmful proteins.

The pair identified new mitochondrial proteins that Omi cuts. Fresh substrates point to a wider regulatory role in nerve cell survival. That role was not the one most researchers assumed. Their findings may redirect how Omi is viewed in neurodegeneration, from simple guard to active manager.
plos-pone-0007200:
Jason W. Bohland, Hemant Bokil, Cara B. Allen, and colleagues tackled a naming problem in brain science in 2009. Neuroscientists divide the brain into regions using atlases. Different atlases draw those borders differently, and no single standard is widely accepted for cortex or deeper structures.

Their PLOS ONE paper calls this the brain atlas concordance problem. They offer a quantitative way to compare anatomical parcellations from different atlases. Such comparisons help researchers judge whether two studies that name the same brain region actually mean the same patch of brain tissue. The comparison method is the paper's main tool for that judgment.
plos-pone-0007300:
Jean-Noël Arsac, Dominique Bétemps, Eric Morignat, and colleagues tested transmission of an unusual sheep prion disease in 2009. Atypical scrapie, also called Nor98, is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy. It is clearly distinct from classical scrapie and from BSE, the cattle disease often called mad cow disease.

The differences show in the biochemistry of the resistant prion protein. Genetic factors also differ between the diseases. The authors use transgenic mice that carry sheep prion genes. They report major effects of host prion protein levels and donor prion genotype on transmission. Their work guides surveillance of atypical scrapie.
plos-pone-0007400:
Holly E. Copeland, Kevin E. Doherty, David E. Naugle, and colleagues mapped energy development against wildlife in the American West in 2009. Many studies quantified indirect effects of hydrocarbon economies on climate and biodiversity. Few had measured the direct effect of new energy production on species where drilling actually occurs on the ground.

The authors map oil and gas development potential in the US Intermountain West. They estimate impacts to species from that footprint. Their PLOS ONE maps show where future development is likely and which habitats overlap. Land managers can use the overlap to plan protections before leasing decisions.
plos-pone-0007500:
Mélanie Bilodeau and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on cystatin genes and blood formation in mice. Cystatins are proteins that block enzymes which chew up other proteins.
