Haoran Wu led a team of six authors reviewing how cars judge driver readiness, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In conditional self-driving, the car handles the road until it asks the human to take over. That handover is only safe if the driver is alert and ready at that moment.

Wu's group surveyed the methods cars use to read driver state, from eye tracking to steering patterns. Their review maps which tools best detect drowsiness and distraction, and where the gaps remain. Carmakers and regulators can use that map to set standards for handovers. As partly automated cars spread, this quiet technology may prevent many crashes.
plos-pone-0359100: Matsuoka and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on older patients after stomach cancer surgery. They asked what later problems after the operation mean for survival. Complications can hit older patients harder and slow their recovery. Knowing which complications most affect outlook helps surgical teams watch for them, act early, and talk honestly with families about risk.
plos-pone-0359300:
Sarra Ayouni, Maha Sliti, Abeer Alghanem, Fatimah Alhayan, and Mohamed Maddeh published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works on wearable activity monitoring, where wrist or body sensors record movement. The authors present a feature selection method, a way to choose which sensor signals matter, that is compact, target-aware, and stability-based.

The test is cross-dataset: a method tuned on one group of wearers must still work on another. Choosing fewer, steadier features can make activity recognition cheaper and more reliable on real devices. Engineers building fitness trackers and health monitors are the audience for selection methods that survive a change of dataset.
plos-pone-0359400: Huang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on finding flaws on factory surfaces with very few examples. Their network learns from a handful of defect photos by matching new images against stored prototypes. Attention at several scales helps it catch both tiny and large flaws. Inspectors often have few samples of rare defects, so methods that learn from little are valuable.
plos-pone-0360300:
Lei Wang and Xiaowei Zhang drew in 2026 on a big national survey of Chinese life, run in 2021, to study media habits and action against pollution. The survey lets them link what media people use with what those people do. Do they report pollution? Do they join efforts to stop it?

Their study asks which kinds of media use move people from knowing to acting, and in which groups the link is strong. The answer matters for public agencies. They spend large sums on campaigns that may inform the public without moving it to act. Sound survey evidence can show whether campaigns should spread facts, build social norms, or open clear paths for citizens to report and take part.
pmc-12418700:
Fettiplace and colleagues report a modified Delphi study on disclosing artificial intelligence use in scientific writing. The work was done for regional anesthesia and pain medicine publishing. AI tools can polish language and speed editing, the authors note, but they can also make things up, carry bias, and blur who is to blame.

A steering group ran two survey rounds with authors, reviewers, editors, and AI researchers. Focused talks followed. The group agreed on what AI means here, what must be reported, and where reports belong. It also agreed on authorship rules. Reviewers gained guidance too, including checklists and support for detection software. The aim is openness, with human duty for the work kept intact.
pmc-13197800:
Ammar Almarghlani and colleagues compared two ceramic tooth implants in a 2026 clinical study. Root-analog implants are custom-made to copy the shape of the pulled tooth root. Standard ceramic implants come in fixed shapes. The team weighed gum health, bone stability, and early comfort for each type.

Thirty patients got one type or the other, based on fit for a custom copy. Scans and gum checks ran at one and three months. Plaque and bleeding scores did not differ between groups. Bone height held steady for both, with a slight dip for standard implants. The custom group had less swelling, pain, and redness at one month. By three months, both groups looked alike.
pmc-13201900:

pmc-13277000:

pmc-13277100:
Amal R Khanolkar wrote a 2026 study of health gaps among teens in the United Kingdom who use sexual identity labels other than lesbian, gay, or bisexual. That group includes teens who did not state an identity. Data came from a national cohort study of 9,998 seventeen-year-olds across the country.

pmc-13278800:

pmc-13279000:

The group compared tool scores with slow hand tracing in two small patient groups. For ventricle size, the tools matched hand tracing well, though two tools shrank large values. pmc-13279200:

pmc-13279500: Xinying Li and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their 2025 study on a gene regulator that boosts output of a farm chemical in a soil germ. pmc-13280300:

pmc-13281300:

pmc-13282400:

pmc-13283400:
Chinese-medicine body types enter a machine-built screening nomogram for early memory loss in Qixin Xu's 2026 Guangzhou study. The tool mixes body type classes from Chinese medicine with machine learning picks. Early spotting in primary care is the main goal.

A total of 1,503 adults aged 60 years and older had community health exams in 2025. About a quarter met the study cutoff for mild cognitive impairment. Four learning methods agreed on seven stable predictors for the final chart. Age, female sex, and two deficiency body types raised risk in the model. Regular exercise and a balanced body type lowered risk in the results. Chart accuracy was checked in a held-out group.
pmc-13283900:
A heart that stopped outside hospital beat again through combined machine support in a 2026 case by Hiroki Moriuchi and colleagues. Survival and return to daily life after such arrests remain very low. Two support devices together can steady blood flow and rest the heart.

After brain recovery was confirmed, bypass surgery used only artery grafts. All grafts stayed open, heart function improved, and he rejoined society at three months.
pmc-13284900:
Al Mahmud and co-authors propose a hybrid forecasting model for COVID-19 cases in Malaysia in a 2026 time-series study. The authors present the design as a stronger tool for public health planning.
pmc-13285700:
Roberta Martinez Novaes and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026 on portal vein thrombosis in newborns. pmc-13286300:

pmc-13286700:
Elmer E Gutierrez and Breanna J Putman watch how fence lizards cope when fire strips their cover in a 2026 field study. Clay model lizards measured attack pressure across sites, while real lizards from burned and unburned habitats were scored for back darkness and perch choices under an avian vision model.

Open, freshly burned plots drew more predator attacks on the models. Lizards matched darker ground with darker backs, improving their camouflage against charred surfaces. pmc-13287100:

pmc-13287200:

Shifts were tiny, usually toward the back and outer side, and centres did not reliably move to the middle with age. Knowing the variant should help clinicians avoid mistaking normal growth for disease.
pmc-13287300:
Maike E Lindemann and colleagues tested in 2026 how well combined PET and MRI scanning finds and measures tiny prostate cancer spots with weak tracer uptake. pmc-13288700:
Xun Yang and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for comparing ways of teaching inhaler technique to adults with asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Separate networks for each disease will use standard control questionnaires, with a pooled analysis kept secondary.
pmc-13288800:
Vanessa Le and colleagues survey German gynecologists on abortion care in 2026. The survey used the Theory of Planned Behavior. It ran online from June to November 2024. In all, 213 doctors completed it. All worked in offices. Cluster sampling drew them in.

pmc-13289100:

Boys got them less than girls. Wait-and-see scripts were filled less often. Fill timing did not split by group.
pmc-13289300:
Anna Wilhelmina de Boer and colleagues propose a 2026 framework called Panel Management Next Level for proactive, joined-up care. pmc-13289400:

pmc-13289500:

pmc-13290800:

pmc-13290900:

pmc-13291300:

pmc-13291500:

pmc-13292300:

pmc-13292400:

pmc-13292900:

pmc-13293600:

pmc-13293900:

pmc-13294400:

pmc-13295000:

pmc-13295100:

pmc-13296900:

pmc-13297800:

pmc-13298600:

pmc-13299100:

pmc-13299800:

pmc-13301900:

pmc-13303200:

pmc-13306200:

pmc-13307500:

pmc-13308700:

pmc-13308800:

pmc-13309200:

pmc-13309800:

pmc-13309900:
Abdullah Gazioğlu and co-authors compare blood chemistry in calves sick with a cattle germ against healthy calves in a 2026 study. The germ, Mycoplasma bovis, causes lung disease in young cattle. pmc-13310400:

pmc-13310700:

pmc-13310900:

pmc-13311000:

pmc-13311100:

pmc-13311300:

pmc-13311600:

pmc-13311700:

pmc-13312000:

pmc-13313600:

pmc-13314400:
Yanhong Ding and Ai Zhang present a 2026 case of morning glory syndrome, a rare birth defect of the optic disc, joined with retinal detachment. The condition was first described in detail by Kindler in 1970 and named for the flower-like look of the back of the eye.

pmc-13314600:
Khaled Mohammad Khwaileh and Naheda Mohammad Makhadmeh study Jordan law on fake news in work published in 2026. They ask how the 2023 Jordanian Cybercrime Law juggles free speech rights against state security claims.

pmc-13314900:
Lei Zhang and co-workers give a step-by-step surgical protocol for reaching the rat inner ear, published in 2026. Getting drugs or viruses into the inner ear is key for hearing and balance research. But the common rat routes are tight and risk harm to the ear bones or a key artery.

pmc-13315500:
Huan-Ran Hou and colleagues used advanced MRI in 2026 to track brain blood flow during a week of head-down tilt, a standard way to mimic weightlessness. Tilting the body sends fluid toward the head, which can disturb pressure and flow in the brain and may affect thinking.

The schedule lets the team map how flow adapts over time and returns afterward.
pmc-13315900:
Phoebe Thomson, Philip Shaw, and Divyangana Rakesh used long-term data in 2026 to ask whether childhood thinking ability predicts how the teenage brain develops. Earlier work tied ability to brain structure and wiring at single time points, but growth paths over years were less clear.

pmc-13316200:
Caroline Klint Johannesen and colleagues report in 2026 the early effect of RSV prevention on baby hospital stays in Denmark. pmc-13316300:
Jingjing Zhang and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on engineered T cell treatment for acute myeloid leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer with high relapse rates. The therapy, proven in some B cell cancers, faces special barriers in this disease, and the review maps both progress and roadblocks.

pmc-13317200:

pmc-13318500:
Naoto Fukunaga and co-workers describe a 2026 surgical case involving a 71-year-old man with complex aneurysms of the aorta and iliac arteries who was referred for open repair. Stent grafts had already been placed in both internal iliac arteries ahead of the main operation.

pmc-13318900:
Katya Grander, Victoria Mosub, and Sigal Kordova present a 2026 comparative study of thinking biases in large language models across languages. pmc-13320400:
Brittany H. File and co-authors study hospice referral patterns in returned neck of womb cancer in a 2026 article on uneven care. pmc-13320500:
Lucile Broséus and a large cohort team examine in 2026 how air pollution before birth may shape a baby's lung function. pmc-13321000:
Luciana Vilela Gomide and co-authors write a 2026 letter on a little known lesion pattern in hidradenitis suppurativa, a long term skin disease with painful lumps and draining tunnels. pmc-13322800:

pmc-13322900:

pmc-13323300:

pmc-13324300:

pmc-13324500:

pmc-13327900:

pmc-13328000:

pmc-13329700:

pmc-13330700:

pmc-13331100:

pmc-13332400:

pmc-13332500:

pmc-13333300:

pmc-13333400:

pmc-13333900:

pmc-13334300:

pmc-13334400:

pmc-13335800:

pmc-13336500:

pmc-13337400:

pmc-13338700:

pmc-13341300:

pmc-13341600:

pmc-13341800:

pmc-13342400:

pmc-13400300:

pmc-13400600:

pmc-13402100:

pmc-13403700:

pmc-13404300:

The authors present enzyme treatment as a possible complement to mechanical cleaning in preventing or managing caries.
pmc-13421700:
Swelam and colleagues report a 2026 survey of how farmers in Egypt perceive climate change and respond to it. The team gathered answers from 2,953 farmers across seven major farming regions and built combined scores for awareness, felt impacts, adaptation steps, barriers, and support from institutions.

Awareness of climate change ran high, but uptake of technical fixes stayed low. Farmers leaned on cheap, step-by-step changes, while costly tools such as modern irrigation and digital aids were rarely used, and old irrigation methods still ruled. Many reported steep drops in key crop yields. Adaptation steps linked strongly with reported yield changes, while feeling impacts more strongly did not predict adapting more. The gap suggests money and support, not knowledge, are the binding limits, a key point for farm policy in dry regions.
pmc-13421800:
Benard O Ayieko leads a ten-author team describing, in a 2026 paper, how they carried the results of an HIV study back to everyone with a stake in it. Their Kenyan trial offered fishermen HIV self-testing through social networks, with linkage into treatment and prevention, and the team treated dissemination as part of the research rather than an afterthought.

Guided by stakeholder theory and diffusion of innovations, they engaged participants, beach communities, facility staff, county health managers and the national AIDS programme leadership in sequence. Feedback gathered at each level is reported in their own words. The authors sort the audience into institutions, watchers acting as intermediaries, and stakeholders themselves, offering the exercise as a template other trials can copy.
pmc-13422100:
Quayyum and co-authors interviewed Canadian clinicians, researchers, and health-system and community staff about how food insecurity and disease-related malnutrition, poor nutrition driven by illness itself, feed into each other. Little earlier work had examined the two problems together despite their shared roots in poverty and unequal access.

Twelve participants from four provinces took part in seven interviews and two focus groups for the study. The overarching theme was that structural inequities connect both problems, captured in the complaint that services treat the symptom, not the system. Participants backed screening for both conditions only when results could link people to real services beyond food charity, delivered without bias or stigma. They called for system-level change supported by research, intervention, and professional education, and ranked a generated list of research questions.
pmc-13422300:
Daniela Virgintino leads a thirteen-author team studying, in a 2026 paper, how the smallest brain vessels sprout branches with help from support cells. In the developing human forebrain, pericytes at the growing front extend hair-thin tunnels called tunnelling nanotubes. These tunnels bridge toward other vessels. The team asked whether the SCF signal and its c-KIT receptor steer this partnership.

High-resolution confocal microscopy and three-dimensional modelling of developing brain and glioblastoma tissue located both molecules. The nanotubes, marked by the protein NG2, were counted across healthy and tumour vascular networks, and double staining with an endothelial marker fixed each signal's cellular home. The authors read the pattern as a non-canonical route of vessel-pericyte communication worth targeting in tumours.
pmc-13422800:
Juliana Viola leads a nine-author team reporting, in a 2026 case study, a complete response to dual immunotherapy in a rare kidney tumour. The patient had a locally advanced epithelioid angiomyolipoma — a growth that can turn malignant — and such tumours usually receive drugs aimed at the mTOR pathway, with inconsistent durability.

She received ipilimumab plus nivolumab as first treatment and improved fast, in symptoms and on scans. Immune-related sarcoidosis then appeared, settling after the drugs stopped and steroids were given. Delayed kidney removal found no living cancer in the specimen. Genetic testing revealed an inherited FLCN mutation, the mark of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, and a single expanded T-cell clone was shared between her blood and tumour. Over five years on, she remains in remission.
pmc-13423900:
Rick Burgess and ten co-authors write as a lived experience advisory board attached to a mental health research centre. Their position paper sets out what people with personal experience of mental illness bring to research. It also asks what blocks their real influence. The paper grew out of facilitated workshops where board members, a survivor researcher, and support staff pooled their experience of involvement work in universities and charities.

Six themes structure their advice. They cover defining lived experience, moving from one voice to research impact, and naming the value added. They also cover respecting different kinds of knowledge, confronting power gaps, and hearing what organisations must change. Token involvement, they argue, wastes a resource that can sharpen questions, methods, and the meaning of results.
pmc-13424500:
Sumina Shrestha and three colleagues survey 1,202 Australian adults on death literacy, the knowledge and skills that help people navigate dying, care, and grief, asking whether two recent upheavals shifted it. The COVID-19 pandemic and the arrival of voluntary assisted dying laws both changed how Australians encounter death, and the team tested whether those exposures relate to literacy scores on a standard index.

The sample was drawn from a national online panel balanced by age, gender, and region. Regression models adjusted for background factors, and mediation analysis probed whether the two events carried the influence of social capital, attitudes, and supportive behaviour into literacy outcomes. The study frames death literacy as something societies, not just individuals, build.
pmc-13424800:
Lu and colleagues measure in 2026 how much facial angiofibroma, the small red growths on the face caused by tuberous sclerosis complex, lowers quality of life. No one had previously converted that burden into a health utility, the number economists use to value health states.

Interviewers asked 100 dermatology patients to imagine living with almost-clear and with moderate facial growths, alongside blindness in one or both eyes for comparison, and valued each state three ways. Moderate growths scored clearly worse than almost-clear ones on every method. On average, participants said they would give up about 12 percent of their remaining life to be cured of moderate growths. That meant roughly seven of 57 years, or accepting a nine percent risk of immediate death. The authors argue that shrinking these growths can deliver real quality-of-life gains.
pmc-13425100:
Greta M. Massetti, Ghenet Besera, Laura Chiang, and Sherri Pals report 2026 survey findings on workers separated from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Since January 2025 the agency lost more than a quarter of its workforce through layoffs, contract cancellations, and fellowship endings. The CDC WISE Survey gathered answers from 430 former employees, contractors, and fellows.

Respondents together held over 7,300 years of public health experience, nearly 80 percent left involuntarily, and more than half were still unemployed when surveyed. Three quarters faced financial barriers to health care, while sleep problems and psychological distress were widespread across career stages.
pmc-13425600:
Lukas H. A. Edwards and Isabel M. Smallegange tested what prompts dispersal in the bulb mite Rhizoglyphus robini in a 2026 multigenerational experiment. Mites can develop a phoretic form that hitches rides to new patches, and food spread within the home patch may signal competition. Populations lived under patchy, uniform, or intermediate food layouts at low or high density maintained by culling.

Tracking dispersal form expression across generations separated effects of local food heterogeneity from density itself. Evolutionary ecologists gain experimental evidence that conditions inside the source habitat, not only differences between habitats, shape movement decisions. The work shows how food spread in a small space can push a whole group to roam, rest, feed, or stay put in new ways.
pmc-13426200:
Yuko Makihara and colleagues report a spinal epidural angiolipoma of the vascular-predominant type in a 2026 case study. An 80-year-old man developed progressive gait instability from a thoracic epidural mass. MRI showed a rim of fatty tissue around a strongly enhancing vascular center, with growth into the right intervertebral opening.

Surgeons removed the tumor, and pathology confirmed angiolipoma, a benign growth mixing mature fat with small vessels. Seeing both fat and vascular parts on preoperative imaging is presented as the key clue for diagnosis and for planning the operation. The mass sat in the spine of a man of four score years, and its slow growth gave him time to seek care while he could still walk with some ease.
pmc-13426500:
Akkari and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on banana waste as a water cleaner. Banana peels and stems are cheap, common farm leftovers in many lands. Ground and treated, they can trap drug residues that slip through water plants. The review gathers how these materials are made and how well they work.

The authors walk through soak tests that measure speed, capacity, and heat effects. They also weigh how often the materials can be rinsed and reused. Banana-based traps rival costlier options for several common drug pollutants in studies. Gaps remain on real wastewater mixes and large-scale plant trials, they note. Their map of open questions sets an agenda for greener cleanup work. Turning waste into a useful product also cuts disposal costs for farmers.
pmc-13426900:
Çiftci and colleagues reported in 2026 on the best timing for a hormone test in children. The test checks for a mild form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a gland disorder caused by low levels of one enzyme. Doctors use the Synacthen test, which prompts the adrenal glands to make hormones. They then measure a hormone called 17-hydroxyprogesterone in the blood. The team asked whether a sample at 30 minutes is as useful as one at 60 minutes.

Çiftci reviewed records for 150 patients aged up to 18 years tested between 2000 and 2024. Twenty-nine patients reached the diagnostic level, and three looked normal at 30 minutes but showed the clear result at 60 minutes. No case was found early that was missed later, so the later sample caught every case. The V281L gene variant was the most common cause found.
pmc-13427100:
Shira Gertsman and coauthors discuss pregnancy in a young woman with bipolar disorder in a 2026 clinical review built around a case. Their patient was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder at twenty-five during a mixed episode. She switched from quetiapine to lithium at twenty-seven after another episode. She has stayed stable for three years on lithium, with a level in the therapeutic range. The article asks what risks bipolar disorder brings in the perinatal period.

Complications span preterm birth, gestational hypertension, low birth weight, small head size, and congenital malformations, driven by mixed factors including smoking, cannabis use, obesity, and disrupted prenatal care. Balanced medication decisions weigh relapse risk against fetal exposure.
pmc-13427400:
M. Cruellas and a large multicenter group examined whether inherited BRCA2 damage changes outcomes on first-line CDK4/6 inhibitors plus hormone therapy in metastatic breast cancer in a 2026 study. Three such inhibitors are approved with endocrine therapy for hormone receptor positive, HER2-negative metastatic disease. Whether homologous recombination repair gene variants, including BRCA2, alter benefit from this standard combination was uncertain.

Tracking outcomes by variant status could reveal a subgroup needing different first-line strategy, such as earlier use of PARP-directed approaches. Genomic stratification of a widely used regimen matters for thousands of patients starting metastatic treatment each year. Most sick women start this pair of drugs at once, so a gene test that flags who gains less could change the first plan of care for them.
pmc-13427600:
Hisato Takagi writes, in a 2026 letter, about an extremely rare pattern in the great artery arch above the heart. Normally three branches leave the arch. In the avian-type pattern, named for its likeness to birds, only two shared trunks appear: one for both neck arteries and one for both arm arteries. Takagi pulls together every published case and the larger anatomy studies since the year 2000.

Pooling those studies puts the pattern at about two people in every 10,000, a figure he offers as a sharper estimate. In two reported patients an arm artery passed behind the food pipe, forming a full ring, yet caused no symptoms. No case showed a spontaneous tear of the artery wall. Clinicians who spot this variant on scans gain a calm summary of what is actually known.
pmc-13427800:
Christina Høstmælingen and co-authors review, in a 2026 study, slipped discs in teenagers treated at one center over ten years. Lumbar disc herniation is rare under age 18 and can look unusual, so referral often comes late. Records covered 21 patients who had a small disc operation between 2015 and 2025. The average age was about 15, and every patient had low back pain.

The typical wait from first symptoms to an MRI scan was six months, and to surgery a full year. Most operations involved a single disc level low in the back. Three months after surgery, nearly all patients reported better back pain, and all had relief of leg symptoms. Good results despite long delays may reflect young bodies healing well, though the group is small and follow-up short.
pmc-13428000:
Daniel Pinggera and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether a second MRI scan soon after severe head injury adds anything. Brain MRI refines what doctors know about injury patterns and outlook, yet patients are often scanned twice in the first two weeks. The team studied 17 adults with severe injuries who had both an early scan within three days and another near day 12 to 14. Three specialists rated the scan pairs without knowing which came first.

In about 71 percent of cases the two scans were judged equally useful. Lesion counts overlapped heavily across all scan types, with no steady gain at the later time point. Monitor wires caused frequent image artifacts but rarely blocked reading. The authors advise timing scans to the clinical question rather than repeating them by routine.
pmc-13429100:
Natalie Ong and co-authors evaluate the Motivated for Change programme, a training and quality improvement effort in a paediatric emergency department. Their 2026 mixed methods study asks whether the programme helps staff give safer, better-adjusted care to children and young people who have intellectual or developmental disabilities.

The programme combined behaviour change, adult learning, and quality improvement methods. The team surveyed 131 staff before and 89 after the programme, interviewed parents, and observed care in the department in both phases. Staff knowledge, skills, and experience in providing reasonable adjustments rose significantly after the programme. Parents' accounts and observations also showed practice changes, and staff went on to start their own improvement projects and an in-house training programme for new staff.
pmc-13429900:
Lázaro Antonio Campanha Novaes and colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, a Brazilian biobank built to fix the ancestry gap in cancer genetics. Genome-wide studies have mapped cancer risk variants mostly in Europeans, who supply over 90 percent of participants. Risk scores trained on them can misfire in Brazil's highly mixed population. The repository focuses on colorectal, breast, and cervical cancers, enrolling both patients and cancer-free controls.

Enrollment reached 4,062 people from every Brazilian state, yielding nearly 40,000 blood-derived specimens in storage. Genetic typing is complete for 2,844 participants so far. Ancestry analysis confirms the expected blend, led by European roots with African, Native American, and Asian shares. The resource will let researchers retest known associations and recalibrate risk scores for admixed populations, a step toward fairer precision medicine.
pmc-13430000:
José Ferrer Costa and colleagues built a decision tool to help health services judge whether to adopt extended reality, meaning virtual and mixed reality systems, in daily care. Their 2026 framework turns known adoption factors into a structured check that managers run before spending money.

The team first set draft criteria from theory and past studies, then refined them with 33 stakeholders from hospitals, primary care, and universities. The final tool holds ten criteria in three groups, covering human, organisational, and technical concerns. Each criterion gets two scores, one for importance and one for readiness, so gaps stand out clearly. Safety and comfort scored highest for importance, while fitting tools into daily workflow scored lowest and needs most work.
pmc-13430200:
Yijun Wang and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a pomegranate compound against age-related bone loss. Senile osteoporosis thins bones as marrow stem cells age and lose their bone-building drive. Punicalagin, an antioxidant from pomegranate peel, was applied to stem cells aged artificially with peroxide in the lab. Standard aging stains, protein checks, and bone-formation assays tracked the response. Aging rats with the disease then received injections to test the effect in a living body.

The compound reversed aging signs in the stem cells and restored their bone-building activity in a dose-dependent way. Gene sequencing traced the action to a protective pathway that switches on antioxidant defenses. Treated rats formed more bone and lost less to aging than untreated ones. Many osteoporosis drugs slow loss without rebuilding, so a stem-cell rejuvenator would fill a real gap if human studies follow.
pmc-13430300:
Danfeng Shen and Hongxing Xu published a letter in 2026 that questions a study of how food changes the way the body handles bersiporocin, a drug for lung scarring. The writers accept that meal timing was described with care. They argue that key flaws in method and in reading of the results weaken the claim that food has no real effect.

One concern centers on peak blood levels. Total exposure stayed inside the usual range, yet peak levels fell sharply after meals, and the letter notes that regulators treat peak level and total exposure as equally important. A second concern targets the proposed reason for more gut side effects soon after eating. The writers call that reason hard to square with slower peak times, and they offer delayed stomach emptying as a better fit.
pmc-13432000:
Cuestas, writing in Spanish, looks at how mental models are built and reshaped during medical training. Mental models are the maps doctors use to picture how the body works. He gives special attention to cardiovascular physiology. Unlike memorizing facts, a mental model lets a doctor predict what a hemorrhage will do to blood pressure. It also helps explain breathlessness in worsening heart failure.

Robust models keep working when cases vary. Fragile ones collapse outside known conditions, a split Cuestas applies to students' grasp of body processes. Knowledge does not pile up with training, he argues. It gets rebuilt, with basic-science groups giving way to shapes in the final years and early practice. Next to physics, where deep grasp has been probed through interviews and problem-solving tasks, basic medicine has had little probing. The piece targets final-year students and new doctors at that settling-in stage.
pmc-13432900:
Felix Schöpf, Gian Luca Marongiu, and Daniel Roderer reviewed in 2026 how grip proteins on a mouth germ help drive bowel cancer, with fresh sharp structures of those grips in hand. The germ turns up often in the bowel crowds of bowel cancer patients. Far from a bystander, it spurs tumor growth, spread, and immune dodge through grips on its outer skin.

Each grip locks onto a host port on tumor or immune cells, which fires chains that free cell growth or mute immune guards. For three grips, host ports have been known for years, and fresh structures now show the lock in fine detail. Two more grips have only just won named ports, or still lack one, so their moves stay dim. The review weighs each grip's share in the cancer's march.
pmc-13434600:
Qi Liu and coauthors report a catalyst that gets better as it works in 2026. The target products are Schiff bases frozen in a twisted shape, a class that had resisted clean making. A palladium catalyst joins two parts with strong control of the twist.

Starting amines trade places on the catalyst and reshape it into a faster form. As the trade goes on, purity of the twist climbs with time, up to 96 percent. Yields reach 83 percent with full control of one bond shape. Computer models and bench tests agree on the path. Self tuning catalysts may suit other hard reactions.
pmc-13436100:
Judith Tanner and colleagues interviewed heart surgery patients and hospital staff in England about using artificial intelligence to watch surgical wounds heal. The interviews sat inside a trial of digital wound monitoring, where patients send wound images for review instead of travelling in.

Twenty patients and ten staff took part across two hospitals that perform heart surgery. Both groups backed the tool, saying it should improve safety, widen access, and speed up care. They also expected it to catch wound problems early and let monitoring cover every patient at scale. Some worried about data security, staff leaning too hard on the software, and losing human contact, concerns Tanner says wider testing must answer.
pmc-13437200:
Su Min Ha, Inyoung Youn, and Jung Min Chang answer a letter about their work on automated breast ultrasound for women with dense breasts. In the 2026 response, they clarify that their aim went beyond finding more cancers. They tested whether the automated scan, paired with mammography and an artificial intelligence reading aid, could make screening work faster and lighter for busy radiologists.

Their plan let clear cases skip human review: women with a negative mammogram and a negative AI-guided scan would need no extra reading. Radiologists could then focus on scans the AI flagged or mammograms raised doubts about. The authors grant that their study held few cancers and that false alarms must stay low for the plan to be safe. Larger screening groups should compare reading every scan against the selective plan, they say, and future work might automate both imaging steps together.
pmc-13437300:
Xiang Li and colleagues examine a gene called UAP1 as a warning marker and possible drug target in multiple myeloma, a plasma cell cancer of the marrow. The gene helps build sugar-coated proteins, and it fuels growth in several other cancers. Their 2026 study mined six data sets covering 3,117 patients, plus single-cell readings and tests in two myeloma cell lines.

Patients whose tumors made more UAP1 died sooner and relapsed faster on every survival measure the team used. Single-cell data placed UAP1 mainly inside tumor cells, tied to how far those cells had matured and to signals that mute the immune system. In the lab, switching the gene off slowed cell growth, pushed cells toward death, and made them more sensitive to a standard steroid drug. The authors present UAP1 as a sign of worse outlook and a lever future treatments might pull.
pmc-13437400:
Cemre Cukaci, Ulrich Rabl, and Richard Frey ran a small pilot trial of a ketogenic diet for treatment-resistant depression. The very low carbohydrate diet forces the body to burn fat, and early hints suggested mood benefits. Thirteen eligible patients were offered a place in late 2023; five declined, eight joined, and only four finished the six weeks. Daily finger-prick tests checked whether each person stayed in the fat-burning state.

All four finishers reached that state, and three improved markedly, with two meeting full remission marks on a standard depression scale. Others left early: one quit at week two, one after a changed diagnosis, and two could not reach the target state. The authors call the diet workable for a subset of patients and the early signals worth chasing. Recruitment and dropout were hard enough that only larger, controlled trials can judge the approach fairly.
pmc-13437500:
Yuanshuang Jiang, Jing Kang, and Yan Chen linked wearable glucose readings with early kidney damage in young people with type 2 diabetes. Cases found before forty tends to run a harsher course, and kidney injury can start silently. Their 2026 study covered 810 Chinese patients who wore a glucose sensor for a week. Early kidney disease meant protein leaking into urine while filtering power still held.

About twenty-three percent met that definition. The more time a patient spent in the target sugar range, the lower their odds of kidney damage, even after standard measures were weighed. Sugar swing showed a U-shaped tie, risk lowest in a middle band. Blood fats called triglycerides carried a small share of both links, hinting fat handling travels with sugar control. The authors advise a three-part guard: steady sugar, time in range, and lipid care together, not glucose alone.
pmc-13438400:
Jiacheng Shen and colleagues tested a lab-made single allergen against the crude pollen extract now used to retrain the immune systems of people allergic to Artemisia. Their 2026 study worked in female mice made asthmatic with mugwort pollen. Groups received the standard extract, the recombinant allergen Art an 3, or a dummy treatment. The team then read airway sensitivity, lung tissue, wash fluid, blood antibodies, and immune cell mixes.

The extract edged ahead on tissue healing and cut allergy-linked cells and antibodies more clearly. The single allergen answered with a different signature: it raised calming signals and grew more regulatory and helper T cells of the protective kind, plus more blocking antibody. The authors judge the defined molecule roughly the extract's equal in protection, with a tidier, more standardizable makeup. That profile makes Art an 3 a serious candidate for the next generation of allergy shots, pending human trials.
pmc-13439300:
Ji Yong Ahn presents a 2026 quiz case of a stomach illness first read as cancer. A 45-year-old woman arrived at a large hospital after a month of upper belly pain and heartburn that acid pills had not eased. Scopes at her first clinic showed a mass-like ulcer spreading across the stomach, extra raised yellowish spots, and swollen nearby glands. Biopsies, though, showed only inflamed tissue and heavy long-term gastritis, with no cancer cells.

Repeat scopes and deeper tissue study at the referral centre pointed to gastric syphilis, a rare stomach form of the widespread infection. Dense plasma-cell inflammation fits that picture, and staining for the syphilis germ settles the question. Penicillin, the standard cure, usually brings fast relief in body and scope views alike. Ahn urges doctors to keep the infection in mind when stomach lesions look malignant but tissue tests stay inconclusive.
pmc-13440700:
Manat Singh Chopra and colleagues describe emergency brain surgery for a bleeding metastasis from testicular cancer, reporting a 2026 case. Choriocarcinoma, an aggressive germ cell tumour, spreads through blood and bleeds easily in the brain. Their patient, a 22-year-old man with repeated recurrences, arrived with fresh bleeding in the right frontal lobe. He had already survived earlier operations for brain deposits.

Surgeons opened the skull and removed tumour and clot using a novel suction device carrying its own camera, easing work in a narrow field. Tissue study confirmed metastatic choriocarcinoma matching his history. Chemotherapy resumed after surgery, with radiation aimed at the emptied cavity. Disease still advanced quickly afterward. The authors present the camera-suction tool as a practical aid for resecting deep, bleeding tumours, while stressing the grim outlook these deposits carry.
pmc-13441500:
Hidehito Sumiya and colleagues report the first known case of a bile duct stent knocked loose while placing a duodenal stent, publishing in 2026. Their patient, an 81-year-old woman with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, already carried a covered metal biliary stent for drainage. A malignant narrowing then blocked her duodenum, and a second stent was planned. The scope could pass only partway, so the delivery system advanced over a guidewire.

The wire apparently threaded the mesh at the biliary stent's lower end and dragged it downward into the duodenum. The team withdrew the delivery system without deploying, avoiding trapped or clashing stents. Since the bile duct opening could not be seen, they cannulated under X-ray guidance with a novel rotatable cutting tool and placed a plastic stent. The duodenal stent then followed successfully, and the case is presented as an endoscopically rescued first.
pmc-13441900:
Qian and a large IMAGEN consortium mined blood multi-omics from 1,274 healthy teens. They hunted molecular drivers shared across mental disorders, using genetic variants as anchors to argue cause. They mapped variants that set DNA methylation and gene expression, and checked them in outside data. Then they ran Mendelian randomization across six disorders, from ADHD to schizophrenia and insomnia.

The analysis named 73 potentially causal methylation sites and 62 genes. Some were tied to one disorder, and some were shared across the panel. Found genes grouped in pathways tied to both psychiatric and autoimmune disease. That backs a shared genomic structure between the two domains. Two-step tests showed expression of three genes, MAD1L1, MRPL2, and HLA-DRB1, carrying methylation effects on schizophrenia and insomnia in the modeled pathways. One methylation site turned down MRPL2, which looked causal for insomnia. That shows a concrete transdiagnostic chain.
pmc-13442000:
Heegwang Roh and colleagues rebuild tetanus toxin into a light-switchable synapse silencer, reporting in 2026. The toxin's cutting chain normally snips VAMP2, a protein synapses need to release cargo, and it never switches off. The team threaded a light-sensing domain into a control site and tuned the design through directed evolution. The result, named LATeNT, sat idle in darkness and woke after ten to twenty minutes of weak blue light.

Lit tissue showed potent silencing across several brain regions and along long-range projections, with recovery inside a day. The switch let the team unmask a hippocampal interneuron group governing anxiety-like behaviour and prove a point about local cannabis-like signalling. Beyond the brain, the tool governed insulin release from pancreatic cells and turned chemical signals into gene output in cultured cells. The authors offer it as a general inducible proteolysis platform.
pmc-13443200:
Ashraf Ezzat Attia reports a blood swap rescue for a man with sickle cell disease after heart arrest in a 2026 case paper. The patient was 37 years old, with the HbSS gene type plus a G6PD lack. A pain crisis slid into two heart arrests, shock on four pressor drugs, and lung failure with organ harm.

A heart-lung machine was weighed, then set aside for a twin swap plan: red cell swaps plus daily plasma swaps. Seven rounds cut his sickle hemoglobin share from 73 percent down to 18 percent by the end. Pressor needs fell within a day and ended by day eight. He came off the breather on day ten and left intensive care on day fourteen, with no brain harm found.
pmc-13443600:
Yanjuan Wang and colleagues read nano-scale mineral guests inside a fluid-rich diamond from South Africa in a 2026 study. Cloudy diamonds hold swarms of tiny fluid pockets that hint at how diamonds form deep down. The guests are so small that their build and birth terms stayed out of reach.

A micro electron beam named one guest as åkermanite and refined its structure, while twin guests proved to be barium-strontium carbonates. Heat-ray checks showed a gem-grade core ringed by a rim rich in dense fluid pockets. Pressure loss during the diamond's rise likely grew the åkermanite from that fluid. Birth terms point to at least 1,000 degrees at about 140 km depth. The fluid marks read as low-magnesium carbonate to silicate mixes.
pmc-13443800:
Deming Li and colleagues strip oxygen from storage air with an electric cell in a 2026 paper. Deep oxygen cuts guard food and drugs from spoilage, yet nitrogen flushing eats power to hold its gradient. Cold chains feel that cost most, since chill bills already rule their budgets.

Their cell moves oxygen out by pairing oxygen intake on one face with oxygen release on the twin face. The path wastes less order than pressure-swing gear, so it runs nearer the physics floor. Paired with mild chill and low oxygen, total energy fell by about 36 percent against standard cold runs, while food quality held or rose. The authors frame the cell as a scalable swap for flush systems in storage and transport.
pmc-13446300:
Joshua Bruinsma and colleagues review bleeding from swollen veins around a bowel stoma, a rare but dangerous problem in patients with high pressure in the portal vein, in a 2026 case-based paper. Their case involves an adult with liver cancer that had spread. Proof for best care is thin, so the team joined past reports with their own center's practice.

Options span drugs that ease portal pressure, local pressure and stitch measures, vessel blocking by catheter, a shunt that reroutes portal flow, and surgery to move the stoma. None worked for all, and each carried its own return-bleed risk. The authors urge stepwise, team-based care tuned to bleed severity, liver reserve, other illness, outlook, and anatomy, with the patient's own goals in the frame.
pmc-13446900:
Sue Han and colleagues use super-fine microscopy to watch single virus particles dock on human cells, and they report a revised entry story for the COVID-19 virus, in a 2026 study. The ACE2 protein was long cast as the doorway handle for attachment and entry. Their images point instead at heparan sulfate, a sugary coat on the cell surface.

The virus grips clusters of some six to over a hundred heparan sulfate strands that rise well above the surface, about one cluster per wide patch of membrane. Those clusters haul the virus inside, while ACE2 acts later to let the genome speak. A cancer drug that binds heparan sulfate blocked the Omicron JN.1 form from infecting human airway cells, which names the grip a drug target.
pmc-13447000:
Cherechi Nwabueze and colleagues review hepatitis B in the vaccine era, arguing that liver care must own prevention, in a 2026 narrative paper. The virus still drives much of the world's cirrhosis and liver cancer, with over two hundred fifty million people living with chronic infection. Catching it at birth carries the highest risk of that grim path, which makes early shots vital.

The vaccine was the first ever shown to prevent a cancer, and full courses protect nearly all young recipients for decades. Yet series completion lags in many places, and the bill arrives years later as failing livers and tumors. The authors trace how policy and delivery gaps feed clinic wards, and they urge gut and liver doctors to push coverage as core work.
pmc-13447200:
Chang Sun and co-authors combine exercise with a drug in mouse work on Alzheimer's-like disease published in 2026. A key enzyme that helps recycle a vital cell fuel called NAD+ sat in the wrong cell types in these mice, low in neurons yet high in immune brain cells. Blocking the enzyme alone might calm inflammation while starving cells of energy.

Six-month-old mice with amyloid build-up showed memory loss, brain inflammation and damaged cell power units. The blocker drug alone helped little over twelve weeks. Treadmill exercise improved memory, lowered amyloid and protected cell power units, even when the enzyme was blocked. Adding the drug to exercise improved some measures further, which the authors link to backup fuel pathways and lower fuel waste.
pmc-13447300:

pmc-13476300:

pmc-13476900:

pmc-13477100:

pmc-13477400:

pmc-13478600:

pmc-13479700:
Cuo Yi and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of ultrasound-based prediction models for judging breast cancer response to chemotherapy given before surgery. pmc-13479900:

pmc-13480100:
Zhou Ye and colleagues present a 2026 study of severe belly infection after a hole forms in the gut. They weighed lab values, illness scores, timing of care, and germ types to find what drives outcome.

pmc-13480200:
Xiao Zhu and co-authors report a 2026 survey of emergency medical workers in China and the forces that shape pride in their role. Staff rated how much support they felt from their workplace, how they handled feelings on the job, and how strongly they identified with their profession.

pmc-13480600:

pmc-13482100:

pmc-13482600:

pmc-13483600:

pmc-13483700:

pmc-13488200:

pmc-13493400:

pmc-13493800:

pmc-13494100:

pmc-13495200:

pmc-13495800:

pmc-13495900:

pmc-13499600:

pmc-13501700:

pmc-13501800:

pmc-13503800:

pmc-13505100:

pmc-13507200:

pmc-13507300:

pmc-13508300:

pmc-13508800:

pmc-13509500:

pmc-13511200:

pmc-13512900:

pmc-13514800:

pmc-13515100:

pmc-13515500:

pmc-13516000:

pmc-13517800:

pmc-13518300:

pmc-13518900:

pmc-13519000:

pmc-13520300:

pmc-13520400:

pmc-13520500:

pmc-13520900:

pmc-13521900:

pmc-13522300:

pmc-13522500:

pmc-13522700:

Mixed trial results for native T1 as a predictor of death are discussed. The authors weigh differing patient groups and measurement methods across studies. Their own study excluded several heart conditions, which shapes how the findings should be read alongside other work.
pmc-13522800:

pmc-13523200:

pmc-13523300:

pmc-13524100:

pmc-13524900:

pmc-13525200:

pmc-13528000:

pmc-13529400:

pmc-13529800:

pmc-13531800:

pmc-13534700:

pmc-13536600:

pmc-13536800:

pmc-13538500:

pmc-13538700:

pmc-13540200:

pmc-13540900:

pmc-13542100:

pmc-13543100:

pmc-13545200:

pmc-13547200:

pmc-13548600:

pmc-13550300:

pmc-13550600:

pmc-13551700:

pmc-13551900:

pmc-13554000:

pmc-13554200:

pmc-13555100:

pmc-13556000:

pmc-13556100:

pmc-13557500:

pmc-13558300:

pmc-13558500:

pmc-13559700:

pmc-13561700:

pmc-13562300:
Peter Muris and four colleagues frame a puzzle of autistic social life in this 2026 narrative review. Chosen solitude restores, while forced isolation wounds, and the review keeps the two experiences apart.

pmc-13562500:
Qi Gong and Jing Shi propose an artificial intelligence framework that tailors university teaching to each student and forecasts grades early. pmc-13562600:
Mukesh Khandla and eight colleagues tune a catalyst that turns carbon dioxide back into carbon monoxide, a building block for fuels and chemicals. pmc-13562700:

pmc-13566400:
Eduard Shantsila leads a 2026 analysis of UK Biobank data from nearly half a million adults. pmc-13568400:

pmc-13572500:

pmc-13575200:
Mary Dixon leads a 2026 study comparing a wild tomato with a modern variety and their effects on soil phosphorus. Fertiliser phosphorus often locks into soil in forms plants cannot use. Wild plants, which evolved with nutrient pulses, may handle this lock-up differently from bred crops.

The wild tomato kept growing and fostered helpful soil bacteria that free up phosphorus, leaving more usable phosphorus in soil across its growth. Chemicals leaking from its roots, rich in trehalose and glycerol compounds, drove the effect in lab tests. Modern tomato grew fast, lacked those bacteria, and drained soil phosphorus. Modern plants later grown in wild-conditioned soil gained more biomass. The authors suggest the wild strategy could cut fertiliser waste in farming.
pmc-13576100:

pmc-13576700:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study of a stiff-knee complication after knee replacement, treated with radiation before revision surgery. pmc-13578700:
Vivekamanickam Koothan Venkateswaran and colleagues simulate gas squeezing through a cone shaped nozzle at low pressure, in a 2026 study. At the narrow throat the flow can choke, hitting the speed of sound so that downstream pressure no longer matters. Tiny nozzles on spacecraft and lab gear work where gas grows thin and starts to slip along walls, which bends the simple rules.

Three wall treatments were compared in the models, from sticky walls to full slip to no friction at all. At high pressure ratios all three agreed closely. As pressure fell the slip model let about three percent more gas through than the sticky wall model, thanks to lower drag. The authors warn that one line formulas miss these shifts in micro nozzles.
pmc-13579800:
Praveen Bathini and colleagues trace how Alzheimer's antibody drugs can trigger brain swelling and tiny bleeds, in a 2026 mouse study. pmc-13583200:

pmc-13584600:
Zélie Bouveret and colleagues review how small chemical edits steer the glucocorticoid receptor in this 2026 paper. The receptor is a switch inside nearly every cell that responds to steroid hormones and controls inflammation, immunity, and metabolism. Drugs that hit it are among the most prescribed in the world, used for allergies, skin disease, joint disease, and eye problems.

pmc-13588700:

They also resisted a virulent bacterial challenge better than sanitized mice, and the authors argue the simple method can spread the natural-microbiota model across institutions.
pmc-13592300:

pmc-13592500:

pmc-13595500:

pmc-13595900:

pmc-13599600:

pmc-13611400:

pmc-13612200:

pmc-13615100:

pmc-13619700:

pmc-13620200:

pmc-13620400:

pmc-13621400:

pmc-13622600:

pmc-13623200:

pmc-13623300:

pmc-13623500:

pmc-13624700:

pmc-13629100:

pmc-13630500:

pmc-13633900:

pmc-13634300:

pmc-13635600:
