The tumor cells lost HLA-I, a surface tag that shows cell contents to killer T cells, and fewer of those T cells were inside the tumor. In lab models, the immune signal IFN-gamma restored the missing tag in one model, but not in one carrying a broken JAK1 gene. Injecting the signal into tumors in mice also restored it, which supports pairing it with immune checkpoint drugs.
pmc-13637100:
Haolu Shu and three colleagues published this 2026 survey of daily habits among children in a rural region of southern Japan. Sleep, outdoor play, and screen time shape child health, yet few studies follow all three across childhood in one community. The team collected questionnaire data on nearly twelve hundred children from ten schools, spanning toddlers to junior high students. Parents reported for the youngest, and older children answered for themselves.

Sleep fell short of recommendations at every stage and shrank steadily with age, driven by later bedtimes rather than earlier waking. Screen time climbed to nearly four times its toddler level by junior high. Outdoor play, oddly, rose with age here, though it stayed under an hour daily even for the oldest. The authors argue these habits lock in early and harden over time. They call for health strategies starting in early childhood and growing with the child.
pmc-13637400:
Yan-Lin Wei and five colleagues published this 2026 study probing a puzzling dry eye pattern in a Beijing community cohort. Dry eye disease brings burning, grittiness, and blurred vision as the tear film fails. Eight hundred thirteen adults aged forty-five and over received eye surface measurements and detailed questionnaires. In raw numbers, current smokers showed lower odds of dry eye than non-smokers, a result that might tempt a protective reading.

Careful adjustment erased that apparent benefit entirely. Drinking showed no independent link either. Objective measures pulled in opposite directions at once: smokers and drinkers kept a stable tear film slightly longer, yet showed more loss of the oil glands that protect tears. The authors warn firmly against reading smoking or alcohol as protective. They argue that single flattering measures mislead, and that full eye surface assessment plus standard advice on quitting and moderation should stand.
pmc-13639600:
Jason M Nagata and nine colleagues present an overview of systematic reviews on troubled gaming habits and gaming disorder in teens and young adults. Problem gaming is now treated as a youth health concern, yet findings sit spread across many separate reviews.

The team screened reviews from three databases and kept fifty-one of ninety-eight records. Estimates suggest gaming disorder affects roughly six to ten percent of young people worldwide, with earlier starting age and poorer mental health among the risk factors. Cognitive behavioral therapy carried the strongest treatment evidence, though certainty stayed low to moderate. The authors call for sharper diagnostic rules and proper trials.
pmc-13642100:
Xiaoke Chen and four colleagues present a 2026 optics study on an array of tiny lenses written directly onto the tip of an optical fiber. Putting lenses on fiber ends enables compact probes for imaging, sensing, and handling microscopic objects.

Using a femtosecond laser, the team patterned nineteen graphene oxide microlenses in a film only four hundred nanometers thick on a beam-expanding fiber section. The lenses split and focused light at three common wavelengths used in communications and sensing. The authors describe the single-step fabrication as a scalable route to ultrathin fiber-tip devices for nanophotonics and multi-point sensing.
pmc-13642500:
Wanshou Sun and five colleagues present a 2026 way to reveal hidden stress in silicon chip bases after laser cutting. Stress left in the heat zone can spoil how a chip works. Older tools lack the fine detail or reach to map it well.

Their touch-free method uses weak measurement, a light trick that boosts tiny signals. It reads stress through the way stressed glass-like material bends light. The tool sensed stress below half a kilopascal. It also beat a standard scan method on detail by nearly tenfold. Stress size tracked the laser energy used in a clear way. Chip makers gain a way to watch stress as they work.
pmc-13644000:
Qian Zhao and eight colleagues present a 2026 telomere-to-telomere genome assembly of Metarhizium acridum, a fungus used worldwide to kill locusts without chemicals. Its narrow host choice makes it safe for other life, but the genetic basis of that specialism was murky.

The gap-free assembly covers seven chromosomes totaling about forty-five million bases, the most complete genome yet for its genus, with 11,623 predicted genes. Comparisons with broader-host relatives showed frequent chromosome reshuffling. One toxin gene switched on about ten times more strongly during locust infection, and its activated product lowered host survival. The authors offer the genome as a foundation for better biocontrol.
pmc-13645800:
Louise Birkedal Glenthøj and nine colleagues ask, in a 2026 analysis, whether virtual reality avatar therapy for hearing voices works by improving emotion control. The therapy lets patients confront a digital figure that speaks like their distressing voices. The team reanalyzed a randomized trial of 270 people with persistent voices in psychosis. One group received seven immersive therapy sessions, while the other received standard care plus extra supportive counseling.

Therapy did not measurably change two self-reported emotion strategies, rethinking a situation or holding feelings in. People who rethought more at follow-up did report milder voices, yet that pattern did not explain the therapy's benefit in the statistical tests. The authors conclude the gains likely come from what happens inside the sessions themselves, during direct encounters with the voice figure. Their result steers future research toward those in-session processes rather than broad emotion habits.
pmc-13647100:
Alison L. Calear and nine colleagues run a randomized trial of a web guide that trains parents to act as gatekeepers for their children's mental health, in a 2026 study. Parents often spot distress first yet lack confidence to respond. The Australian trial enrolled 509 parents of children aged five to seventeen, nearly all of them mothers. Half received the guide, and outcomes were measured right after and again at twelve weeks.

Parents given the guide reported stronger confidence in recognizing problems and finding help, for both mental health and suicide risk. Perceived knowledge rose, barriers to seeking help fell, and suicide-related stigma and literacy improved. General mental health literacy and attitudes toward seeking help did not move. Some gains held at twelve weeks. The authors say parent-focused gatekeeper training works, while better engagement with web resources remains the next challenge.
pmc-13647600:
Ryosuke Ikemachi and sixteen colleagues characterize a rare nerve-sheath tumor growing inside a young woman's brainstem, in a 2026 case study. Schwannomas inside the brain tissue itself are rare and usually lack the gene loss that marks their common cousins. The twenty-four-year-old patient arrived with dizziness and facial weakness, and surgery removed the tumor. Tissue appearance fit a schwannoma, so the team layered molecular tests on top.

DNA pattern profiling placed the tumor in an emerging family defined by fusions involving the VGLL gene clan. Gene sequencing found the two halves joined as EWSR1 and VGLL1, with the second gene switched on far above levels in ordinary vestibular tumors. Chromosome checks showed a loss pattern unlike the classic one. The authors say the case strengthens the new molecular subtype and shows why brain tumor diagnosis now needs molecular and tissue evidence read together.
pmc-13649500:
Mavis Puopelle Dakorah and five colleagues mapped gene changes tied to malaria drug resistance across communities in Ghana's Central Region. Resistance to the main drug family would threaten hard-won gains against malaria. The team sequenced blood samples from 358 people and read one key gene in the malaria parasite.

The normal form of the gene still ruled in most places, but mutant forms were rich and varied. More than a hundred samples carried one change, dozens carried two, and a few carried three or four. Neither season nor broad land zone explained the pattern, yet the home district did. Known strong resistance markers stayed rare. The authors urge fine-grained watch work to catch spread early.
pmc-13649700:
Hanbin Wu and three colleagues asked if the timing of folic acid use in early pregnancy links to learning trouble in young children. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy is proven to block spine defects, but its tie to later school skills is less clear. The team used a Dutch birth cohort with 3,216 children aged four to seven.

Most mothers had begun the vitamin before conception, while the rest began in the first three months. Late starts showed no link to poor focus, reading trouble, or trouble keeping up at school. One soft link did appear: late starts tied to more parent reports of trouble with sums. The authors warn that memory-based reports and hidden factors bar any claim of cause.
pmc-13650000:
Wei Shan and four colleagues examine why many people with diabetic foot ulcers reach proper care late. An ulcer is a wound on the foot caused by diabetes, and delays raise the risk of severe disease and amputation. The team studied what patients did first, where they got health information, and what worries held them back.

A single hospital followed 400 adults, joined by interviews with 16 participants. Over half arrived late, and over half had relied on non-professional information. Starting with non-specialist care or home remedies tracked strongly with delay, and delay in turn tracked with worse wounds and more amputations. Among patients who lost a limb, worry about who would support daily life often slowed the decision itself. Interviews pointed to lowered urgency, competing advice, and self-treatment, and the authors call for clearer warning-sign teaching and decision support.
pmc-13650300:
Na Luo and three colleagues review the ion channels that sit in the membrane of lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, and their growing role in cancer treatment resistance. These channels keep the compartment's acidity, calcium, and voltage in balance, and when they go wrong they can help tumors grow, spread, and survive therapy.

The review first explains the structure and normal job of the major channels, then traces how their failure supports resistance to chemotherapy, radiation, and immune therapy. Channels shape the tissue around tumors, control cell death decisions, and manage the recycling that lets cancer cells endure drug pressure. The authors weigh early strategies for blocking or tuning these channels as add-on treatments, while noting how little is yet proven in patients. Their aim is to mark a target class that drug developers have largely overlooked.
pmc-13651600:
Roberto Listo and thirteen colleagues use a single molecule wired between electrodes as an exquisitely sensitive probe of the electric double layer. That layer is the charged skin that forms wherever an electrode meets a liquid. That layer's structure has been studied for a century and a half, while its moment-to-moment dynamics remain murky.

Under a square-wave voltage, the current through single-molecule junctions answered in three distinct dialects depending on the solvent. Strongly polar solvents produced large nonlinear surges, middling solvents behaved like tidy capacitors, and nonpolar solvents showed no measurable transient at all within the tested frequencies. Fitting the responses to a molecular-scale circuit extracted how each solvent shapes the innermost layer's behavior and where the nonlinearity comes from. The authors say single-molecule devices can now interrogate interfacial dynamics that bulk measurements average away, with relevance to molecular memory and sensing devices.
pmc-2910600:
Holt-Lunstad, Smith, and Layton pool studies on social relationships and the risk of death. Their meta-analytic review asks how strongly a person's ties to others predict survival. Many readers know smoking and similar habits as proven risks, yet social life is rarely ranked beside them.

Across the pooled evidence, they find that social relationships carry about as much influence on mortality risk as those well-established factors. People with stronger ties tend to live longer. The result pushed doctors and health planners to treat loneliness and weak social connection as real health risks.
pmc-4349800:
Saito and Rehmsmeier argued in 2015 that precision-recall plots tell more than ROC plots for some tasks. Binary classifiers sort cases into two groups, and they are often judged by sensitivity and specificity. ROC plots are the usual display for that performance.

When datasets are imbalanced, with far more of one class than the other, ROC plots can look too rosy. Precision-recall plots focus on the rare positive class that users actually care about. The paper shows with examples why the second view is more honest in such cases. Choosing the right plot changes which classifier a team trusts and ships.
pmc-4375400:
Suzek, Wang, Huang, and their colleagues described UniRef clusters in 2014. UniRef groups protein sequences from the UniProt database into clusters of close relatives. Similarity searches run far faster against clusters than against every single sequence.

Recent work improved the clusters by cutting redundancy and keeping each group more uniform inside. Users can pick a cluster level that trades detail for speed. These clusters support tasks such as assigning function to new sequences by resemblance. As sequence databases grow without pause, well built clusters are a key way to keep searches practical and results clear.
pmc-4728800:
Conesa, Madrigal, Tarazona, and their co-authors surveyed best practices for RNA-seq analysis in 2016. RNA sequencing serves a wide variety of applications, from gene activity to new transcripts. No single pipeline fits all cases, the authors stress, so choices must match the question.

The survey reviews every major step, from experimental design and quality control to alignment and counting of genes and transcripts. It gives guidance on the tools and settings at each stage. Good practice at the design stage cannot be rescued later by clever computing. The review became a standard reading for labs starting RNA-seq work.
pmc-5335600:
Daina, Michielin, and Zoete presented SwissADME in 2017, a free web tool for drug candidates. A strong molecule fails as a drug if too little of it reaches its target in the body. It must also stay in an active form long enough for the expected events to occur.

SwissADME evaluates pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness, and medicinal chemistry friendliness of small molecules. It predicts absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion from a compound's structure. Early screening of these traits saves money, since many candidates fail for body-handling reasons, not weak action. A free tool puts that screening within reach of any lab.
pmc-545600:
Gentleman, Carey, Bates, and their colleagues described Bioconductor in 2004. Bioconductor is a joint project in which many groups build and share open, extensible software for computational biology. It grew inside the R statistical environment, which many data analysts already used.

The paper lays out, in detail, what the project aims to do and how it works. Bioconductor set standards for how analysis packages are built, documented, and shared, so tools from different groups work together. Its release cycle and quality checks raised the reliability of research software. The project became the main home of open tools for genomic data analysis, used by labs worldwide.
pmc-8504100:
Xiaoqi Mao and co-authors reviewed in 2022 the conversation between cancer-associated fibroblasts and immune cells inside tumors. Fibroblasts are support cells, and those living in a tumor form a varied population that ranks among the most important parts of the tumor's surroundings. Once activated, they can encourage tumor growth, new blood vessels, and spread.

The review gathers newer findings on how these fibroblasts and immune cells influence each other, often to the tumor's advantage. Signals from fibroblasts can blunt immune attack, while immune cells in turn reshape fibroblast behavior. The authors close with prospects for treatments that interrupt this alliance. The work highlights a support crew that cancer depends on more than was once thought.
royce-conception-immortality-1900:
The Conception of Immortality, published in 1900, prints Royce's Ingersoll Lecture at Harvard, the same series in which James had spoken two years earlier. Royce gives the idealist's argument for personal immortality, built to stand without church authority.

The self, he argues, is not a thing but a meaning: a life-plan interpreted within a larger consciousness. Death ends the body's expression, not necessarily the meaning it serves, which the absolute mind holds complete. The lecture is brief, careful, and deeply felt. It shows Royce's philosophy turning toward religion, the path his later work would follow to the Beloved Community.
rubruck-journey-rockhill-1900:
William of Rubruck, a Flemish friar, traveled to the court of the Great Khan in 1253 and wrote a famed report of the journey. W. W. Rockhill edited and translated it for the Hakluyt Society in 1900. Rubruck went seeking converts and news of Prester John, the rumored Christian king of the East.

He found instead the vast Mongol Empire, and described it with a clear eye. Dog-headed peoples and other marvels get tested against what he actually saw. His account covers steppe life, Mongol customs, and religions he met on the road. Scholars call it the most clear-eyed travel book of the Middle Ages. Rockhill's edition pairs the text with rich notes.
russell-philosophy-leibniz-1900:
A Critical Exposition of the Philosophy of Leibniz, published in 1900, made Russell's name in philosophy. He read the German thinker through the new logic he was mastering, and found a system of surprising rigor beneath the metaphysics.

Russell argues that Leibniz's whole philosophy flows from his logic of subject and predicate and his theory of relations. The monads, the pre-established harmony, the best of possible worlds: all are traced to a few premises. The reading was contested, and it founded the analytic style of writing philosophy's history. Few first books in philosophy have carried this much consequence.
santayana-interpretations-poetry-religio:
Interpretations of Poetry and Religion, published in 1900, was Santayana's first book, written while he taught at Harvard. Its essays argue one thesis from many sides: that poetry and religion are twin expressions of the imaginative life.

Religion, at its best, is poetry that has taken hold of conduct; poetry, at its deepest, is religion stilled into contemplation. Essays on Dante, Browning, and Emerson apply the idea with finesse. The young Santayana already writes in the serene manner of his maturity. The book announced a philosopher who would treat faith with an outsider's love and an insider's ear.
schelling-system-transcendental-idealism:
Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling published his System des transcendentalen Idealismus in 1800, at the age of twenty-five. The German first edition is the text here, since no public-domain English translation of the work exists. Schelling had been Fichte's brilliant young ally, and this book marks his step beyond the master.

The System traces how the self builds its world, stage by stage, from raw feeling to full awareness. Nature, in Schelling's hands, is mind made visible, and art becomes the highest proof of the whole scheme. His nature-philosophy and identity system form the bridge from Fichte to Hegel in German thought. The book's daring still draws readers who brave the German.
schiller-mary-stuart-1800:
Mary Stuart, Schiller's tragedy of 1800, reached English in Joseph Mellish's translation of 1801. Mary, Queen of Scots, sits imprisoned in England while her cousin Elizabeth weighs her fate. Schiller imagines a meeting between the two queens that never took place in life.

In that meeting pride defeats mercy, and Mary's death is sealed. Around the queens, lovers, plotters, and counselors pull the state toward the scaffold. Mary walks to her death with a calm that rebukes her judges. Schiller gives both queens full humanity, which keeps the play from taking sides cheaply. It remains the classic drama of two women, one throne, and the price of power.
shaftesbury-characteristics-vol1-1900:
Anthony Ashley Cooper, third Earl of Shaftesbury, issued his Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times in 1711. Volume one here follows the Robertson edition of 1900. The volume holds three works: the Letter Concerning Enthusiasm, Sensus Communis, and the Soliloquy, or Advice to an Author.

Shaftesbury wrote philosophy as a gentleman writes letters: polished, witty, and allergic to gloom. He defends free humor against religious panic, and a common sense of mankind against lone system builders. His Soliloquy teaches the writer to hold a dialogue with his own soul. From these elegant pages flowed the whole moral-sense school of Hutcheson and his heirs. Shaftesbury made goodness look graceful.
shaftesbury-characteristics-vol2-1900:
Volume two of Shaftesbury's Characteristics, in the Robertson edition of 1900, holds the Inquiry Concerning Virtue and The Moralists. The Earl of Shaftesbury first published the Inquiry in 1699, the seed of the whole collection. The Moralists, a rhapsody in dialogue, is his fullest and most poetic statement.

Here the moral-sense doctrine stands complete: virtue is a natural harmony of the affections, known by an inner sense. Shaftesbury sets that doctrine in scenes of friendship, countryside, and dawn light that glow with feeling. Hutcheson took the teaching into the schools, but Shaftesbury gave it beauty first. Volume two is the heart of the Characteristics, and of his influence on the century.
shakespeare-midsummer-nights-dream-1600:
William Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream first reached print in 1600. The comedy mixes lovers, fairies, and a crew of rough workmen in one wood. Few plays in English are loved so widely or staged so often for pure delight.

Two pairs of young lovers flee Athens and get lost in the trees. Fairy king Oberon and his sprite Puck tangle their loves with a magic flower. Meanwhile workmen rehearse a crude play that turns to pure farce. Dawn sorts the loves aright, and a triple wedding ends the night. Dreams, desire, and theater itself are the play's glad themes.
skeat-malay-magic-1900:
Walter William Skeat mapped Malay folk religion in Malay Magic, published in 1900 after his travels in Selangor and the Malay states. Spirits of rice and river, charms, divination, and the craft of the pawang, the village magician, fill his classic study. Skeat gathered much of it at first hand, sitting with practitioners and recording their rites.

Birth, marriage, sickness, and harvest all pass under the pawang's art in these pages. Skeat writes as a scholar-adventurer, precise about what he saw and heard. His book remains the classic English account of Malay magic and the beliefs woven through Malay daily life.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Volume II of the Slave Narratives, Arkansas Narratives, Part 2, gathers talks with former slaves. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 for Arkansas, and the Library of Congress project put the set together at Washington in 1941. The list of those who spoke begins with Frank Cannon, Zenie Cauley, Liney Chambers, and Willie Buck Charleston, Jr., then runs on through Lewis Chase, Katherine Clay, and Maria Sutton Clemments.
strindberg-the-dance-of-death-1900:
August Strindberg wrote The Dance of Death in 1900, here in Edwin Björkman's English translation in print. The two-part marital death-dance of Edgar and Alice is the most savage marriage play ever written, many say. Björkman's version carried its black comedy and dread to English readers with force and care.

Edgar, a retired captain, and Alice, a former actress, mark twenty-five years of marriage in a fortress tower. Isolated on their island, they tear at each other with memories, lies, and a practiced, intimate cruelty daily. Alice's cousin Kurt arrives and is drawn into their dance as witness, judge, and near victim himself. Edgar's heart scares, Alice's plots, and a dance to death's music bind the pair they cannot leave. Part Two turns to the young, who risk repeating the dance in the next generation.
tasso-jerusalem-delivered-fairfax-1600:
Torquato Tasso finished his epic Gerusalemme liberata in Italy in the 1580s, and Edward Fairfax Englished it in 1600 as Jerusalem Delivered. The poem tells of the First Crusade and the Christian siege of Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon. Knights, sorcerers, and lovers crowd its twenty cantos of stately verse.

Armida the enchantress, Tancred, and the warrior maid Clorinda give the war its human tangle. Fairfax rendered Tasso in rich Spenserian stanzas that English poets admired for generations. Milton and Dryden both studied his version closely. The translation stands as a landmark of English Renaissance writing in its own right. Fairfax's Tasso taught England how an epic could sing.
tauler-following-of-christ-1900:
The Following of Christ is a small book of German mystic teaching, linked to John Tauler, the Dominican preacher of Strasburg who lived about 1300 to 1361. A note at the front grants that the book may come not from Tauler himself but from his circle, the Friends of God.

That circle worked along the Rhine in the fourteenth century, in the same deep movement that gave rise to the Imitation of Christ. The note praises Mr. Morell's rendering for keeping the plain, earnest tone of the source. Readers are urged to heed what the book says, not who wrote it. Plain counsel on the inner life, grief, and trust fills its short pages.
tesla-problem-of-increasing-human-energy:
Nikola Tesla set out his grand plea in The Century Magazine in 1900. The Problem of Increasing Human Energy deals with how man may gain more force for his work. Tesla was then at the peak of his fame for his work with power. The piece is long, bold, and full of plans.

Food, sun, and the spin of Earth all come up as wells of force. Tesla dreams of power sent through air with no wires, and of craft that move at a word from far off. He tells of his bid to tap the sun's heat by new means. The piece is the root text of Tesla lore.
the-french-impressionists-1860-1900:
Camille Mauclair wrote this study of the French Impressionists from 1860 to 1900, turned into English by P. G. Konody and printed in 1903. Fifty pictures, most lent by the dealer Durand-Ruel, fill the book.

Mauclair notes that Durand-Ruel stood by the painters from the first and built a store of their work over thirty years. A plate shows Renoir at the piano. The text traces how a mocked band of painters, working out of doors in bright color, won their place. Mauclair writes as a critic who knew the men and could sort canvas from canvas by hand and eye.
the-jargon-file-version-4-2-2-20-aug-200: The hacker’s dictionary, version 4.2.2: slang of the computer folk. Witty definitions from the early net, essential for tech culture, a geek time capsule, still fun, a geek time capsule from August 2000, still fun to read.
the-phrenological-physiological-register: The Phrenological and Physiological Register, 1900. Another edition. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. Time has kept the file intact. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
tob-0100:
Solomon's name crowns the Greater Key of Solomon, the most famous grimoire of the Renaissance. S. L. MacGregor Mathers translated it into English in 1889 from old manuscripts. Kings and magicians had copied its rites for centuries, crediting the wise king of Israel as author.

Inside stand planetary pentacles, prayers, and conjurations for aims from finding treasure to becoming unseen. Tools, robes, and timing all follow strict rules. Mathers's edition became a foundation text for the modern ritual magic revival, including the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. This entry uses a verified scan of the public-domain edition.
tob-10200:
Saint Catherine of Siena never learned to write fluently, so the letters gathered in Vida Scudder's translation were dictated to scribes. That did not limit their reach. During the fourteenth century her counsel arrived in the courts of popes and princes, and in prisons and private homes as well.

To popes she sent blunt demands for reform and for a return from Avignon to Rome. To suffering individuals she offered tender spiritual direction, urging trust in Christ. The collection reveals a woman of action as much as contemplation, directing church affairs from her sickbed. Her letters remain a primary record of her influence.
tob-4185-78000:
Plutarch, the Greek essayist of the first century, wrote far more than his famous Lives of great men. His essays and talks, called the Moralia, fill five English volumes in William Watson Goodwin's edition. Volume five closes the set with the miscellany's last pieces.

Late essays treat fate, music, and the views of old philosophers on nature. Some pieces are dialogues, some lectures, some letters of comfort. Plutarch's curiosity never narrows: gods, animals, and dinner talk all interest him. Goodwin's Victorian translation made the full Moralia open to English readers. The final volume rounds off the ancient world's most humane essayist.
tob-4200:
An unknown English mystic of the fourteenth century wrote the Cloud of Unknowing for a young disciple of prayer. The author teaches a way past words and images: put a cloud of forgetting beneath you, over all created things. Then pierce the cloud of unknowing above you. The tool for that piercing is a sharp dart of longing love.

Thought cannot reach God, the book insists, but love can. Its Middle English voice, in modern dress here, stays brisk and funny about idle curiosity. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Cloud is the West's great manual of apophatic prayer, the way of negation, and it still finds contemplatives ready for its discipline.
tob-9100:
Griffith's name attaches to this record of the Rig Veda, the collection of 1,028 Sanskrit hymns that forms the oldest religious literature of India. Composed more than three thousand years ago, the hymns praise Agni, Indra, and the powers of nature and order. Priests at the soma sacrifice sang them.

The evidence notes Griffith's translation is referenced here but is not on Gutenberg, and no public-domain text is attached to this entry. What the record certifies is the work itself: creation hymns, wedding songs, and battle prayers that anchor Hindu worship to this day. No older scripture of a living faith survives in such bulk.
tolstoy-resurrection-maude-1900:
Louise and Aylmer Maude published their authorized translation of Leo Tolstoy's Resurrection in 1900. Resurrection was Tolstoy's last novel, written after his religious crisis had changed his view of art and society. The Maudes, friends of Tolstoy, worked with his approval on many of his books.

Prince Nekhludov serves on a jury and finds the accused is a woman he wronged in his youth. Guilt drives him to follow her into Siberian exile and to question land, courts, and church. Tolstoy used the plot to attack the systems he thought crushed the poor. The novel's force lies in that moral charge as much as in its story.
trevisanvs-de-chymico-miracvlo-qvod-lapi: Dionysius Zacharius wrote of the chemical miracle in this 1600 edition. The philosophers' stone treatise, reprinted. The Latin alchemy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This book preserves that work. Kept for readers. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
un-ga-res-1000:
Blueprint became command in Resolution 1000, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 5 November 1956. A day before, the Secretary-General had been told to draft a plan for an emergency force to halt the Suez fighting. His first report was now in hand. The Assembly acts on it at once, in the depths of the crisis over Egypt.

A United Nations Command is set up for the emergency force. Its task: secure and oversee the halt to fighting, on the terms of the cease-fire call of 2 November. Major-General E. L. M. Burns, chief of staff of the UN truce body in Palestine, takes command. He may draw officers at once from the truce observer corps, barring nationals of the five big powers.
un-ga-res-500:
Trade can be a weapon too, and Resolution 500, adopted by the General Assembly on 18 May 1951, turns it on the foes in Korea. A special team had weighed fresh steps to meet the attack in Korea, after the Assembly's vote of 1 February 1951. Some states had already acted to deny goods that fed the strength of the forces fighting the UN.

The team found that wider trade steps would back the fight and help end the attack. So the Assembly urges every state to place a ban on shipments to the areas held by the Beijing government and by North Korea. The ban covers arms, war goods, and the raw stock from which war strength is built. The vote was the trade arm of the Korean War.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1000 (ES-I) was adopted on 5 November 1956, during the Suez crisis. It set up a United Nations Command for an emergency international force. The force was to secure and watch over the end of fighting. It was to act on the terms the Assembly had laid down in resolution 997 (ES-I) two days before.

The Assembly named the Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization as the force's chief. He was named on an emergency basis. He could at once draw officers from that observer corps. With the Secretary-General, he could also recruit more officers. They would come from member states other than the permanent members of the Security Council.

General Assembly Resolution 500 (V), adopted on 18 May 1951, added economic pressure to the United Nations war effort in Korea. The Assembly acted on its Additional Measures Committee's report. It held that cutting off war goods to the forces fighting the United Nations would back the military action and help end the aggression.

Every state was urged to bar shipments to areas held by the Chinese and North Korean authorities. The ban covered arms, war gear, atomic energy materials, oil, and key transport goods. States were to police their own exports and stop cheating on others' controls. They were to work together and report their steps within thirty days. The drive for a peaceful settlement went on.
un-sc-res-100:
Works in a demilitarized zone between Israel and Jordan troubled the truce in 1953. Construction had begun on 2 September in the zone near the Jordan River. The truce chief of staff reported on the dispute in October. On 27 October 1953 the Council said the works should pause. A pause would let the Council study the question with care. It would not prejudice either side's rights or claims.

Israel's representative told the Council his government would suspend the works. The Council noted that pledge with satisfaction. It relied on the chief of staff to report whether the pledge held. The dispute concerned a planned hydroelectric project at Bnot Yaakov. Water, as often in the region, sat at the heart of the quarrel.
un-sc-res-1300:
The Golan observer force was renewed in May 2000 on standard terms. On 31 May 2000 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 30 November 2000. The Secretary-General had reported on the force eight days earlier. The Council noted United Nations work to protect peacekeepers from disease. The mission's shape stayed the same. Its observers manned the line set after the 1973 war.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. A closing report was due at the term's end. It would describe events and steps taken toward 338. The vote came as Israel completed its Lebanon withdrawal. Attention shifted, but the Syrian front stayed quiet under UNDOF's watch.
un-sc-res-1400:
UNAMSIL was extended through Sierra Leone's elections on 28 March 2002. The Mano River Union presidents had met in Rabat on 27 February. The state of emergency had been lifted, and disarmament stood complete. Refugee numbers across the region were swelling, and their plight caused concern. Election preparations by the government and the electoral commission were moving ahead.

The Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for six months from 30 March 2002. Troop-giving states won thanks for their service. The mission's 2002 concept of operations, set out in the Secretary-General's report of 14 March, was welcomed. The government and the Revolutionary United Front were urged to carry out the ceasefire and peace terms in full. They had to deepen dialogue and national reconciliation. The Council noted the funding gap in the trust fund for disarming and reintegrating fighters. Building the government's own capacity was named essential to lasting peace.
un-sc-res-1500:
The matter of Iraq was settled for the Council in Resolution 1500, adopted on 14 August 2003 by fourteen votes to none, with one abstention. Iraqis had formed a Governing Council on 13 July 2003. The United Nations needed staff on the ground to support the political path ahead. The Secretary-General had laid out a mission plan that July.

The Council welcomes the Governing Council as a step toward a recognized Iraqi government. It creates the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, called UNAMI. The mission starts with a twelve-month term. Its job is to back the Secretary-General's mandate under the post-war framework. That work spans aid, rebuilding, and help with the move to elected rule.
un-sc-res-1600: Resolution 1600 opens a new hundred in the Security Council's sequence, adopted in 2005. The text kept here follows the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Its structure rewards attention: concern stated, facts recalled, and then the decision itself, which is the part with legal force for the states it addresses.
un-sc-res-1700:
Iraq's United Nations assistance mission was renewed by the Security Council on 10 August 2006. Iraq's foreign minister had written on 3 August that the elected government still saw a vital role for the mission. The United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, UNAMI, had been set up in August 2003. The Council stressed that national dialogue, which UNAMI should assist, is crucial to Iraq's stability and unity.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve months from the date of the resolution. It said it would review the mandate within twelve months, or sooner if Iraq's government asked. The Secretary-General had to update the Council regularly on progress in Iraq. The text welcomed the United Nations role as co-chair of the International Compact of Iraq, launched on 27 July 2006. The compact aimed to tie international support to Iraq's own programme for peace and prosperity.
un-sc-res-1900: Resolution 1900, adopted in 2010, opens the Council's 1900s run in this collection, preserved through English Wikisource. The act follows the long-settled form: a preamble weighing the situation, operative paragraphs settling the response. Its placement at a round number makes it an easy landmark in the sequence the collection preserves number by number.
un-sc-res-2000:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2000, adopted on 27 July 2011. The post-election crisis had ended, and the elected president had taken office on 21 May. Grave abuses during the crisis still needed investigation. Armed ex-guards, militias, and escaped prisoners kept the security picture shaky.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the peacekeeping mission, called UNOCI, until 31 July 2012. Its strength stays at 9,792 troops and 1,350 police, plus 205 added police advisers. The mission guards civilians, watches the arms embargo, and collects stray weapons. It backs a fresh disarmament program and deep reform of the security forces. Legislative polls, the first since 2000, must be certified as free and fair.
un-sc-res-300: An official UN record text, Resolution 300 is catalogued in this library with a 1971 date. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-400:
Security Council Resolution 400, adopted on December 7, 1976, recommended Kurt Waldheim for a second term as Secretary-General. Catalog copies dated 1978 are off by two years. Waldheim, a former Austrian foreign minister, had held the post since 1972. China had opposed his first term bid at first, but by 1976 the council settled on him with little open strife.

The Assembly confirmed him, and he served until the end of 1981. His decade at the top covered the end of the Vietnam War, Middle East crises, and Africa's wars of liberation. Later claims about his wartime past, raised after he left office, cast a long shadow over that record.
un-sc-res-800:
Security Council Resolution 800, adopted on January 8, 1993, recommended Slovakia for membership in the United Nations. Eight days earlier, Czechoslovakia had split by agreement into the Czech Republic and Slovakia, a parting so calm it gained the name Velvet Divorce. Neither half kept the old state's seat, so both applied as new members.

The Assembly seated Slovakia on January 19, the same day as the Czech Republic. The council's brief text records a rare event in the life of nations: a country dividing by talks rather than war, with both successors welcomed at once. For Slovakia, the vote marked its first seat of its own in the world body.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Digging in a no-go zone sparked a sharp clash in 1953. Work had begun on 2 September in the demilitarized strip between Israel and Syria. The strip sat by the Jordan River's headwaters. UN truce staff sent a report on 23 October. Resolution 100 passed with no dissent on 27 October 1953.

The Council said the works should pause. The pause would last while the case was probed with care. Israel's envoy told the room his state would halt the work. That pledge was noted with warmth. The truce staff's chief had to confirm the halt had in fact come. The text took care to guard each side's claims. No rights were judged; the diggers simply had to stop while the Council looked.

Spring of 2000 brought one more Golan renewal. The chief's report of 22 May set out a calm scene. UNDOF's term was near its end. The force had kept the Israel-Syria line still since 1974. Resolution 1300 passed on 31 May 2000.

The mandate grew by six months, to 30 November 2000. The Council called on both sides to act on the 1973 text at once. A report was due when the term closed. It would tell of events and steps toward a peace. A fresh clause in this text stands out. The UN's push to school its peace staff on health risks won a warm note. HIV and other ills were now a named care in each such file.

Sierra Leone's move from war toward elections fills Resolution 1400, adopted on 28 March 2002. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, had helped lift the state of emergency and finish disarmament. Peace talks in the wider Mano River region were moving ahead, though refugees were growing in number and the situation stayed fragile.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months from 30 March 2002, including help for the vote then being prepared. It welcomes the deal for a Special Court for Sierra Leone and backs UNAMSIL giving that court office support. It urges the government to restore its authority across the country, above all in diamond areas, and presses for funds for fighter reintegration and for the planned Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Iraq was under foreign occupation when Resolution 1500 passed on 14 August 2003. Fourteen members voted yes. Syria abstained. The invasion had toppled Saddam Hussein months earlier. A Governing Council of Iraqis had formed on 13 July 2003. The Council welcomed it as a step toward a sovereign, elected government.

The resolution created UNAMI, the UN Assistance Mission for Iraq. It would run for an initial twelve months. Its job was to support the Secretary-General's work in the country. That work followed the plan in his report of 15 July 2003. It covered aid, rebuilding, and help toward self-government.

Côte d'Ivoire's peace process gets one more month of cover on 4 May 2005. Ivorian parties had signed the Pretoria Agreement in April 2005, adding to the Linas-Marcoussis and Accra deals. The African Union, the regional bloc ECOWAS, and the United Nations were all working to get the agreements carried out.

All parties are called on to implement the Pretoria Agreement fully and to ensure a safe setting for the steps ahead, including elections. The mandate of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, and of the French forces supporting it is extended for one month, until 4 June 2005. That short bridge kept the operation lawful while the parties' compliance was tested.

Resolution 1700, adopted on 10 August 2006, renews the UN's political mission in Iraq for another year. UNAMI, the assistance mission created in 2003, advised Iraq on elections, a constitution, and rebuilding institutions. Iraq's foreign minister had written on 3 August saying the elected government still saw a vital role for the mission in building a stable, prosperous nation at peace with its neighbors.

The Council extended UNAMI's mandate for twelve months. It stressed that Iraqi national dialogue, which the mission should support, was crucial to the country's political stability and unity. The renewal came as sectarian violence was climbing sharply, and the text thanks the UN for working in Iraq with international backing.

On 16 December 2009, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1900 about the war crimes court for the former Yugoslavia. The court, set up in 1993, was trying cases from the Balkan wars. Its judges reported that they could not finish all their work in 2010, as earlier decisions had asked.

The Council said it planned to keep the trial judges in their posts past the end of their terms. Appeals judges would stay until the end of 2012, or until their cases ended. Two temporary judges could also stay on to finish the Popović trial. For a short time the court could use thirteen temporary judges at once, one more than the normal limit. The aim was simple: trials should end with a proper judgment, not stop in the middle.

The Gambia is the subject of Resolution 200. The Council passed it by a full vote on 15 March 1965. The Gambia is a thin strip of land along a river, ringed by Senegal. It had won its freedom from Britain the month before, in February 1965.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit the Gambia as a member. The Assembly then gave it a seat. The text is one of the shortest kinds the Council writes. Yet it sealed the place of one of Africa's smallest states in the world. Some had doubted so small a land could stand on its own. Membership helped prove them wrong.

Côte d'Ivoire's mission is renewed for the post-crisis rebuilding year in Resolution 2000, adopted on 27 July 2011. The new president had been inaugurated on 21 May 2011 after a post-election crisis marked by atrocities. The International Criminal Court prosecutor was seeking to open an investigation into crimes since 28 November 2010, and legislative elections, the first since 2000, were due.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends UNOCI until 31 July 2012. It keeps its military component at 9,792 personnel, including the 2,400 surge troops, its police at 1,350, and adds 205 police advisers. The Special Representative must certify every stage of the legislative elections. UNOCI's mandate covers protecting civilians, watching the Liberia border with UNMIL, monitoring the arms embargo with no-notice inspections, collecting weapons, and building a new disarmament programme. It covers reviewing the security sector, whose forces were reorganized as the FRCI in March 2011.

Zambia complained that South Africa was violating its sovereignty, its airspace, and its territory. Forty-seven member states backed the complaint. The trouble lay near the Caprivi Strip, along the border with Namibia. South Africa's foreign minister gave his side as well. Resolution 300 was adopted unanimously on 12 October 1971.

The Council restated a basic rule of the Charter. Any violation of a member state's sovereignty and territory goes against the United Nations Charter. South Africa was called on to respect Zambia's sovereignty and territorial integrity in full. The Council also gave a clear warning. If South Africa violated them again, the Council would meet once more. It would then examine the situation under the relevant parts of the Charter.

Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim's first term was ending in 1976. The Austrian diplomat had led the UN since 1972. At a private meeting, the Council considered who should follow or continue. Resolution 400 records the outcome. No public debate or vote count appears in the text.

Members recommended Waldheim for a second term. The new stretch would run from 1 January 1977 to 31 December 1981. The General Assembly made the appointment. Waldheim's second term covered the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran-Iraq war's start. Years later, his wartime record in the German army drew scrutiny. The resolution itself is a single calm sentence of recommendation, preserved from a closed session.

A peaceful divorce brought this new applicant to the Council in 1993. On 8 January, it adopted Resolution 800 without a vote. The Slovak Republic had come into being a week before, on New Year's Day. Czechoslovakia had split into two states without a shot fired. The parting is often called the Velvet Divorce.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Slovak Republic. The Assembly did so on 19 January 1993. Its Czech twin entered on the same day. Swift seats for both halves showed how orderly the split had been. Yugoslavia's violent breakup made the contrast plain to all.
